the Book of the Wheel, marginal gloss on Section 3.7, in a Waymaster’s pencil
Carver’s Notes: The Book of the Wheel

The hook. A Guest who is a Bonded Hand already has a copy; a Guest who is not can buy one at Gristmoot and use it, with a Hard (14) Eye + Lore roll, to pass for a Hand at a Company post for a night. Copies older than 619 still have Section 14 in them, and are therefore worth a great deal to several people: the Wheel, which has been buying them up quietly for twenty years at 300 lacks each and burning them at Toll Nine; the Auditor-General, Lysander Coyle, who wants one for reasons of his own; and the Second Table, whose agents on the Rim have been told that Section 14 contains “the Company’s terms of service to the thing that pays it.” A drover’s widow at Thimble Cross has an Eighth Revision copy in her late husband’s sea-chest, and does not know what it is worth.

The rule. Following the Book exactly is good protection. A Guest working a Company house who has read the Book and follows Section 11 to the letter when a table appears gains +2 on every Caul + Resolve roll made against the table’s pull for that night, and nobody in the house is lost to it unless they choose to sit. A Hand who breaks Section 11.6 (reads a place card) finds the name on it is their own, and from that night is followed down the Rim by tables, one every Plate, each a little closer to the road.

The secret: what Section 14 said. The full text, as printed in every revision up to the Eighth, is reproduced below for the Carver. It does not name anyone. It is the only document on the Table, outside the oldest carvings, that sets out a procedure for the eighth chair, and the Company swore it at Tacit in 61 A.G., before the Ring Charter, in the Company’s first bond, the one the Ledger at Tacit records and nobody has read aloud in five hundred years. The Wheel cut it from the Ninth Revision in 619 because a Factor at Lampwick Halt followed it, one dawn when the count was higher by one, and was found sitting at the head of his table with the ledger open in front of him, smiling, every question in it answered in his own hand, and the last page blank except for the words paid in full.

SECTION 14. OF THE HEAD OF THE TABLE, AND OF THE COMPANY’S PRINCIPAL. (Eighth Revision, 588 A.G.; text as sworn at Tacit, 61 A.G., under the first bond of the seven houses.)

14.1. The Chair at the head of every table in every house of the Company is kept for the Company’s Principal, who is the party to whom the Company is bound before all others, and on whose account the road was built.

14.2. Whether the Principal has come is known by the Night Count. When the count at dawn is higher than the count at dusk, the Principal has been in the house.

14.3. The Principal is not to be asked a name, nor charged, nor counted on the ledger, nor turned away. The Principal is to be served from the Company’s chair as from any other, with the best the house has. The Principal’s account has been paid in advance, and the Company is in the Principal’s debt, and not the other way round.

14.4. The ledger of the house is to be presented to the Principal, open, if the Principal asks for it, and every question the Principal puts is to be answered truly, by the Factor, in writing, in the ledger.

14.5. The page of the ledger on which the higher count is written is to be burned at noon. This is not to hide it from the Principal. It is to hide it from everyone else.

14.6. If the dawn count is higher by more than one, the Factor is to set as many more places as the count requires, and is not to ask how many more will be needed, nor for how long.

14.7. Bonded Hands are reminded that the Bond is sworn as long as the wheel turns. When the wheel stops turning, the road is the Principal’s, and every house on it, and everything carried on it, and every Hand.

14.8. The Company will know that the wheel has stopped turning when the Principal sits in the Chair.

14.9. Until then, keep the place laid.

Ask a Spoke what fourteen is. Go on. Ask her.
pencilled in a secondhand copy of the Book of the Wheel, Gristmoot, price two lacks

Wick Tallow's Catalogue

Steady light, sixth bell light, light that will not leave you!
— the chandlers’ cry on Wick Lane, Lastgate

What it is. Tallow’s of Wick Lane: A Catalogue of Lights, With Prices, For the Carving and Lack of 641. Sixteen pages of coarse reed-paper, stitched with waxed thread, printed by an Heirs’ press in the drying-loft over Saul Brindle’s tannery (Wick pays in candles), and handed out free at the shop door and at the Rim Market at Gristmoot, where Wick’s man keeps a stall each season for the Vigil trade. The cover is a woodcut of the shop sign, a candle with a face. The paper is greasy at the edges, because every copy has been handled by someone who works with fat, and every copy smells, faintly and permanently, of the Lane: hot tallow, lye, singed hair.

Where it is found. Everywhere in Lastgate; in the Lofts, where the Wardens order by the gross; in the Vigil, where Lamplighters’ agents mark it up and pass it round; folded in Rim Road saddlebags as far as Mumchance. Free. A copy carries no Taint. The candles do: a common Tallow candle is Taint Dread 1; a named candle is Dread 2; a few of the stock below are worse, and the Carver’s notes say which.

TALLOW’S OF WICK LANE. ESTABLISHED 551. CHANDLERS TO THE LOFTS, THE HALL OF HANDS, THE SINKS AND THE VIGIL TRADE. LIGHTS THAT DO NOT GUTTER.

TO OUR CUSTOMERS.

Friends, here is the new list. The prices are up a crumb or two on last Lack, because the Court has started charging me for the Jar Room ends, which it used to give away, and because the Vigil cannot get enough of us, and when the Vigil cannot get enough of a thing the Lamplighters’ men turn up on the Lane with a cart and buy the shop bare by noon. I will not have my neighbours going dark for the sake of a city that will not shut its eyes. So the Vigil price is the Vigil price, and the Lane price is the Lane price, and if a Vigil man tries to buy at the Lane price, my boy will know him by his eyes.

Everything on this list is made in my own vats from my own stock and lit from my own coal, which has been burning since the year 551 and has lit every candle I ever sold. Every candle is rendered three times, strained through linen, poured round a wick of Brinemoss reed-pith, and cooled slow in the cellar so it will not crack. They give a steady yellow light that does not gutter, smoke or spit, and they lean, a little, toward whoever lit them. That is not a draught. It is a selling point.

You will hear them. I will not pretend you won’t. Most say nothing anyone could make out. Some say one thing, over and over, the way the Lofts do. I have written down, beside each one on the list, what it says, as best I and my journeymen can make out, so that you can choose. A customer who knows what a candle says will not bring it back.

— W. Tallow, Wick Lane, at the sign of the face.

I. COMMON LIGHTS. UNCLAIMED STOCK, BY THE CANDLE OR THE BOX.

From the Sump-sacks, the Court’s unclaimed, and the Guild’s leavings. I do not know their names. Nobody does. That is what unclaimed means.

No. 1. Plain Sixth-Bell. A hand-length taper, yellow. Burns three nights. Says: nothing you could swear to; a sort of humming. 6 crumbs; 5 lacks the box of a hundred.

No. 2. Long Reader. Thick, for students and clerks of the Upper Boards; doubled wick. Burns six nights. Says: one more page. Very popular with the Court’s copyists. 1 lack.

No. 3. Sinks Stub. Offcuts and the bottoms of vats, pressed together. Burns two nights, a little blue at the edge. Says: several things at once, none of them to you. Not for nurseries. 3 crumbs.

No. 4. Loft Box. As supplied to the Wardens of the Lofts, a gross at a time; squat, so they will not tip on the ladders. Burns four nights. Says: read to me. The shelved like them; they say they keep each other company. 7 lacks the gross.

No. 5. Weir Lantern Candle. Short and fat, for a shuttered tin on the eel-traps. Burns a week in the wet. Says: is it cold out there. The weir-men say it is kind company at the fourth bell. 9 crumbs.

No. 6. The Black Noon. Wick dipped in fen-pitch; a smoky flame that flies will not cross. For fly-fronts. Burns one night. Says: a sound like someone swatting, and then sorry. 1 lack.

No. 7. Door-Candle. For the window by the door, at the Court’s door-duty. Burns a night exactly; out at first bell. Says: who’s there. Every house on the Boards burns one. Half the city goes to bed to the sound of its own windows asking who is there. 4 crumbs (and a crumb to the Court, which is not my doing).

II. JAR ROOM ENDS. COURT STOCK.

The rendered remains of the Court’s long-sentenced, from the Jar Room, when a jar has been sat on the shelf so long there is nothing left in it that will answer to a name. The Court sold me these free until this year. They are hard candles, white, very bright. Some customers prefer them. They are bright because they are angry.

No. 8. Penitent. Tall, white, dead straight. Burns five nights. Says: I didn’t, I didn’t, I didn’t. They all say that, the Court’s clerk tells me. 2 lacks.

No. 9. Fen Murderer. From a man jarred in 402 for killing his brother in a punt with a pole. Burns nine nights and is the brightest thing I sell. Says: the brother’s name, and get up, get up. Leans hard. Reading by it you will feel you are being read. 4 lacks.

No. 10. Heir of 288. One of a batch from the War of the Heirs, a young man who killed his father nineteen times; the father kept coming back to his desk; the son was jarred. Burns four nights. Says: stay down. Bought mostly by the Heirs, who light it at their meetings for luck. 3 lacks.

No. 11. The Forger. A clerk jarred for forging Closing licenses. Burns three nights. Says: a very soft scratching, like a nib. Two customers have told me it writes. I have not seen it. 2 lacks.

III. NAMED LIGHTS. FAMILY STOCK, ALREADY POURED.

Families who commission a named candle sometimes find, afterward, that they cannot bear to burn it, or that they owe me for the pouring and cannot pay, or that there are a great many more candles in a grandmother than anyone expects. These are from such families, sold on with their permission or their debt. I give the first name only. A name is a thing you should have to come in and ask for.

No. 12. Ide. A grandmother of Weir Row, a hundred and eighty years Kept, sold by the family to pay for a great-uncle’s restitching. Burns a week. Says: you have cold hands, girl. Very fond of children; leans toward them across a room. 5 lacks.

No. 13. Fenwick. A carpenter of the Landing. Burns five nights. Says: measure twice. A customer of the Boards reads her household accounts by him and says she has never made a mistake since. 5 lacks.

No. 14. Aldous and Merrit. Husband and wife, poured into one candle at their request, two wicks. Burns a week; the flames lean toward each other and will not stand up straight. Says: both talking at once, quarrelling, it sounds like, for six nights, and on the seventh night, before the end, silent. 9 lacks.

No. 15. The Small. A child of the undercity, two hundred years seven, from one of the Drowned Storeys; given to me by Queen Nell’s own runners, who said she asked to be light. One candle only. Burns three nights. Says: a counting game. One for the lamp and two for the wick. I will not sell her to anyone who laughs at the price. 5 lacks.

No. 16. Josse. An uncle, gone Ripe, beyond stitching. Burns four nights, smokes a little, cannot be helped. Says: is it a feast day yet. 4 lacks, reduced.

No. 17. Mother. That is all the family would give me. Thirty candles, one Mother. Burns three nights each. Says: where are you going. Sold singly or the lot. The family asks that the lot not go to one house. 5 lacks each; 120 the lot.

IV. SPECIALTIES.

No. 18. Wedding Pair. Two thin white tapers from one source, twisted together. Lit at the betrothal supper and pinched out at the vow, then kept. Burn: one hour, every anniversary, for as long as the marriage lasts. In Sallowreach that is long. Say: I do, I do, I do, softer each year. 3 lacks the pair.

No. 19. Quease Taper. Made to the order of Dr. Halloran Quease, of a stock he selects, for his studies. Burns two nights. Says: precisely where it hurts, in detail, and the doctor writes it down. Not for general sale; listed because people ask. Price on application to the doctor.

No. 20. The Long Watch. For the Vigil trade. Rendered four times, the hardest tallow I can make, a wrist thick. Burns a month and does not shorten, which I cannot explain and do not try to. Says: don’t close your eyes, don’t close your eyes. The Lamplighters buy every one. Lane price 2 lacks; Vigil price 9.

No. 21. Nudger’s Candle. For the Vigil trade. Small, with a pin pressed into the side at the half-burn. Says: pinch me. When the flame reaches the pin, the pin falls, hot, wherever the candle has been set, which is meant to be the back of your hand. 6 crumbs Lane, 2 lacks Vigil.

No. 22. Hush-Edge Candle. For the Finishers, who walk into the silences with lights. Plain, steady. Burns until it crosses the edge of a Hush, and then it is not burning, and has never been burning, and is not even warm. Says: thank you on the way in. Sister Lorn’s people buy them by the box and I let them have the loft free. 1 lack.

No. 23. Seamer’s Lamp-Wick. Tallow-dipped wick by the yard, for the Guild’s lamps. Says: little things, threadlike, in and out, in and out. The Guild buys it because a seamer working by it never misses a stitch. 2 crumbs the yard.

No. 24. Ferry Candle. For Tam Ruddock’s clients waiting in the back room at the Long Farewell. Made from the unclaimed foreign dead, the ones who came across the Drop to not die and then did, eventually, of what they had. Burns two nights. Says: things in other dialects. Tam asks for them. I think it helps his clients to hear someone from home. 8 crumbs.

V. COMMISSIONS.

Your own. A named candle of your own dead, from your own family, rendered in my own vat, alone, never mixed. You bring them to the back door on Tanner’s Boards before the first bell, wrapped, labelled, with the release signed by the eldest Kept of the house. My journeymen do the rest. They are gentle. You may wait in the front shop. You may not wait in the back. You collect in nine days: forty to sixty candles from an adult, depending, and a cedar box. The candle-blessing is yours to arrange. 50 lacks.

Yourself. A customer of the Upper Boards asked me last Plenty whether I would take her before she was finished, while she was still Kept, so that she could be the light her grandchildren read by, rather than a woman on a shelf they visit on feast days. I said I would think about it. I have thought about it. I will, for those who ask in writing, before witnesses, with the eldest of the house consenting. The vat is hot. It is very quick, and very slow, and then it is over, and then it is not over. My wife Bess asked me the same thing, in 618, and I did it myself, and I burn one of her each Tablenight, and she is the steadiest light I have ever made. 50 lacks, the same. I do not charge more for a willing customer.

VI. TERMS.

No returns on any candle that has been lit.

No returns on any candle that has not been lit but has been heard, because once you have heard it you will always hear it, and there is nothing I can do about that.

Candles that run in the heat and stand up are not to be brought back to the shop. Send a boy for me. Do not let it out of the room, and do not let it near the stove, and do not let anyone in the house call it by any name. I will come with the cold-barrel and the hook.

Candles are not to be lit in a Hush, on Tablenight by anyone not of the family, or within a bowshot of the Ferrying Post at the midnight bell, for a reason I cannot give, as I do not know it, but my journeymen will not go near the Post at midnight with a lit candle and I have stopped asking them to.

Snapped candles burn as two. Both halves lean the same way. Both halves say the same thing, out of time with each other, which is worse. Do not snap your candles.

Steady light. Sixth bell light. Light that will not leave you.

Snapped candles burn as two. Both halves lean the same way. Both halves say the same thing, out of time with each other, which is worse.
Tallow’s Catalogue, Terms
d10What the candle by the bed says tonight (for any Tallow light, unnamed)
1Turn the page. It says it a breath before you do, every time.
2Your mother’s pet name for you. You never told anyone in Lastgate what it was.
3It’s warm in here. Is it warm in here. Then, slowly, as the night goes on: it’s too warm.
4A bell-count, one to six, over and over, like a child learning. It stops at five once. Something in the house stops with it.
5Nothing at all. It is the only silent candle you have ever owned. In the morning the wick has been pinched out from the inside.
6Don’t let them put me in the Sump. The flame leans toward the window, toward the deep fen, and stays there.
7The name of someone in the house, and I know what you did. It is not talking to you. It is talking to the person behind you.
8A tune. Every Kept in the house hums along before they know they are doing it.
9Eight. Then it counts down, slowly, to one. Then it folds, and goes out.
10Your own voice, saying the last thing you said before you lit it.
Carver’s Notes: Tallow’s Catalogue

The hooks. The catalogue is a shopping list for the Guests and a map of Lastgate’s quieter griefs. No. 17, Mother: thirty candles, sold singly to thirty houses, each of which now hears where are you going from its window, and the family that sold her would like her collected again, every candle, before the last one burns down; three are already in the Vigil. No. 9, the Fen Murderer: a buyer on the Upper Boards has died, properly died, in a house where no one is supposed to be able to, with his chair pulled up close to the candle and his book open; the candle was saying get up and he did not. Commissions, Yourself: a Kept Guest, or a Kept companion, may find a relative has written to Wick Lane on their behalf.

The rules. A Tallow light used to read, work or watch by gives +1 to Eye rolls made by its light for long tasks, because it does not gutter and it does not let you stop. No. 2, Long Reader raises that to +2 and its user cannot willingly end the task before the candle is out (Caul + Resolve, Hard 14, to put it down). No. 21, Nudger’s Candle lets a Vigil Guest pass one Weariness check automatically per candle. No. 22, Hush-Edge is the only light that will tell you, by going out and never having been lit, exactly where a Hush begins; it is Taint Dread 2. No. 9 and No. 19 are Taint Dread 3. A candle that runs and stands is a Tallow-Saint: treat it as a man-sized Kept thing of soft warm fat (Threat 3 · Flesh 14 · Guard 9 · Attack +4, smothering 2, and the victim catches light · Armor 0 · Dread 3) that wants only to be lit, and to be called by its name, and does not know it no longer has one.

The secret. Wick has been honest in every line of this catalogue but one. The Sinks Stub, No. 3, is made of offcuts and vat-bottoms, and the vat-bottoms have not been strained since Lack 640, because what is in the bottom of the vats has started to move toward the north side of the copper at midnight and Wick’s journeymen no longer like to put their arms in. Every Sinks Stub sold since then has a little of everything in it, and every one of them, at the midnight bell, leans for one minute toward the Ferrying Post. The Sinks are full of them. On the night a Guest happens to be on the Post at midnight, they will see a thousand little lights in the low windows of the undercity all leaning at them at once, and hear, on the fen wind, a thousand very small voices saying, together, the same short word Bed One said in the Vigil, which none of them can pronounce.

The worthless gift. No. 12, Ide, was sold by her great-granddaughter to pay for an uncle’s restitching. The uncle is Josse, No. 16: he went Ripe anyway, the restitching failed in a month, and he was sold to Wick too, at a reduced price. The family has two candles in the window now and a debt to the Guild still owing. They light both on feast days. The two candles lean toward each other and argue.

The Weighing Almanac

Plant at the Plate’s waxing, reap at its full, and never be the last in the row at dusk.
— the Almanac’s motto, printed under the title since 503 A.G.

What it is. Garbel’s Weighing Almanac for the Year 642 A.G., Being the Six Hundred and Forty-Second Year of Plenty: Containing the Calendar of the Fields, the Plate’s Changes, the Reckoning of the Reaping by District, the Weights of the Board, Receipts for the Hungry Month, Weather-Signs, Sayings, and Notices. Thirty-two pages, octavo, printed every Carving at Registry Close in Sated by the house of Garbel and Daughters under licence of the Board, and sold for 3 crumbs at every mill, cookshop and Bailiff’s post in the south. The paper is cheap and soaks up grease beautifully; most copies hang on a nail by the stove and are read to tatters by the Lack. It is the one book in nearly every Fatland house, and in many the only one.

Where it is found. Everywhere south of the Chute; in Company houses on the southern stretch; and, lately, in the north, where the Long Count has made its Reaping tables the most-read pages of any book on the Table outside the Lofts. The Board licenses it, reads it in proof, and has twice tried to have the Reckoning removed. It sold out both years. No Taint, but a reader who finds their own village’s odds and their own household’s weight makes a Dread 1 check, and Fatland readers make it at Dread 2 in Carving.

TO THE READER.

Here is the Almanac again, friend, as it has been since my great-grandmother’s day. You will find in it what you always find: when to plough and when to sow, what the Plate is doing, how heavy the Board is, and how to feed a family through the hungry month on less than you’d like. You will also find the Reckoning, which some of you have written to say you would rather not, and others have written to say is the only reason you buy us. I print it because it is true, and because a thing printed in an almanac is a thing you can plan around, like frost. My mother printed it. Her mother printed it under the title Wolf-Odds, which the Board preferred. I have dropped the wolves. The Board has noted this.

Eat well. Lack keep away. And when the light goes red in Carving, come in from the field.

— Mistress Hennet Garbel, Registry Close, Carving 641.

THE CALENDAR OF THE FIELDS.

GRACE. The Weighing falls on the third day of the Grace Plate; Board Members are asked to fast from the night before for an honest scale, and none ever has. First Furrow on the first fair morning after: the heaviest man in the village pulls the plough and the furrow is fed a loaf, butter side down. Sow the toothed wheat at the Plate’s waxing, roots at its waning. Prune the Orchards in the second week, with wax in your ears. Lucky days: the 4th, the 9th, the 15th. Unlucky: any day the soil is warmer than your hand at dawn; sow nothing, it is already full.

PLENTY. Second sowing; first cut of hay; cherries from the Bleeding Orchards, which must be stoned at once, before they set their own stones. The fields sweat in the last week. Sweating Night falls when the drip-pans fill without rain; carry the bedding out, sleep on the warm ground, and count your children at dawn, by touching, not by looking. Lucky days: the 2nd, the 11th. Unlucky: the day the Belch first blows; do not marry, butcher, or sign anything with a Union man.

CARVING. Harvest. The Plate is full on the 14th of Carving this year and the Almanac’s counsel is that no one under three hundred pounds be in the far rows after the red light from the 10th to the 18th. Marbling Morning, the first frost, is expected in the third week; a white vein running east-west across your own yard means a gain in the house, north-south a loss. Harvest Home after the Lists are read. Lucky days: none we will print. Unlucky: the Lists.

LACK. Slaughter, salting, the barrels down the Chute. Feed the hills. Tablenight on the longest night; the national fast begins at sundown on the eve. The Almanac wishes every village luck with it, and prints on page 26, as always, the receipts for breaking it gracefully, since you will. Lucky days: the first three of the Plate, when the fat is hardest. Unlucky: Tablenight, for reasons it is not the Almanac’s business to discuss.

THE REAPING NOTICES.

(Being the Almanac’s Reckoning of the Reaping for the coming Carving, by district, worked from last year’s Lists, the Board’s published Returns, and the Long Count, which the Almanac thanks. Odds are given as one in so many souls of the district who will go out to the field at dusk and not come in. They are a reckoning, not a sentence. Plan accordingly. See the table.)

NOTICE OF BRAWNMOUTH. The Almanac has been asked by the Deacon’s widow of Brawnmouth to print the following, and does so as an advertisement, paid. In the Grace of 641, at the advice of the Dowager Hill of Brawnmouth, that the field would be easier on the village if it were given the best of us early, the village gave Deacon Amos Pruett, our heaviest and best, three hundred and eighty pounds, of his own will, to the Long Strip at First Furrow, with music. He went down singing. The village was promised a gentler Carving. The village has this year lost twenty-two, which is two more than the year before. The widow asks that other villages being offered the same counsel by their hills should know this. She asks nothing else. The Almanac’s Reckoning for Brawnmouth is unchanged by the gift, and is printed below at the same odds it would have been.

NOTE ON THE CHAIRMAN’S WEIGHT. The Weigher records the Chairman, as for the last three Weighings, at nineteen hundred pounds, being the weight of the Chairman at the last Weighing at which the Chairman could be lifted from the dray. The question whether the Chairman’s roots, and the soil, cellar-flooring and foundation-stone of the Weighhouse to which the roots now adhere, ought in fairness to be weighed with him, was put to the Board by the Deacon for Low Tilth, who estimated the whole at thirty thousand pounds, or three hundred votes, which would give the Chairman the Board outright. The Board declined, by weight, to consider the question. The Deacon for Low Tilth has since resigned and gone home to Kettle Furrow, where we understand he is helping with the Count.

RECEIPTS FOR THE HUNGRY MONTH.

Every month is hungry in the south, friend; we know. But the Lack Plate before Tablenight is the hungriest, when the fat is all in the barrels and the barrels are all down the Chute, and the Feasting Laws still want five plates a day off you, and the Bailiff is still coming round. These receipts are cheap, filling, and good for a crowd, and each will go round a family five times if you are clever. None of them has any meat in it of which you need wonder where it came from. The Almanac thinks that you should have, once in a while, a meal you need not think about.

Barley and Onion Broth. Take a cupful of pearl barley and wash it well. Cut three onions and two carrots small and soften them in a spoonful of good dripping or butter in your pot, slowly, till the onions are gold. Add the barley, a bay leaf, a pinch of thyme, and eight cupfuls of water or any stock, and a good pinch of salt. Simmer with the lid half on for an hour, stirring now and then, till the barley is soft and the broth thick. Add a handful of chopped greens or a turnip, cut fine, in the last quarter hour. Pepper it. Serve it with bread. It is better the next day, and better still the day after, and so lasts for three of your five meals, which is the point.

Pease Pudding. Soak a pound of yellow split peas overnight in cold water. Drain. Put them in a pot with an onion, cut in half, a bay leaf, and water to cover by a finger’s width, and simmer gently for an hour and a half, skimming, till very soft and nearly all the water is gone; add a little more if it catches. Take out the onion and bay. Beat in a knob of butter, salt and plenty of pepper, and, if you have one, an egg, beaten. Spoon it into a buttered basin, cover it with a cloth, and steam it for an hour in a pan of simmering water, or bake it in a slow oven. Turn it out. Eat it hot in slices, or cold with bread. A pudding of a pound will feed six twice.

Oatcakes on the Griddle. Mix two cupfuls of fine oatmeal with half a teaspoon of salt and a pinch of soda. Melt a spoonful of dripping or butter in half a cupful of hot water and stir it in to make a stiff dough. Turn it out onto a board dusted with oatmeal, press it flat with your knuckles and roll it as thin as you dare. Cut it into wedges and bake it on a hot dry griddle or in a pan, a few minutes a side, till the edges curl and the cakes are crisp. Cool them on a rack. They keep a week in a tin, which in a Fatland house they will not be asked to do.

Baked Apples for Tablenight Eve. Core as many apples as you have mouths, without cutting through the bottom. Fill each with a spoon of oats, a spoon of brown sugar or honey, a few raisins and a little butter, and a pinch of cinnamon if you are rich. Stand them in a dish with a finger of water and bake in a moderate oven for three quarters of an hour, till soft and splitting. These are the last thing to eat before the fast begins at sundown, and the first thing to eat when it ends, which is usually about an hour later.

WEATHER-SIGNS AND SAYINGS.

When the drip leaves a skin you can lift with a spoon, the Belch is three days off.

Red sky at evening, the field is eating; red sky at morning, it has eaten.

If the ground rises under your palm at dawn and falls at dusk, all’s well. If it rises at dusk, keep the children in.

When the scarecrow faces the village, the frost is early.

A Marbling that runs to your door is a gift. A Marbling that runs from your door is a bill.

Wheat that whispers is ripe. Wheat that hushes is hungry. Wheat that turns its heads when you pass is neither, and you should keep walking, and not look back to see if it is still turned.

A fat man casts a short shadow at dusk. The Almanac has nothing more to say about that, and neither should you.

Wheat that whispers is ripe. Wheat that hushes is hungry. Wheat that turns its heads when you pass is neither, and you should keep walking.
the Weighing Almanac, Weather-Signs
Carver’s Notes: The Weighing Almanac

The hooks. The Reckoning is the most dangerous table in the south, because it is accurate, and nobody knows where Hennet Garbel gets the figures for districts the Long Count does not reach. She gets them from the Board’s own cellar Returns, through the Chairman’s Washer, the same channel that sends the Inner Committee’s minutes to Kettle Furrow folded in a shoe; the Board suspects a leak at Registry Close and the Cullmasters have been told to find it before the 642 edition is set. The Guests may be hired to protect the press, to find the leak, or to deliver the proofs. Separately, the Dusk Acres, not printed line has a twin in Hennet’s locked drawer: the odds there are given as one in one.

The rules. A Guest who plans a journey through the south using the Calendar and the Reckoning, and keeps to the Almanac’s counsel, may reduce any one Reaping scene that season by one step of danger: the field’s pull is Routine (10) rather than Hard (14) for one roll. A Guest who ignores the counsel on an unlucky day the Almanac names raises it to Grim (18). The Weight Chart is a Clause and Persuade tool: knowing a Member’s weight and change gives +2 to bargain with or about that Member at the Weighhouse, because in Sated a man’s gains and losses are his politics.

The secrets. The Hessops’ new Deacon each year weighs exactly 880 pounds because it is not a new Deacon. Deacon Cobb Lardner resigned because he did the Chairman’s arithmetic aloud. Cullmaster-General Sweetbread lost thirty pounds because he has stopped being able to eat at the Board’s table since he read the cellar figures for the Dusk Acres, which are his own figures, and saw that the dusk-shift no longer lowers the general Reaping at all. The Cullmasters’ whole justification is that the field can be steered with the poor, so the rest are spared; it cannot, and the Inner Committee knows it can no longer be minuted otherwise. Brawnmouth’s gift was worthless, and so is every other dusk-shift.

Real recipes. The four receipts are ordinary, safe kitchen recipes and work as written.

The Glovemaker's Ledger

Never shake her hand, love. Never laugh near her. And never ask her what she’s thinking. She’ll tell you.
— a cedar-warden of Hand Street

What it is. A tall narrow account-book bound in black kid, the binding soft and cold to the touch, kept for forty years by the glovers Stave of Needle Street, Lastgate: by Josias Stave from 602 to 619, and by his daughter Merrit from 619 to this day. It records one account only. Every pair of gloves made for Lady Corrow Vane, the Left Hand of the Court, since the year her fingers went grey, is entered by number, with its pattern, its leather, the date it went to Glovehall, the date it came back, why it was replaced, and what it touched while she wore it, as far as the glovers could learn or tell from the leather. There are four hundred and seventy-one pairs. The ledger is the only record anywhere of the inside of Corrow Vane’s life.

Where it is. In the locked press at the back of the Staves’ shop, beside the cedar drawers in which Merrit keeps every returned pair, because she has never been able to decide whom it would be safe to sell them to. Taint Dread 2 to read; Dread 3 to open the drawers. The returned gloves are cold, and keep the shape of the hand that left them. A returned pair worn for a day is Taint 2 Regrowth (Ossel).

ACCOUNT OF THE LADY CORROW VANE OF GLOVEHALL, HAND-LINE, IN GLOVES. Opened by Josias Stave, glover, of the sign of the Open Hand, Needle Street, in the Grace of 602.

On the leather. My lady’s hands are cold enough to sting through ordinary kid, and ordinary kid, which in this country is from beasts that do not finish, feels them. I learned this with the first pair. I cut them from good fen-goat, Kept stock, the softest skin on the Boards, and when I fitted them to her, the leather flinched. It tightened on her hand of itself like a face screwing up its eyes, and on the second day the gloves were found on the floor of her chamber, having crawled off her in the night. So there is only one leather that will hold her. It must be finished leather. My lady comes to my yard on the first of each month, and I bring out the kid, and her Glovebearer unpicks her stitches, and she lays her bare hand on the kid’s brow, and it lies down. Then I flay it, and cure it in alum and egg, and cut it to her pattern, and the leather does not mind her, because it is past minding. Neighbours come to the yard gate on the first of the month to watch her hand. I let them. It is the only time anyone sees it.

Pair 1. Grace 602. Black kid, finished. Pattern: three joints to the finger, as for any lady. Returned in Plenty. Replaced because: the fingers had grown. Touched: her mother’s Closing-desk; the oath-book of the Court; her husband’s sleeve, at table, once (he wrote to tell me, as a joke; he is a kind man).

Pair 4. Lack 602. Replaced because: split at the right forefinger, from the inside, as if the finger had tried to come out. Touched: nothing of note. She has been told by the Court not to touch anything of note until she is licensed.

Pair 9. Carving 603. Her first Closing. Replaced because: she asked. Touched: a Kept fisherman of the Glad Century, aged three hundred and four, who had asked for it for two hundred years. She told me, when she came for the new pair, that he said “oh” when it happened, as though he had remembered where he left something. The returned right glove had a smell of river on it that would not wash out. I have it still.

Pair 31. Lack 605. Pattern widened at the palm, the wrist let out, for the lying-in. Touched: the swaddling of her son Teodor, at arm’s length, as she gave him to the nurse. Only the swaddling. The nurse told my wife that my lady held the bundle out with both hands straight in front of her, like a woman holding a pot too hot for her, and when the nurse took it she sat down on the floor. Replaced because: the left glove was found in the cot. Nobody would say how it got there. The child was well. I made a new pair and charged nothing.

Pair 92. Grace 610. Replaced because: the right forefinger and middle finger would not open. Touched: the face of the Regent, Ansel Grue, at his own request, in his own office, with nobody else present. When the pair came back the two fingers were bent in, hard, cold as iron, closed on nothing, as if gripping something the size of a walnut. I could not straighten them with the stretchers. I could not cut them with my best shears. I put them in a box and the box is in the press and the fingers are still closed. Sometimes in damp weather the box is heavier.

Pair 117. Plenty 612. Pattern lengthened: a fourth joint to every finger. I cut it the way I was taught to cut a child’s glove, with room. Touched: four hundred clients this year, by her count. She brings her little black book to the fitting and reads me the numbers while I measure.

Pair 186. Carving 617. Replaced because: the stitches. The Glovebearer then, Old Halse, had begun to sew too tight, from fear; the wrists came back with the silk sunk into the skin and the leather gone white around it. Touched: Old Halse. She did not mean it. He was unpicking the left wrist and his thumb slipped inside the glove against her palm. He was living. He fell where he stood and rose an hour later Kept, and asked to go on working, and did, and sewed better, without fear, because he had nothing left to fear from her. He sewed until 634. I make his gloves now too.

Pair 199. Grace 618. Black kid, finished, with nine stitches of black silk at the wrist, the Court’s pattern for the Left Hand. Her investiture. Touched: the Regent’s ring, which she kissed through the glove, and the nine Closers of the Court, each on the brow, each through the glove, so that they would know what it was to be held by her and not finished. Two of them wept. The pair came back with the fingertips frosted, in Plenty, in a warm room.

Pair 211. Lack 619. My last pattern. My hands are no good. I am giving the bench to Merrit, who cuts better than I did at her age, and I am going to ask my lady a thing I should not ask.

Pair 212. Lack 619. (in a different hand from here on) Pattern as 211, cut by me, Merrit Stave. Touched: my father. He asked her at the fitting, and she said nothing, and her Glovebearer looked at the door, and she looked at my father’s hands, which were swollen like plums with forty years of the shears, and she said, “Mr. Stave, there is no license.” He said he knew. She took off the right glove herself, which she never does. She laid her hand on his brow the way she lays it on the kid, and he said “thank you,” and lay down on the yard stones, and that was all. We are not to speak of it. I am writing it here because this is his book, and he would want the account kept, and because it was the kindest thing anyone in this city has ever done for us, and it is a crime.

Pair 240. Plenty 622. Replaced because: the water. Touched: the moat at Glovehall, to the shoulders, and her husband in it. Lord Merriman went into the moat in the night and she found him at dawn under the weed and went in after him, gloved, and brought him up by the hair. He was Kept by then, of course. She had her hands on him all the way to the bank. The gloves came back full of green water that I could not pour out, as though they were still cupping it, and when I left them on the sill overnight the water was still there in the morning, and warm. Lord Merriman is in the south wing. He declines to be closed. He sent me a note thanking me for the gloves. He says they were the first time she had held him in twenty years, and he would rather keep that than be finished.

Pair 301. Carving 628. Replaced because: split at every seam at once. Touched: a Weir Row family who laughed. The old man was to be closed on Tablenight and wanted to go out laughing, and the house laughed with him, and my lady stood in the middle of it with her hands clenched, and the gloves gave at all ten seams like a burst sausage. She finished him. The family are still laughing about it, I am told. She cannot pass Weir Row.

Pair 344. Grace 633. Touched: the lead mittens of her brother Osric, through the hatch in his door, at the padlock. That is all of him she touches. She asked me if I could make a glove for him. I said that I could make a glove for any hand. She said, “Could you make one that he could not take off?” I said I was not sure that I could make one he could not see through. She said, “No. Of course.”

Pair 371. Carving 635. New Glovebearer, Miss Prudence Lisk, a living girl, careful. Replaced because: wet inside. Miss Lisk brings them back herself and does not look at me. They are wet every month now. It is not water. It is salt.

Pair 402. Lack 637. Pattern lengthened again: a fifth joint. The fingers are as long as my forearm from wrist to elbow. When I measure her she lays her hand flat on my bench and I can hear the knuckles settle one after another like beads on a counting-frame. Touched: nine thousand and some clients since Pair 9, by her little black book, which she reads to me while I measure. And a christening cap in a glass case, the glass only, never the cap. The glove came back with a little round frost-mark on each fingertip, as though she had pressed the glass, hard, for a long time.

Pair 446. Carving 639. Touched: the face of a living rebel in a back room of the Hall, by order, without license, without consent. Replaced because: she brought them to me herself and put them in my hands and said, “Burn these, Miss Stave.” I did not burn them. They are in the press. I do not know why I disobeyed her. I think I wanted someone to have to remember him.

Pair 459. Lack 640. Replaced because: silent. The leather of the fingertips, when I bent them, made no sound. Kid creaks. All leather creaks. These did not, in the last inch of every finger, and when I held the glove to my ear and rubbed it there was a place at the very tip where my own fingers made no sound against it either. A little silence in the leather the size of a pea. I have put them in a lead box. My lady’s estate has a Hush in the orchard now. I know what this is. I have not said.

Pair 470. Plenty 641. Touched: a pear. That is all she would tell me. Replaced because: the silence in the fingertips had reached the second knuckle.

Pair 471. Carving 641. Pattern lengthened: room for a sixth joint. I did not ask. She did not say. I cut it with room, the way my father taught me to cut for a child, so that it will fit her next year, if there is a next year, and if she has hands. She asked me, while I measured, whether a glover could make a glove for a whole house. I said not a glove, my lady. A glove is for a hand. She said, “Then something to put over it,” and looked out of my window toward the fen, toward Glovehall, for a long time, and I could hear the knuckles settle.

It must be finished leather. My lady comes to my yard on the first of each month, and I bring out the kid, and she lays her bare hand on its brow, and it lies down.
Josias Stave, the Glovemaker’s Ledger, 602
Carver’s Notes: The Glovemaker’s Ledger

The hooks. Pair 212 is a confession to an unlicensed Closing by the Left Hand of the Court, in writing, in a hand any Court clerk could match; it would ruin her, or make whoever holds it her creature for life. Pair 446 names, in effect, a political murder done on the Court’s order. The Guests may be hired by the Heirs to steal the ledger, by Corrow herself to recover it quietly (she knows Merrit keeps one; she has never asked to see it, and that is the most frightening thing about her), or by Merrit, who wants it carried out of Sallowreach to somewhere it can be read after the Glovehall Hush has taken everything.

The rules. The returned gloves hold what they held. Pair 92, the closed fingers, can be pried open only by a Guest with Cut 4 or higher in the Hand-line, at a Dire (22) Hand + Godsign roll; what is in them is the Carver’s to decide, but it is the size of a walnut and it is whatever the Regent was supposed to finish of, and it is still warm. Pair 240 never empties; it is a carried cupful of water from a Kept moat, which will drown anything small put into it and keep it alive. Pair 459, worn, makes the wearer’s touch silent: Filch and Stealth rolls with the hands gain +2, and each day worn is Taint 2 Regrowth (Ossel) and a Dread 1 check, as the wearer’s fingertips begin to feel nothing at all.

The secret. Ivo Vane, Corrow’s son, who has never touched his mother’s skin, buys her old gloves from Merrit, a pair at a time, by night, at a price she cannot refuse, and Merrit has entered none of these sales in the ledger. He wears them in bed. He wears them to sign the forged Closing licenses he sells to the Heirs, and the cold of his mother’s hands, still in the leather, leaves on the paper the frost-print the Court’s clerks test for, which is why his forgeries have never once been caught. He is wearing Pair 186 at present, the one that finished Old Halse, because it is the only pair that has ever held a living man’s hand, even by accident.

Confessions to the Bench

The accused will repeat the oath, in its words, from the beginning. The court will listen. The court will not interrupt. The god does not need the court’s help.
— Judge Thane Urrow, opening his eleven thousandth trial, Lack 640

What it is. Six transcripts from the Breaking courts of Tacit and the gorges, copied out of the Keeners’ fair records by a student of the Bench of Clauses for a commonplace-book of “Instructive Cases,” which the Bench confiscated in 641 and which has since been copied, quietly, several more times. The Keener of a Breaking court writes down every word spoken, and every sound, in a column of its own: the sound column is what makes these transcripts famous. In a Breaking court, the sound is the verdict.

Where it is found. The original is in the Bench’s archive on the Bench Terrace. Copies circulate among law students at Tacit, among the Forsworn of the Breakdowns, who read them aloud for the pleasure of hearing the great made small, and on the Rim, where a Company Waymaster at Quillhouse rents one out by the night. Reading these transcripts is safe. Reading the oaths in them aloud, in Oathen, in the first person, is not: an oath read aloud is an oath said, and the Bench has records. The third transcript is Taint Dread 3 and should not be read aloud anywhere.

I. The Matter of Hollen Brisk

BREAKING COURT OF THE BENCH TERRACE, TACIT. GRACE 638. JUDGE T. URROW PRESIDING. THE ACCUSED: HOLLEN BRISK, WATER-CARRIER, OF THE SHADEWARD. THE OATH ALLEGED BROKEN: SWORN TO HER FATHER, ORREN BRISK, BEDRIDDEN, IN 631, BEFORE HER BROTHER. WEIGHT 3.

JUDGE URROW: The accused will repeat the oath.

BRISK: “Father, I will bring you water every day as long as you live.”

(Sound column: none.)

JUDGE URROW: The court will wait.

(Sound column: none. The court waited the customary span of three breaths, then three more at the Judge’s sign.)

JUDGE URROW: The oath is kept. The court notes that it is kept.

THE BROTHER, from the gallery: He died of thirst. He died of thirst in his bed with a full cup beside him. Ask her where the cup was.

JUDGE URROW: The gallery will be silent or will be sworn silent. The court will put the Question, since the brother has laid it. Hollen Brisk. Did you kill your father?

BRISK: (after a long pause) I brought him water every day. I set it on the shelf by the window. Every day. It was always there. He could see it.

JUDGE URROW: That is not an answer. Did you kill your father?

BRISK: No. The thirst did.

(Sound column: a sound like a wet thread parting. A split, a hair’s breadth, at the left corner of the accused’s mouth. One drop of blood, no more. The Keener measures it with the rule: one-eighth of an inch.)

JUDGE URROW: The court records a hairline. The god has found the answer nearly true. So does the court. Sentence to be drafted: the accused is to carry water every day for nine years to the Witnessing Vaults, and set a cup within reach of every niche in her father’s gallery, and she is to swear that it is within reach. Next.

II. The Matter of the Forty Pages

BREAKING COURT, BENCH TERRACE. CARVING 639. URROW PRESIDING. THE ACCUSED: ALDER MASKE, DRAPER. THE OATH ALLEGED BROKEN: HIS MARRIAGE VOW TO ISOLT MASKE, NÉE VERE, FORTY PAGES, NEGOTIATED ELEVEN MONTHS, SWORN 626. WEIGHT 4. THE WIFE ATTENDS.

JUDGE URROW: The accused will repeat the vow. All of it. The court has set aside the morning.

MASKE: Article one. “I take her as she is, and as she will be, barring only...”

(Sound column, articles one to ten: none. Two hours.)

MASKE: Article eleven, clause three. “I will not lie down with another, nor rise with another, nor...”

(Sound column: the left hand. Each finger, in order from the smallest, folding back to the wrist with five distinct reports. The accused continues reading without being told to. The Keener notes that he does not look at his wife.)

MASKE: Article fourteen. “I will not speak of her in her absence to any person in a manner I would not repeat in her presence.”

(Sound column: the lower lip. A split to the chin.)

MASKE: (indistinct) Article nineteen. “I will not spend the household’s silver without...”

(Sound column: none. The wife, in the gallery, laughs once, aloud, and is fined.)

MASKE: Article twenty-six. “I will keep her warm in Lack.”

(Sound column: none.)

MASKE: Article thirty-one. “I will not let her be alone in the dark at the time of her mother’s dying.”

(Sound column: the breastbone. A crack, one, long, like a branch under snow. The accused sits down on the sand of his own accord. The Judge permits it. He reads the rest sitting.)

MASKE: Article forty. The last. “And I will love her.”

(Sound column: none.)

JUDGE URROW: The court will wait.

(Sound column: none. Three breaths. Three more. Nine more, at the Judge’s sign, which is irregular.)

JUDGE URROW: Article forty is kept. The court so records.

THE WIFE, from the gallery: (Keener’s note: she spoke without rising, and was not fined, and the court did not look at her, because it was not looking.) Then I would rather it had broken. Then I would know what the rest of it was for.

JUDGE URROW: Sentence to be drafted. Next.

III. The Shepherd of Sworn Gorge

BREAKING COURT, BENCH TERRACE. LACK 640. URROW PRESIDING, WITH TWO WARDENS OF THE ECHO SEATED, AT THEIR REQUEST. THE ACCUSED: TOBEN HALE, GOATHERD OF THE UPPER GULLET. THE OATH ALLEGED BROKEN: UNKNOWN. THE ACCUSED HAS BEEN BREAKING FOR THREE YEARS, A PART A MONTH, FOR NO CAUSE HE CAN NAME. HE STATES THAT IN 637 HE FOLLOWED A GOAT INTO A SEALED RAVINE AND HEARD THE ECHO THERE. WEIGHT: UNKNOWN.

JUDGE URROW: Toben Hale. The court cannot ask you to repeat an oath it does not know. The court will ask you instead to repeat what you heard.

WARDEN STANE: Judge, I’d ask you not to.

JUDGE URROW: Noted. The court has the duty of the god’s record. Toben Hale, repeat what you heard in the gorge, in its words, from the beginning.

HALE: I only heard the end of it. It comes round. You have to wait for it to come round. I waited a day.

JUDGE URROW: Then repeat what you heard.

HALE: It was a man’s voice and it was very young. He said, “I swear, on everything I ate, that when it comes back I will...”

(Sound column: see below.)

(Keener’s note, in a different ink, made the same day: The remainder of this transcript is struck by order of the Bench, Lack 640, and the Keener’s original sheet burned in the presence of the Chief Clausewright. All persons present in the court, numbering forty-one, have been sworn by the Bench to silence on its contents, at Weight 5, on the bones, and also sworn to the oath the accused repeated, since they had heard it, and are bound by it, as he is. The accused completed it. He did not break while repeating it. He broke after, when the court rose, and had been breaking for an hour when the Wardens carried him out. The Judge’s ear-trumpet was found afterward on the bench, closed flat, as if it had been stepped on. Nobody stepped on it. The two Wardens of the Echo resigned their posts that evening, and have taken the Quiet.)

IV. The Matter of Corse Ottery, Forsworn

QUESTION COURT, REMOVED TO THE WITNESSING VAULTS BY ORDER OF THE JUDGE. PLENTY 640. URROW PRESIDING. THE ACCUSED: CORSE OTTERY, FORSWORN OF THE BREAKDOWNS, WHOSE JAW BROKE IN 622 ON A FALSE OATH OF DEBT AND HAS SET CROOKED. THE CHARGE: THE MURDER OF ONA DRAY, A SURETY, IN THE LOW CANYON. THE VICTIM IS STANDING IN HER NICHE.

JUDGE URROW: Corse Ottery, did you kill Ona Dray?

OTTERY: No.

(Sound column: none. The jaw, already broken, has nothing left to break with. The gallery, which is Forsworn, laughs. The Judge waits for it to stop.)

JUDGE URROW: The court is aware of the difficulty. That is why we are here and not on the Terrace. Corse Ottery, lay your hand on the bones of Ona Dray and swear, before her as second witness, that you did not kill her.

OTTERY: (laying his hand on the dead woman’s foot, which is cured hard and dark as a saddle) I swear on Ona Dray that I never laid a hand on her.

JUDGE URROW: That is not the oath the court asked for.

OTTERY: It’s the one I’m giving.

(Sound column: a dry sound from the niche. Cured leather giving. The victim’s jaw, wired shut at her standing, opens against the wire, which parts. Keener’s note: the face of the dead in the Vaults wears the look of having just heard something. It is the only time I have seen one look as if it were about to answer.)

THE DEAD WOMAN: (in the accused’s own voice, exactly, from inside her) Never laid a hand on her.

(Sound column: a pause. Then the same voice, lower.)

THE DEAD WOMAN: Used the rope.

(Sound column: the accused’s hand, on the dead woman’s foot. Every bone of it, at once. He cannot lift it off her. He has to be cut free at the wrist by the Vault-keepers, and the hand is left on the foot, by the Judge’s order, as testimony.)

JUDGE URROW: The dead have testified. Sentence: the Breaker. Next.

V. The Ninefold at Tallow-Clan Narrows

REPORT OF THE BENCH’S INSPECTOR OF THE UPPER GORGES, ENTERED WITH THE BREAKING COURT’S RECORDS AS A TRANSCRIPT OF A PROCEEDING NOT RECOGNISED BY THE BENCH. CARVING 637. THE ACCUSED: DAVIT OF THE TALLOW-CLAN, WHO KILLED HIS BROTHER AT THE GOATFOLD WITH A HOOK. THE NARROWS: A NINEFOLD, BY THE CLAN’S COUNT. THE INSPECTOR WATCHED FROM THE RIM AND WROTE, AT THE ELDER’S PERMISSION, BY GESTURE.

THE MOTHER, from the rim: Davit. Did you do it?

(Echo, from the narrows, nine times, dying: did you do it, did you do it, did you, did you, do it, do it, it, it, it.)

DAVIT, from the floor of the narrows: I didn’t. Mam, I didn’t.

(Echo: I didn’t. Sound: the jaw, once, a crack like a stick. Mam, I didn’t. The lower lip goes. I didn’t. The teeth on the left side, all of them, a sound like gravel shaken in a cup. I didn’t. The tongue. I will not write what the tongue did. I didn’t. He is on his knees. Mam. He is trying to hold his face together with both hands. The echo does not care that he has stopped speaking; the walls are still saying it in his voice, and every time they say it, it is said again, and it is still a lie. I didn’t. The upper jaw. I didn’t. I am holding my pencil so hard I have broken the lead. Didn’t. The throat, down the front, to the breastbone, and then there is no more sound from him and the narrows go quiet, slowly, the way a bell does.)

THE MOTHER: (to the clan, after the silence) Bring him up. Put him with his brother. Facing in.

(Inspector’s addendum: Nobody touched him. That is the clans’ whole defence of it, and having watched it I find I cannot answer it. I asked the mother on the walk down whether she had believed him. She said she had believed him until the third echo. I asked what changed at the third. She said, He was still saying it. A man telling the truth would have stopped to listen.)

VI. The Late Verdict

BREAKING COURT, BENCH TERRACE. LACK 641, THE FOURTH DAY AFTER THE KEPT RAIN CAME LATE. URROW PRESIDING. THE ACCUSED: SELKE VARRA, CANYON WATCH, WHO SWORE TO HOLD THE NORTH STAIR OF THE TERRACE AND WAS SEEN BY THE WHOLE COURT TO LEAVE IT, THIS MORNING, TO RUN FROM A SOUND IN THE CISTERNS. THE BREACH IS WITNESSED BY THE COURT ITSELF. WEIGHT 3.

JUDGE URROW: This is a formality. The accused will repeat the oath.

VARRA: “I will hold the north stair of the Terrace through my watch and not leave it for any cause.”

(Sound column: none.)

JUDGE URROW: The court will wait.

(Sound column: none. Three breaths. Three more. Nine more.)

JUDGE URROW: (after a time) The accused left the stair. Forty people saw it. The court saw it.

VARRA: Yes, Judge.

JUDGE URROW: Then the court will wait.

(Sound column: none. The Keener has turned the sand-glass twice. Eleven minutes by the glass. The court does not move. In the gallery a Forsworn begins to laugh and stops by himself. The accused is weeping and does not know where to put her hands. The Judge has lowered his ear-trumpet and is sitting very still with his eyes shut, which the Keener has not seen him do in twenty years of this court.)

JUDGE URROW: (quietly, not to the court) Are you there?

(Sound column, at the twelfth minute, all at once: the accused’s knees, both, backward, like a heron’s, on the sand. She goes down without a cry. And at the same moment, from the Judge’s chair, a second sound, smaller, from inside the red robe: a creak, as of a rib taking a weight it was not built for.)

(Keener’s note: I record, because it is my office to record every sound in the court, and every face, that when the accused’s knees broke the Judge opened his eyes and smiled. Openly. In front of the court. It was the first time in my service I have seen him do it. I do not think he knew. I have not told him. I am entering it here so that the court, if it ever has to, can hear it read back.)

JUDGE URROW: The verdict was late. The court notes that it was late. The court notes that it came. Sentence to be drafted. Next.

He was still saying it. A man telling the truth would have stopped to listen.
a mother of the Tallow-clan, to the Bench’s Inspector, Carving 637
Carver’s Notes: Confessions to the Bench

The hooks. Each transcript is a seed. Hollen Brisk is carrying water to the Vaults every day, and has begun to find the cups empty in the morning, in the niches of the dead, who do not drink. Alder Maske broke his breastbone on Article thirty-one because his wife’s mother died alone in the dark while he was elsewhere; Isolt Maske wants the Guests to find out where, and with whom, and she does not want to know. Toben Hale’s forty-one witnesses are all bound by an oath sworn in 419 A.G. by a young man “on everything he ate,” to do something “when it comes back”; one of them is a Guest’s contact, and has begun breaking, a part a month, in the same order as Hale. Corse Ottery’s hand is still on the dead woman’s foot, and the Forsworn want it back for burial; the Bench will not release testimony. The Ninefold is still practised in the Gullet, and the Inspector who wrote the report has asked to be sent back, which worries the Bench more than anything else in it. The Late Verdict is the newest: Urrow wants to know whether the god was late, or deliberating, and whether it was deliberating about him, and he will pay the Guests well to find another case where it happens.

The rule: running a trial from these. Read the oath in full; have the player repeat it in character, word for word; then let the silence run. These transcripts are models for the Carver’s pacing. Since Lack 641, when a Breaking is due, the Carver may roll a d6 in secret: on a 1 the verdict comes late, from one minute to an hour, and anyone in the court when it lands makes a Dread 2 check, Dread 3 if they were the one who had begun to hope.

The rule: reading the oaths. A Guest who reads aloud, in Oathen, the oaths in the first, second, fourth or sixth transcripts has said them; the Carver should treat any of them as a binding Weight 1 promise for a day, and let the dice and the Guest’s conduct decide whether anything happens. Reading the fragment in the third transcript aloud binds the reader to the Sworn Gorge oath at Weight 5. The Bench has only the first eleven words of it on record, and wishes it had none.

The secret. The late verdicts are not the god growing careless. The god has begun to listen for longer, the way a listener does when the speaker has stopped being the most important voice in the room, as though it were waiting to hear something else said first. The Judge’s smile is the Appetite of the Witness taking a man who has spent forty years listening for it, and the creak in his ribs is his judicial oath, neither pleasure nor pity, beginning to come due.

Part Two
Engines and Songs
The machinery of the Grace, and what the Table sings while it works.
Chapter 3

Engines of the Grace

Machinery and Devices
There is no gunpowder on the Table. There is no need of it. We have found other ways to make a thing go off in a person’s hands.
— Ambrel Coyle, clockwright of the Vigil, in the preface to his Book of Escapements, 371 A.G.

A letter from a Rim Road tinker to her apprentice, found folded in a tin of brass pins sold at Gristmoot. The apprentice’s name has been scraped off.

You asked me what the trade is. I will tell you, since you will not stop asking, and since you have good hands and a bad memory, which is the right way round.

The trade is this. Every land on the Table has a god in it that is coming back, and every land has decided to hold the god down with a machine. Not a prayer. Prayers are cheap and everybody has one. A machine. The sleepless have engines that stab them on the quarter-hour. The coast has a bell that rings off a man’s chest. The highlands have a clock that runs on a dead woman’s brick and a frame for sewing strangers’ hands together. The red canyons have traps for words. The fen has wax that makes a small silence and mittens of lead the size of a bucket. The Fatlands have a scale that has elected three governments. The Fast has an axe and an axe and an axe.

None of them work, girl. That is the first thing to know. They hold. Holding is not working. A thing that holds is a thing that will one day let go, and you must sell it to the customer as though it never will, and you must be standing a long way off on the day it does.

The second thing to know is that every one of these engines has a part in it that is a person. Look for it. It is always there. Sometimes it is the operator, sometimes the one who is operated upon, sometimes a body that was put in at the bottom when the thing was built and never taken out again. When you are asked to mend a machine, find the person in it first, and ask whether they would like to be mended, and then do the job anyway, because you have been paid.

The third thing to know is that brass goes green, iron goes red, lead goes white and people go every colour, and you must carry polish for all four.

Mind the pins. Some are dipped.

This chapter describes the great and small machines of the Table: the engines by which seven peoples have tried to hold their eaten gods in check, measure them, steer them, profit by them, or follow them down. Some are famous and singular, like the Follow in its slip at Mile Nineteen or the Great Scales under the bone dome of the Weighhouse. Some are common trade goods sold on every Rim market, like lead mittens and jaw-wires. All of them have a history, an operator, a cost, and a way of going wrong.

Every device is described in the same order. First comes its lore and history: who made it, why, and what it has done. Then a diagram in words: a parts table and a plain account of how the thing works, written so that a Carver can describe it to the players, or a player whose character has Craft or Reckoning can understand it, sketch it, sabotage it, or build a worse one. Then who builds it and who uses it; then what it is like in operation, to every sense; then the rules; then a d6 failure table; then cost and availability; then a hook.

Engines and the Grace Roll

Using a device that is built for the purpose is normally automatic; the rules for each device say when a roll is needed. When one is, mechanisms answer to Eye + Reckoning (setting, reading, calibrating, timing), building and mending to Hand + Craft, and anything that is fitted to a living or Kept body to Hand + Stitching.

Building a device is a Long Task (see the Rules chapter): the device lists the difficulty, the time for each roll, and the number of successes needed. Materials must be bought first, at the listed cost, and are spent whether the work succeeds or not.

Failure tables. Every device has a d6 failure table. Roll on it when a roll to use the device is a Lack, when a device is used past its limits, when a saboteur has been at it, or whenever the device’s own rules tell you to. A failure on an ordinary roll is just a failure; the table is for when the thing itself goes wrong.

Sabotage. Fouling a device without being noticed is Hand + Craft (or Hand + Filch for a quick job) against the device’s Sabotage difficulty. Finding the fault afterwards is Eye + Reckoning at the same difficulty. Each Helping on the sabotage lets the saboteur choose the failure result instead of rolling it.

Find the person in the machine. It is always there. Ask if they want mending. Then mend it anyway.
the Gristmoot tinker’s letter

The Vigil Waking-Engine

Tick, and prick. Tick, and prick. The engine does not love you. That is why it never tires of you.
— slogan painted over the door of the Rattlehouse on the Slope

Lore and History

In the first winter after the First Night, when the city of Ludmere had lost half its people to the long room and had not yet renamed itself, every survivor needed a nudger, and there were not enough hands to go round. Spouses kept each other awake until one of them failed. Children were paid by the hour and fell asleep on the job. Whole streets went down together in the warm afternoon of the third day of Carving 341 because the last waking person in each house had nobody left to pinch them. What the city needed, said a clockwright named Ambrel Coyle, was a nudger that did not get tired, did not love you, and could not be bribed with a minute’s rest.

He built the first Waking-Engine in his workshop on what is now Lampwrights’ Row in the spring of 344: a spring-driven escapement in a walnut case, strapped to the back of a chair, that every ninety beats of its balance wheel drove a steel pin a quarter-inch into the sitter’s thigh, rattled a tin clapper by their ear, and tightened a leather strap across their chest until they gasped. He sat in it himself for nine days and nights and came out raving, bloodied down both legs, and awake. The Watch of Watches bought the patent in 346. By 360 there was an engine in every guardhouse, every counting-room, and every orphanage.

The engines have grown since. The personal kind, called a coffer after the walnut case, is now carried on the back like a pedlar’s pack and wired by cords to cuffs on the wrists and thighs. The civic kind, the Great Engine, fills a whole building: the Rattlehouse on the Slope, a long brick hall built in 388, where four hundred of the city’s poorest stand in numbered stalls on a sloped floor while a single driveshaft the length of the hall turns cams that work four hundred arms, each arm tipped with a needle, a rattle, and a cold wet sponge. They pay a crumb a watch. It is the cheapest way to stay awake in the Vigil, and every night the Wakers carry out three or four who failed anyway, still standing in their stalls, eyes shut, the needle-arm going in and out of their thigh like a sewing machine.

Ambrel Coyle died in 371, awake, of a burst heart, in his own engine. He had written in the margin of his last drawing: I have built a thing that keeps a man from sleeping. I have not built a thing that lets him rest. The city does not know the difference. I am beginning to.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunction
Mainspring and barrelblued steel, brass drumstores the force; wound by crank every watch
Balance wheel and hairspringbrass, steelkeeps the beat; ninety beats to a “prick”
Cam-drumoak, iron pegssets the order of insults: pin, rattle, strap, sponge
Pin-cuffs (four)leather, brass, steel pinsdrive pins into wrists and thighs on the cam’s word
Rattle-boxtin, dried peasclatters at the ear
Chest-strapwaxed leather, ratchettightens on the breath, forcing a gasp
Lull-catchbrass feeler on the browsenses a nodding head and fires everything at once
Wake-glasssmall mirror on a stalkholds a lamp’s glare in the eyes

The coffer works like any clock, except that its hands are needles and its face is the wearer. The mainspring drives a train of brass wheels that turns the cam-drum one full revolution every quarter-hour. Pegs on the drum lift levers in a set order: at the first peg a cuff fires its pin; at the second the rattle-box shakes; at the third the chest-strap ratchets one notch tighter and then lets go; at the fourth a sponge of cold water on a stalk slaps the neck. The order can be changed by moving the pegs, and a good Waker-valet sets a client’s drum like a musician sets a tune, so that the insults come irregularly and the body cannot learn them. The cleverest part is the lull-catch, a brass feeler resting against the forehead: if the head drops by more than a finger’s width, the feeler trips a sear and the whole drum fires at once, every pin, rattle and strap together. The wearer comes up screaming. That is the point.

The Great Engine is the same thing built into a building. A water-wheel in the Slope’s main sewer turns the driveshaft; the shaft runs the length of the Rattlehouse; four hundred cams on it work four hundred stalls. There are no lull-catches in the Great Engine, because the Rattlehouse cannot afford them. Instead there are walkers: Rattlehouse boys who pace the aisles with Waker’s needles and look for drooping heads.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

Coffers are made on Lampwrights’ Row by six licensed clockwright families, of which the Coyle-Harrows are the oldest, and repaired on the Slope by everyone. The Wakers use them on prisoners and on themselves; the Watch of Watches uses gilded ones with silk cuffs, in which the pins are gold and the sponge is scented; clerks, night-porters, lamp-tenders and soldiers wear plain ones. Parents buy small coffers for children, with blunt pins, and the Watch pretends not to know that the pins are always sharpened within a year. The Rattlehouse is run by a Slope family, the Grainers, under a Watch licence, and is never empty. The Tuckers hate the engines: an engine-wearer does not need a minute’s guarded sleep, and an engine that has been fouled is the commonest way a Tucker’s competitor is put down.

In Operation

A coffer ticks loudly, by design, because a tick is a comfort and comfort is death, and so the tick is pitched just off the beat of a resting heart, a little fast, so that the body feels hurried by it. The wearer smells of brass polish, sweat and old blood, because the pin-cuffs are never quite clean and the punctures on the thighs of a ten-year wearer are a lace of white scar and fresh scab, weeping clear fluid into the cloth. The first prick comes with a click and a cold small bite, and then the warm thread of blood. The rattle is a sound like a handful of teeth in a tin. The chest-strap is the worst: it squeezes until the ribs creak and the breath goes out in a grunt, and holds a moment too long, and lets go, and the lungs heave in a gasp that is half a sob. In the Rattlehouse four hundred of these happen in one long ripple down the hall, every quarter-hour, a wave of grunts and gasps and little cries, and then a silence full of ticking, and then the boys walking the aisles calling up, up, up, up in bored sing-song voices.

Old wearers twitch in time with their drums even when the engine is off. They flinch on the quarter-hour. Some of them cannot hear a clock without their thighs bleeding.

It’s not the pin. You get used to the pin. It’s the click before the pin. I hear it in my sleep. I don’t sleep. I hear it anyway.
Rattlehouse stall-holder, number 211

Rules

Wearing a coffer. A wound coffer runs one watch (eight hours). While it runs, the wearer gains no Weariness from the watch’s passing, as though they had taken rouse, and gains +2 on all blink checks; the lull-catch fires on any failed blink check before the blink resolves, cancelling it, but the wearer loses 1 Flesh and the rest of their action. Each watch in a coffer costs 1 Flesh from the pins, which heals normally. A coffer stacks with rouse: a character on rouse and in a coffer may shed 1 further Weariness each watch, but must make a Gut + Endure roll (Hard 14) at the end of the watch or gain the Engine-Twitch (−1 to all Hand rolls requiring stillness, such as Shooting, Stitching and Filch, until they have spent a full day out of the coffer).

Stealth and comfort. A coffer is Noisy. Its wearer is at −4 to Stealth. In the Vigil this is good manners; abroad, it is a confession.

Torture. A coffer set to a cruel tune by a Waker or a wake-valet is a torture device (see Torture in the Rules chapter): the operator rolls Hand + Reckoning instead of the usual roll, and the subject cannot blink, faint or fall unconscious while it runs. Anyone forced into a cruel coffer for a full watch makes a Dread 2 check.

The Rattlehouse. A stall costs a crumb a watch. A character in a stall makes no blink checks for the watch, but the Rattlehouse is a scene of monotony, and at the end of each watch the GM rolls a d20 for each PC; on a 1 the character has gone under in their stall and must be fetched as described under Falling Asleep, by a Rattlehouse boy whose Tongue + Intimidate is +5.

Building a coffer is a Long Task: Hand + Craft at Grim 18, a day per roll, five successes, materials 60 lacks. Its Sabotage difficulty is Hard 14.

Failure Table (d6)

d6The engine fails
1The mainspring breaks with a crack like a slapped face. The engine stops. The silence afterward is so restful that the wearer must make a blink check at once, at +4.
2The cam-drum slips a peg. Every insult comes at once, every beat, until someone cuts the cords: 1 Flesh per round, and the wearer cannot act except to scream.
3The lull-catch sticks. The engine runs on, but the head may drop freely now. The wearer does not know. Their next failed blink resolves as normal, in harness, and the people around them assume the engine is working.
4The tick falls into time with the wearer’s resting heart. The engine has become a lullaby. +1 Weariness every hour until it is reset (Routine 10 Eye + Reckoning; the wearer must notice first).
5A pin breaks off in the thigh and works its way in. Nothing happens for a week. Then, each morning, roll a d6: on 1–2 the wearer loses 2 Flesh and limps all day, until a surgeon digs the pin out (Hard 14 Hand + Stitching).
6The wearer goes under in the engine and is Counted, and the engine goes on running. Nobody thinks to unstrap it. At the Dormitory they find the cuffs still pricking a sleeping body every quarter-hour, and the body still gasping on cue. Dread 3 for whoever finds it. They may not be allowed to take it off: the Matron says it is the only bed in the row that still breathes on its own schedule.

Cost and Availability

ItemCostAvailabilityNotes
Coffer, plain40 LCommon in the Vigil; Scarce elsewherewalnut, steel pins
Coffer, gilded400 LUncommongold pins, silk cuffs, scented sponge
Child’s coffer15 LCommonblunt pins, for now
Re-pegging by a valet2 LCommona new tune for the drum
Rattlehouse stall1 c a watchCommonthe Slope; bring your own rag

Hook

The Stall That Never Empties. Stall 400 in the Rattlehouse, at the very end of the hall, has been rented every watch for eleven years by somebody who pays in advance and is never seen to arrive or leave. Its needle-arm is always wet. The Grainers want to know who it is. The PCs, keeping watch through a night, see the arm working on nothing, quarter-hour by quarter-hour, and on the stroke of the Tablenight bell they see the empty stall gasp. When the Grainers finally open the stall’s floor they find that the stall was built over Ambrel Coyle’s first workshop, and that under the boards is a walnut chair with nobody in it, still strapped shut.

Finn Undertow's Tide-Bell Mechanism

The sea says dawn’s at the half-bell. Your chests say it’s now. I ring for the chests.
— Finn Undertow, Tide-Bellman of Lowmark

Lore and History

Lowmark has rung a tide bell since before the Beaching. The first was a ship’s bell hung on a post at the harbour mouth, struck by hand when the water turned so the fleet knew when to sail. After the Brimming of 60 A.G., when the first generation was born coughing brine, the bell took on a second task: to tell the city when to bail. For four hundred years the two tasks were one, because the tide in the chest rose and fell with the tide in the sea, and a bellman needed only to watch the water and ring.

The bell that hangs now on the Headland, called Old Gannet, was cast in 61 A.G. from the bronze fittings of the Admiralty’s first stranded ships, and it is the size of a small room. In 402 the Bellmen’s Company built a tower for it and fitted it with a tide-engine: a float in a stone well, the Tide-Well, fed by a culvert from the harbour, whose rise and fall turned a pegged drum that tripped the hammer at each turn of the tide. The bellman’s work became the keeping of the engine.

Then the sea began to leave. The culvert ran dry in 530. The Bellmen kept a clockwork reckoner set by the Salt Assay’s tables instead, and that was well enough until the body’s tide began to drift from the sea’s. By 600 the two were half an hour apart. By 630 they were two hours apart, and the Admiralty had ordered that the bell follow the sea, because the sea was the navy’s business and the chest was not.

The Admiralty had tried, before that, to make the engine ring the chest. In 604 a Tenanted volunteer named Ysolde Prow, a net-maker’s widow from Mile Three, was sealed into a glass cistern in the base of the tower with a leather cuff around her ribs and a cord from the cuff to the escapement, so that the slow fill and empty of her body’s tide would drive the hammer. The Bench approved it. The Deepening blessed it. Her family were given a pension and a plaque. For three years the bell rang off Ysolde Prow’s chest, and the city bailed in time. Then it drifted, exactly as before: a Tenanted chest, it turned out, followed something else, something deeper than the city’s tide, and the engine rang the wrong hours for Lowmark as surely as the sea did. The Admiralty unhooked the cord and went back to the sea-drum. Nobody unsealed the cistern. Ysolde Prow is still down there, thirty-seven years later, in the base of the tower, in green water gone thick as broth, breathing slowly, and nobody remembers whose job it is to feed her. She was the city’s sacrifice to the bell, and she was worth nothing.

Finn Undertow took the rope in 627. For four years he rang the sea, as ordered.
