Then one dawn he felt his own chest fill, and heard the whole Headland cough with him, a full hour before the sea-drum tripped, and he went down into the gear-room with a knife and a coil of tarred cord and wired the engine to himself.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunction
Old Gannetbronze, eleven tonsthe bell; heard to Mile Twelve on a still day
Hammer and seariron, oak beamstrikes the bell when the sear is tripped
Sea-Drumoak, iron pegs, clockworkthe old engine; trips the sear at the Assay’s tide
Chest-Drumbrass, gut cordthe new engine; trips the sear off Finn’s ribs
Selector leveriron, brass plate marked SEA and CHESTchooses which drum commands the hammer
Rib-cufftarred leather, whalebone staysbuckled around Finn’s chest, day and night
The Count Wheelbrass, scratched by handFinn’s drift-counter; a notch for every minute the tides close
The Prow Cisternglass, iron bands, lead sealthe old chest-engine; disconnected, still occupied

The tower is three storeys of grey stone. At the top hangs Old Gannet, with its hammer on an oak beam above it. In the gear-room beneath, two drums sit side by side, and a long iron selector lever chooses which of them will lift the hammer’s sear. The Sea-Drum is the old engine, driven now by clockwork set to the Salt Assay’s tables. The Chest-Drum is Finn’s: a small brass drum with a ratchet, connected by forty feet of gut cord, running over pulleys and down through a hole in the floor, to a buckled leather cuff around Finn Undertow’s ribs. When his chest fills with the body’s tide, his ribs swell; the cord draws taut; the ratchet turns the drum by one tooth; and when it has turned far enough, the sear trips, and the bell rings for the chests of Lowmark.

Finn is roped to the tower, as bellmen always were, so that the Calling cannot walk him off the Headland. But his rope is short, because the cord is short. He sleeps, eats, bails and lives within forty feet of the Chest-Drum. Beside it, on the wall, is the Count Wheel: a brass wheel he has marked by hand, one scratch for every minute by which the body’s tide has drifted from the sea’s, and a second ring of scratches counting down the days until the drift closes. By the wheel, the tide in every chest on the coast will fill at the same moment at the Low Water of Carving 642.

At the bottom of the stair, behind a door that has been bricked and then unbricked and then bricked again, is the Prow Cistern.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

The Bellmen’s Company of Lowmark, which is now Finn Undertow and two apprentices, keeps the engine. The Admiralty owns it and has three times ordered the selector set to SEA; each time Finn has set it to CHEST again, and the city has refused to support the Admiralty’s officers in arresting him, because the city coughs when Finn rings, and it is easier to cough on time. Skerrow and the other coastal towns have their own bells and bellmen, and most of them still ring the sea. The Deepening want the cistern opened, and Ysolde brought out to be walked into the Trench with the honour she was owed. The Wreckwives bring her flowers, which they push through a crack in the bricks.

In Operation

The tower smells of tar, wet bronze, and the sour green breath that rises up the stair from the cistern. It sounds of ticking, of gulls, and of Finn’s breathing, which every visitor notices: slow, and deep, and a little too long, and accompanied, at each breath’s end, by the small dry click of the ratchet forty feet above him. He wears the rib-cuff under his shirt; the leather has worn a raw red band around his torso, weeping at the edges, and the whalebone stays have pressed white grooves into his skin like the marks of a corset. When the body’s tide comes, he stops whatever he is doing. His chest fills, visibly, the ribs rising and staying risen; his face goes dark; water comes up into his throat and he bends over his bucket and bails, retching, and above him the ratchet clicks, and clicks, and the sear trips, and Old Gannet speaks, a sound so deep it is felt in the teeth before it is heard. Across the Headland, a mile of Lowmark coughs, together, at once, a sound like surf on shingle.

When the bell rings, a deep, slow knocking answers from the bottom of the stair, three times, and then stops. Finn says it is the pipes.

Every hour I’m the city’s chest. Every hour I’m drowning for all of you. It’s a living.
Finn Undertow, to the Admiralty’s third arresting officer, who went home

Rules

Ringing the chests. While the selector is set to CHEST, everyone in Lowmark who hears Old Gannet bails on time. Brinehollowers within earshot gain +1 on Calling rolls on any night the bell rings the chest, because they are bailed and steady; they gain the same bonus against drowning effects of their own tide. When the selector is set to SEA, Brinehollowers in earshot suffer the −2 penalty for a missed bailing for 1d6 × 10 minutes each turn of the tide, as the bell lies to them.

Wearing the cuff. Anyone may take Finn’s place on the cord. The wearer must be a Brinehollower (anyone else’s chest does not have the tide) and must stay within forty feet of the drum. Each turn of the tide, the wearer makes a Gut + Endure roll at Hard 14 or loses 2 Flesh to the cuff’s bite as the chest swells against it. A wearer at the Appetite or beyond feels the coast’s tide as one swell; they may roll Caul + Godsign at Grim 18 to learn, for one turn, who on the Headland is closest to being Called, as a direction and a distance. A Lack gives them the Want The West for a day.

Reading the Count Wheel. Eye + Reckoning at Hard 14 gives the date of the closing. A Helping reveals that the drift is not steady but follows a slow rhythm of its own, four breaths in a day; a Grace lets the character recognise the rhythm as a single great breath taken by something very large, somewhere below, and make a Dread 3 check.

The cistern. Opening the bricks is Hand + Labor at Routine 10. Seeing what is inside is Dread 3. Ysolde Prow is Tenanted, at the Seating, and has not been bailed by anyone but herself in thirty-seven years. She can speak, very slowly, through water. Whatever is wearing her is courteous, and asks after the bell.

Sabotage difficulty: Hard 14 for the drums, Routine 10 to cut the cord.

Failure Table (d6)

d6The bell fails
1The cord snaps. The bell rings no tide at all until it is spliced. In the silence, the Headland’s chests come on unannounced, in the street, at table, in bed; d6 deaths by drowning in the night among the old and the drunk.
2The ratchet slips backward. The bell rings twice, a turn apart, and half the city bails for nothing and half not at all. Brawls at every pump.
3The selector jumps to SEA in the night. Nobody touched it. The ratchet has been moved by a hand that left wet prints on the lever, small and long-fingered.
4The cuff tightens itself. The wearer’s chest goes on filling past the tide and will not stop until the cuff is cut: Gut + Endure at Grim 18 or begin drowning on dry stone (1 Flesh per round).
5Old Gannet rings for the cistern instead of the cuff. Its note drops a full tone. Everyone in earshot at the Appetite or beyond must make a Calling roll at once, in daylight.
6The drift closes early. For one turn, every chest on the coast fills at the same moment, and the bell rings it, and in the silence after, a mile of Lowmark hears something very large, far to the west, draw breath with them. Dread 4.

Cost and Availability

The Tide-Bell Mechanism is Unique. A small chest-engine for a household (a rib-cuff, cord and clapper bell that rings the wearer’s own tide for the house) can be had from a Mile Six bell-founder for 35 lacks (Uncommon in Brinehollow, Rare elsewhere); it is popular with Wreckwives, who strap it to their returned spouses and listen, at night, to see whose tide it rings.

Hook

The Third Knock. The Admiralty wants the selector set to SEA permanently and has hired the PCs to replace Finn with a reliable man, quietly. Finn’s apprentices have hired the same PCs to find out what is knocking on the cistern’s bricks. Inside the cistern, Ysolde Prow has been keeping her own count, scratched on the glass with a fingernail: a count that closes on the same night as Finn’s, and a list of names under it, nine hundred long, every one of them a volunteer from Dagna Hull’s wall.

The Assemblers' Joining Frame

Whose is the hand? Every mother’s. What does the needle do? It makes the god whole.
— the Gatherers’ Catechism

Lore and History

The first Joinings in the Barn were done on a threshing floor, on straw, by lamplight, with the Part held in place by the hands of six kneeling Seamsters for a whole night while the seam took. Hands tire. In 566 a Seamster fell asleep at the far end of the figure, and the ear she was holding against the figure’s jaw crawled away into the straw and was not found for a week; when it was, it had begun to take root in the floorboards. Dov Marrin’s predecessor, a wheelwright’s widow named Hanne Spokes, built the first Joining Frame that winter from a cart-bed, a loom and a midwife’s birthing chair, and every Joining since has been done in it or in one of its children.

There are now four frames in the Barn and perhaps a dozen elsewhere, in the cellars of Assembler households across the highlands, where Gatherers join two or three Parts together before carrying them to the Barn, so that the god arrives in larger pieces. The Attendance has found and burned nine of these lesser frames since 620. They are always warm when found, and there is always something in them.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunction
The Bedoak cart-bed on trestles, padded with fleeceholds the figure or the receiving body
The Armseight jointed oak arms with brass clampshold a Part exactly against its seam for a night
Warming Troughscopper, under the bed, fed from a kettle-stovekeep bed and Parts at blood-heat
The Listening Slabred clay, hollowed, with a brass ear-cupwhere a Part is laid to be Heard before joining
Hum-Pipea bone flute with five holessounds the five-note tune that calls the Parts
Seam-rackcurved needles, sheep-gut, silver wirethe stitching itself
Cord-Pegsiron, set in the bed’s rimwhere a Carrier’s living cord is pegged, if they are Uncut

The frame is a bed with arms. The receiving body (Herself, or a lesser assemblage, or a living Carrier who has agreed to bear the piece) is laid on the fleece and kept at blood-heat by the troughs. The Part is first laid on the Listening Slab, a hollowed brick of warm red clay with a brass cup set into its side, and a Fitter puts her ear to the cup and listens, sometimes for days, until she knows where the Part wants to go. Then the arms are swung in and their clamps set: soft brass jaws lined with lambskin, adjusted by thumbscrews, one arm for each edge of the seam. The clamps hold the Part against the body, edge to edge, raw to raw, with exactly the pressure of a mother’s hand. The Fitter sews with curved needles, sheep-gut for the skin and silver wire for anything that bears weight. Then the hum-pipe is played, the five notes, over and over, by relays of brothers and sisters, all night, while the seam takes. By morning, in Cradlewrack, the arms can be swung back. The Part is part of something.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

Frames are built by Assembler carpenters to Hanne Spokes’s pattern, and only Fitters and Assembler-Prime may join in them. Seamsters assist. The Attendance keeps two confiscated frames in the Lying-In, and the rumour in Kest is that it uses them, for the births it permits but cannot look at: to sew back what came out wrong. Lazar Voss has drawn a frame in exact detail. The Second Table has paid for a frame to be shipped, in pieces, to a cellar on the Rim.

In Operation

The room smells of hot copper, wet fleece, milk, and a sweetish smell beneath it like a cut pear left out. The troughs gurgle. The clamps tick as they are tightened. The Part, on the Slab, is never quite still: a hand flexes, a tongue curls, an eye rolls in its socket of clay to look at the Fitter. When it is laid against the body, the edges of both wounds are seen to be wet and raw and to tremble toward each other, like the lips of a cut that wants to close. The gut squeaks through skin. Through the long night, under the hum, the seam begins to pulse, first out of time with the body’s heart, then in. By dawn the scar is pink, puckered, and warm as a cheek. The worst moment, those who have seen it say, is the first twitch: when the joined hand closes, not by its own will but by the body’s, and the whole figure on the bed seems to shiver once, from end to end, the way a sleeper shivers when someone sits down on the bed.

It took at four bells. I felt it take. The whole barn felt it. Everybody looked at the door, as if someone had come in.
Seamster’s account of a Joining, Plenty 639

Rules

The Hearing. Laying a Part on the Slab and finding where it belongs is Caul + Instinct at Hard 14, one roll per day; a Fitter adds her rank. Each Helping reveals one true thing about the Part’s bearer or its place in the figure. A Lack means the Part has been heard wrong: it will be joined where it does not belong (roll on the failure table at the Joining’s end, regardless of success).

The Joining. Hand + Stitching at Grim 18 (Hard 14 for a Fitter in a proper frame). The frame gives +2 to the roll; without one, six steady assistants are needed and the difficulty is Dire 22. A success means the Part takes by dawn. Inside Cradlewrack this is certain; outside it, the Part takes only on a Grace, and otherwise dies in the night, cold and grey.

Bearing the piece. A living body joined to a Part becomes a Carrier. The Part has Taint 2 Regrowth (Cradlewrack’s god, foreign to most) and counts as worn against the skin every day. It feeds through the seam: the Carrier’s maximum Flesh drops by 2 for as long as it is carried. It has a will: once a session the GM may have it reach, grip, stroke or point, and the Carrier must win an opposed Gut + Brawl roll against the Part’s Threat 3 to stop it. Witnesses of a Joining make a Dread 2 check; the Carrier makes Dread 3 the first morning they see it move.

Building a frame is a Long Task: Hand + Craft at Hard 14, a day per roll, four successes, 90 lacks of oak, brass and copper. Its Sabotage difficulty is Hard 14.

Failure Table (d6)

d6The Joining fails
1The seam will not take. The Part is cold by morning. It is still moving.
2It takes, wrong side out. The hand is joined palm-outward, the eye facing in. It works.
3The clamps were too tight. The Part takes, and the brass arm takes with it: the clamp is fused into the flesh, and must stay, or be sawn.
4The Fitter’s ear was against the cup for too long. Her own hearing is joined into the Part: from now on she hears what it hears, everywhere it goes.
5The receiving body takes the Part and then reaches past it, in the night, and takes one of the assistants’ hands as well. The assistant must be cut free (Grim 18 Hand + Stitching) or join the figure.
6The Part’s bearer, wherever they are in the highlands, feels the seam take, at dawn, as a pain in the place it came from. They will come to the Barn. They will want it back, or they will want to lie down beside it. Neither ends well.

Cost and Availability

A frame is Rare, never openly sold, and costs 300 lacks from an Assembler carpenter who trusts the buyer, or 900 through the Second Table’s agents. Assembler joining-gut (sheep-gut cured in posset) is 3 lacks a skein, Uncommon in Cradlewrack. Possession of a frame in Kest is a matter for the Second Opinion.

Hook

The Frame in the Cellar. A Rim innkeeper at Knocking Gate has asked the PCs to clear a cellar he has inherited. In it is a small Joining Frame, still warm, the troughs still bubbling, the kettle-stove still lit by someone who comes in at night. On the fleece, in the clamps, are two ears and a mouth, already joined into something like a face, and the face is humming the five notes. It is waiting for its eyes. The innkeeper’s own children have started humming them too.

Hush-Wax Lanterns

It does not light the room. It finishes a little of it.
— Loft-Warden’s description, given in sign, because there was no sound to give it in

Lore and History

When Dunmere went silent in 633, the Court sent surveyors to the edge, and the surveyors brought back what they could reach without crossing: a dead heron with every feather perfect, a stalk of grey grass that did not wilt, and, from an apple tree just inside the line, a wild bees’ nest. The bees had fallen in rows on the comb. The honey had stopped. The wax, when it was cut, did not smell of anything at all.

A chandler named Wick Tallow bought the comb. He had built his fortune rendering the unclaimed dead into candles that feel themselves burn, and he wanted to know what a candle would do that could feel nothing. He rendered the Dunmere wax, poured it into a single taper, and lit it in his shop in the Lower Pilings. The flame was perfectly still. Around it, for a stride in every direction, there was no sound. The flies in the shop dropped out of the air. And the Kept candles on the next shelf, the ones made from people, stopped moaning in their wax and went out.

Wick Tallow is a businessman. Within a year he had sent gatherers to the edge of every Hush in the country for comb, for tallow from things that died at the line, for the fat of birds that fell. The product is called Hush-wax. Rendered into lanterns, it makes a small, moving silence: a little Hush on a pole. The Court declared it a licensed good in 636, since a thing that finishes even a little is a Closing by another name. The licence is never granted. The lanterns are everywhere.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunction
Hush-wax taperwax or tallow from inside a Hush’s edgethe source; burns three hours a finger
Lead cowlsheet lead, hingedshutters the silence; open, it spills, closed, it stops
Wickgrey grass from a Hush, plaitedwill not burn without Hush-wax around it
Glass chimneythick green fen-glasskeeps the flame from the air, which it dislikes
Pole or bailash, ironheld at arm’s length, always
Cork ear-stopscork and waxworn by the bearer, out of habit; they do nothing

A Hush-wax lantern is a plain fen-glass chimney in a hinged lead cowl, on a pole or a bail. The taper inside is grey, odourless, and slightly cold to the touch. The wick is a plait of Hush grass, which will not catch from any ordinary flame unless it is wrapped in Hush-wax, and which, once lit, burns with a small, upright, motionless flame, pale as milk, that casts no flicker. Around that flame, while the cowl is open, is a sphere of hush about two strides across: no sound passes into or out of it; flies, moths and fen-midges die at its rim and fall; decay stops within it; and the Kept, inside its light, grow still. Closing the lead cowl stops it at once. Lead is the only thing that does.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

Wick Tallow’s shop makes the best, with a small mark of a closed eye pressed into the base of every taper. Hush-gatherers, mostly Heirs and Finishers desperate for money, risk the edges to supply him; a gatherer who leans an inch too far simply stops. The Loft-Wardens buy lanterns quietly and carry them through the shelving on the worst nights, so that the Set-Aside nearest the light can have an hour without pain. Burglars and assassins use them for silence. Kept families buy them to sit by a grandmother’s shelf. The Finishers burn them at their services. The Court’s Closers hate them, with reason.

In Operation

Inside the sphere, the world stops making sound. A voice is a mouth moving. A footstep is a jolt felt through the heel. The bearer hears only their own heartbeat, carried through bone, very loud. The air goes perfectly dry and smells of nothing, which is the most frightening smell in Sallowreach, where everything smells. Outside the sphere, the fen goes on, buzzing and dripping and moaning; inside it, the flies come in out of the fog and drop onto the boards with tiny dry ticks that nobody hears, and pile in a ring at the edge of the light like black sand. And the Kept in the light change. Their faces slacken. The perpetual small motion of the fen dead, the twitch of the eyelid, the working of the jaw, the restless fingers, stops. Some weep. Some smile. All of them, if the light stays long enough, begin to lie down.

My mother had been screaming for ninety years. I held the lantern to her shelf and her mouth stopped and she looked at me. That was the first time she knew me since I was born. Then I closed the cowl, because it was not licensed, and she started again.
confession to the Loft-Wardens, unsigned

Rules

The silence. While the cowl is open, no sound enters or leaves the sphere (two paces radius). Characters inside gain +4 on Stealth against anyone outside and cannot be heard, speak to one another, or cast spoken oaths; Oathen echoes cannot reach them. The bearer must roll Caul + Resolve at Routine 10 each scene or gain 1 Fray from the silence.

The Kept. A Kept creature in the light is at −2 to all rolls and moves at half pace. Each full hour a Kept body remains in the light, roll a d6: on a 6 it finishes, properly and finally dead. This is an unlicensed Closing and a capital offence in Sallowreach. Kept PCs in the light feel no pain and must make a Caul + Resolve roll at Hard 14 to leave it voluntarily.

Taint. Hush-wax carries Taint 2 Dread, taken each scene the lantern burns. A Hand-line character at the Appetite or beyond who holds an open lantern gains +2 to any Closing touch, but also gains 1 Hunger each scene; at the Course, a Lack on any roll while holding it begins a small Hush, a pace across, at their feet, permanent.

Burning down. A finger of taper burns three hours. When the last of it gutters, the silence does not vanish at once: it drains out of the sphere in a sudden rush of noise that is a Dread 1 check for all inside.

Failure Table (d6)

d6The lantern fails
1The cowl will not close. The bearer must smother it with lead, or carry it open until it burns out.
2The flame stands still and the silence keeps spreading: a pace more each minute, until someone snuffs it with a lead cap (Hard 14 Hand + Craft).
3The silence comes off the lantern and stays where it was set down, the size of a hearth, after the flame is out. The Court will want to know whose it is.
4The bearer’s own sound goes out with it and does not come back for a day: no voice, no footsteps, no heartbeat anyone else can hear. Physicians pronounce them dead.
5A Kept body finishes in the light, and it was not the one meant.
6Something answers inside the silence: a voice heard only within it, close by the ear, clear as a bell, saying one word. Edda Thrush will want to know which word. Dread 3.

Cost and Availability

A Hush-wax lantern is Rare and illegal: 120 lacks from Wick Tallow’s back room, 250 abroad, where Vigil buyers want it for sleepless sickrooms and the Fatlands want it to quiet the Bleeding Orchards at pruning. Spare tapers are 30 lacks a finger. Counterfeits are common: ordinary wax dyed grey, which burns, flickers, and stinks of mutton.

Hook

The Wardens’ Night. Old Bettany Shroud wants a lantern carried up through all nine storeys of the Lofts, one shelf at a time, so that each of her forty thousand can have a minute’s peace on Tablenight. It will take all night and every taper in Lastgate. The Court has heard and sent a Closer to stop it. Halfway up, the PCs begin to notice that the shelves the lantern has passed do not start moaning again when the cowl is closed. They lie very still, and very quiet, and on the fifth storey every one of them has turned their head to watch the lantern go.

Oathen Echo-Traps

A word is a bird. It must land somewhere. We build it a nest, and close the lid.
— Echo-Warden teaching, in handtalk

Lore and History

The Echo-Wardens were chartered in 422 to clean the canyons of old sworn words, and for their first century they did it with felt, wool, sand and rockfall: smothering. Smothering kills an echo but takes days, and a long echo can bind a dozen travellers before it dies. In 531 a Warden-Tracker named Iolo Thrane, who had been a bell-founder before the knife took his right ear, built the first echo-trap: a long spiral horn of fired clay, lined with wax, that a living echo would fly into and not fly out of. The word went round the spiral, smaller and smaller, until it reached a wax-lined chamber at the centre, where it pressed itself into the soft wax like a seal into a letter, and stopped.

The traps worked. They also kept. A trap pulled from the rock forty years later was found to contain its echo still, pressed into the wax, and anyone who put their ear to the horn’s mouth heard it, faintly, and was bound by it. The Wardens now break every full trap on an anvil in a felt-hung room, and grind the wax with sand. Not all of them do. Kept words are worth a great deal to the wrong people.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunction
The Mouthflared clay bell, a forearm widefaces up-canyon; takes the echo in
The Spiralcoiled clay tube, wax-lined, nine turnsnarrows the word and keeps it turning
The Nestwax chamber at the centre, fist-sizedwhere the word lands and presses in
The Lidlead plug on a chainseals the nest; never removed in hearing of anyone
Felt jacketwool felt, stitched tightstops the trap ringing like a bell
Mountingiron pins, rope cradleset into the rock at an echo’s turning-point

An echo-trap looks like a great clay snail-shell, wrapped in grey felt, with a flared mouth. The Wardens track a living echo by ear, find the bend where it turns from one wall to the other, and pin the trap there, mouth facing the oncoming word. An echo is a sound that wants a wall to strike. The trap gives it a softer one, then another, nine turns down a narrowing spiral of wax, each turn taking a little of its force, until it is small enough to enter the nest. There it presses into the wax and is still. A Warden listens at the felt for silence, then fits the lead lid by touch. Then the trap is carried down, unspeaking, wrapped in a quilt, to be broken.

Smugglers and Forsworn have learned to build traps backwards: with a lid that can be opened. A trap with a kept word in it, unstopped in a narrow place, sends the word out again into the rock to bind whoever walks there. These are called loaded horns, and owning one is a crime equal to breaking the oath inside it.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

Echo-Warden potters at the Wardens’ house in Tacit build the true traps, and each is numbered and must be returned, full, to be broken. Smugglers in the Breakdowns build cruder ones from cracked water-jars lined with tallow. Grandam Cess, the Vow-Eater, is said to keep a shelf of loaded horns in her back canyon, each holding an oath she has lifted from a client, waiting to be sold to someone who wants that client bound again. The Bench owns a single horn from Sworn Gorge, sealed in lead, taken by Halvar Stane in 611 from the outermost bend of the gorge. It holds only one word. Nobody knows which.

In Operation

A trap being set is the quietest work on the Table. The Wardens move by touch and gesture, felt slippers on rock, breath held. Then the echo comes down the canyon: a voice, thin and distant and urgent, bouncing from wall to wall, the same few words over and over, getting louder as it nears, I will not leave you, I will not leave you, I will not, a man’s voice from sixty years ago, and the hair stands up on the Wardens’ arms, because every time it passes them they must not hear it. Then it enters the mouth of the trap and the clay begins to hum, a low warm buzzing like a jar full of bees, and the felt jacket shivers, and the word goes round and round inside, smaller and smaller, in a voice that grows tinny and frantic, like someone shouting from the bottom of a well, until at the centre it stops with a sound like a thumb pressed into butter. The Wardens say a full trap is warm for a day afterwards. They carry it like a sleeping child.

I will not leave you. Sixty years it went up and down that gorge. We trapped it on a Tuesday. I hope whoever he was meant it. I hope she knew.
Echo-Warden Tracker’s report, Low Dray, 638

Rules

Trapping an echo. Tracking a living echo to its turning-point is Eye + Search at Hard 14 (Grim 18 for an echo older than a century). Setting the trap is Hand + Craft at Hard 14. Each round the work takes in hearing of the echo, every character without ear-stops must make a Caul + Resolve roll at Hard 14 or hear the words and be bound by them, at the oath’s Weight (see Oaths in Oathen). Wax and lead plugs give +4 to this roll.

The kept word. A full trap holds one oath. Anyone who puts their ear to an unlidded full trap is bound by it as if they had sworn it, at Weight −1 (minimum 1), and makes a Dread check of that Weight. Breaking the trap on an anvil destroys the word; grinding the wax ensures it.

Loaded horns. Unstopping a loaded horn in a narrow place releases its word as a living echo for 1d6 hours. Everyone who walks through must resist as above. Using one against a pursuer is a Hand + Craft roll at Hard 14 to place it where they will pass.

Building a trap is a Long Task: Hand + Craft at Grim 18, two days a roll, three successes, 25 lacks. Sabotage difficulty Hard 14: a hairline crack in the spiral.

Failure Table (d6)

d6The trap fails
1A crack in the spiral. The word goes in and comes out again, faster, angrier, and now it knows what a trap sounds like.
2The lid slips in the carrying. The word escapes at the bearer’s ear, at full voice, as though they had said it. Bound at full Weight.
3The trap catches the wrong word: one of the Wardens’, spoken under the breath at the wrong moment. Now it keeps that.
4The wax was soft from the sun. The word is pressed in, but blurred: anyone who hears it is bound to something like it, and the GM decides what.
5The trap takes two echoes at once, and they are pressed together in the nest. The oath that comes out of that wax, if anyone opens it, is a new one that neither speaker made.
6The word is too old and too large for the nest. The trap fills and bursts on its mounting, and the canyon rings with it from end to end. Every Warden present is bound.

Cost and Availability

Echo-traps are Scarce and Warden property; a Warden-made trap sold out of the Wardens’ house costs 40 lacks and a bribe. A smuggler’s jar-trap is 8 lacks, Uncommon in the Breakdowns, and holds a word one time in three. A loaded horn with a known oath in it is Rare, and its price depends on whose oath it is: from 50 lacks for a stranger’s idle promise to more than a platter a word for a notary’s vow.

Hook

The Horn on the Market. A loaded horn has turned up for sale in the Gristmoot black market, and the seller says it holds an oath of Jessamy Quill’s, caught in the Gullet in her youth. If it is real, and is uncorked in a narrow place, the Company’s notary will be bound by something she said at nineteen. The Company wants it bought. Grandam Cess wants it stolen. Jessamy Quill wants to hear it first, privately, with no one else in the room, which is the one thing no one will let her do.

The Weighing Scales of Sated

Heavy hand, heavy vote. Light hand, light supper.
— Sated proverb, said of Garrick Tripe’s rings

Lore and History

The Great Scales were cast in 261 A.G., a year after the Weighing became law, by the bell-founders of the Chute, from the bronze of every church bell in Sated that had rung for the Gorging. They stand at the centre of the Weighhouse under the dome of glazed bone tiles: an iron beam forty feet long on a knife-edge fulcrum of black steel, with two bronze pans, each large enough to hold a loaded cart. On one pan sits the member. On the other, the city’s standard weights, cast in lead and stamped with the Board’s sheaf, are added by Weighmen with block and tackle until the beam hangs level. The result is cried aloud and chalked on the great slate, and becomes that member’s vote for a year.

Every Weighing since 261 has been rigged. The Board knows it. The crowds know it. The proverb says that the Scales have never once told the truth and never once been wrong, because the Board has always been exactly as heavy as it needed to be. The present Weigher, Garrick Tripe, inherited the office from an uncle and the methods from a long line of Weighers before him, and has elected three governments.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunctionHow it is rigged
The Beamiron, forty feetbalances member against weightsa hollow at the member’s end, filled with shot
The Knifeblack steel fulcrumthe pivotshaved off-true by a hair; favours one side
Member’s Panbronze, cart-sizedwhere the member sitswetted with dripping; a pan “sweats” pounds
Weight Panbronzeholds the standard weightsthe weights are short; see below
Standard Weightslead, stamped with the sheafmeasure the memberhollow-cored “light lead” kept in a second set
The Lever Belowiron rod through the floornone, officiallya boy in the cellar presses up on the member’s pan
The Slateslate, chalkrecords the resultthe chalk-boy is paid too

The Scales are honest in their bones and crooked in every joint. Garrick Tripe’s methods, as recorded in a confession he has written and hidden against the day the Chairman turns on him, are these. The pockets: the member’s Weighing-day coat is sewn with lead, at 200 lacks a vote. The sweat: the member’s pan is wiped down with hot dripping before the Weighing “for the member’s comfort,” and a thick enough coat adds the weight of a child. The light lead: the standard weights have a twin set, identical, stamped, cored hollow and packed with sawdust, which can be swapped in by the Weighmen at the tackle. The knife: the fulcrum was re-ground in 588 a hair off-true, so that the beam favours whichever end the Weigher chooses to hang the member from. The lever: an iron rod rises from the root-choked cellars beneath the Weighhouse floor to the underside of the member’s pan, where a boy lying on his back in the dark pushes up, or pulls down, on a signal from Tripe’s left boot.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

The Board owns the Scales and Garrick Tripe keeps them, with nine Weighmen, a chalk-boy, and the cellar boy. The cellar boy is always an orphan, because it is cold and wet down there and the roots move. The present one is Nib, aged twelve; his predecessor went down one Weighing in 637 and did not come back up, and the roots around the base of the lever are thicker than they were. Chairman Obb Tullow’s vote, at nineteen hundred pounds, is the only one on the slate that has never been rigged. The Chairman insists on this. He has sent word to Tripe, three years running, that if a Weighing ever goes against him, Tripe will be sitting on the member’s pan at the next one, and Nib will be told to pull.

In Operation

The Weighing is three days of noise and gravy. The Weighhouse is packed to the dome. The members are brought in on drays and lifted onto the pan by tackle and twenty men, while the crowd chants the weights. The beam groans like a ship’s mast. The bronze pan, wiped with dripping, glistens and smells of roast. Garrick Tripe, in his brass-buttoned coat and his twelve rings, walks the length of the beam with his hand on it, feeling her settle, he says, and taps his left boot, and far below in the dark a boy lying among warm roots, breathing loam, puts his hands on an iron rod and pushes until his shoulders crack. The beam dips. The crowd roars. The chalk squeaks. Somewhere, a deacon of Low Tilth has lost his vote to a woman who weighs less than her coat.

She weighed nine hundred and four. Her coat weighed three hundred. The Board weighed her twice to be sure, and both times she came out heavier. That’s the Scales. They know what you’re worth.
tavern talk at the Pie Gate, Weighing Week

Rules

Rigging the Weighing. Each method adds weight, and votes, at a price and a risk. Pockets add up to a fifth of the member’s own weight; the sweat adds 1d6 × 10 pounds; light lead adds a tenth; the knife a twentieth; the lever, up to a hundred pounds either way. Arranging each requires Tripe or his people, a fee (see below), and for the PCs to do it themselves, Hand + Filch or Hand + Craft at Hard 14 (pockets, sweat), Grim 18 (light lead, the knife) or Dire 22 (the lever, without Nib’s cooperation).

Detecting the rig. An observer may roll Eye + Reckoning at Grim 18 to notice that the result is wrong; a Helping identifies one method. Proving it before the Board is another matter: Tongue + Clause at Dire 22, and the Board will weigh the accuser.

Under the floor. The cellars are dark, warm, and full of roots that flinch when touched. A character who goes down to the lever must make a Dread 2 check and, each hour below, a Lung + Athletics roll at Hard 14 or be held by the roots (Entangling, Gut + Athletics at Grim 18 to break free). After a full Weighing down there, roll a d6: on a 1 the character has begun to root.

Failure Table (d6)

d6The rig fails
1A pocket tears on the pan. Lead shot pours across the bronze and rolls, clattering, into the crowd. The member is stripped in public, then fed, then weighed again.
2Light lead and true lead are mixed up at the tackle. Every member weighed that hour gains or loses a tenth. Three Board seats change hands. Nobody can say why.
3The cellar boy pushes when he should have pulled. The beam slams, and the member on the pan is thrown. Bailiffs drag Tripe’s boot-signals out of him by evening.
4The knife-edge, re-ground once too often, cracks. The beam drops a foot and stops, perfectly level, by itself, with nobody on it. Dread 1 for the hall.
5The roots take the lever. It pushes on its own, from now on, at every Weighing, for whoever the Dowager Hills prefer.
6The Chairman is weighed and the beam does not move. Nineteen hundred pounds of man on one pan, and the city’s full set of weights on the other, and the beam level. Then it dips toward the Chairman, slowly, as if pulled from below. He has rooted through the pan.

Cost and Availability

ServiceCostAvailabilityNotes
Lead pockets200 LRareTripe; a vote’s worth
The sweat40 LScarcepaid to the pan-wipers
Light lead for a member150 LRarethe Weighmen want a cut
The lever500 LRareTripe’s left boot; and a meal for Nib
A Weighing-day coat30 LUncommonempty; legal

Hook

Nib. The cellar boy has stopped coming up between Weighings. He sends his wages up the lever on a string. Tripe wants him brought out before the Grace Weighing, because a boy who will not come up will not take signals. The PCs go down among the roots and find Nib quite happy, warm and well fed, and sitting on the knee of something in the dark that he calls the old Weigher, which has been teaching him to feel what each member weighs before they are ever lifted onto the pan.

Lark Ninedays' Pang-Clock

Thirtydays. Twentydays. Fourteendays. Elevendays. Ninedays. I keep the names in a drawer, like gloves I have outgrown.
— Lark Ninedays, to the Tally clerks

Lore and History

Cradlewrack has always timed its pangs, at first with sun-marks and the memory of old women, later with water. The state’s first pang-clock was a cistern on the Tally-house roof in Kest, built in 420 when the interval was a full season, with a float that fell a finger a day and a bell struck by hand. Lark’s mother, Ide Thirtydays, inherited the post when the interval was thirty days, and named her daughter for it; when Ide died in 609 she was mortared into the clock’s base, a brick at a time, as she had asked, so that she would always be where the count was kept.

Lark rebuilt the clock in 612, around her mother’s brick. Her improvement was to let the pang itself strike the bell. The earth’s contraction, felt everywhere in the country, sloshes water; Lark mounted a small brass surge-cup on the clock’s rim, balanced so finely that the slosh of a pang tips it, and the tipping trips the bell. The bell no longer needs a hand. It rings at the instant of the pang, and the float tells her how long it has been since the last. Every time the interval shortens, she grinds the old graduations off the brass ribbon and marks new ones, and changes her name.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunction
The Vesselcopper, tall as a womanholds the water that falls
The Floatcork in a brass cupfalls as the vessel drains, marking time
The Ribbonbrass strip, hand-graduated in daysthe scale the float points to
The Surge-Cupbrass, balanced on a needletips at the pang’s slosh and trips the bell
The Bellbronze, a yard acrossthe loudest thing in Kest
The Mother’s Brickfired red clay, mortaredthe base; Ide Thirtydays inside
The Interval Wheelwood, notcheda notch for every pang since 612

Water drips at a steady rate from the vessel through a narrow brass nipple into a basin. As it drains, the float sinks, and a pointer on it slides down the graduated ribbon. When the pang comes, the surge-cup tips, the bell rings, and Lark reads the ribbon: so many days, so many hours. She notches the wheel. Then she refills the vessel to its mark, resets the cup, and waits. When the pangs begin to fall consistently short of the lowest mark on the ribbon, she grinds it smooth and re-marks it, shorter.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

Lark alone keeps the state clock, and sleeps beside it. Copies of her design are kept in every Attendance hall, every Foundling barracks (General Tibb times his drills to her bell), and the households of anyone who can afford one. Small household pang-clocks are sold in every market in the highlands. They are all, without exception, less accurate than Lark’s, because they were not built on a mother.

In Operation

The roof room is bare and cold, and the clock ticks with its drip, a small wet sound like a tap in an empty house. Lark keeps a hand on the vessel when she sleeps. Before a pang the water warms, and Lark wakes. It begins to smell faintly of iron. The surface trembles in fine rings, then in coarser ones; the copper creaks; the brick under it is warm as a cheek. And at the pang the whole vessel bulges, visibly, the copper swelling outward between its bands like a belly, and the water inside goes pink for a breath, and the surge-cup tips with a click, and the bell goes off like a slap across the whole of Kest. Then the copper eases, the water clears, and the drip goes on. Lark notches the wheel with a knife, and if the notch is shorter than the last, she says nothing for an hour, and then begins to grind the ribbon.

The brick gets warm before the water does. I don’t write that down. I just put my hand on it, the way you’d put your hand on your mother’s arm in the night to see if she’s still breathing.
Lark Ninedays

Rules

Reading the clock. Anyone may read the ribbon (no roll). Predicting the next pang to the hour is Eye + Reckoning at Hard 14 with Lark’s clock or a good copy, Grim 18 with a household clock, Dire 22 without one. Each Helping narrows it further; a Grace gives the minute. Knowing the pang is coming lets a character prepare: re-stitch old wounds in advance (see Doors and the Body Is a Door), brick in, or be somewhere a crowning is not.

Lark’s arithmetic. With access to the Interval Wheel and the old ribbons, Eye + Reckoning at Grim 18 over a day gives the date on which the interval will reach one day. It is in the sealed letter Orla Kest has read once. A character who works it out makes a Dread 3 check.

The brick. Laying a hand on the Mother’s Brick before a pang gives +2 to the roll above. Doing so during a pang is a Dread 2 check, because something inside it pushes back.

Building a household pang-clock is a Long Task: Hand + Craft at Hard 14, a day a roll, three successes, 40 lacks. Sabotage difficulty: Routine 10 (it is a pot of water).

Failure Table (d6)

d6The clock fails
1The drip blocks with silt. The float stops. The clock reads the same hour for a day, and anyone relying on it is caught by the pang.
2The surge-cup tips at a cart passing. The bell rings false. Half of Kest bricks itself in for a pang that does not come, and the real one finds them in the street.
3The water goes pink and stays pink.
4The bell does not ring. The surge-cup has tipped, but the clapper is held, gently, as though by a small hand.
5The vessel bulges and does not ease. In a week it bursts, and what is found in the basin is the length of a forearm and warm.
6Two pangs. The cup tips once for the earth and once, a little after, for something underneath it, and the gap between them is shorter than the interval. Lark has heard this twice now. She has not ground it into the ribbon. Dread 3.

Cost and Availability

Household pang-clocks are Common in Cradlewrack at 40 lacks (see the water clock in the Rim Market chapter), Uncommon elsewhere. A pang-bell that rings itself a breath early is 6 lacks. Lark’s clock is Unique, and it is not for sale, though the Second Table has asked.

Hook

Lark Sixdays. The interval has shortened again and Lark has not changed her name. She has stopped grinding the ribbon. She has been seen at night with her ear to the brick, talking. The Attendance needs to know the true interval, and sends the PCs to read the clock while she sleeps. The ribbon has been marked, in a careful new hand, with a single graduation near the bottom. Beside it, scratched into the brass, is a name she has never used, and it has no number in it.

Lung-line Breather Tanks

The prince will receive you now. Kneel at the glass. Speak slowly. He reads lips. Do not tap.
— usher’s instructions, Hall of Tanks, Fathomhouse

Lore and History

By 388 the Lung-lines of the House of Vasht could no longer breathe air for long, and the first prince held court from a glass tank. But a prince must travel, inspect the fleet, appear at the Lowering, review the Netwatch, and visit his estates, and the great tanks of Fathomhouse weigh as much as a ship. The Admiralty’s glass-wrights built the first breather tank for Prince Corin Vasht in 412: a walking tank, an upright glass coffin full of brine on a wheeled carriage, drawn by eight bearers. He rode in it to the Lowering and back, and lost two bearers on the Mile when the carriage slipped, and was very pleased.

The modern breather is smaller and grimmer. There are three kinds. The carriage-tank is a great glass case on wheels for the highest of the House. The water-helm is a sealed globe of glass and brass over the head, fed with brine from a back-pack bladder by a hand pump worked by a servant who walks behind; it lets a Lung-line at the Course walk and work in air for half a day. And the lung-bag is a simple oiled-leather bag of brine strapped over the mouth and nose, bought by commoners at the Course, which holds an hour.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunction
Water-helm globethick glass, brass collarholds brine around the head
Neck-sealoiled leather, tallow, brass clampkeeps the brine in at the throat
Back-bladdertarred sealskin, two gallonsthe reserve of brine
Feed-pumpbrass hand-pump, gut hosepushes fresh brine into the helm
Bleed-cockbrass tap at the helm’s baselets foul brine out, onto the road
Tank-tendera personworks the pump, every minute, for life

A Lung-line at the Course breathes water and suffocates in air; the water must be salt and cold and moving, or it fouls with the breather’s own sloughed skin and the body’s exhalations, which are cloudy. The water-helm keeps it moving. The tank-tender walks a pace behind, one hand on the brass pump, pressing it slowly, a stroke for every breath the wearer takes, pushing clean brine from the bladder into the helm while the bleed-cock lets the foul water dribble out at the collar and down the wearer’s chest. The bladder is refilled at any salt basin or from the bailing of the household. Carriage-tanks are the same, larger, with four tenders and a cistern-cart behind.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

The Admiralty’s glass-wrights at Fathomhouse make helms and carriage-tanks for the House of Vasht and its cadet branches. Commoners’ lung-bags are sewn on Mile Six. Tank-tenders are a hereditary servant caste, chosen young, trained in the stroke until it is as steady as a heartbeat, and they wear rubber aprons and never go below the fourth stair. A good tender’s family serves one prince for generations. A tender who falters for a minute kills their master; the punishment is to be weighted and lowered into the master’s tank, to breathe what he breathes. None have managed it.

In Operation

A Lung-line in a water-helm is a thing out of a nightmare walking in daylight: a grey face in a globe of greenish water, hair drifting like weed, eyes huge and black and unblinking, and the mouth opening and closing slowly, like a fish. Bubbles do not rise; the wearer does not breathe out air. Lips read through glass, words written on a slate. The collar leaks a steady drip of cloudy brine that smells of the bottom of a rock pool, and leaves a white crust of salt on the wearer’s coat from collar to hem. The pump wheezes, stroke by stroke, behind. When the brine fouls, it fouls fast: the water clouds from the bottom up, the face inside darkens and swells, the eyes bulge against the glass, the hands go to the collar and scrabble, and the tender pumps faster, and faster, and if the bladder is dry, the wearer drowns in air in front of everyone, slowly, standing up, looking out through clouding water at the people who are failing to save them.

Thirty years I’ve pumped for His Grace. I hear the stroke in my sleep. If I stop in my sleep, I wake, every time, gasping, because I think it’s me drowning.
a tank-tender of the cadet House of Vasht-Ennor

Rules

Wearing a breather. A character at the Course with Fathom-Body suffers −1 to all rolls for each hour spent in open air beyond the first, cumulative, until they are immersed (this replaces the core rule while the character is in Brinehollow’s dry air and not wearing a breather). A water-helm with a tender removes the penalty for half a day before the bladder must be refilled. A lung-bag removes it for one hour. While helmed, the wearer cannot speak aloud, is at −2 to Search by sound, and gains +1 Armor to the head.

Tending. A tender must make a Gut + Endure roll at Routine 10 each hour. A failure lets the brine foul: the wearer loses 1 Flesh per round until the tender succeeds or the bladder is changed. Combat, running and fright make the roll Hard 14.

Foreigners. A non-Brinehollower who puts on a water-helm drowns, as anyone would. A Brinehollower at the Taste or Appetite who wears one for an hour makes a Caul + Resolve roll at Hard 14; on a failure, they find it comfortable, and gain 1 Regrowth on a Lack.

Failure Table (d6)

d6The tank fails
1The neck-seal fails. Brine floods down the wearer’s chest and the globe empties in a minute. The tender must re-seal it with tallow (Hard 14 Hand + Craft) before the wearer drowns in air.
2The pump jams. The tender must pump by mouth through the hose. The brine tastes of the wearer.
3The globe cracks. It holds for an hour. Then it does not.
4The bladder was filled from a basin someone was Called from last night. The wearer is calm, and courteous, and faces west, and asks the tender to stop pumping.
5The foul brine is not foul. It is thickening, and darkening, and moving of its own accord around the wearer’s face, and the wearer is breathing it with every sign of pleasure.
6The tender falters, from exhaustion or malice, and the wearer drowns in front of the court. Dread 2 for all present. The House will want the tender weighted.

Cost and Availability

ItemCostAvailabilityNotes
Lung-bag6 LCommon in Brinehollowholds an hour; leaks
Water-helm with bladder and pump220 LRareAdmiralty glass; noble only by law
Carriage-tank3 plattersUnique to ordereight bearers and four tenders not included
A tender’s service5 L a dayUncommona hereditary tender cannot be hired; they can be stolen

Hook

The Prince Wants a Walk. Prince Aurel Vasht, who has not surfaced in nine days, asks the PCs secretly to take him out of Fathomhouse in a water-helm to see the sea, the real sea, at the Trench edge, once, before he can no longer bear the air at all. His tender, an old woman named Sorrel Cask whose family have pumped for Vashts for nine generations, will come, and will pump. On the road west Aurel stops writing on his slate. In the globe his lips are shaping words in a rhythm the PCs have heard once before, knocked from the bottom of the Headland tower.

The Pantry's Ration Scales

Four months of grain. Six of winter. I can do it to the day. I cannot do it to the name.
— Mother Stint Avery

Lore and History

The Measure is older than Wanting. It is a brass balance with a beam the length of a forearm and two shallow pans, and it was brought out of Hallowboard in the spring of 1 A.G. by the survivors of the Refusal, wrapped in a blanket, carried by a girl of eleven named Meagre Avery who would not let anyone else hold it. Nobody knows what it weighed before. The Unfed say it weighed out the Host’s bread for the great table, and that it is the one thing from Orrum’s house that they kept. The Abstinent say this is a lie and punish anyone who repeats it. It hangs now from an iron hook in the cool dark of the Pantry’s ground floor, and every ration in the Fast has been weighed on it since 41 A.G.

The public weights are a set of nine lead discs, stamped by the Abstinent with a hand held up, palm out: the Decline. Every Unfed child is shown them once, so they know the measure is true. They are true. Mother Stint Avery, Avery’s descendant and Keeper of the Pantry, uses them every morning in front of the Ration Line.

She also has a second set.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunction
The Beambrass, worn bright at the centrebalances grain against weight
Two Pansbrass, shallow, dentedone for grain, one for weight
The Hookiron, set in the ceiling beamhangs the Measure; eight notches cut in it
Public Weights (nine)lead, stamped with the Declinethe true measure, shown to the Line
Stint’s Weights (fourteen)lead, unstamped, in a felt-lined boxthe short measure; one for each list-village
The Ledgerbound paper, back to 41 A.G.every ration, by name, by day, by weight

Stint Avery’s private weights are fourteen lead discs, each a little lighter than the true half-ration, each scratched with the name of a village and kept in a felt-lined box under her apron. When a list-village’s carter comes to the iron door, she weighs out their measure with that village’s weight. The furthest are lightest. The oldest are lighter. The ones with fewest children are lightest of all. The difference between the true weight and each private weight is a matter of grains: a pinch, a spoonful, a crust. Across a winter, across fourteen villages, it is the difference between four months of grain and six. She shaves the weights herself, with a file, by lamplight, after the Line has gone, and weighs the filings, and writes them in a column in the back of the Ledger that nobody else reads.

The lightest weight is marked Avery Steading.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

Only the Keeper of the Pantry uses the Measure, and only Stint Avery has the second box. Forbear Wend knows there is a list but not that there are weights; he believes the list is of names to be omitted entirely, and he prays over it, and Stint Avery has not corrected him, because a short measure keeps more people alive than an omission and she cannot bear his prayers. Two Pantry clerks suspect. One Crumb-Runner, Tarry Moss, who counts his cargo to the bean, knows exactly how much grain goes in and how much is handed out, and has done the subtraction.

In Operation

The Pantry’s ground floor is cool, dim, and smells of dust, sacking, and mouse, which to an Unfed nose is the richest smell in the world. Grain whispers from the scoop into the pan. The beam dips, rises, hangs level, trembling. Stint Avery watches it with her whole face. The Line watches her. Nobody speaks; the only sound is the grain and the small creak of the hook. When a list-village’s carter comes in at the end of the day, alone, she takes the felt box out of her apron and chooses the weight by touch, without looking, the way you choose a coin in your pocket, and the grain falls, and the beam hangs level, and it is a lie, and it is the only kindness the arithmetic will allow. The carter cannot tell. Over the winter the people of that village will grow a little thinner, and a little colder, and the old will die a week or two sooner than they would have, and nobody will be omitted, and nobody will walk to the Lean House, and the Seated on the valley road will wave.

The hook has eight notches in it. Seven are worn smooth. The eighth is sharp, as if nothing has ever hung there.

It is not cruelty to weigh short. It is arithmetic. Cruelty would be weighing true until the grain ran out, and then nothing.
from the back of the Pantry Ledger, in Stint Avery’s hand

Rules

Detecting the short measure. A character watching the weighing may roll Eye + Reckoning at Grim 18 to notice that the list-village weights are unstamped; weighing a private weight against a public one on any honest scale reveals it at once. Working out the scheme from the Ledger’s back column is Eye + Reckoning at Hard 14 and takes an evening.

Living on the short measure. A Pantry measure is half a ration. The short measure is less: a character on it gains +1 Pang every three days instead of holding steady (see Pangs: Starvation). Over a six-month winter, an Unfed village on the short measure loses its oldest, about one in ten. On a true measure until the grain ran out, it would lose half.

Exposure. Revealing the private weights to the Ration Line is a Tongue + Persuade roll at Hard 14 to be believed. The Line will riot (see Madness in the Community); the Pantry’s grain will be distributed true for six weeks and then run out, and the Lean House will fill. A PC who causes this and then sees the Lean House makes a Dread 3 check.

Failure Table (d6)

d6The measure fails
1A clerk swaps a private weight for a public one by mistake. One village gets its true half-ration for a month, and another goes on the list to pay for it. Stint chooses which.
2The felt box is dropped in front of the Line. The weights roll out across the flagstones, each with its village’s name scratched in.
3A weight is shaved too far. A hamlet’s oldest begin to walk west.
4Stint’s hands, at last, refuse. She stands holding the Avery Steading weight over the pan and cannot put it down. Someone must decide for her.
5The beam hangs level before the grain is poured. Something is already in the pan, unseen, weighing exactly a ration. The grain poured on top of it comes out warm.
6One morning there is a fifteenth weight in the box. It is not shaved. It is heavier than a ration by a great deal, smooth and warm as bread, and it is marked, in brown ink the colour of gravy, Wanting.

Cost and Availability

The Measure and Stint’s weights are Unique. Common ration scales are 12 lacks anywhere on the Rim; Fast-made ones, with the Decline stamped on the beam, are 4 lacks in Wanting and are honest, which no buyer abroad believes.

Hook

The Back Column. Tarry Moss has done the subtraction and asks the PCs to check it, because he cannot believe it and cannot say it aloud. The PCs find the weights, the column, and the name Avery Steading. Then they must decide whether to tell Avery Steading. When they get there, the villagers are thin and cheerful and grateful for the Pantry’s fairness, and have laid a little extra on Stint Avery’s mother’s grave as thanks: a crust, saved from their own short measure.

The Follow

She is not a ship. A ship comes back. She is a question with rivets in it.
— Dagna Hull, shouting, as she does

Lore and History

The Follow is Dagna Hull’s answer to the sea leaving: an iron vessel built to chase the water down into the Trench and come back to say where it is going. She began it in 636 after a pressure day burst every port-glass on Mile Nineteen and the water was lower at noon than at breakfast. The Admiralty funded it through Commodore Lysander Vell, who calls it a sounding vessel for the fleet’s return. Nine hundred people have chalked their names on the wall of her shed as volunteers. Someone loosens a dozen of its rivets every week, and the marks on them are the marks of Dagna’s own hammer, struck backward. It has been nearly finished for a year.

The Deck Plan in Words

The Follow is a riveted iron egg forty feet long and fourteen feet across at the widest, lying on its side in a timber cradle in a slip at the end of the Mile. Its skin is plate iron three fingers thick, overlapped and riveted in courses like the scales of a fish, with eight round glass ports a hand thick set in brass collars. Beneath, a weighted keel of cast lead. Above, a tarred sailcloth air-bladder the size of a barn, deflated and folded in a net cage, which is filled from bellows at the surface to float the vessel and let out by a valve, from inside, to sink it; to rise, ballast is dropped and the bladder refilled from a bank of pressed-air bottles. It has one deck and three compartments, entered by a single hatch at the top, sealed with a wheel-lock and a gasket of tallowed leather.

The forward chamber, called the Eye, is the observation room: a curved bench facing four of the eight ports, a sounding-well (a sealed tube through the floor through which a lead line can be let out and drawn back without letting the sea in), the depth-glass (a mercury column in a brass case, graduated in fathoms by Dagna’s hand down to a mark she has labelled Here I stop writing), and a lamp-box of whale-oil lanterns burning behind glass. It smells of oil and cold iron.

The midships chamber, the Works, is the heart: the valve-wheel for the bladder, the ballast-releases (six iron levers, each dropping a pig of lead), the air-bottles in a rack, the bellows for the cabin air, a sand-glass, a log-slate, a hand-pump for bilge, and Dagna’s hammer on a hook. Two bunks fold from the walls. A bail-trough runs along the floor for the crew’s tides.

The aft chamber, the Stores, holds water, biscuit, salt fish, rope, a spare gasket, a medicine chest, and a bulkhead behind which, according to Dagna’s drawings, there is nothing but the lead of the keel. Commodore Vell’s annotations, in a neat red hand on her plans, say otherwise.

The secret hold lies behind that bulkhead, between the Stores and the stern plating: a narrow iron room eight feet deep, reached by a panel that unbolts from inside the Stores. Dagna did not draw it. Vell’s own riveters built it in a week while she was ill in the Lack of 640. It is lined with lead. It holds four barrels of salt, a rack of flensing knives of grey bone each marked with a course-name, a set of butcher’s saws, a folding table, a lead box that weeps cold water, and a rail of iron meat-hooks bolted to the ceiling. There are eight hooks. Seven are tagged in red ink: Fish, and six names of other courses. The eighth tag is blank. The hold is for carving.

The Crew Roster

PostWhoWhat they want
Master and pilotDagna Hullto see where the water goes, and come back to say
Mate and riveterHollis Brineto go down and never come back; and to stop her going
Sounding-manHask Tarn, if he willto call the depth; he has said maybe
Admiralty observerCommodore Lysander Vellto carve a god at the bottom of the Trench
Vell’s men (three)Second Table Scullionswages; they do not know what the hooks are for
Volunteers’ placeone name from the wallchosen by lot; nine hundred hope; four want to know

The Follow carries six. Dagna intends the sixth place to be drawn by lot from the wall. Vell intends it for one of his own. The PCs may fill any place: Dagna will take divers, a pilot, or a strong back; Vell will take anyone who does not ask about the Stores.

The Launch Checklist

Pinned inside the hatch of the Follow, in Dagna Hull’s hand, chalk on slate. To be read aloud, shouted, and answered, before every descent.

1. Rivets. Count the lowest seam. Count it again. Count it with me watching.

2. Gasket. Tallow it. Press it. Look at it in the lamp. No dry patch.

3. Ports. Eight. Wipe each. Knock each with the knuckle. It should ring, not thud.

4. Bladder. Full. Cage net tight. Valve shut, lashed, my knot.

5. Ballast. Six pigs. Six levers. Each lever tried and returned.

6. Air bottles. Twelve. Each hisses. Each shut.

7. Lamp-box. Lit. Spare oil. Spare wick. Spare flint.

8. Line. Forty fathoms, marked. Second line, four hundred. Third line I do not talk about.

9. Bail-trough. Clear. Everybody bails before the hatch shuts. Everybody.

10. Ropes. Each of us roped to the ring by the Works. My knots. Hollis checks mine. I check his.

11. Names. Say your name. Say where you are going. Say: and back.

12. Hatch. Wheel it shut. Lock it. Tap it twice for luck.

13. Last: Nobody touches the valve but me. If I am not able, nobody touches it at all.

(scratched under, smaller, in another hand) 14. Stores bulkhead: do not knock on it.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

Dagna Hull and forty riveters from the slum Miles built the Follow; Vell’s men built the hold. Hollis Brine, Dagna’s apprentice and the first name on the wall, loosens the rivets at night with her own hammer, taken from beside her sleeping hand, weeping, because he knows from Nerys Colm’s invitation that there is no coming back from the deep places, and he wants to go more than anything, and he will not let Dagna go there. Mother Limpet wants to bless it. Four hundred of the nine hundred are Deepening.

In Operation

Inside, the Follow is a cold iron throat lit by whale-oil. Every sound rings. The crew sit roped to the ring, knees touching, breath fogging. When the valve opens there is a long roar as the bladder empties overhead, and the egg tilts, and lurches, and drops, and the ports go green, then grey-green, then black. The iron begins to talk: ticks, groans, a long low moan from the lowest seam as the pressure takes it. The air thickens. Ears pop, then bleed. The Brinehollowers’ chests fill, all together, out of turn, and they bail into the trough with the iron ringing around them. At the ports, things come up to the glass out of the black and look in: pale, ribbed, too many eyes or none, and at depth, faces, the calm courteous faces of the Called, drifting upward past the ports in their nightshirts, looking in at the lamp with polite interest, and one of them always knocks. On a pressure night in the slip, the iron hums a single note, and the nine hundred come to the shed in silence, and stand.

I wrote her the question: what is at the bottom? She wrote me back one word. I’ve had it framed. I look at it before I go in to work.
Dagna Hull, of Nerys Colm’s letter, which says Don’t

Rules

The vessel. The Follow has 60 points of Hull (treat as Flesh for the vessel) and Armor 6 against blows. Each hundred fathoms of descent past the first, the pilot rolls Eye + Reckoning at a difficulty that starts at Routine 10 and rises one step every hundred fathoms. A failure costs 1d6 Hull as seams strain. At 0 Hull the vessel floods. Each loosened rivet on the lowest seam (Hollis’s work, a dozen a week) costs 1 Hull before launch unless found (Eye + Search, Hard 14, per inspection).

Aboard. Every hundred fathoms, all aboard make a Gut + Endure roll at Hard 14 or lose 1 Flesh to the pressure. Brinehollowers make a Calling roll at every three hundred fathoms, even awake, and their companions may hold them only by the ropes. Seeing the Called at the ports is Dread 2; the knocking is Dread 3. The depth-glass passes Here I stop writing at nine hundred fathoms. Below that, the GM decides what the line finds.

Rising. Dropping ballast is automatic; refilling the bladder from the bottles needs Hand + Craft at Hard 14 at depth. The valve may be closed by hand from inside, by anyone, at any time, and once closed against the bottles, the Follow cannot rise.

The hold. Finding the panel is Eye + Search at Grim 18. What is inside is Dread 2, and Dread 3 for anyone who understands the hooks. The lead box contains a piece of Dromm’s flesh from the Beaching (Taint 3 Regrowth, Brinehollow), which still weeps.

Failure Table (d6)

d6The Follow fails
1The gasket weeps. A thin jet of black water as hard as a nail across the Works. Hand + Craft at Grim 18 to stop it; each round it runs, 1 Flesh to whoever is in its path and 1 Hull.
2A port crazes. White lines run across the glass like frost. It will hold for 1d6 × 10 fathoms more.
3The lamp-box goes out. In the dark, the crew hear the iron, the sea, and the slow, polite knocking, moving round the hull from port to port.
4A ballast lever will not drop. Someone tied it, with a knot from the Mile.
5The valve is closed by hand from inside. Nobody admits it. The bottles cannot refill the bladder. The Follow goes on down.
6The stores bulkhead is knocked on, from the inside of the hold, where nobody is. Then the eighth hook rings, like a bell, by itself.

Cost and Availability

The Follow is Unique. A place aboard is not for sale: Dagna gives one to the PCs, or Vell does, or the lot does. A berth on the wall costs a chalk and a name, and the Mile bets on the draw at 900 to 1.

Hook

Low Water, 642. If nobody intervenes, the Follow makes its trial descent at the Low Water of Carving 642, the very night Finn Undertow’s count closes, with Dagna, Hollis and four of Vell’s men aboard, and the air-bladder rises to the surface without them, its valve shut by hand from inside. The PCs can be aboard, or on the surface at the bellows, or in the hold, or on the Headland with Finn, or at the slip at midnight, when Hollis Brine comes with the hammer one last time and finds them waiting.

Tablebreaker Axes

Lamp, plates, legs, top, chairs. Chairs last. Every chair. Every one.
— Decline Marsh, teaching a new Axe

Lore and History

The first table was broken with a spade, in 46 A.G., by a boy named Forgo Hallam, two years after his neighbours were found seated in their kitchen; he broke a different table, in a ruin, before anyone could sit, and walked home, and was sick, and was praised. For a century Unfed broke tables with whatever was to hand. Then, in 151, a smith of Wanting named Abjure Coll forged the first true Tablebreaker’s axe, and wrote down the rite for making it, and every Axe since has carried one made to her rite or has carried nothing.

The Diagram in Words

PartMaterialFunction
The Headgrey iron, quenched in snow-watera broad bit for splitting, a hammer-poll for legs
The Haftash from a Rim tree, never a Fast treethe length of the bearer’s arm and a hand
The Notchesknife-cuts down the haftone for every table broken
The Wraplinen, unbleached, bound at the gripnever oiled, never with fat
The Gauze-Ringiron ring at the buttties the Rope-Holder’s tether to the Axe’s belt

A Tablebreaker’s axe is a felling axe with a longer haft and a broad grey head, unpolished, its poll flattened to a hammer for knocking out legs. Nothing about it is beautiful. It is heavy at the head and thin in the throat, so that it bites deep and hates to come out, because the wood of Orrum’s tables is like no other wood: it closes on the blade, gently, the way a hand closes on a hand.

The forging rites, as Abjure Coll wrote them. The iron must come from the Rim, bought, never accepted. It is worked at an outdoor forge on bare ground, because a hearth is offered. It is quenched in snow-water or rain, never in a well, because a drawn bucket is offered. The haft is ash from a Rim tree, cut by the bearer, because Fast wood grows in Orrum’s soil. No fat, oil or tallow touches it, ever; it is waxed, if at all, with beeswax from Cradlewrack. When it is finished it is carried, by the new Axe, to the Barrows below Hallowboard, and laid on the warm grass of the mounds overnight, alone, while the new Axe stands with their back to it until dawn. In the morning the axe is cold. If it is warm, it is not blessed, and must be broken and forged again.

Notch-lore. Every table broken earns a notch, cut with the bearer’s own knife on the evening after, in silence. Notches are cut in rows of nine, from the head down; a full haft holds about four hundred. A notch cut crooked means the bearer looked at the food. A notch cut twice means a chair was missed. A haft with a notch the bearer does not remember cutting is retired at once and buried in the Barrows: it has broken a table the Axe never saw.

Who Builds It, Who Uses It

Three outdoor forges in Wanting make the axes, and the smiths are honoured. Tablebreaker bands of three to six carry them; Old Breakers carry the oldest. Rim buyers want them as curiosities and as weapons against Orrum’s tables abroad, which have been found now at crossroads in three lands.

In Operation

A Tablebreaker band approaches a table blindfolded in loose gauze, with wax in their ears and linen over their mouths, so that the food is a blur and the smell is muffled and the voice that says sit down, love, it’s still hot is muffled too. The Sniffer leads. The Rope-Holder holds the tether. The Axe goes in. The first blow is to the lamp, so that the food cannot be seen clearly. Then the plates, which shatter and spray gravy, warm and fragrant, across the Axe’s gauze, and the smell comes through the linen and the mouth floods. Then the legs. The wood does not splinter like wood. It gives, and sighs, a long sound, like a mother setting down a heavy dish she carried all that way for you. Then the top, which splits along the grain, and inside the grain is warm and pink and smells of bread. Then the chairs, every one, while the Rope-Holder pulls the Axe back by the belt each time they lean toward a seat. When it is done the Axe stands in the ruin, shaking, and the band waits in silence until the smell has gone.

Four hundred and ten notches. One I don’t remember cutting. I buried it at the Barrows and it was warm when I set it down.
Old Breaker Shun Ellery, at Tablenight

Rules

A Tablebreaker’s axe is a weapon: (5) Brutal, Two-Handed; +4 vs furniture, as in the Rim Market chapter. A Barrow-blessed axe also ignores any warding of Orrum’s tables, and a laid table broken with one is broken: it will not be found laid again in that place for a season.

Breaking a table takes a number of successful Hand + Blades rolls at Hard 14 equal to the number of places laid plus one. While breaking, the Axe must make an Invitation check each round at the table’s strength (Hard 14 for a table seen at arm’s length; Grim 18 if a card bears their name); gauze and wax give +2, and a Rope-Holder may haul them back once a round (opposed Gut + Brawl against the table’s pull, which the GM rolls at +6). Each table broken gives the Axe +2 Want and 1 Fray.

The notch. A character who has broken 100 tables gains +1 on every Invitation check against a laid table; 400 tables, +2. A character who finds a notch on their haft they did not cut makes a Dread 2 check and must retire the axe.

Forging is a Long Task: Hand + Craft at Hard 14, a day a roll, three successes, 25 lacks of Rim iron and ash, then the night on the Barrows (Caul + Resolve at Hard 14 to keep one’s back turned until dawn; a failure means the bearer looked, and the axe is warm in the morning).

Failure Table (d6)

d6The axe fails
1The blade sticks fast in the table-top, which closes on it like a mouth. Grim 18 Gut + Labor to pull it free; until then, the Axe is standing at an open chair with their hands on the haft.
2The haft cracks along a row of notches. It will hold one more table.
3A splinter of the table goes into the Axe’s palm and will not come out. It is warm. It smells of bread. Taint 1 Regrowth (the Host) each day it stays in.
4The Axe broke the table and missed a chair. Nobody noticed until morning, when it is found standing whole in the ruin, pulled out.
5The axe-head comes off on the backswing and flies into the dark. When it is found it is lying on a laid table a mile west, on a folded napkin, at a place set for the Axe.
6There is a new notch in the haft in the morning, neatly cut, in a hand not the bearer’s, and a crumb in it.

Cost and Availability

40 lacks, Scarce, from a Wanting forge to an Unfed buyer; Rare and 120 lacks to anyone else, and the smith will not forge for a Godeater at any price. A Tablebreaker’s wedge (+2 to break furniture) is 3 lacks.

Hook

The Axe in the Window. A Rim pawnbroker in Gristmoot has a Tablebreaker’s axe in his window with four hundred notches on it and a card tied to the haft. It is Decline Marsh’s. Decline swears it is beside his bed, and it is. There are two of them. The one in the window has one more notch than his, and the card tied to it is in his mother’s hand, and says thank you.

Kept-Restraints

Mittens on the hands. Wire on the jaw. Frame on the neck. Name on the shelf.
— Seamers’ Guild skipping rhyme, Lastgate undercity

Lore and History

Sallowreach has restrained its own for six hundred years, for three reasons: the Hand-lines whose touch has become too strong, the Kept whose bodies are too far gone to hold themselves together, and the criminals of both kinds. The Stitching Laws of 130 A.G. made falling apart in public a fineable offence and created a trade in braces, binders, wires and frames that is now the Seamers’ Guild’s second income after thread. The Licensing of 301 made the Hand-lines’ touch a sold good, and the lead mitten its lock.

The Diagram in Words

DeviceMaterialFunctionWorn by
Lead mittenssheet lead, lambskin lining, padlocked cuffblock a Hand-line’s touchHand-lines in the Course; Osric Vane
Appetite mittenswool and wirestop compulsive closingHand-lines at the Appetite
Jaw-wiresilver or iron wire, cork padsholds a dropping jaw shut, or a biting oneLoose Kept; criminals; screamers
Quiet-wireiron wire through the lipsCourt sentence for the noisy deadthe Kept of Lastgate’s lower courts
Neck-frameiron hoops, leather, brass screwsholds up a head whose neck has rottedLoose and Ruinous Kept
Shelf-collariron, chained to the Loft shelfholds the Set-Aside on their shelvesthe Lofts

Lead mittens are buckets of sheet lead a finger thick, shaped to a fist, lined with lambskin, closing at the wrist with a hinged cuff and a padlock whose key is held by someone else. Lead is the only thing through which a Closing touch will not pass. Osric Vane’s are the largest ever made, because his nine-jointed fingers are a span and a half long; they weigh thirty pounds each, and the floors of his wing at Glovehall are scored with the marks of him dragging them. Jaw-wires are a Seamer’s craft: a loop of wire passed under the cheekbones and around the jaw, padded with cork, twisted tight at the temple, so that a Kept whose jaw muscles have rotted can keep their mouth closed in company. A tight jaw-wire also stops a biter, and the courts use it, as the quiet-wire, through the lips, on Kept sentenced for screaming at the living. Neck-frames are three iron hoops at collarbone, throat and jaw, joined by sliding rods and brass screws, so that a head whose neck has gone to string can be held upright and turned by hand.

In Operation

Lead mittens are cold, heavy, and always faintly damp inside from the hands’ own chill. The arms of a long-time wearer are thick at the shoulder and wasted at the wrist; the padlock rattles against the lead at every step. When the mitten is unlocked, the smell that comes out is of damp stone and lamb’s wool and something like an empty room. The jaw-wire squeaks when a Kept speaks through it, the words forced out between locked teeth; the cork pads go black with seepage and must be changed weekly. The neck-frame creaks when its wearer turns, and a well-fitted one lets a grandmother nod at a dinner party with only a faint ratcheting sound from her collar.
