  • Bake the burnt honey cakes, the biscotti and the oatcakes. All keep in tins.
  • Start the beetroot pot bread if you are ambitious (it rises overnight).

The Morning

  • Bake the black rye bread (it needs an afternoon to rise and an hour to cool).
  • Make the chickpea stew (it reheats perfectly).
  • Roll the labneh in its black seeds.
  • Make the jam thumbprints with whoever is around to press a thumb.

The Running Order

TimeAt the tableIn the gameWhat to do
ArrivalHot scones at the door; the slate by the doorCharacter creation or recapHand every player a scone wrapped in a cloth. Say Come for a week. Take wagers on who leaves last.
First hourThe grace; rye, cheese, picklesThe opening sceneHave each player say the grace of their character’s land. Set the empty chair now, with a plate.
Second hourSalt-baked fish, cracked at the table; soda breadThe first troubleCrack the crust as the first horror lands. Put a bowl of water at the head of the table.
The quiet courseChickpea stew and flatbreadsA silent scene: a search, a vigil, a waitFor one course, nobody at the real table speaks: the scene is played in gestures, notes and dice. It is harder and better than it sounds.
The Great RemovePie or stew, and the peppersThe crisisPass the peppers whenever someone flags. Whoever gets the hot one gets a bonus die on their next roll.
SweetsJelly, honey cakes, thumbprintsThe turnPut the thumbprints on a plate by the door. If any are gone at the end, do not ask.
MidnightHot punchThe climax, or a cliffhangerAt midnight, stop the game. Turn off the lights for one minute, as the Vigil does. Everyone counts aloud, together, to sixty. Then May we all finish, and drink.
The endWarm milk, lamps down; oatcakesEpiloguesEach player says what their character ate on Tablenight, and what they did not eat, and why.
The Empty Chair

Every Tablenight on the Table has an empty place in it: the chair at the end of the old northern tables that nobody may sit in; the bowl of seawater at Brinehollow’s head; the plate nearest the door in the highlands; the table laid behind the backs of the Unfed. At your Tablenight, set one more chair than you need, with a plate, a glass, and a little of every course. Nobody sits there. Do not explain it. If a player asks who it is for, the Carver says, it was always so, and it would be rude to sit there, and changes the subject. At the end of the night, count the chairs. Then count them again.

Keeping Game Night Safe and Kind

Ask about allergies and dietary needs when you invite people, and label the dishes that contain nuts, gluten, dairy, egg, fish or shellfish. Keep a non-alcoholic punch for everyone and let adults add their own. Have one thing on the table (the oatcakes, the scones, the soda bread) that almost everyone can eat. Agree before you start how dark the evening’s fiction will go, and remember that the horror is in the book and the food is just food: a player who wants to skip the wake-bill and just eat the stew is doing Tablenight exactly right.

The last page of The Receipts of the Seven Tables and the Road Between, in Odo Pellance’s hand, which is unsteady here, and written, the College’s clerk notes, in a different ink from the rest, very fresh, though the book had been on the rag-stall for a season.

I have eaten everything in this book and I am still hungry. Everyone is. That is the one true receipt on the Table, and I have saved it for the end.

Last night at Saltlick a man came in at the common-room door very late, very tall, stooping under the lintel, and stood a long time at the end of the long table with his hat in his hands, counting the chairs. He was polite. He was warm; you could feel it across the room, like a banked oven. He did not sit. When he had counted, he looked at me, and he looked so tired, and so kind, and so sorry, and he said that there would be one more for supper soon, and that he hoped I would not mind laying for them, since he could not, since it was not his place to; and he asked me, very courteously, whether I knew what they liked.

I said I did not know who he meant.

He said, no, and that was the trouble, nobody did, nobody had asked in such a long time.

Then he was gone and the chair at the end was pulled out, and it is still pulled out, and I have not pushed it in, and I have been sitting in the kitchen all night writing this by the banked fire with my back to the door, trying to think of a dish for someone whose name has been chiselled off every grace-stone on the Table, and every receipt I know is a receipt for a god we ate, and I cannot think of a single thing to serve that it has not already had.

Lack keep away. Lack keep away. Lack keep away.

It didn’t.

Chapter 7

Pocket and Shelf

Trinkets of the Table
Show me what a man carries and I will tell you what he is afraid of. Show me what his widow kept and I will tell you whether she was right to be.
— Nan Pickering, limb-broker, to a buyer at Gristmoot

From the day-book of the lost-property cupboard at the Weeping Post waystation, Rim Road Company, kept by Under-Warden Ibbet Lusk. The cupboard is a press of nine shelves under the stair. By Company rule, anything left behind is kept a year and a day and then sold, for the poor-box, at the Carving fair.

Third of Grace. Found in the snug, under the settle: one glove, grey kid, Sallowreach make, sewn shut at the wrist with the hand still in it. The hand is not attached to anything. It is warm. Shelved, top, at the back, wrapped in a bar-towel. Note: it has moved to the front by evening. Moved it back.

Fifth of Grace. Left in Room Six by the Vigil gentleman who paid in tabs: a hatpin, very long, the head a little enamel eye, open. On the shaft, scratched with a needle, sixty-one small notches. The chambermaid says he sat up all night pricking his thumb with it and saying the numbers. Shelved, middle.

Ninth of Grace. In the yard, after the Fatlands drovers left: a child’s milk tooth on a string. Not a child’s. Too many roots. Shelved, middle, in a cup.

Tenth of Grace. A bail-bucket, small, tin, painted with two names and a heart, one name scratched out. Left on the mounting block by a Brinehollow woman going east. She did not forget it. I saw her put it down and look at it and walk away. Shelved, bottom.

Eleventh of Grace. A bit. Child’s, leather, Oathen, very worn on the left side where it was chewed. Inside the strap, burnt with a hot nail: SHE SAID SHE WOULD. Shelved, middle.

Twelfth of Grace. A cord, three yards, dried, plaited back on itself like a rope. Found tied to the leg of the bed in Room Two. Tied very well. Could not be untied. Cut it. It bled a little, which I have not written down anywhere else. Shelved, bottom, in a basin.

Fourteenth of Grace. A place card, stiff, cream, gilt edge. Found on the common-room table at dawn, set square at the head, where nobody sits. No name on it. Only one mark, very old, that the Oathen notary who was staying would not look at twice. Shelved, top, face down. Gone by evening. Nobody has been under the stair.

(In a later hand, the Warden’s:) Lusk, you are not to keep a day-book of this cupboard any longer. Sell the lot at the fair. Burn the card if it comes back. (Below that, Lusk again:) It came back. It is in the cupboard. I have shelved it, top, face down, and I have put a plate in front of it, because I did not know what else to do.

Everyone on the Table carries something they cannot explain to a stranger. The Lastgate porter has a black wax breath in his cheek, sucked smooth, a twelfth of a twelfth of a death he will never afford. The Netwatch hooker has a knotted cord around her wrist, one knot for every face she pulled out of the surf. The Unfed child has her one toy, a stone the size of an egg, which she is not allowed to pretend is food. These are trinkets: small things with no price worth haggling over and a story worth a night’s drinking.

This chapter is a cupboard of them. It opens with a d100 table of trinkets from every land and the Rim, each a single line with a hint of the story behind it. It then gives eleven d20 tables for more particular searches: what the dead have in their pockets in each of the seven lands, what the bereaved keep, the charms people trust that do not work, the toys of children, and the things the cautious sew into their hems. It closes with twelve Trinkets with a Story, written up at length, with lore, rules and a hook, for the Carver who wants a small thing to open into a large one.

A trinket is a sentence with the rest of the page torn off.
Cutwright marginal note, On the Evidence of Pockets

Using Trinkets

At creation. Every Guest begins play with one trinket, rolled on the d100 table or chosen. The player and the Carver decide together where it came from, but the player should leave at least one question about it unanswered. The Carver will answer it later, and not always kindly. A Guest from one land may perfectly well carry a trinket from another: the Rim Road moves everything, and most trinkets are bought, found, stolen or inherited from someone who was not their maker.

In play. A trinket has no rules value unless the Carver gives it one. Most never need one. But once per story, when a trinket becomes important in a scene (it is recognized, it is the thing that proves who you are, it is the last thing you have to give), the player may tell the trinket: say, in a sentence or two, what it means. If the telling is good, the Guest gains +2 on one roll in that scene that the trinket could plausibly touch, or recovers 1 Fray. This is the same small mercy as the Strength of the Dead and, like it, it is meant to be earned with a story rather than spent like a coin.

As clues. The tables of pockets and hems are for the Carver above all. A corpse is a document. A dead woman’s pockets in Lowmark tell you whether she was Called or pushed; a Kept man’s lining in Lastgate tells you who has been paying his Seamer. When the Guests search a body, a room or a bundle, roll on the matching table and let the result be true. Several results are written to open a scene by themselves.

Selling them. Trinkets are worth almost nothing, a crumb to a lack, unless they are something more. A Hard (14) Eye + Lore roll tells whether a trinket is godflesh (and so carries Taint, as given in the Rim Market chapter) or only ordinary sorrow. The ones that are godflesh are marked in the text; most are not. Most trinkets are only the things people keep because they cannot keep the people.

Land Tags

Each trinket on the d100 table carries a land tag: Sallowreach, the Fatlands, Brinehollow, the Vigil, Cradlewrack, Oathen, the Fast, or the Rim (the Road itself, its inns and its Company). The tag says where the thing was made or where its story belongs, not where it is found. When the Guests rummage in a place, the Carver may reroll results whose tag would make no sense there, or may keep them: a Vigil hatpin in a Fatlands wake-house is a better story than a Fatlands spoon.

The Hundred Trinkets

Roll d100, or let the player read down the list until something catches.

d100TrinketLand

a pedlar of salvage at Gristmoot

What's in a Dead Person's Pockets

The dead are the most honest witnesses on the Table, except in Sallowreach, where they are also the most talkative. Each table below is for a body found in that land, or the body of someone from that land found anywhere. Roll once for the main find; roll twice more and take the lesser results as small change, string and lint. Several results are the beginnings of scenes.

Sallowreach: The Pockets of the Kept

In Sallowreach a “dead person” may be lying there quite awake, watching you go through their coat. Ask first. It is the law, and it is good manners.

d20In the pockets
1A jar of breath-tokens with a slotted lid, three filled of sixty; the body has been saving for its own Closing for a century.
2A Seamer’s receipt for a new left foot, not original, fitted 588, and an older receipt for the same foot, original, reattached 412.
3A sprig of rosemary, a twist of vinegar-rag and a scrap of cedar shaving: three classes of smell, one coat.
4A finger, not the body’s own, wrapped in a handkerchief; the body cannot explain it, and it does not match any Seamer’s register.
5A letter to a son, written in 431, re-dated in fresh ink every year since, never sent.
6Lead mittens, folded, too small; a Hand-line child’s, which the body was paid to dispose of and did not.
7A page of a Loft-Warden’s ledger of whispers: forty lines, all the same word, which has been scratched out so hard the paper is through.
8A small dried flower from Dunmere Hush, perfect, which makes no sound when crushed; not the rustle a dried flower makes, nothing at all.
9Teeth, loose, the body’s own, in a twist of paper labelled for the Seamer, Tuesday.
10A forged minute of Closing with the Regent’s signature spelled wrong.
11A pocket-book of jaw-clicks, the body’s own private code, so it can still talk to its wife after her jaw went.
12Maggots, in a tin, labelled Justice Lathe’s, borrowed.
13A ticket for the Finishing Post with a pilgrimage date six weeks from now.
14A list of the forty-one petitions its widow has filed for its Closing, copied out neatly by the body itself.
15A Tallow candle-stub and a receipt from Wick Tallow’s shop: rendering, one, unclaimed, your uncle.
16A key to a Loft shelf, numbered, and a note: read to her, she likes the sea ones.
17A child’s milk-tooth, a lock of hair and a seven-year-old’s drawing, labelled Nell, from the undercity, with a price.
18Earth from outside the border, kept in a twist of oilcloth: a pinch of the country it can never visit.
19Nothing at all; its pockets were cut out long ago, and its hands are not its own, and the hands remember picking pockets.
20A Closer’s glove, empty, which is warm, and which flexes its fingers once when it is touched.

The Fatlands: Pockets of the Eaten

There are no graves in the south. A body found with its pockets intact has not yet been to its wake, and someone is waiting for it, plate in hand.

d20In the pockets
1Food. Always food first: a cold chop, half a pie, a fistful of sweet toothed-wheat biscuits; the body died eating, and its jaw is still working.
2A Board fine-book, every page stamped, for insufficient appetite, which in the Fatlands is suspicious.
3A Reaping tally in the hand of Pell Hogget’s copyists, with this year’s number written in and a line drawn under it.
4Lead shot, a great deal of it, sewn into the coat: a man who wanted to vote heavier at the Weighing.
5A dusk-shift summons from the Cullmasters, for tonight.
6Ash in a twist of paper and a tin cup of water: one of the Thin, who has starved down to the bone and died of it, or been caught.
7A wake invitation for tomorrow noon. The name on it is the body’s own.
8A root, small, with a birthmark on it, wrapped in a wet cloth to keep it alive.
9A Renderers’ Union card, lapsed, and a barrel-mark written on the back with a notch beside it.
10A spoon, tied to the wrist with a cord, because the owner could no longer remember to pick one up.
11Seed, a handful, from a field the owner’s grandmother became.
12A letter home to the Fast from a pilgrim of Osanna Blythe’s, saying I am almost there, and I am so hungry, and it smells like bread.
13A thumb-length of Ummer’s fat in waxed paper, white and sweet, Taint 1 Hunger; the body’s last meal was going to be this.
14A set of false teeth made of toothed-wheat teeth. Good ones; somebody’s.
15A funnel.
16A meat scrip of the side denomination, a fortune, stained, with a hole in it the shape of a bite.
17A Second Helping pledge-card, signed in blood, promising one hand, the left, at the next feast. The left hand is missing.
18A notched barrel-stamp, Quartermaster Stockpot’s mark, stolen or given.
19A child’s gleaning sack, empty, with a girl’s name embroidered on it, and a smaller sack inside, with a smaller name.
20Soil in every pocket, warm, moving a little, packed in so tightly that the seams have split; there are roots in the cloth.

Brinehollow: Pockets of the Drowned and the Dry

Bodies are rare on the coast. The Called go west and do not leave much behind. When one is found on the Uncovered, Netwatch law says to turn out the pockets before anybody says the name aloud.

d20In the pockets
1Water. The pockets are full of it, and it is warm, and it is still coming.
2A bail-bucket, small, with a hole punched in the bottom: a person who did not want to bail any more.
3A length of anchor-rope, cut, and in the other pocket the knife that cut it, and the hand that held the knife is the body’s own.
4Shells, dozens, all the same species, none of them known, all of them alive and closing tight when touched.
5A Netwatch tally, earned, and a scrap of paper on which the hooker wrote the name of the one they dragged home.
6A pier-note for nine yards of the Mile not yet built.
7A tide-table for the body’s own lungs, written in a Wreckwife’s careful hand.
8The key to a cistern, and on the key-ring a little tin label: his dinner, six bells.
9Salt crystals the size of teeth, which turn out, under a lens, to be teeth.
10A sketch of a stone table with eight chairs, on wet paper, with a heading: Lobbett’s Drop, bearing west by south, nineteen hours walking.
11A Deepening lantern, small, its wick drowned, and a hymn sheet.
12A letter of complaint to the Salt Assay about the numbers, unsent.
13A Tenanted judge’s ruling on a land dispute, which the body won, and which says at the bottom, in the second ink, you will not need it.
14Kelp from the cellar stairs, wrapped like a keepsake.
15A pair of glass ear-stoppers for pressure days, one cracked, and blood in the cracked one.
16A wedding ring, coughed up at the dawn bailing, still with a little shell growing on it.
17A Netwatch hook-head, broken off its pole, with a scrap of oilskin still on the barb.
18A hand-drawn map of the Hanging Abbey with one anchorite’s chain marked in red, and a note: he says he will open his lock for me.
19Nothing but a smooth grey stone, very heavy, the size of a fist, in every pocket; someone wanted this body to stay under.
20A ticket for the Follow, Dagna Hull’s iron vessel, berth 412 of 900, and a farewell letter that has not been written yet; only the date and Dear.

The Vigil: Pockets of the Awake

A dead Vigilant is almost always a dead Vigilant who could not stop; the heart goes, from rouse, at fifty, at forty, younger on the Slope. Their pockets are a record of the last hours of a long day.

d20In the pockets
1Rouse-tabs, many, loose, and the teeth that rouse took, kept together in the same pocket.
2A pin-case with forty pins, each one bent from use, and a forty-first, straight, unused, saved.
3A nudger’s contract, three years left to run, for a child whose name is followed by bell-hours owed: 1,140.
4A Seeming form, filled out but not filed, describing a figure laying a table in the street.
5A Dormitory visitor’s pass for Bed 40,112.
6A note in their own hand: if you are reading this I blinked; I did not mean it; tell Hale Grimmer it was the same way.
7A tiny bottle of Brinehollow brine, cheap rouse-cutting, and sand in the hems that smells of the sea.
8A pillow-feather, one, hidden in a locket.
9Eye-drops in a phial and a soft brush: a lidless servant, or a lidless lord in a servant’s coat.
10A Tuckers’ receipt, one minute, guarded, returned, and the guard’s thumbprint in soot.
11A mirror the size of a lack, for checking that one’s eyes are still open.
12Bells, little ones, sewn into the cuffs, so that nodding hands would ring.
13A lullaby, written down, the words crossed out one by one as though someone was trying very hard to forget it.
14A map of the long room in the dream, paced out, thirty paces from the eye, with a mark where a voice spoke.
15A page from the Hourkeeper’s pendulum log, stolen: the hour of the third bell, Plenty 641, sixty-one minutes and nine seconds.
16A slapping-glove, the polite kind, kid leather, very worn on the palm.
17A child’s drawing of a bed, which is contraband.
18Lamp-oil in a hip flask, for drinking, which is the last thing the Slope does when the rouse runs out.
19A key to a room in the Glass House, the yawners’ quarantine, and a mask with the mouth sewn shut.
20Nothing at all; the body has been laid out in the street, on its back, eyes closed, hands folded, by someone who wanted to give it the one thing the city could not.

Cradlewrack: Pockets of the Born

In the highlands, ask first whether the body is the body or only the part of it you can see; and check for cords.

d20In the pockets
1A neck-kit: needle, gut thread and a little mirror, for restitching wounds that open in the night.
2A brick, and a trowel, and a pot of lime: someone who meant to brick themselves in tonight.
3A naming-right certificate for a birth not due for three months, bought for two lacks.
4A Tally extract with the body’s own birth recorded twice, in two different years, to two different mothers.
5A tiny hand, wrapped in swaddling, warm, holding the body’s finger even now.
6The pang-interval, chalked on a slate, and crossed out, and chalked again, smaller each time.
7An Agnes Latch door-key and a promise in writing from the doorwright: holds, or your money back.
8A hymn of the Barren Order, and a surgeon’s bill for the cutting.
9A cord-clamp of horn, still clamped on nothing.
10A drawing of the Assemblers’ figure, measured, with the left hand coloured in by someone hopeful.
11A lock of white hair, and a note: my son’s, aged one.
12A Foundling Company pay-chit, and a list of things children do copied out to learn, with play underlined.
13A knocker, small, unscrewed from a door, kept so that the door could never again be knocked on.
14A wet-nurse’s receipt from Dolour Pym for a month of feeding the one with the voice.
15Clay from the rim of the Dilation, warm, with a faint, slow pulse in it.
16A Second Opinion’s warrant, blank, with the Attendance’s seal. Someone stole this to fill in a name.
17A half-sentence written on a scrap of paper, and when the door is open, and an offer of reward for whoever has the rest.
18Swaddling bands, very long, for something very long.
19A midwife’s tally-pin and a fetal skull the size of a walnut with too many sutures.
20A door, folded somehow, a whole cupboard door, in a coat pocket that should not hold it; it is ajar.

Oathen: Pockets of the Sworn

An Oathener’s pockets are full of paper. Read it carefully. Any of it may still bind someone.

d20In the pockets
1A sworn note, unpaid, backed by the issuer’s left eye.
2A bit, iron, for an Appetite-struck relative, with the key on a separate string.
3A slate and chalk for silent talk, the last words on it if able.
4Tally-sticks from the Breakdowns, which are held not to bind, and which the body seems to have been chewing.
5A list of every promise the body made in the last year, each with an Exit beside it, in their own careful hand; one has no Exit.
6A Surety’s fee-receipt for standing behind one marriage, forty pages.
7A wax plug for each ear, used in echoing gorges.
8A fragment of the Ledger, a flake of red stone with three carved words on it, chipped from the cliff by a tourist.
9A finger, the body’s own, lost to a broken promise, kept in a little velvet bag.
10A copy of the Mute King’s latest gesture, drawn in nine panels, with the Bench’s forty-page reading folded inside.
11A lie, written down, sealed in wax, never spoken: the body wanted to know what it would feel like to own one.
12A rain-cup, empty, from the Kept Rain of this year, three days late.
13Handtalk rings, the copper finger-bands that make signing clearer across a canyon, two of them snapped.
14A marriage contract with one clause underlined: the parties shall not speak of the well.
15A child’s first sentence after the bit came off, on a card, framed in silver: I will try.
16Teeth, loose, the price of a lie.
17A note from Grandam Cess: paid in full; the larger oath to be called in at my pleasure.
18A small gold coin with Tolm’s ear on it, from before the Gorging.
19A breaking-bill: a Clausewright’s invoice for the drafting of a defence for the body’s broken promise, which the god did not accept.
20A card bearing two words, which the body was carrying from Sworn Gorge to the Bench; whoever reads them aloud is bound by an oath they do not know.

The Fast: Pockets of the Unfed

Unfed pockets are lean. What is in them was carried, every crumb, and carried far.

d20In the pockets
1Half an oatcake, wrapped, untouched, saved for tomorrow, for three weeks of tomorrows.
2A ration chit and a list of who else in the household was struck off.
3A stone, egg-sized, smooth: a child’s toy, carried by an adult.
4A place card with the body’s own name.
5A Reckoner’s tally of high-Cut bloodlines, with a smear of someone’s blood on the last name.
6A Crumb-Runner’s grain-count in a tiny ledger, down to the bean, and a line at the bottom: ate none.
7A little brass bell, a dusk-bell, and a name.
8Honey cake, iced, perfect, warm. The body did not carry this.
9A Hostwatch chalk-stick for marking warm ground, worn to a nub.
10A silver fork, which the body refused to use, kept to prove it.
11A splinter of an axed table, sharp, the wood still warm.
12A letter from a Fatlands cousin begging the body to come south and eat.
13The Five Rules, written on a strip of cloth, in a child’s hand, for an adult who was forgetting them.
14A seed. One. Green at the tip.
15A poacher’s price-slate with the body’s own weight on it, in bone.
16Crumbs on the lips, crumbs in every pocket, crumbs in the seams, and nothing in the stomach at all.
17A copy of Meek Garrity’s seating plan, in a hand that has copied it many times.
18A Decline-cord: three knots, for no, thank you thrice, and a fourth knot, half-tied.
19A napkin, linen, folded into a crown, from a table that was laid for them.
20An invitation, engraved, to dinner, at a house that has stood empty for six hundred years, eight o’clock, do not dress.

Keepsakes of the Bereaved

Every land grieves in its own shape. What the mourners keep tells the Guests who was loved, how they were lost, and whether the mourning has gone wrong. Use this table for a widow’s drawer, a Wreckwife’s shelf, a Loft-Warden’s desk, or a parent’s coat.

d20KeepsakeWhere it is kept
1A plait of hair cut from a Kept husband in the year he was still handsome, tied with the ribbon from his first restitching.Sallowreach
2The marrow-spoon from a wake, given to the most beloved; it was never washed.Fatlands
3The cut end of an anchor-rope, wrapped in a bride’s veil.Brinehollow
4A bed number, painted on a slate, and a chair beside the Dormitory row, carried there daily for eleven years.Vigil
5The first-year bracelet of a child who was returned and did not come home, worn on the mother’s ankle, under the stocking, where the Attendance will not look.Cradlewrack
6A widow’s copy of a forty-page marriage vow, with the clause until death circled, and beside it, in her hand, he kept it.Oathen
7A crust left on a sill each night for a child who was Seated, replaced each morning with something better, which the mother cannot bring herself to eat or throw away.Fast
8A death-license, bought and paid for and never used, because when the Closer came, the widow found she could not let him do it.Sallowreach
9A jar of rendered fat, labelled with a name and a date, on the top shelf of the larder, not for cooking.Fatlands
10A pair of shoes, left at the high-water mark, filled with sand by the tide; the family will not empty them.Brinehollow
11A nudger’s pin, kept by the one who was nudged, from the night the nudger fell asleep first.Vigil
12The knocker from the door of the room where it happened; the door has been bricked over, but the knocker was saved, and is knocked on, softly, on the anniversary.Cradlewrack
13A bitten bit: the leather muzzle a child chewed through in her last illness, saying something that nobody will repeat.Oathen
14A tablebreaker’s axe, cleaned and hung on the wall, and a place card tucked into the bindings with the dead man’s name in his mother’s handwriting.Fast
15Forty years of letters read aloud to someone on a Loft shelf, bound into a book, with the answers the shelf whispered written in the margins.Sallowreach
16A field. The whole field. The bereaved has stopped planting it and sits at its edge in the evenings, and it is warm.Fatlands
17A bowl of seawater at the head of the table, changed every day for nine years instead of once a year.Brinehollow
18The last words of a sleeper’s mouth, written down by the Matron’s clerk and sold to the family for a season’s Bed-Due.Vigil
19A Part, in a jar, which the bereaved is quite sure is the dead person come back, and which grasps at the glass when they come home.Cradlewrack
20A promise, given by the dead and never kept, on a scrap of paper in a locket; the bereaved checks it every morning for blood.Oathen
They say keep nothing. They say the dead want to be let go. Those people have never been to Lastgate, where the dead are standing in the hall with their hats on, asking where you put their things.
[ Henna Farrow, the Widow Unmade, to a Rim Road mourner ]

Charms and Wards (That Don't Work)

The trade in cures never ends, and below the trade in cures is the trade in charms, which is cheaper, and fails more pleasantly. Every land has its little protections. None of the ones on this table does what it says. A Hard (14) Eye + Lore roll knows that; a Guest who carries one anyway may, at the Carver’s option, take +1 on a Dread check while it is in hand, because believing in a thing is not nothing. On a Lack on that check the charm breaks, and with it something in the believer: gain 1 extra Fray.

d20CharmWhat it is meant to do
1A grey glove-finger stuffed with salt and cedar.Turn aside a Closer’s touch. It has been tested. Ask the families of the testers.
2A Thin rebel’s knotted string, one knot per day of fasting, tied round the belly.Shrink the hunger. It shrinks the belly, and the hunger stays the same size.
3A west-facing door painted shut with tar and fish-blood.Keep out the Calling. The Called go out of the windows, or the chimney, or through the wall of the cellar where the indoor tide comes in.
4A rouse-tab worn under the tongue at all times, never swallowed.Prevent the blink. It dissolves. It always dissolves.
5An open-weave basket hung over the cradle, so that whatever comes through the night-door will be caught in it.Catch what comes. It has caught things. Nobody has opened it to see.
6A word written on the inside of the wrist in ink and licked off before speaking.Take back a careless promise. Tolm does not read wrists.
7A stone placed in the mouth before entering any house, so that nothing can be offered and nothing accepted.Turn the Host. The Host is patient. It waits for you to take the stone out to breathe.
8A Hand-line lady’s nail-paring, bought from her maid.Grant an easy death. In the north, it grants nothing. Outside the north, it does not need to.
9A sugar-mouse left in the far field at dusk.Feed the Reaping instead of the family. The Reaping does not eat sugar.
10Iron filings sewn into the sleeves to weigh down the arms.Keep a sleeper from rising to walk west. It holds the arms. It does not hold the legs.
11A Waker’s needle-tip, blunted, hung at the throat.Ward off sleep. People sleep in it. Whole streets of people went down in their needles.
12A circle of red clay drawn on the belly of anyone who has had false labour.Keep it false. The circle opens, a crack at a time, along with whatever is under it.
13A handtalk sign, no, held with the left hand while speaking with the mouth.Cancel the words. The hand is the next thing to break.
14A crumb from an axed table, carried in the cheek.Make you smell of refusal, so the Host passes you by. It makes you smell of crumbs.
15A Rim Road waystation’s grace, Lack keep away, painted round the rim of a bowl.Make any meal safe. It is very well painted.
16A small bag of Sump-mud, from the bottom of the fen.Make the wearer unkillable outside Sallowreach. Sold on the Rim at a high price, to soldiers. The soldiers do not return to complain.
17A drop of a Tenanted judge’s sweat, in oil.Make the wearer impossible to lie to. It makes them believe everyone is lying, which is a different thing, and quite as useful in Lowmark.
18A cast of a newborn’s first word, made in wax, of a child who said not yet.Delay a birth until a midwife can come. Some births are delayed. They come all at once, later.
19A lock of the Fasting Girl’s hair, sold in every market on the Rim.Kill the hunger, as hers was killed. There is not that much hair in the world. These are horse.
20A little enamel table with eight chairs, all pushed in, worn on a chain.Keep the eighth chair empty. Nobody quite says what this charm is for, only that it is very old, and that it is sold by people who will not take payment for it.
Of course it doesn’t work, dear. Nothing works. That’s why it’s only two crumbs.
Widow Prosper Gammage, cure-seller of Gristmoot

Children's Toys

The children of the Table play, everywhere, with whatever the god has left them. The toys on this table may be found in an abandoned nursery, in a pedlar’s tray, in a dead child’s grave-goods (where there are graves), or in the fist of a child who should not have it. Treat with care; the Carver should imply rather than dwell.

d20ToyLand
1A rag doll with its mouth and eyes stitched shut, in the fashion of a well-kept grandmother, and a tiny Seamer’s kit to restitch her.Sallowreach
2A clay pig, glazed red, with a slot in its back for meat scrip and a slot in its belly to take it out.Fatlands
3A toy bail-bucket on a string, for practice coughing, with a tin fish painted at the bottom so the child knows when it is empty.Brinehollow
4A spinning top that never falls while it is watched and falls at once if every eye in the room closes.Vigil
5A rattle made from a door-hinge, so that babies learn the sound before they learn the danger.Cradlewrack
6A set of handtalk finger-puppets, each one wearing a tiny bit.Oathen
7A stone, egg-sized, smooth; the Unfed child’s one toy, which she is not allowed to pretend is food, and which she sometimes holds against her cheek at night as though it were warm.Fast
8A Kept-doll: a jointed wooden figure with every joint wired, designed to fall apart and be put back together, and a lid-shaped box to keep the pieces in.Sallowreach
9A tiny scale and weights, for playing at the Weighing; the child’s favourite doll always wins, because she is stuffed with lead.Fatlands
10A paper ship, folded from an Admiralty notice, set to sail in the cellar on the indoor tide.Brinehollow
11A cup-and-ball with a bell on the cup, so a child who nods loses the game loudly.Vigil
12A wooden baby in a wooden mother that opens, and inside the baby another, and inside that another, and the smallest is a hand.Cradlewrack
13A whistle that makes no sound, given to children so they have something to blow while they are learning not to talk.Oathen
14A kite of grey cloth, flown at dusk in the Fast on the day the warm front comes, so that children can see which way the god is walking.Fast
15A set of marbles made from Sump-glass, each with a bubble in it that, in the right light, looks like a face.Sallowreach
16A corn dolly with teeth in its ears.Fatlands
17A pair of tin stilts, for wading, painted with the high-water marks of a sea long gone.Brinehollow
18A pinwheel on a stick, carried by street-nudgers to keep their hands moving and their charge looking.Vigil
19A skipping rope of dried cord that, when nobody is holding the ends, slowly coils toward the nearest woman.Cradlewrack
20A tiny tea-set, a cup and a saucer and a little plate, forbidden in the Fast; this one was left on a doorstep there, beautifully wrapped, with a card.Fast
The little ones play at Weighing, and the littlest is always the Chairman, and they push her about in a barrow. It is the sweetest thing.
a nursemaid of Sated

Things Sewn into Hems

The cautious of the Table sew the things they must not lose, or must not be caught with, into the hems of coats, the waistbands of skirts and the soles of boots. A Hard (14) Eye + Search finds a sewn hem. A Grace finds the second thing sewn in behind the first.

d20Sewn inWhy
1Three minutes of Closing, flat, in a shoulder-seam.A whole family’s savings, carried by the one member who can leave the country, to sell where it is worth less.
2Lead weights, flattened, round the whole hem of a skirt.To weigh more at the Weighing; or to sink; the coat does not say which.
3A rope’s end, knotted, and a note: tie me if I stand.A Brinehollower travelling without family, asking strangers for help in the only way that does not need to be said aloud.
4A row of pins, points outward, round the inside of a collar.So that nodding forward hurts. Vigil travellers wear these on long Rim journeys.
5A strip of caul, dried, folded like a bandage.Taken from a noble’s birth by a midwife who was told to burn it. It is worth more than the coat, and more than the woman wearing it.
6A sworn note backed by the wearer’s own hands.So that if the wearer is robbed of it, the robber has nothing; and if the wearer breaks the promise in it, the hands go anyway.
7Oatcake crumbs, a pinch, in every seam.An Unfed habit: never be without food you carried yourself, however little.
8A Company platter, sewn into the sole.Twenty lacks, for a bribe at the border.
9A forged College certificate of Cut, one lower than the truth.To stay off the Reckoners’ lists and away from the Second Table’s.
10A tooth, human, in a little pocket made for it.A Fatlands traveller’s own milk tooth, sewn in by a mother, so that if the Reaping takes them on the road there will be something left to serve.
11A letter to the Drowned Bench, explaining why the wearer is not Tenanted, in case anyone asks.Because people do ask, and the Tenanted cannot lie, and the wearer can.
12A list of every door the wearer has shut behind them in the last month.A Cradlewrack precaution, to check against in the morning.
13A tongue-shaped silver plate.An Oathen trick: something to bite down on, so that the mouth stays shut when the Appetite rises.
14A map of the warm ground between the wearer’s village and the Rim, inked on silk.A Hostwatch map, for running away by.
15A small knife of grey bone with the Sweet scratched on the handle.A Second Table Carver’s mark, carried by someone who should not have it; possibly a thief, possibly a servant, possibly a Carver travelling quietly.
16A pinch of Hush-dust in a fold of lead foil.Death in a pinch, for the wearer, if the north will not let them finish any other way. The wearer is not in the north. They are going home.
17A single eyelash, very long, in a paper envelope.A lash from the eye of Iss, a relic, worth a fortune, carried by someone who has not slept in a week for fear of losing it.
18Fifty lacks in bone, quilted flat into a child’s coat, and the child’s name sewn in red beneath.The mother’s whole fortune, sent with a child who was being sent somewhere safer. The coat is here. The child is not.
19A rag with come in written on it in a careful, old-fashioned hand.Nobody knows. It was not sewn there by the wearer. The stitches are very fine.
20A place card, folded in four, bearing no name at all, only a single mark in the oldest Table-speech.The wearer found it at their own table, one morning, and sewed it into their coat so that it would not be found at anyone else’s. It is warm.

Trinkets with a Story

The twelve trinkets below are written up at length. Each can be dropped into a Guest’s pocket at creation, found on a body, sold across a stall at Gristmoot, or left in the lost-property cupboard of the Weeping Post. Each has its lore, its rules (if it has any), and a hook for the Carver who wants it to open up.

The Fifty-Ninth Crock

A stoneware crock, brown-glazed, the size of a man’s head, with a lid of grey slate cut with sixty narrow slots. Fifty-nine slots hold a lacquered minute of Closing, each one a sliver of coffin-wood with Regent Grue’s signature and a license number. The sixtieth slot is empty and has been empty, the family says, since 509 A.G.

The crock belonged to the Doweys of Lower Pilings, porters for eleven generations, who saved toward the Closing of their founder, Aunt Merriel Dowey, who was Kept in the Glad Century and had been coming apart since before the War of the Heirs. Every Dowey child was told that when the crock was full, Aunt Merriel would be allowed. Every slot filled was a supper. In 509 the fifty-ninth went in, and the family carried the crock to the Hall of Closings to ask, humbly, if the Court would accept fifty-nine and a promise. The Court counted the minutes, slowly, checked every number against the register, found the thirty-first forged, removed it, and sent the crock home with fifty-eight. The family saved for another eighty years and replaced it. By then the fifty-fourth had been found forged as well. This has happened, the Doweys say, four times. The Court is never wrong about forgeries. The Court also prints the minutes.

Aunt Merriel is still in the house, on a chair by the hearth, mostly wire. When a slot is filled she claps, which sounds like sticks. The last Dowey sold the crock to pay her own Seamer’s bill and walked into the Finishing Post with the Finishers in the spring of 640.

RULES: The fifty-nine minutes are worth about 3,800 lacks at the Court’s rate, and they are all genuine; a Grim (18) Eye + Reckoning roll against the Court’s register proves it. Whoever brings the crock to the Hall of Closings with one more minute will find, on a Hard (14) Tongue + Clause roll, that the Court cannot refuse it, because a crock has never before been returned with every number checked in advance. On a failure, a clerk discovers one forged, whatever the truth.

HOOK: Aunt Merriel has asked, through an interpreter of jaw-clicks, for the crock back. She does not want to be Closed. She wants to know which of her great-grandchildren forged the minutes that were taken out, because the Court gave each one back to her, privately, every time, with the name of the forger on the reverse. She has four. All four names are of children who are still alive, and one of them now sits on the Mortuary Court.

Brawnley's Shoe

A child’s shoe of good red leather, the sole hardly worn, a little silver buckle in the shape of a wheat-ear. It is the right shoe. It is always cold, even in the Belch, and it smells of the far field at dusk: turned earth, warm fat, and something sweet underneath.

In Carving of 618 the village of Brawnley in Low Tilth, frightened by its own count, gave a child to the field. Nobody would call it that. The Cullmaster for the district, a man named Harl Peasgood, preached at the meeting-house that the Reaping was hunger and that hunger could be satisfied, and that if the village chose one, freely, and sent her out at dusk dressed for a wake, the field would be full and would take nobody else that season. They chose by lot, as such things are chosen. The lot fell on a miller’s daughter named Pippa Ash, eight years old. Her mother dressed her in her best, with new red shoes, and walked her to the far furrow herself, and Pippa stood there, as she had been told, facing the Scarecrow, until the others had counted a hundred, and then the field was empty, and one shoe was standing upright in the furrow.

The Reaping took twelve from Brawnley that Carving. Its usual number was nine. Harl Peasgood was one of them. The shoe was given back to the mother, who kept it in the oven, where it is warm, for twenty years, and then walked out to the same furrow herself, in the left shoe.

RULES: The shoe carries Taint 1 Dread (a cold thing that smells of the field). Anyone who holds it at dusk in the Fatlands knows, without a roll, the direction of the nearest Reaping that night. It is the only known instrument that can tell, and the Cullmasters would pay 300 lacks for it, or have it taken.

HOOK: Pell Hogget’s tally shows that Brawnley has lost exactly twelve every Carving since 618. Not nine, not ten. Twelve. Somebody in the village has been choosing by lot every year since, quietly, to keep the number from rising; the lot has fallen, every year, on a family that has not been told it was drawn. The Guests are in Brawnley in the week of the drawing, and somebody has just bought them a drink.

We gave her up so the rest would be spared, and we were not spared, and she was not spared, and we have gone on doing it since, because what else would it have been for?
Brawnley meeting-house, overheard

The Unwashed Marrow-Spoon

A long, narrow spoon of horn, the kind used at a Fatlands wake to scoop the marrow from the long bones and feed it to the most beloved of the dead. The bowl is stained dark gold and has never been washed. Wake custom says the marrow-spoon is given to its eater to keep, and is washed only when that person is themselves served, so that the last mouthful they ate is the last mouthful the spoon ever held.

This one was given to a boy of fourteen at his father’s wake in Sated in 590, and the boy, who is now an old man and a Bonded Hand of the Rim Road Company, has never been served, because he left the Fatlands to escape being served, and there is no wake on the Rim. The spoon still tastes of his father. Not of marrow: of his father, of the specific man, the pipe-smoke and the bad tooth and the rum, so that the old man can lick it and be, for a moment, sitting on his father’s knee.

He has let other people lick it. Some of them have wept. One of them, a Second Helping celebrant, offered him two hundred lacks for it.

RULES: Taint 1 Hunger. Licking the spoon gives the taste of the last person served with it, so precisely that a Hard (14) Eye + Feast roll can name a stranger’s age, trade, health and last meal from it. Used on a different dead person’s marrow, it changes allegiance at once, and the old flavour is gone for ever.

HOOK: The old man is dying, on the Rim, outside the Fatlands, where no one will serve him. He wants the Guests to carry him home to Sated alive, so that his own children can do it properly, with the spoon. His children have been told he died thirty years ago, and they have already held his wake, with somebody else.

Westward

A brass pocket compass in a case of sharkskin, the lid engraved with a Brinehollow ship under full sail and the motto Home Is Down. The needle points west. It does not point to the west of the compass; it points to the west, wherever that is, however the case is turned, even indoors, even underground, even on the Rim Road on the far side of the Fast, where west is through the middle of the world. Under a lens the needle is a sliver of grey bone, faintly ridged, with a pore at one end.

It belonged to a Netwatch officer called Hollis Teague, a hooker with nineteen years on the Raw Mile and a reputation for always knowing where the Called would walk in. He used the compass for it. On calling nights he would stand on the pier with the lid open, watching the needle, and when it trembled, he knew the Called were moving and which way. He pulled two hundred and seven people off the shore. In the winter of 633, his wife was Called. He had the compass open in his hand. It was pointing at her. He followed it out across the Uncovered for nine miles before the Netwatch caught up with him and roped him, and he spent the next eight years in the cistern of his own house, Tenanted, writing letters to the Admiralty in two inks about the error of their charts.

RULES: The compass carries Taint 2 Regrowth (Dromm, foreign to all but Brinehollowers). Holding it open gives +2 to any roll to track the Called, find water, or navigate the Uncovered. Each night it is kept within reach, a Brinehollower who carries it must resist The West at +2 Difficulty.

HOOK: The needle has started, in the last month, to point slightly downward.

The Sixty-First Notch

A hatpin, eleven inches long, the shaft of good steel, the head a bead of enamel painted as a small open eye. Along the shaft, scratched with a needle, are sixty-one tiny notches. It was left in Room Six of the Weeping Post by a Vigil gentleman who paid in tabs, and it is the work of one of the Hourkeeper’s under-clerks, Absalom Ferrule, who carried the pendulum count from the Pendulum Hall to the Watch of Watches every bell for nine years.

Each notch is a minute. Ferrule began by marking the hour as sixty notches, as an hour should be. In 637 he added the sixty-first, a very small one, because the pendulums said so. He was told to remove it. He did not. In 640 he came down to the Rim with leave to visit a sister in Brinehollow and a pin in his hat, and sat up at the Weeping Post through the night, pricking his thumb at the sixty-first notch, saying the numbers aloud, until the chambermaid fetched the warden. He left before dawn without the pin. He never reached his sister. He was found two days later at the Netwatch line on the Raw Mile, standing on the last pier with his eyes open and his face toward the Trench, perfectly awake, and he said he was waiting for the hour to end.

RULES: Pricking the thumb with the sixty-first notch removes 2 Weariness and adds 1 Fray, because for one second the pricker feels how long the hour actually is. Anyone who uses it more than once in a day begins to count the minutes of every hour aloud.

HOOK: Maud Sexton, the Hourkeeper, wants the pin back; it is the only record of the stretching that was made outside her office and cannot be suppressed. The Watch of Watches wants it destroyed. Ferrule’s sister in Brinehollow wants to know why her brother walked west, when the god of the west is not his god.

The Pillowcase

A pillowcase of fine grey linen, darned at one corner, with a laundry-mark in red thread: D. 40,112. It is a Dormitory pillowcase, and it has been on the head of a sleeper. Nobody in the Vigil may legally own one. It has never been washed, and it smells of sleep: warm hair, warm skin, the indefinable, heavy, clean smell of a room where someone has been unconscious for a long time. People who have never slept, and there are many in the Vigil, have wept at the smell and not known why.

It was taken from Bed 40,112 by the sleeper’s mother, Odile Farthing, in 637, when the boy in it had grown too large for it, and the Dormitory changed his linen to the larger size. She asked for the old case and was refused. She took it anyway, under her skirt, and carried it home, and for four years has pressed her face into it each evening for exactly as long as she can stand. Then she sold it, to a Tucker on the Slope, for enough rouse to stay awake for her son’s birthday. The Tucker sold it on. It has passed through nine hands since and is now on the Rim, in a box of salvage, being sold as a curiosity of the Vigil.

RULES: Taint 1 Regrowth (Iss). Anyone who presses their face to it gains 2 Weariness and makes a blink check at Hard (14). A blink with the case pressed to the face goes, unmistakably, to the long room, and for that second the blinker is lying in Bed 40,112, and somebody very large is lying beside them, smiling.

HOOK: Odile has asked the Guests to find it and bring it back. She does not want to smell it. She wants to put it back on his pillow, because last week the Matron’s clerk told her that the boy has begun, in his sleep, to turn his head from side to side as if he were looking for something.

The Little Bone Door

A door the size of a thumbnail, carved from a single piece of bone, with a frame, a lintel, two hinges no thicker than a hair, and a latch. Its maker is unknown; it was born. A baby in Rudge, a girl, came into the world on the third night of a pang in 619 holding it in her fist, so tightly that the midwife had to open the fingers one at a time. The Attendance asked the Two Questions of the child and permitted her, and asked them of the door and were unsure, and permitted it, provisionally. It was entered in the Tally as a birth: a door, bone, twin to the above.

The door was shut when it was born. It has been opening. A Rudge clay-digger with a lens measured the gap each year, and then each season, and now each pang, and it widens a hair’s breadth every pang, which is to say every nine days. Through the gap there is nothing visible but dark, and a draught, warm and faintly salt, like the air that comes off the Dilation. The girl, now twenty-two, says that when the door is fully open she will be able to go home. She does not say where home is. She has carried the door in her mouth for safety since she was a child and has worn a groove in her back teeth with it.

RULES: Taint 2 Regrowth (Vey). Anyone who looks through the gap for more than a moment must make a Dread 2 check, because they see an eye on the other side, looking back, and the eye is their own. Anyone in Cradlewrack carrying the door finds every door they pass ajar.

HOOK: The girl has been murdered, and the door is missing. The Attendance wants it found before the next pang. The Assemblers want it for the figure, which lacks a voice and a left hand, and which, they say, also lacks a way out.

A Lie in Wax

A ball of red sealing wax the size of a walnut, with a strip of paper rolled inside it; the seal on the outside is the mark of the Murmuring House, where the Bench of Clauses keeps its witnessed silences. It is a lie. A single sentence, untrue, written down by a Tongue-line cadet of the House of Esk in 588, who wanted to know, before he died, what it would be to own a falsehood. He wrote it, sealed it without reading it back, and gave it to the Murmuring House to keep, and the House, which had never been asked to keep a lie before, kept it, because no law said it could not.

In Oathen, writing has been held not to bind. It is now binding a little, at half Weight, as everyone knows. The lie in the wax has been gaining weight as the widening goes on. The Clausewrights who examined it in 640 report that the wax is warm, that the paper inside can be heard rustling, and that the cadet, now an old man of the Breakdowns, has begun to lose his teeth, one a year, without any promise to account for it.

Nobody knows what the lie says. The cadet does not remember. If it is unsealed and read aloud in Oathen, it becomes a spoken lie, and someone will break: the reader, or the writer, or the god, who has never before been asked to listen to a falsehood it was holding in its hand.

RULES: Unread, it carries Taint 1 Dread. Read aloud in Oathen, it is a lie of Weight 3; the reader breaks at the mouth, and the writer breaks again. Read aloud outside Oathen, it is only words. A Sayer could make it true.

HOOK: The Bench wants it destroyed, which is a decision that would itself need to be sworn. Tavish Crook, called Loophole, wants to buy it, and has asked, in questions, whether the Guests would like to be rich. And the cadet has sent word that he remembers, now, what he wrote; it was a sentence about the rain.

The Better Crust

A crust of bread, the heel of a dark loaf, hard as fired clay, wrapped in a square of clean white napkin. It is perfect: no mould, no staleness beyond hardness, and when broken (it has been broken, once, and the halves fit), the crumb inside is soft and warm and smells of a kitchen on a winter morning. It has been eleven years since it was baked.

It came from Wanting, from the window of a widow named Lessen Hode who, the winter after her daughter was Seated, broke the rule and left a crust on her sill. She did it for the reason everyone does: so that if the child was hungry, there would be something there. In the morning it had been taken, and in its place was this, wrapped in this napkin, still warm. She did not eat it. She did not throw it away. She did not leave anything on the sill again. She kept it under her pillow for eleven years and every morning, before the Decline, she held it to her face and smelled the kitchen her daughter is sitting in.

Abstain Rooke, called Abby, has been leaving crusts on her own sill for a month and has been getting back better things. When she heard about the widow’s crust she went to see it, and the widow, who is dying, gave it to her.

RULES: The Better Crust is an offer, and the Unfed treat it as one. Any Unfed who holds it must make an Invitation check at Routine 10 each night it is in their keeping; any who eats it is Seated, wherever they are, at a table that appears around them. Godeaters who eat it are fed, perfectly, completely, for the first time in their lives, and lose all Hunger, and from then on find all other food tasteless.

HOOK: Lessen Hode has died. Abby has the crust. Tonight there is a table in the street outside Abby’s house, laid for two, with two cards; one says Abstain, and the other says the name of the widow’s daughter.

The Room Nine Key

A key-fob of polished elm, carved in the Company style with the wheel on one side and, on the other, a number: 9. The key on its ring is iron, old, heavy, good for a mortice lock. It was found by a Bonded Hand on the floor of the stable at the Hollow Halt, a waystation of the eastern Rim that has eight guest-rooms and has never had nine.

The Hollow Halt’s ledgers go back to 402. The Company’s builder’s plans show an inn of eight rooms, on two floors, four and four. There is, however, a ninth door. It is in the upper corridor, at the end, where the corridor should end in a window. It is painted the same as the others. It has no number on it. It has a lock. The key fits it.

Nobody has opened it. The warden of the Hollow Halt, a careful Oathener named Tamsin Orle, swore when she took the post that she would keep the house in good order and turn no paying guest away; she has decided, on reflection, that an unnumbered door is not a room, and has had it painted over, twice, and both times found it clean in the morning. On busy nights, when all eight rooms are let and travellers are sleeping in the common room, guests have been heard to say that they saw a light under the ninth door, and smelled supper, and heard a chair being drawn back from a table.

RULES: None, until it is used. When the key is turned, the Carver should run the room as an Orrum table laid for one more than the party, with the Invitation checks of the Fast chapter, Dread 3 to stand in the doorway.

HOOK: The Bonded Hand who found the key sold it to a Guest for three lacks. Next morning the Company issued a notice offering three hundred for its return, no questions asked, and Jessamy Quill’s seal was on the notice.

The Missing Chair

A carving of a round table, dark wood, polished by long handling, about the width of a palm, with eight little chairs around it, each no bigger than a fingertip, each perfectly made, down to the turned legs and the carved slats of the backs. Seven chairs are glued firmly in place, pushed in. The eighth socket is empty. The owner, whoever the owner currently is, keeps finding the eighth chair: in a coat pocket, in a boot, on a windowsill, under the pillow, on the plate at breakfast. It is always pulled out, facing the table. And whenever the owner puts it in its socket and turns away, it is gone again.

Salvagers say it came up out of the Uncovered in Cray Lobbett’s net, years before he found the table at the place that now bears his name. Collectors on the Rim say it is Fast-work, from a temple of Orrum, before the Gorging. A Cutwright in Quire who examined it says only that the wood is no wood she knows, that there are tool-marks on the table’s eighth side where a figure carved in relief has been chiselled away, and that the chiselling is newer than the table by a great deal and older than the College by more.

RULES: Owning it costs nothing. Losing it is impossible; it returns. Each time the eighth chair is found, the owner makes a Dread 1 check. On a Lack, the owner finds the chair at a real table, a full-sized one, pulled out, with nobody in it, and the people at that table do not see it at all.

HOOK: Do not explain it. Let the chair keep turning up. Let it turn up at Thimble Cross, at the Long Table, at a Second Table dinner beside the empty chair of the Head. Let somebody at last glue it into place, and in the morning let all eight chairs be gone, and the table bare, and a smell of cold in the room like a door opened onto winter.

There is no eighth chair. Put it back.
note pinned to a curiosity in a Gristmoot salvage stall, in the stallholder’s hand, and under it, in another: it was never there to put back

Marrow Jack's Glove

A man’s glove of black kid, Lastgate make, very good, lined in grey silk, with the right hand still inside it. The hand is Kept: cold, grey at the nails, slightly soft at the knuckles, entirely alive. It grips. It is the right hand of a Lastgate notary, a Kept man named Absolon Wray, which was taken from him on a Loft shelf in 629, while he lay Set Aside and dreaming, by the part-thief called Marrow Jack, and sold to a back-alley Seamer, and from the Seamer to a glover who thought it would make a fine curiosity.

The hand still writes. Give it a pen and it writes notarial hands, Lastgate formulae, sworn copies of documents the notary witnessed in the three hundred years before his shelving. And Absolon Wray, on his shelf, can feel everything it does. The Loft-Wardens have written down what he whispers, these twelve years: the names of everyone who has held his hand, and what they had it write.

RULES: Taint 2 Dread (it is a living hand in a glove). Anyone who gives the hand a pen may make a Hard (14) Eye + Clause roll to have it reproduce any Lastgate document Wray witnessed before 597; the copy is in his hand and passes as genuine. Each use, Wray feels it; each use, a Loft-Warden writes the user’s name down.

HOOK: Wray witnessed the Licensing of 301, the first written record of the Hand-lines’ bargain with the Court, of which the original was lost. Jory Welt of the Heirs would give anything for a copy. So would the Regent, to burn it. And Wray, on his shelf, has begun to whisper that he wants his hand back, and that he knows the name of the person who is holding it right now.

Chapter 8

Games of the Table

The house fed me once. It was good. I lost the rest of my life here anyway, but it was very good soup.
— scratched beneath the Grace-and-Lack house rules, taproom of Thimble Cross

Deposition of Josse Haverick, Warden of Thimble Cross, to a Company inquiry at Saltbridge, 640 A.G., concerning a game of chance played on Company premises against Company rule. Sworn, with Exits.

I state, if able, that the game in question was played in the taproom between the second and fifth bells of the night of the twelfth of Carving. I state that I did not stop it, as I now intend to explain. The players were five. Two drovers of the Fatlands, a Brinehollow woman with a rope at her wrist, an old Kept man of Sallowreach travelling under licence to his border and no further, and a gentleman of the Vigil who did not give his name and did not blink. The game was Grace-and-Lack. It is always Grace-and-Lack.

The stakes, as I understood them at the first bell, were coin. At the second bell they were coin and a bail-bucket. At the third, the drovers had staked their dusk shifts, which is to say their places on a Cullmaster’s list, which is a thing that can be traded in the south, and the Brinehollow woman had staked her rope. At the fourth bell the old Kept man staked his own Closing: a license, paid for, in his coat, for which his family had saved two hundred years. He lost it to the Vigil gentleman on a pair of fours. I state that I have never seen a man so happy to lose. He said, through his interpreter, that he had been afraid to use it.

At the fifth bell the Vigil gentleman, who now held a Closing he could not use, a rope he did not need, two places in a field at dusk, and a Kept man’s two hundred years, staked all of it on one throw against the Brinehollow woman’s oath on her drowned husband. She threw two tens. I did not stop it. I state that nobody could have.

She tore up the license. She gave the drovers back their dusk shifts, which they did not want. She kept the rope. She would not say what the oath had been. The Vigil gentleman went up to his room, and in the morning he was asleep in his chair, and he did not wake, and the chambermaid says that he was smiling.

The people of the Table play. They play in the Loft-galleries of Lastgate with cards that have been in the same game for a hundred years; on the props of the Dry Fleet with knucklebones that are not all sheep’s; in the Pinchmarket with a deck that keeps them awake; in the silent galleries of Tacit with dominoes that make no sound on felt. They play for coin, and then for what they have instead of coin, and on the Table what people have instead of coin is very strange.

This chapter gives eleven games of the Table with full rules that can be played at the real table, using ordinary dice, a standard deck of cards, dominoes, coins or pebbles. Each game comes with its history, who plays it and where, how it is cheated, what is staked on it, and the horror that has grown up around it. It opens with rules for gambling in play: how to resolve a game quickly with the Grace Roll when you would rather not play it out, what can be staked, how cheats are caught, how debts are collected in each land, and what happens when someone stakes an oath on the dead.

Every game on the Table is the same game. Somebody puts something on the board that they cannot afford to lose, and somebody else wants it. The dice only decide the order.
Honor Pyle, surety-broker of Mumchance

Gambling in Play

Playing It Out or Rolling It

A game in the fiction can be handled in three ways, and the Carver should choose by how much the game matters.

  • Play it for real. Get out the dice, the cards or the pebbles and play the game in this chapter, the Carver taking the parts of the other players at the board. This is the best choice for a game that is a scene in itself: a wager with the Second Table, a hand of Who Finishes against the Regent’s clerk, Grace-and-Lack for a Kept man’s license. A short game played for real takes ten minutes and is remembered for years. Players may still roll to cheat, to read a tell, or to Partake (see below).
  • Roll it. Each player rolls the pair given for that game (Quick roll in each game’s entry) as an opposed roll; the highest total wins. Pure games of chance are rolled on 2d10 alone, with no Attribute or Skill: the Table’s dice are honest even if its people are not. Helpings in the opposed roll mean the winner took more than the stake from the losers, or won it with style, or noticed something about them while they lost.
  • Let it run. A night of gambling in the background is a single roll: Tongue + Haggle or Eye + Reckoning (the player’s choice), Hard (14). Success: break even, or win a little (a lack per Helping). Failure: lose a day’s cost of living. Lack: lose much more, and be offered credit. Grace: win, and be noticed by someone who matters.

What Can Be Staked

The Table gambles in layers. A game begins with coin and, if nobody leaves, works its way down through the ladder. The Carver may use this to pace a gambling scene: each hour of play, the stakes go one rung lower.

RungStakeExamplesCost of losing
1Coinlacks, crumbs, platters, regional moneymoney
2Goodsa weapon, a bail-bucket, a crock of minutes, rousekit, and the regional money it stood for
3Servicea day’s labour, a shift on watch, a dusk shift, a nudgingtime, and sometimes your life
4Bodya sworn note backed by a hand; a Surety’s fee; a Kept limbFlesh; a permanent mark
5Kina naming-right, a bed in the Dormitory, a share in a wake, a Kept relativea Dread check; the family’s opinion
6The Deadan oath on the dead, the remains of the dead, the dead themselvessee below

Every land has rules against the lower rungs, and every land breaks them. The Thimble Cross chalkboard forbids rungs 4 to 6 by name, which tells you how often they are played.

Cheating

Every game in this chapter lists the common cheats. To cheat, roll Hand + Filch (for marked cards, loaded dice, palmed pebbles) or Tongue + Deceive (for false counts, false promises, signals to a partner) against the most watchful opponent’s Eye + Search (or Eye + Instinct, for a lie). If the game is being played for real, a successful cheat lets the player do one thing the rules forbid: look at a card, set a die to a chosen face, move a pebble. If the game is rolled, a successful cheat adds +4 to the cheat’s game roll.

A failed cheat is not always noticed. The opponent who beats the cheat’s roll knows, and may say so or hold the knowledge for later. A Lack on a cheat is caught in public, and the consequences are those of the land, as in the table below. A Grace on a cheat goes so well that the cheat is believed to be lucky, and the next game in that house will be harder to win honestly, because everyone is now watching the lucky one.

Partaking at the Board

The god in the blood wants to win as much as its host does, and Partaking is the oldest cheat on the Table. A Guest who Partakes during a game adds the Tooth as normal to a game roll, or, in a game played for real, may reroll any one die of their own, or look at one hidden card or one closed hand. Every house has a rule against it, and every house can tell: each land’s Tooth has its tell, as the Lands chapters describe (cold fingers, a growling belly, a yawn through the room, a drip of salt at the nose, a door swinging open, a half-second echo, a smell of bread). Anyone at the board may roll Eye + Instinct, Hard (14), to see it. An Unfed Guest’s Gnaw (the Empty Tooth) has no tell at all, which is why the Unfed are not welcome at the dicing-boards of the Rim, and why they are rarely asked twice.

Debts

A gambling debt is a debt like any other on the Table, and each land collects it in its own way. When a Guest owes and cannot pay, roll on, or read, the land’s row.

LandHow it is collectedWhen it goes bad
SallowreachThe debt never dies, because nobody does; it passes to the debtor’s Kept self and is collected in parts.A Kept creditor sells the debt by the limb at auction.
FatlandsThe debtor is read onto a Cullmaster’s list and walks the far field at dusk.The debt is struck off in full. The debtor is not.
BrinehollowImpressment into the Dry Fleet, a year for every hundred lacks.The debt is sold to the Raw Mile, where pier-haulers die.
VigilPaid in waking hours: the debtor or their child nudges for the creditor, by the bell.A nudger who sleeps is delivered to the Dormitory, and the family billed a new Bed-Due.
CradlewrackPaid in naming-rights: the creditor names the debtor’s next birth, of any kind.The debtor bears it.
OathenEvery wager in Oathen is a promise. Default is a Breaking at the wager’s Weight.The Surety who stood for it breaks too, and comes to visit.
FastNo coin; debts are in chits, and a defaulter’s name is quietly left off the next list.Murder by omission. Nobody’s hands are dirty.
RimThe Company buys the debt and ships the debtor as cargo, on a sworn manifest.Nobody knows who buys. The manifests are sworn.

Oaths on the Dead as Stakes

The deepest stake on the Table is a dead person. It can be laid down in three ways.

  • Staking the oath. A Guest who has sworn an oath on the dead may stake the oath itself: if they lose, they must release the winner’s choice of their own sworn purpose and swear a new oath on the same dead, drafted by the winner. Releasing an oath this way is not a deliberate breach, because the dead were wagered and lost, but the dead do not like it: gain 2 Fray, and the next Visitation the Carver rolls for that dead person comes without the courtesy of a broken oath to explain it. The new oath grants the Strength of the Dead as normal. It is, however, the winner’s oath, and the winner wrote it.
  • Swearing as the stake. The loser swears, at the board, an oath on their own dead, drafted by the winner, at once. This is an ordinary Oath on the Dead in every respect, Strength and Breaking and Visitation, except that it was sworn under duress, and the dead know it: the Strength is +1, not +2. Oatheners will not play for this stake. Sureties will not stand for it. Everybody else does it constantly.
  • Staking the dead themselves. A Kept grandmother, a Loft shelf, a share in a wake, a sleeper’s bed and the Bed-Due with it, a Seated relative’s place at the Long Table, the location of a body. The winner gets what the dead are worth in the land where they lie, which may be a great deal. The loser makes a Dread 3 check at the moment of losing, and a Guest who has staked their own dead gains the Fray even on a success: a minimum of 1, as always, and the knowledge that they did it.

An oath sworn at a board over a desecrated corpse (a Kept man’s severed hand, the plate at a wake, a body pulled from the surf and robbed) binds twice as hard, as the Oaths on the Dead rules say. The Rim Road’s worst houses keep a corpse in the cellar for this purpose. The Thimble Cross chalkboard forbids it, which, again, tells you something.

Chasing

A Guest who has lost more than a week’s cost of living in a single sitting must roll Caul + Resolve, Routine (10), to get up from the board. On a failure they stay for one more round, one rung lower on the ladder of stakes. On a Lack, the god in their blood has noticed the game, and the next roll is made with a Tooth whether they wished to Partake or not. A Guest who reaches rung 6 in a single sitting, and loses, gains a Derangement of the player’s choice from the Common Madnesses if they Break within the week; it will be about luck.

It is not the losing. It is the next throw. There is always a next throw, and in that throw, I win back everything, including Mam.
a Fatlands drover, at the Weeping Post, before his dusk shift

Grace-and-Lack

The great dice game of the Rim Road, played in every taproom from Thimble Cross to the Weeping Post, on Company premises, against Company rule. It is older than the Company. Every Cutwright on the Table insists that it is older than the Gorging, because the dice used are the Table’s own: two ten-sided bones, cut from the knuckles of oxen, numbered one to ten with drilled pips, and thrown together from a leather cup. The doubles are named for the meal. A pair on a winning throw is a Grace; a pair on a losing throw, a Lack. Two ones is Licked Clean, two tens a Second Helping. Scholars argue whether the game borrowed its words from the Table’s oldest grace or the grace from the game. The Purgation preaches that the game is a blasphemy, a mockery of the meal. The Purgation’s preachers are among the best players on the road.

Who and where. Everyone. Drovers, Bonded Hands, couriers, pilgrims, Netwatch on leave, Kept men at their border with an interpreter, Cutwrights on circuit. The inns of the Rim keep a dicing-board in the taproom: a shallow tray of oak lined with green felt and edged with a lip so the bones cannot escape, and a house cup that may not be refused.

What you need. Two ten-sided dice (numbered 1 to 10; on a die numbered 0 to 9, the 0 counts as 10) and a cup. Coins, pebbles or counters for stakes. Three to eight players.

The Rules

  • The House. One player is the House, who banks the game. The first House is whoever holds the cup; thereafter, see step 6.
  • The stake. Every other player, a punter, puts a stake in front of them. Rim houses set a minimum (a crumb) and a maximum (whatever the House can cover).
  • The House throws. The House throws both dice from the cup, once. The total is the House’s mark. If the House throws Licked Clean (two ones), the House pays every punter even money at once and the round is over. If the House throws a Second Helping (two tens), every punter loses their stake at once, unless a punter chooses to throw anyway and also throws two tens (see below).
  • The punters throw. Each punter in turn, going left, throws both dice from the cup, once. Compare their total to the House’s mark.
  • Higher than the mark: the punter wins; the House pays even money (stake for stake).
  • Equal to or lower than the mark: the punter loses the stake to the House. (A tie goes to the House: whoever is keeping things as they are wins.)
  • A pair on a winning throw (a Grace): the House pays double, and stands the punter a drink.
  • A pair on a losing throw (a Lack): the punter pays double, and stands the House a drink, and drinks it in front of everybody, which is to say, the punter must buy the House’s drink and the House may make them watch it drunk.
  • Licked Clean (two ones): the punter loses double, whatever the House threw.
  • Second Helping (two tens): the punter wins double, whatever the House threw, even if the House threw two tens.
  • Settling. Stakes are paid or taken as each punter throws.
  • Passing the cup. The House keeps the bank until it has been cleared (every punter beat it in a single round) or has banked five rounds, whichever comes first. Then the cup passes to the left, and the new House banks.

Grace-and-Lack favours the House by a little: about one throw in fifteen, House and punter tie, and the tie goes to the House. That is why the House rotates. It is also why Rim inns like to bank the game themselves, and why the Thimble Cross chalkboard says even if Jem is throwing.

The Biting Game. In rougher houses, a punter may Partake before throwing: they double their stake and add one six-sided die, the Tooth, to their total. If the Tooth shows a 1, the god bit back: the punter loses the doubled stake whatever they threw, and the House takes a drink at the punter’s expense. The Tooth never counts toward a pair. This is the version played at the Weeping Post on Tablenight and nowhere respectable. It is the version Guests will want to play.

Quick roll. Pure chance: 2d10 against the House’s 2d10, ties to the House.

Cheating. Loaded bones, weighted toward the tens with a bead of lead under the one face, are called fat dice on the Rim and are sold at Gristmoot for two lacks a pair. They are detected by dropping them in a glass of water, which every honest house keeps on the counter for the purpose. A cup with a false bottom, a tureen, lets the thrower set the bones rather than throw them. The commonest cheat is the House’s own: a House that throws its mark with a bad cup can always see its own dice first. That is why the cup is the house cup and may not be refused.

Stakes. Coin, everywhere. On the Rim, below coin, every rung of the ladder. The Thimble Cross board forbids wagering kin, the Kept, licenses, places in Mother Gall’s queue and dusk shifts, which are the five things most commonly wagered at Thimble Cross.

The horror around it. On Tablenight at the Weeping Post, the house leaves an empty place at the dicing-board, with a stake in front of it: one lack, very old, worn smooth on one face. The House throws for it as for any punter, from the cup, and the warden’s boy throws the empty place’s dice. Nobody remembers why. Nobody will stop. In 638 the empty place threw two tens, a Second Helping, and the warden paid out double, two lacks, onto the felt in front of the empty chair. In the morning the coins were gone, and the chair had been pulled out, and the warden would not let anyone push it back in for a year.

Throw from the cup, not the hand. The hand remembers what it wants.
Rim saying

The Last Plate

The Fatlands eating contest is not a game of who can eat the most. Everyone in the south can eat without end; the hunger does not care for the stomach. It is a game of who can eat the most before the Split: before the belly, which in a Fatlander is a bag the god has stretched for six centuries, finally gives at a seam. The Board of Plenty calls the contest a civic festivity and licenses it at every Weighing fair. The Renderers’ Union sponsors the plates.
