You used a figure of speech. The Carver chooses the one you said (“I could eat a horse”, “I’d kill for a drink”, “I’ll be right back”) and the god takes it literally, at Weight 1. In the Course, at Weight 3.
Say less.
the whole of Oathen’s law, as taught to children

The Fast

Lack · Fast · 55
Come In
A voice from a lit window, warm, tired, glad: “Come in.” Everyone who hears it makes an Invitation check at Grim (18); Godeaters roll Caul + Resolve the same. A failure is a step toward the door. The door is open. The bread is warm.
Lack · Fast · 56
Smell of Bread
The wind turns, and smells of a kitchen. Walk into the wind, as the rule says, and lose the day’s travel; or make an Invitation check at Routine (10). The Unfed in the company look at you as if you had said something filthy.
Lack · Fast · 57
Accepted on the First
Without thinking, you took what was offered the first time it was offered: a cup, a coat, a seat by the fire. −4 Tongue with the Unfed for the session. Wanting will sell you nothing until you have publicly refused three things, three times each.
Lack · Fast · 58
The Hearth Was Lit
You walked into a house where the hearth was already lit. The door is still open behind you. Dread 2. When you turn, there is a table, laid for exactly as many of you as there are, and one more.
Lack · Fast · 59
Warm Ground
The frost is melted in a long stoop-shouldered track. The Host passed here within the hour. Lose 1 Pang or 1 Hunger: it feels like kindness. Every Invitation check you make for the rest of the day is at +2 Difficulty.
Lack · Fast · 60
The Chalk Cross
Someone has chalked a small cross between your shoulders: the Blank trade’s mark. Unfed and Blanks: a poacher tries to take you tonight, alive, and has brought good food for the road. Godeaters: they think you are carrying one, and will look.
No, thank you. No, thank you. No, thank you.
the Decline, as said at every Unfed deathbed

The Knife: Combat Lacks

Lack · Knife · 61
Stuck in the Bone
It goes in, and it stays in: bone, a beam, a Kept man’s ribs. Spend your next action wrenching it free (Gut + Labor, Hard 14) or fight empty-handed. If the one it is stuck in is still standing, they now have your weapon.
Lack · Knife · 62
Blood on the Bread
The blow lands, hard and true, on someone you did not mean. Your attack hits the nearest bystander or ally instead, for full damage. If it is a stranger, they are somebody’s kin, and the Carver will tell you whose.
Lack · Knife · 63
Overreach
You put your whole weight into it and the weight keeps going. The target makes a free attack against you at +2, now. If it hits, you are also prone.
Lack · Knife · 64
Lost Grip
It flies from your hand, turning, and lands in the worst place in reach: a fire, the fen, a Laden’s open mouth, a laid table. Your weapon is 1d6 paces away. To take it back from a table you must reach across a chair, and an Unfed must make an Invitation check to do it.
Lack · Knife · 65
Your Own Swing
Your blade, your elbow, your own momentum, against your own body. Roll a d10 on the Mangling table and take the result yourself. The Carver narrates how you did it. Everyone who cares about you checks Dread 2.
Lack · Knife · 66
Slipped in It
Blood, brine, fat, gravy, something from the Sump. Down you go. You are prone. Until you wash, −2 to Stealth and Persuade, and dogs follow you down the street with great interest.
Lack · Knife · 67
It Breaks
The blade snaps, the haft splits, the string parts. The piece that came off is in someone. Your weapon is ruined. Roll a d6: on 1–3 the shard is in them, on 4–6 in you. 1 damage, ignoring Armor, and it will need cutting out.
Lack · Knife · 68
Somebody’s Mother
In the crowd, a woman screams a name. It is the name of the one you are fighting. She is his mother. Anyone who strikes him again this fight makes a Dread 2 check first. If he falls, she comes for whoever did it.
Lack · Knife · 69
The Lamp Goes Over
Your swing, or your fall, takes the nearest light with it. Darkness at once. In 1d6 rounds, fire. In the Vigil, every Waker in the district is on the way, and they will blame whoever is still standing.
Lack · Knife · 70
The Face
For the first time, you see your enemy’s face properly. They look like someone you love. Lose your next action and make a Dread 1 check. For the rest of the story you will see that face on every opponent you kill.
Lack · Knife · 71
The Tooth Comes Uninvited
The god does not wait to be asked when there is blood. Roll a Tooth: it adds nothing, but you gain Hunger exactly as though you had Partaken, and suffer your land’s bite on a 1. Unfed: gain 1 Pang.
Lack · Knife · 72
Yielded Too Late
He drops his weapon and goes to his knees, begging, as your blow is already falling. Hand + Blades (Hard 14) to pull it. Fail, and it lands: full damage, and a Mangling if he lives. His friends will not check morale again this fight. They have seen what you are.
A man on his knees is still a man. Remember that, after. You’ll have time.
Abate Kell, Tablebreaker, to a younger axe

Rolling the Lack

For groups without printed cards, roll for the Lack instead and read the card of that number in the lists above. Seventy-two is a d6 and a d12 together, read like a clock: the d6 picks a band of twelve cards, and the d12 picks the card within it. The card’s number is (d6 − 1) × 12 + d12: a 3 on the d6 and a 5 on the d12 is card 29, Origin Stamped Twice. (With a d8 and a d10 on hand, the arithmetic is worse; use the d6 and d12.)

d6CardsWhat falls there
101–12General
213–24General (13–18); Sallowreach (19–24)
325–36The Fatlands (25–30); Brinehollow (31–36)
437–48The Vigil (37–42); Cradlewrack (43–48)
549–60Oathen (49–54); the Fast (55–60)
661–72The Knife (combat only)

The full d72 obeys the same rules as the deck: if the number falls on a card that is not in play (another land’s card, or a Knife card outside a fight), roll again. Faster, roll only what is in play:

  • In a fight, on an attack or defense: roll a d12 and read cards 61 to 72.
  • Anywhere else, in a land: roll a d6 and a d12. On a d6 of 1–3, read the general card numbered the same as the d12 (01–12). On 4–6, a d12 of 1–6 reads general cards 13–18 in order, and a d12 of 7–12 reads the land’s six cards in order (7 is its first card, 12 its last).
  • On the Rim Road, between lands: roll a d6 and a d12 as above, and on 4–6 with a d12 of 7–12, roll again.

A rolled card that is already on the Plate this session (keep a tally on scrap paper) is rolled again, as the deck would have it.

The Grace Deck

Forty-eight gold cards. They are beautiful, and every one of them is a little wrong, because on the Table kindness usually is. Twelve fall anywhere; four belong to each land; eight are for the Knife. A Guest may refuse any of them, as the rules above allow, and the Unfed are paid in Want for doing it.

The General Graces

Grace · 01
May You Finish
What you did is done, wholly and for good, as things were done before the Gorging. It cannot come undone: the lock stays locked, the wound stays closed, the argument is over, even in Cradlewrack. In Sallowreach a stranger weeps with envy and offers you 1d6 lacks to touch them.
Grace · 02
Almost Full
The next meal you eat is right. Not good: right. Remove 1d6 Hunger (Unfed: 1 Pang) and heal 2 Flesh. You will compare every meal for the rest of your life to this one, and every one will lose.
Grace · 03
Wanted to Believe
They want to believe you, and so they do, entirely. The one you are dealing with believes what you said and will defend it to others for the rest of the story. If it was a lie, they will learn the truth one day. They will not be angry. Only sad.
Grace · 04
The Lock Was Never Locked
The guard was asleep. The page was already turned. The door was on the latch. Gain one extra Helping. Ask the Carver who left it open for you. She does not have to answer, and if she smiles, do not ask again.
Grace · 05
A Face Remembered
Someone here will remember your face, kindly, for the rest of their life. Once, later, they help you without being asked, at exactly the right moment. It costs them something terrible, and you hear about it afterward.
Grace · 06
The House Stands You a Drink
A stranger at the next table raises a cup to you. You have never seen them. They know your name. Gain one extra Helping, and the next Guest to roll this scene adds +2. The drink is paid for. Do not ask by whom.
Grace · 07
The God Turns Over
The thing in your blood sighs, turns over, and sleeps. Remove 2 Hunger. For the rest of the scene, Partaking costs no Hunger and no Tooth bites. The next time you Partake after the scene, roll one more Tooth than you meant to. It woke hungry.
Grace · 08
Ordinary Decency
You see a stranger do a plain kind thing for no reason at all: a widow feeding a neighbour’s children, a guard looking away. Remove 1d6 Fray. You will try to repay it. The Carver will make sure you cannot.
Grace · 09
As Though Expected
The flies part. The crowd parts. The rain parts. Doors are held. +2 to Stealth and Athletics for the scene, and nobody stops you. Dogs lower their heads as you pass. Somewhere, a place has been set for you, and everything here knows it.
Grace · 10
And Something Besides
You learn what you came for, and one thing more, true and unasked, about someone at this table. Gain one true answer. Then the Carver tells you, privately, a secret belonging to another Guest or a trusted NPC. You may never use it. You will never forget it.
Grace · 11
Clean Hands
No blood. No witness. No mark a Cutwright can read. Nobody will ever connect you with what you just did. Not even you: from now on, when you remember it, the hands are somebody else’s.
Grace · 12
Lack Keep Away (Said)
You said the grace, properly, and it held. For the rest of the session you know which food is safe. Once, cancel a Taint or a poison you swallow. Then you notice the plate beside yours: empty, clean, and warm.
On the Table, a good day is one where you do not find out what it cost until tomorrow.
Rim Road proverb

Sallowreach

Grace · Sallowreach · 13
A Steady Light
A Tallow candle, made of somebody, gives you its light. +2 to Search for the session. It whispers the name of anyone hiding inside its glow. It does not want to go out. When it gutters at the end, it thanks you, and you recognise the voice.
Grace · Sallowreach · 14
The Shelf Remembers
A woman shelved on the ninth storey heard everything, and tells you through the wrapping. Gain one true answer from the Carver. She asks you to come back and read to her. If you do not, she tells someone else something about you.
Grace · Sallowreach · 15
The Unlicensed Mercy
For one breath, the Closing Hand is in yours. Once, now, you may let one Kept person finish: they go still, with a sigh, properly dead. It is a crime against the Court. Their family will love you, owe you and report you, in that order.
Grace · Sallowreach · 16
Sewn Right
The thread pulls through clean and the skin lies down like it was waiting. Heal 1d6 Flesh and stop one bleeding wound. The stitching is so fine that a Seamer asks to buy the scar, when you are finished with it.
May you finish.
the polite greeting of the north

The Fatlands

Grace · Fatlands · 17
You Look Heavy
Everyone who sees you today thinks you look heavy, which is to say beautiful. +2 Tongue with Fatlanders for the session. A Gut-line household sends a dinner invitation, gilt-edged. Declining it would be sedition.
Grace · Fatlands · 18
The Field Knows Your Name
You thanked the field by name, and it was the right name. The next time the Reaping would take you, it takes someone else. You will learn whom, at their wake, from the menu.
Grace · Fatlands · 19
The Honest Cut
You know, by smell and grain, exactly what this meat was. If it was beast, eat it and heal 2 Flesh. If it was not, you know whose it was, and you are spared tasting them. The Carver tells you which.
Grace · Fatlands · 20
Fruit with a Bone Pit
An orchard tree lowers a branch to you, a fruit at the end of it, skinned and fat and warm. Eat it: remove all Pangs or 1d6 Fray, and gain Taint 1 Hunger. It is the best thing you have ever tasted, and it has a face, if you look.
You look heavy, sister. You look so heavy.
the kindest thing one Fatlander can say to another

Brinehollow

Grace · Brinehollow · 21
Slack Water
For one tide the sea in you lies still. Until next dawn you need not bail and are immune to the Calling. You dream of a stone table far out on the seabed, and the chairs around it, all pushed in but one.
Grace · Brinehollow · 22
Fathom Sense
You feel the depth of everything: water, wounds, lies. +2 to Search and Instinct for the scene, and you may ask one question about what lies beneath this place. The answer comes as pressure in your ears.
Grace · Brinehollow · 23
A Rope Thrown
Someone throws you a rope at the right moment: Netwatch, Wreckwife, a stranger with a boathook. You are pulled clear of whatever had you. They want nothing for it. They look at you the way they look at all the Called.
Grace · Brinehollow · 24
The Tenant’s Courtesy
A Tenanted person, calm and fair, offers help: a ruling, a secret of the Uncovered, safe passage. It is sincere. Gain the help. It asks, very politely, for the use of your left arm for one afternoon, someday. Saying yes is optional. Remembering is not.
The sea is not going out. It is going in.
the Lowmark tide-post

The Vigil

Grace · Vigil · 25
Pinch Me
A stranger pinches your wrist at exactly the right moment, and stays. Remove 3 Weariness. They nudge you through the night unasked and leave at dawn without a word. You will look for them. You will not find them.
Grace · Vigil · 26
The Seeming Agrees
The street sees what you want it to: you as a Waker, a saint, nobody. Gain one extra Helping on a deception this scene, and it goes into the public record as news, which makes it true until disproven.
Grace · Vigil · 27
Rouse That Holds
The dose takes, clean and bright. Gain no Weariness this watch or the next, and +2 Eye for the watch: every thread in a coat, every flicker in a face. All day your heartbeat is loud enough for others to hear.
Grace · Vigil · 28
Thirty Paces
In a blink you are in the long room, close to the wall, and back. Gain one true answer: a name, a direction, a word from behind the lid. The eye did not open. You are sure the eye did not open.
Rain on a roof is the most dangerous sound in the city. Build in tin.
Benedikt Lour, the Architect

Cradlewrack

Grace · Cradlewrack · 29
The Door Held
A door you shut stays shut till dawn. Here. Everyone inside rests properly: double Flesh healed overnight, and 1 Fray removed. In the morning there are small handprints on the outside of the door, at every height.
Grace · Cradlewrack · 30
First Breath
Something begins again. Try one failed task again at once, at +2. Somewhere in the highlands tonight, something is born with your face. The Tally will list it, under your mother’s name.
Grace · Cradlewrack · 31
Both Questions
A birth you witness goes right: “A child,” and “Yes.” Every witness removes 1d6 Fray. The child’s first word, said clearly and at once, is your name.
Grace · Cradlewrack · 32
The Hand Holds Yours
A small warm Part takes your finger and leads. +2 to Search and Wayfaring for the scene, and it always knows the way out. It does not let go when the scene ends. You will have to decide something about it.
Knock first. It isn’t for you.
Cradlewrack manners, to visitors

Oathen

Grace · Oathen · 33
The Good Clause
Your words had an exit in them you never put there. One promise you have made, of any Weight, gains a condition the Carver drafts in your favour. A Clausewright who hears of it offers to buy the phrasing.
Grace · Oathen · 34
Believed
Everyone here believes you, completely, because here everything said is so. +4 to your next Persuade or Deceive roll in Oathen. If it was a lie, it is now carved on the Ledger, and will be there when the cliff falls.
Grace · Oathen · 35
A Drop of the Kept Rain
From a hard white sky, one drop, on your face. Remove 1d6 Fray and heal 2 Flesh. Somebody saw it. The Rainwarden would like a word, in writing, about why it chose you.
Grace · Oathen · 36
The Canyon Does Not Answer
No echo. For the rest of the scene nothing you say binds unless you mean it to. Speak freely, once in your life. Afterward the quiet feels like a mouth that has closed on you.
If able. As I now intend. Barring death, illness or weather. Yes.
Sorrin Vael, Chief Clausewright, accepting a cup of water

The Fast

Grace · Fast · 37
No, Thank You
Your refusal is heard, and accepted. Gain 2 Want (Godeaters: remove 2 Hunger). The table you did not sit at folds itself away, like a host who understands. Next time it will have learned your favourite dish.
Grace · Fast · 38
A Crust Replaced
Good bread, warm, on the sill where you left none. Eat it: remove all Pangs (Godeaters: 1d6 Hunger). It is not Tainted. That is the frightening part. Eating what you did not carry breaks the third rule; the Unfed will know.
Grace · Fast · 39
The Warm Track
You find where the Host has walked, and where it is walking. You avoid it for the rest of the session without a roll. Once, at the edge of sight, something tall stops on a hill and waits for you to catch up. You do not.
Grace · Fast · 40
The Blank Card
Tonight’s place card has no name on it. Every Invitation check you make this session is at −4 Difficulty. Tomorrow there will be a name on it, and you will know them.
If a chair is pulled out for you, do not thank it.
the fifth rule of the Fast

The Knife: Combat Graces

Grace · Knife · 41
Through the Joint
Your blade finds the gap the way a Renderer’s does, without looking. Add one extra Helping, and choose the Mangling instead of rolling it. Butchers who see it nod. You dream of the sound.
Grace · Knife · 42
They Yield
Your enemy drops the weapon and begs, and the rest lose the stomach for it. Every enemy checks morale now, at Grim (18). The one on his knees calls you by name and asks after your mother.
Grace · Knife · 43
The Blow Turned
It strikes a buckle, a bone button, a little book in your coat. Ignore the damage from the next hit against you this fight. Afterward, look at what stopped it. It was a gift from someone dead.
Grace · Knife · 44
Seen Coming
You see the next blow before its owner has thought of it. +4 Guard until your next turn, and a free attack on anyone who misses you. The god in you is enjoying this, and you can feel it enjoying it.
Grace · Knife · 45
The Light Behind You
Every lamp in the room is suddenly at your back. Enemies suffer −2 to attack you this round and the next, and you see every face clearly. You will see them all again tonight, when you close your eyes.
Grace · Knife · 46
Second Wind
Breath comes back into you, sweet. Heal 1d6 Flesh and ignore Bloodied for the rest of the fight. Your breath smells of fresh bread. Someone across the room turns to look.
Grace · Knife · 47
A Clean Stroke
If this blow kills, it kills quickly and well, as every killing should. No Dread check for the kill, no Stain, no Pall in any watching crowd. The dead face is peaceful. That bothers everyone more than blood would.
Grace · Knife · 48
Into the Worse Thing
Your enemy stumbles back into the fire, the fen, the Hush, the crowning, the laid table. As a free Cast Into, with no roll. Whatever is down there is grateful, and remembers who sent it dinner.
A good blow is a gift. Mind who it is from.
Purgation tract, nailed to a waystation door

Rolling the Grace

Forty-eight is a d4 and a d12, read the same way as the Lack: the d4 picks a band of twelve, the d12 the card within it, and the card’s number is (d4 − 1) × 12 + d12. A 2 on the d4 and a 9 on the d12 is card 21, Slack Water. With no d4, roll a d6 and reroll 5s and 6s; or roll a d6 and a d8 and read (d6 − 1) × 8 + d8, which gives the same 48 by a different road.

d4CardsWhat falls there
101–12General
213–24Sallowreach (13–16); the Fatlands (17–20); Brinehollow (21–24)
325–36The Vigil (25–28); Cradlewrack (29–32); Oathen (33–36)
437–48The Fast (37–40); the Knife (41–48, combat only)

As with the Lack, reroll any number that is not in play, or roll only what is:

  • In a fight, on an attack or defense: roll a d8 and read cards 41 to 48.
  • Anywhere else, in a land: roll a d6 and a d8. On a d6 of 1–3, read general card 01–08 by the d8. On 4–6, a d8 of 1–4 reads general cards 09–12 in order, and 5–8 reads the land’s four cards in order.
  • On the Rim Road, between lands: roll a d12 and read the general cards alone.

A Grace refused is still a Grace served. Put its number on the tally with the rest.

Chapter 10

The Hunger, Pall, Tablenight and Market Decks

Shuffle it, love. It’s all been dealt before. You’re only finding out the order.
— a card-sharp at the Full Measure, Gristmoot, to a Brinehollow pilot who asked what he was playing

Four decks follow. Each one replaces a moment at the table where the Carver would otherwise reach for a d10 table and read out a line: the moment a Guest’s god takes a step forward, the moment a village fails its Turn, the long night of Tablenight, and the moment a purse opens at a stall nobody has vouched for. A card is a better instrument for these moments than a die, for one reason. A card can be handed across the table. The player holds it, reads it, keeps it, and it stays on their side of the table for the rest of the campaign, face-up beside the character sheet, where everyone can see what the god did.

Every land is certain its own luck is honest. Every land has a deck it doesn’t let strangers cut.
Rim Road saying

Using the Decks

None of these cards replaces a roll. The Grace Roll still decides whether a Guest succeeds, the Turn still decides whether a village holds, Hunger still fills at 10. The cards tell you what it means: what the body did, what the village did, what the night brought, what the stall was really selling. Where a card gives a rules effect it is in bold, and it uses the numbers of the core rules exactly: Difficulties of Routine 10, Hard 14, Grim 18, Dire 22 and Impossible 26; Dread ratings 1 to 5; Hunger, Regrowth, Fray, Pall, Steadiness, Hold, Want and Pangs as the Rules chapter and the land chapters define them.

  • The Hunger Deck is seventy cards, ten for each of the seven lands. A Guest draws one each time Hunger fills and Regrowth rises. It is kept.
  • The Pall Deck is thirty-six cards in three bands of twelve. The Carver draws one each week a community fails its Turn.
  • The Tablenight Deck is thirty cards. It comes out of the box once a year, at dusk on the longest night of Lack, and goes back in at dawn.
  • The Market Deck is thirty-six cards. The Carver draws one, in secret, when a Guest buys from a stall nobody can vouch for.
DeckCardsDrawn byWhenKept?
Hunger70The playerRegrowth risesYes, for good
Pall36The CarverA failed TurnUntil the event ends
Tablenight30BothDusk to dawn, Tablenight onlyUntil dawn
Market36The Carver, secretlyA doubtful purchaseUntil it betrays you

No cards? Every deck below is printed in order, so it doubles as a table. For the Hunger Deck roll a d10 down the land’s ten cards, rerolling any the Guest already holds. For the Pall Deck roll a d12 down the community’s band. For the Tablenight Deck roll a d10 and a d6: on a d6 of 1–2 read the d10 against the first ten cards, 3–4 the second ten, 5–6 the last ten. For the Market Deck roll a d6 and a d6 and read them as tens and units of a number from 11 to 66, counting down the thirty-six cards in order: 11–16 are the first six cards, 21–26 the next six, and so on to 61–66. Cross off what is used. Cards are better. Players remember a thing they were handed.

Printing the Decks

The card pages are laid out three to a row. Print them on the heaviest card stock your printer will take (250 gsm or more), single-sided, and cut along the gutters. Each card is sized to fit a standard poker sleeve (63 × 88 mm), and sleeving is recommended for the Hunger Deck, which will be handled for years and will, in most groups, end up with gravy on it.

Give each deck its own back so they cannot be mixed in a hurry. The suggested backs, if you draw or print your own, are these:

  • Hunger: a white plate on black, with a single bite out of the rim.
  • Pall: a row of roofs against a grey sky, every chimney cold.
  • Tablenight: a chair, seen from behind, turned to face a wall.
  • Market: a lack coin, shut-mouth face, with the little crack at the corner of the lips.

Print the Hunger Deck’s seven land sections on seven tints of card if you can (fen-green, wheat-gold, slate-blue, lamp-amber, clay-red, canyon-ochre, and for the Fast a clean, pressed white), so that a player can find their land’s stack by colour. Keep each Guest’s drawn Hunger cards in a small envelope clipped to their sheet between sessions. When a Guest is Seated, give the player the envelope. Some groups bury it. One group known to the authors bakes it into a loaf at the wake session and nobody eats the slice with the card in it, and nobody throws it away either.

Carver’s Advice: The Card Is Not a Verdict

A drawn card is a suggestion with authority, not a law. If a Hunger card describes a change that collides with something already established (a Guest who has lost the hand the card would grey), move the change to the nearest part that makes sense, keep the rules effect, and say so out loud. If a Pall card names a figure the community does not have (a Celebrant in a village with no chapel), give the role to whoever holds it in fact: the midwife, the oldest man, the Netwatch sergeant. If a Market card does not fit what was bought, hold it back and play it on the next purchase that it does fit. The only thing a Carver should never do with a card is soften what it says the god does. The god does not soften.

The Hunger Deck

It doesn’t come back the same way twice. That’s how you know it’s alive. Dead things repeat.
— Dr. Halloran Quease, catalogue entry No. 402

The Rules chapter says it plainly: when Hunger reaches 10, Regrowth rises by 1, Hunger empties, and something in the body is different now, and it does not change back. The Hunger Deck is that something. It turns the most important moment a Guest will have in a session into a physical object, dealt from the god’s own stack, and it makes every Guest of the same land different from every other. Two Sallowreachers at the Course both have grey hands. Only one of them has no smell, and only the other has Kept following her to market.

Drawing

  • When Hunger fills and Regrowth rises, stop play. The player shuffles their land’s ten cards, minus any they already hold, and draws one. They read it aloud. The Carver describes it happening, now, at the table, in the scene. Let it breathe.
  • The change is permanent. The card goes face-up beside the character sheet and stays there. Its rules effect applies from this moment until the Guest is Seated. Nothing on the Table reverses it. (A Purger’s Grace that rolls Regrowth back by one does not return the card; the god takes a step back, and leaves its footprint.)
  • A Guest never draws the same card twice. Ten cards are exactly enough for ten steps, from the first rise of the Taste to the last rise of the Brink. A Scrapling who begins at Regrowth 0 takes their first step into the Taste without a card, showing only the land’s Taste tell from its chapter. If a Guest ever reaches for the stack and finds it empty, they are at Regrowth 11, the Carver has already told them so, and the next time Hunger fills there will be no card. There will be the Seating.
  • Stage scales the description, never the rules. The cards are not stages. The stage says how far the god has come; the card says where it came through this time. A Guest at the Taste who draws a Course-looking card has the first, small, deniable version of it (a knuckle, not a hand; a cupful in the lungs, not a cistern), and it will grow at every stage that follows. A Guest at the Brink who draws a Taste-looking card has it as the god’s afterthought, total and at once. The rules effect is the same either way.
  • Foreign points. When Taint from another land’s god gives a Guest a point of foreign Regrowth (see the Rim Market), they draw from that land’s stack instead of their own, and mark the card foreign. Two gods are now leaving marks on one body. The Carver may spend a foreign card, once per session, to make it flare for a scene.
  • The Returned (Unfed who have eaten a god) draw from the stack of the land whose god they ate. Their Regrowth rises by 2 each time Hunger empties: they draw two cards, and the second is always the worse, by the player’s own judgment, read aloud.
  • The Unfed have no Regrowth and draw from the Fast’s ten cards on different triggers, given with that stack.
I kept the cards in a tin. Nine of them. My wife counted them every night while I was asleep, which I never was, and I listened to her count, and when she got to nine she’d stop, and breathe, and put the lid on.
a Hand-line clerk of the Lofts, Regrowth 10
The Hunger Deck at the Table

The best moments with this deck are quiet ones. Do not draw at the end of a session in a rush; draw at the moment it happens, mid-fight if need be, and pause the fight. Ask the player where the character feels it first. Ask who sees it. The other players should be invited to say what their Guests notice: it is in the companions’ faces that the change becomes real. If the player wants to, let them hide the card, face-down beside the sheet, and play the Guest concealing it, until someone sees. The Carver always knows what it says. So, eventually, does everyone.

Sallowreach: Ossel, the Closing

Ossel comes back as an ending. Its marks are cold, grey, silent, and finished, and the Kept of the fen can smell every one of them. Sallowreach Guests draw these ten.

Hunger · Sallowreach
The Extra Joint
In the night a finger grew. Your right forefinger has a new knuckle between the second joint and the nail, and it bends backward with a dry click like a beetle turning over. Rings will not fit. You slit your gloves. +1 Filch. Anyone who sees it flex makes a Dread 1 check.
Hunger · Sallowreach
Rinsed
You stop smelling of anything. Sweat, soap, breath, the warm salt of a palm: gone. Your pillow smells rinsed, like air after snow. Flies cross the room rather than pass you. Dogs will not come. +1 Stealth against beasts. −1 Persuade with anyone who must sleep beside you; they cannot tell if you are there.
Hunger · Sallowreach
The Low Lid
Your left eyelid grows cold and heavy and sits a fingerbreadth lower than the right, as if someone had begun to close it and been interrupted. It is the first part of you that is ready. You always know whether any eye within ten paces is open or shut, even in darkness. −1 to Search by sight.
Hunger · Sallowreach
Ash Nails
Your nails go black from the root, thick and dull as horn, and stop growing. Where they scratch living skin they leave white lines that never redden. One tears off on a door; the bed beneath is smooth grey slate and does not bleed. Unarmed blows deal 2. Kept people flinch from your bare hands.
Hunger · Sallowreach
The Swallowed Ending
You reach the end of a sentence and the end is gone, and everyone listening has lost it too. It will happen again. Once per session the Carver may end something you are saying, and nobody will remember where it was going. Once per session you may do the same to someone else, by touch, without a roll or cost.
Hunger · Sallowreach
The Footstep in the Chest
Your heartbeat stops carrying. A Seamer laying an ear to your chest hears nothing, then, a long way off, one step, as of someone walking toward her who never arrives. Your pulse is a clock in an empty house. +1 Stealth. Anyone treating your wounds rolls at −2: they cannot tell if you are dying.
Hunger · Sallowreach
Grey to the Wrist
The grey crosses your wrist overnight like a tide-line. The skin above it is smooth, seamless, shining, and the lines of your palms are gone. Lastgate palmists say a palm with no lines is a life already finished. Your hands feel no heat: you will burn them without knowing, and the Carver will tell you when. +1 Rites to Close.
Hunger · Sallowreach
The Pile on the Pillow
Flies within an arm’s length fall out of the air and do not get up. Each morning there is a small dry pile of them on your pillow, neat as swept ash. In Sallowreach, anyone who sees the pile knows what you are. Every Kept who learns of it will come, sooner or later, and ask you to finish them.
Hunger · Sallowreach
The Following
The Kept begin to follow you at a distance, the way starving dogs follow a butcher’s cart. Each morning one more stands outside your door in the drizzle, smelling of the fen, holding its hat. In Sallowreach, 1d3 Kept attend you each day. They will carry, fetch and lie for you. Each dusk, one asks to be closed.
Hunger · Sallowreach
What Nobody Calls a Smile
Your face smooths at the edges like a face seen through fog, and at rest your mouth curves very gently upward. You cannot feel it. In the mirror it looks content. Anyone who watches you sleep makes a Dread 1 check. +1 Intimidate. −1 Persuade when comforting the grieving: they know that look.

The Fatlands: Ummer, the Field

Ummer comes back as soil: warmth, appetite, roots, and things living in the folds. Fatlanders call every one of these cards getting heavy, and some families clap. Fatlands Guests draw these ten.

Hunger · Fatlands
The Night Mouth
You wake chewing. The pillow-corner, a bootlace, the inside of your own cheek, scarred now into ridges like a ploughed field. You do not remember the dream, only the taste of soil. You may eat leather, wax, paper and tallow as food. Each morning the Carver names one small thing of yours that is gone.
Hunger · Fatlands
The Loam Thumb
The pad of your left thumb goes soft and cool and slightly granular. Press it and it crumbles at the surface, dark and moist, smelling of rain on a ploughed field, and fills slowly back from beneath. Your thumbprint no longer holds its shape: it is worthless on any Oathen note. Heal 1 extra Flesh after a night on bare soil.
Hunger · Fatlands
The First Shoot
A pale green shoot uncurls from the crease of your elbow. Pluck it and it bleeds a bead of sweet sap and is back by morning. Washers say it is luck. They say it brightly. +1 Wayfaring to find food or water in any field. Bees find you: −1 Stealth outdoors in Plenty and Carving.
Hunger · Fatlands
The Warm Bed
Your body runs hot. Your bed is warm a full day after you leave it, and nothing kept under it spoils. Bread rises faster in your kitchen. Your companions sleep against you in Lack and do not say why. Ignore the first night’s cold penalty each week. Food carried on your body keeps one day longer.
Hunger · Fatlands
The Bill of Fare
Your eyes begin to rest on people the way a cook reads a menu: the back of a farmhand’s neck in the sun, a soft inner elbow reaching for the salt. It is not malice. It is older. +1 Search to judge weight, weakness and wounds. −1 Persuade with anyone who catches you looking.
Hunger · Fatlands
The Lodger
Something lives in you now. An earthworm, pink and fat and slow, in the deep fold under your arm. When it is picked out you ask, politely, for it back. You eat it. There will be others. Any lover or Seamer who finds them checks Dread 1. Once per session, eat what lives in you to remove 1 Hunger.
Hunger · Fatlands
Straw
Your hair coarsens overnight into something fibrous and dry and the colour of stubble, and it rustles when you turn your head. It will not take dye. It will not lie flat. Mice nest in the brush you leave on the sill. −1 Stealth in silence. +1 Endure against cold.
Hunger · Fatlands
Threads
Pale threads, fine as hair, grow from the soles of your feet. Stand an hour on bare earth and they go down into it, and it feels like being tucked in. You cannot be knocked prone while standing on soil. After an hour standing still on bare ground, leaving costs 1 Flesh or a Caul + Resolve roll at Routine.
Hunger · Fatlands
Sunday Sweat
You sweat a clear, sweet, faintly sticky fluid that smells of roasting and rising dough. Bees come. Flies come. Fatlanders breathe it in and smile and touch your arm. +1 Persuade with Fatlanders, who think you smell like a Sunday. −2 Stealth against anyone with a nose.
Hunger · Fatlands
The Names in the Furrow
When you walk a Fatlands field at dusk you feel its pulse through your boots, and you know, without wanting to, the names of everyone Reaped into it. The wheat leans when you say them. You learn the name of anyone Reaped into ground you cross. Each new name is 1 Fray the first time you hear it.

Brinehollow: Dromm, the Depth

Dromm comes back as weight and water and the patient pull of the west. Every mark is a little more of the deep moved into the house. Brinehollow Guests draw these ten.

Hunger · Brinehollow
Salt at the Corners
Every morning there is a fine white crust at the corners of your mouth, as if you had slept on a beach in the wind. Your lips split and sting. Your kisses taste of the sea. +1 Endure against thirst. Anyone who kisses you hears surf in their sleep for a night.
Hunger · Brinehollow
The Slosh
Your lungs have begun to keep a cupful. When you turn over in bed it shifts in your chest like a half-full cask rolled on a cart. The first breath after bailing makes you sick. Hold your breath one minute longer per point of Gut. −1 Athletics when running. Bailing takes twice as long.
Hunger · Brinehollow
Black Water Eyes
Your pupils swell until there is almost no iris left, black and wet and deep, and in lamplight they shine green like a cat’s. Children stare. Mirrors are unpleasant. See in dim light as if it were day. −1 to all rolls in strong sunlight or the lamplit streets of the Vigil.
Hunger · Brinehollow
Skate Plates
A patch of grey skin, pebbled and cold as wet slate, spreads down your spine to the small of your back, raised like the plates of a skate. It cracks and weeps clear fluid if you go a day dry. +1 Endure against cold. Dry folk who see your back make a Dread 1 check.
Hunger · Brinehollow
The Second Register
Your voice drops and gains an undertone, like a second speaker standing just behind you, a beat slow. It is worse in small rooms. It is worst when you say someone’s name. +1 Intimidate. −2 Deceive: the two voices rarely agree.
Hunger · Brinehollow
The Shell
You cough up a pink, whorled shell, small as a fingernail, and alive. It grew in the wall of your lung. Another is growing. Once a month you cough one up. Any Brinehollow Seamer who sees it knows your stage. Dr. Reave pays 5 lacks each and keeps them in a jar.
Hunger · Brinehollow
Weed in the Bath
Your hair comes away in the basin in long dark ropes that drift on the water like weed. By the next season you are bald, and the scalp is grey and smooth. Every Brinehollower knows the look: −1 Deceive about your stage with them. +1 Athletics when swimming.
Hunger · Brinehollow
The Weight
You are heavier than your size. Floorboards complain. Horses balk at you. Ferrymen look at you, then at the waterline, and charge double. +2 to resist being moved, knocked down or carried off. −1 Athletics. You sink in mud to the knee.
Hunger · Brinehollow
Still Ribs
Your chest stops needing to rise. You take a breath when you remember, perhaps once a minute, and the stillness of your ribs is the thing people notice from across a room. +1 Stealth. Dry folk who watch you for a minute make a Dread 1 check.
Hunger · Brinehollow
North for a Compass
You hear your name in every silence, not as a memory but as a direction, the way a compass hears north. It is patient. It is kind. It is very old. You always know which way the western sea lies. The West Want is one step harder to resist at dusk.

The Vigil: Iss, the Rest

Iss comes back as rest, and rest in the Vigil is the enemy. Its marks are lids and yawns and lost seconds, and the slow terrible comfort that makes the people around you lie down. Vigil Guests draw these ten.

Hunger · Vigil
Thin Lids
Your eyelids go translucent. Shut them and the world is still there, dim and red, like a hand held to a lamp. You will never know true dark again. +1 Instinct against anything that comes while you rest. Dread checks against what is in front of you are one step harder.
Hunger · Vigil
The Bruise Beneath
The skin under your eyes goes raw and purple from rubbing and will not heal; it cracks at the corners and weeps a little in the cold. On the Slope it is a badge. On the Rim, mothers pull children out of your way. +1 Intimidate. −1 Persuade with strangers outside the Vigil.
Hunger · Vigil
The Long Yawn
Your yawn goes too wide and too long. The jaw cracks out of its socket and clicks back, eyes streaming, and the yawn goes through the room like a rumour. You do not choose when. Once per scene, the Carver may make you yawn: everyone in earshot with Weariness 3+ makes a Routine Caul + Resolve roll or gains 1 Weariness.
Hunger · Vigil
Clean Linen
You smell of clean linen, always: starched, sun-dried, a bed just turned down. The Bedded turn their heads in the street. A Ward Sergeant sniffs, and holds out his hand for your blink-book. +1 Persuade with the Bedded and the exhausted. In the Vigil, the Watch stops you once a day.
Hunger · Vigil
Laid Straight
After every blink you find something near you laid very straight: a fork, a pen, a knife, its handle turned toward the nearest person. You never see yourself do it. +1 Craft: your hands are neat now. Anyone who notices the laid things checks Dread 1, and remembers.
Hunger · Vigil
The Left Lid Goes
Your left lid thins, then draws back over a season like a burnt page curling from its edge, and is gone. The eye is naked, wide and wet and permanently looking. +1 Search. That eye must be wetted every half hour or you suffer −1 to all Eye rolls. You cannot wink, wince or weep on that side.
Hunger · Vigil
One Night, Perfectly
You remember one night completely now, every second of it, every face, every sound: the worst one. It plays whenever you are still. Once per session, recall any detail of any scene you have witnessed, exactly. A night’s rest removes no Fray from you unless someone holds your hand through it.
Hunger · Vigil
Nuzzling
You lean into warmth without deciding to: a bakehouse wall, a stove, the cheek of whoever is beside you, eyes half shut. In the Vigil it is grounds for divorce. Gain 1 Weariness whenever you touch something warm for a full minute. +1 Persuade with Fatlanders, who think it is sweet.
Hunger · Vigil
Your Number
Behind your eyes, when they are open too long, you see rows of beds, numbered, warm, breathing. One is empty and has a number, and you know it. So, you suspect, does the Dormitory. +1 Reckoning. Write the number on your sheet. If you are ever Counted, that is your bed.
Hunger · Vigil
The Slow Breath
Your breathing slows to the rhythm of the Dormitory, and the people around you start to breathe with it. Babies go quiet in your presence. Dogs lie down. +2 Persuade to calm the frightened. Anyone who shares a room with you for a night gains 1 Weariness.

Cradlewrack: Vey, the Opening

Vey comes back as beginning: pangs, waters, openings, things carried and things delivered. In any body, of any sex, at any age. Cradlewrack Guests draw these ten.

Hunger · Cradlewrack
The Old Scar Opens
Your oldest scar goes pink, then lipped and moist, and at each pang it dilates a little and weeps clear salt water that smells of the springs. Seamers stitch it. By morning the gut has dissolved. It never closes. +1 Godsign. Anyone who sees it open makes a Dread 1 check.
Hunger · Cradlewrack
The Interval
Cramps roll low in your belly in waves with gaps between, whatever you are, and you count them without wanting to. The gaps are getting shorter. At the start of each session the Carver secretly sets your interval in hours. During a pang, −2 to all rolls for one round. +1 Instinct to feel a quake coming.
Hunger · Cradlewrack
The Waters
Once a week, without warning, a sudden warm flood of clear salt fluid from no clear source, soaking through your clothes and the chair and the boards. It smells of the springs. It is always at the worst time. The Carver chooses when. −2 Persuade in polite company for the scene. You leave a trail.
Hunger · Cradlewrack
The Widening
Your hips widen over a month. At night the bones of your pelvis groan apart like a door on old hinges, and your gait becomes the rolling walk of the eighth month. −1 Athletics. +1 Labor: you carry low and strong. Your clothes must be let out (3 lacks).
Hunger · Cradlewrack
The Latch Three Rooms Away
You hear every latch in a house: lifting, catching, a door easing open three rooms away. You cannot sleep in a room whose door is shut unless someone else shut it. +1 Search for hidden doors, hatches and compartments. A night behind a door you closed yourself is no rest.
Hunger · Cradlewrack
First Lines
You begin things and cannot end them. Your pack fills with half-sewn shirts, first lines of letters, songs that stop at the turn. You set out on roads at dawn and come back by noon. Once per session, reroll the first roll of any task. You can never make the last roll of a Long Task: someone else must finish it.
Hunger · Cradlewrack
Carried
Your belly hardens and swells for nine days. On the tenth you deliver, quickly and alone, a warm smooth stone with your own thumbprint in it. Highland law says the Attendance must be told. While you carry the stone, +1 Endure. Throw it away and it is by your door at dawn.
Hunger · Cradlewrack
The Second Opening
A second opening, where the body has no business having one, low on the flank under the ribs: round, lipped, moist, and breathing. You keep it bandaged. It hears: +1 Instinct to know if something living is beyond a wall. Anyone who unbandages it makes a Dread 2 check.
Hunger · Cradlewrack
The Gathering
You cannot throw away a piece of anything that was alive: nail parings, a pulled tooth, a cut-off braid. You keep them in a crock. In markets, Parts in their jars turn slowly toward you. +1 Haggle when buying Parts. Any severed Part within ten paces moves toward you, by inches, when nobody watches.
Hunger · Cradlewrack
The Voice Underneath
Something inside you has begun to talk, in a small, earnest voice, about what it will do when it arrives: whom it will visit first, which doors it will open. Once per session, ask it one question about anything beginning nearby; it answers truly. Each answer costs 1 Fray.

Oathen: Tolm, the Witness

Tolm comes back as an ear and a tongue. Its marks are echoes, ringing, swearing, and a body that grows more ears than it needs. Oathen Guests draw these ten.

Hunger · Oathen
The Clerk Behind the Ear
Everything you say comes back half a second late, close behind your ear, a little flatter, like a tired clerk reading it back for the record. You hear how it sounds. +1 Clause. In echoing places, any lie you tell comes back aloud for others to hear: −2 Deceive.
Hunger · Oathen
Wet Slate
Whenever a promise is made within earshot, even whispered, even in a language you do not speak, your mouth floods with the taste of wet slate and your back teeth ache. You know when anyone within earshot makes a promise. +1 Instinct to read intentions.
Hunger · Oathen
The Ringing
Your ears ring when anyone near you lies. In a market it never stops. In a family it never stops. You learn to live in the high thin whine of it, the way millers live in the grinding. +2 to detect a lie spoken in your hearing. −1 to all Eye rolls in crowds.
Hunger · Oathen
Sworn in Sleep
You swear in your sleep. Whoever shares your room lies rigid and tries not to hear. You wake not knowing what you promised, or to whom, or on whose bones. Each session the Carver writes one Weight 1 oath you swore in the night, and reveals it when it binds.
Hunger · Oathen
The Liver Tongue
Your tongue thickens and darkens, mottled the colour of raw liver, heavy and cool and faintly ridged, and rests against your teeth even in silence. The Bench’s men measure your jaw with their eyes. +1 Intimidate. −1 Persuade: you lisp. A bit fits you now, and someone will offer one.
Hunger · Oathen
An Ear at the Wrist
A pucker on the inside of your wrist opens over a week: pink, folded, perfectly formed. It turns toward voices. It weeps clear fluid when anyone near you makes a vow. +1 Search by hearing. Anyone who holds your hand makes a Dread 1 check; it turns toward their mouth.
Hunger · Oathen
The Undervoice
A second voice has grown beneath yours, half a step lower, and sometimes it says your next word a moment before you do. Sometimes it says a different one. +1 Rites. Once per session the Carver may choose your next word for you, and you say it.
Hunger · Oathen
Figures Bite
You said you were frozen and there was frost on your lashes. You said you could eat a horse and your companions watched you look at one. Your figures of speech have teeth. Once per day the Carver may make one figure of speech you utter come true, in a small way. Witnesses check Dread 1.
Hunger · Oathen
Mouthing Along
You mouth other people’s words as they say them, and you know how their sentences end before they do. It makes you unbearable at dinner. It makes you very good at the Bench. +1 to oppose any Deceive. −1 Persuade: nobody likes being finished.
Hunger · Oathen
The Weight in the Throat
A pressure has settled behind your teeth, a heat in the throat like a sneeze held back, and only something heavy, said aloud and witnessed, eases it. If a day passes without you swearing an oath of Weight 1 or more, gain 1 Hunger at dusk.

The Fast: Orrum, the Host

The Unfed have no god in their blood, no Hunger track and no Regrowth. What they have is hunger itself, and a Host who has noticed. The Fast’s ten cards are not the god coming through the body. They are the body paying for the Refusal, and Orrum taking note of the bill.

When the Unfed draw. An Unfed Guest draws one card from the Fast’s stack the first time each story that their Want reaches 10 (Hollow) and they survive the night of the laid table, and the first time in their life their Pangs reach Wasting (7). The cards are permanent, as all Hunger cards are. A Blank who has never eaten a god draws nothing; they have nothing to pay with and nobody keeping count. A Returned no longer draws from the Fast: the Host has struck them off its list.

Hunger is honest. It writes its name on you, and it spells it right.
an Abstinent elder of Wanting
Hunger · Fast
White Fingertips
Two fingertips on your left hand go white and dead in a hard wind and never come back. You can hold them in a candle flame and feel nothing. Other Unfed see them and nod. +1 Endure against cold. −1 Filch.
Hunger · Fast
The Pegs
Your gums draw back from your teeth until they stand out like pegs on a board. One loosens, and you keep it in your wax tin, as is proper. Godeaters stare at your smile. +1 Intimidate. −1 Persuade with anyone who has never gone hungry.
Hunger · Fast
The Grandmother’s Recipes
You recite recipes at night that you were never taught, in an old woman’s warm voice: crackling, gravy with a little port in it, seed cake with caraway. Every one is from a table the Host has laid. +1 Lore about Orrum and his tables. Invitation checks against the smell of baking are 2 harder.
Hunger · Fast
Windfall Breath
Your breath smells of nail varnish and windfall apples: the smell of a body burning itself for warmth. Fatlanders catch it from across a yard and come over with a plate. Any Fatlander who smells it must resist The Hollow. Refusing them gains you +1 Want, once per day.
Hunger · Fast
Spelled Right
You wake to find your secret name, the one you were given for refusal and have never once said aloud, written in frost on the inside of your window in a fine round hand. Every letter is correct. Place cards bearing your name are Dire 22 to refuse, not Grim 18.
Hunger · Fast
The Hip Sores
Sores open on your hips where you lie on the bare floor, and they will not close: two raw wet coins of red that stick to your blanket. You learn to sleep sitting up against a wall, as the old ones do. You recover 1 less Flesh from any night’s rest. +1 Resolve against comfort offered as a bed.
Hunger · Fast
The Warm Ground
You feel the earth to the west of you as warm, as a hand feels a hearth across a room, and you know without looking which way the nearest laid table lies. You always know the direction of the nearest of the Host’s tables. Contagion checks for Walking West are one step harder for you.
Hunger · Fast
Gone Quiet
You stop feeling hungry. Not less: not at all. Every Unfed knows this is the worst sign, and you know it, and you feel nothing about it. From now on the Carver tracks your Pangs secretly, and tells you your state only when you reach Brink.
Hunger · Fast
Hair in the Comb
Your hair comes away in handfuls, and you keep it in a cloth so that nothing of you is wasted. One morning the cloth is empty. Somewhere ahead, on a laid table, your hair is woven into the white linen like a darn. When you find it, make a Dread 2 check.
Hunger · Fast
Light as Kindling
You weigh less than your coat. Wind leans on you. A friend lifts you over a stile without trying and goes pale, because it is exactly how the Seated come up out of their chairs. +1 Stealth and Athletics. −1 Labor. Your Flesh maximum falls by 1.

The Pall Deck

You don’t hear a village go. You hear it stop calling names through the wall, one house at a time.
— Lieutenant Sable Reef, Netwatch

The Pall is a community’s Fray: 0 to 20, with a Steadiness of 0 to 5 that holds it together, and a weekly Turn of 2d10 + Steadiness against 10 + the Pall. The Rules chapter gives the Carver d10 tables of events for each band. The Pall Deck replaces those tables with thirty-six weekly events, each with a rule that pushes the Pall up or down and a choice that puts the Guests in the middle of it. It is meant for a community the Guests are going to stay in long enough to love, which is to say, long enough to watch it go.

Drawing

  • Sort the deck into its three bands: Uneasy (Pall 5–9), Feverish (10–14) and Broken (15–19). Each band is twelve cards. A Whole community (0–4) draws nothing; it grieves what it has to grieve, and holds.
  • Once a week, roll the Turn. On a success, the community holds: the Pall falls by 1 and no card is drawn, except at Broken, where one card is drawn even on a success, as the Rules say.
  • On a failure, the Pall rises by 1 and the Carver draws one card from the community’s current band, then applies it. The card’s own Pall change is in addition to the 1 for the failed Turn.
  • On a Lack, the Pall rises by 2. Draw two cards from the band, read both, and play the worse.
  • On a Grace, draw nothing. The Pall falls by 2, and the Carver describes the decency the Guests witness, as the Rules describe.
  • A drawn card is set face-up in front of the Carver’s screen for the week it covers, so the players can see the shape of what the village is doing. Most cards ask the Guests to choose. Let them argue about it. A card that has run its course goes to the bottom of its band.
  • If the band changes mid-week because of a card, the next week’s draw is from the new band. A community that crosses into Lost at Pall 20 belongs to the god; put the deck away.
Carver’s Advice: Tragedy, Not Spectacle

Several cards in the Broken band describe people answering the Pull. Run them as the Rules chapter asks: the camera stays on the people left behind, never on the act. These cards never say how anyone was lost, and you should not either. Say what is missing: the made beds, the rinsed buckets, the cat that needs feeding, the hand that let go. Give the grief room. Check in with your players before you bring out the Broken band, and after. If anyone at the table needs a card set aside, set it aside, and draw again.

A village has a Fray the same as a man. The difference is that a man can be held down till dawn.
Sister Wren Abbotsley of the Hanging Abbey, in a letter to the Netwatch

Uneasy (Pall 5–9)

Rumour, locked doors, quarrels. The community still looks like itself in daylight. These are the cards of the first cracks.

Pall · Uneasy
The Well Tastes Wrong
Someone says the common well tastes of salt, or iron, or a god, and by evening half the street is carrying water from a stream a mile off. Nobody has tested it. Nobody wants to. Pall +1. If a Guest drinks from the well in public and nothing happens, Pall −1. If something does, Pall +2.
Pall · Uneasy
Who Saw the Tall Man
A rumour runs that a tall, stooping figure was seen at dusk looking in at windows, its warm breath fogging the glass, counting. Three people swear to it. Two of them were not there. Pall +1. If the next card drawn is Feverish, it is a shared Seeming of this figure, whatever the card says.
Pall · Uneasy
The Red Door
The house where last month’s Break happened had its door painted red, by nobody. This week a second door is red. Then four. The painters are copying something they do not understand. Steadiness −1 while the painting continues. Catching a painter: Eye + Search, Hard 14. Each painter is someone the village trusts.
Pall · Uneasy
The Celebrant Stops
The village’s Celebrant does not hold the rite this week. He stands at the altar a long time and then says he no longer knows who is listening, and goes home. No rite this week can lower the Pall unless a Guest leads it: Tongue + Rites, Hard 14. Success: Pall −1, and Steadiness +1 for the season.
Pall · Uneasy
Bread Under the Boards
A family is found hoarding: flour, salt-fish, and a side of meat whose provenance nobody asks, under the floorboards. By nightfall three other families have started their own. Pall +1. The next feast lowers the Pall only if the hoards are shared out. Persuading the hoarders: Tongue + Persuade, Hard 14.
Pall · Uneasy
The New Words
The children’s counting game in the square has changed its words. It counts houses now, and the rhyme ends on one of them. The children do not know who taught it to them. Guests who hear it to the end make a Dread 1 check. The house it ends on is the subject of the next Broken card, if one is ever drawn.
Pall · Uneasy
The Denunciation
An old man denounces his neighbour to the Netwatch, the Wakers, the Board or the Bench, as Tenanted, or blinking, or Seasoned, or forsworn. His evidence is that she has been kind to him lately. The Guests are asked to deliver her. Doing so: Pall −1, and they owe the village nothing. Refusing: Pall +1, and the authorities hear of it.
Pall · Uneasy
Supper in the Barn
A preacher arrives (a Deepener, a Bedded sister, a Second Helping brother, a Finisher) and holds a supper in the long barn. Warm bread. Kind words. Twelve go. A cult forms with Hold 1 over 1d6 households. Each week it is not opposed, Pall +1 and its Hold rises by 1 on one household.
Pall · Uneasy
A Quarrel Over a Spade
Two old friends come to blows over a borrowed spade. One loses an eye. Neither can say, a day later, how it started, and both are sure the other is not himself. Pall +1. A Guest who sits them down together (Tongue + Persuade, Hard 14) cancels it. Fail, and both men share a Derangement for a week.
Pall · Uneasy
The Cellar
A family moves its oldest member into the cellar and puts a bolt on the outside. They will not say why. At night something down there sings the old grace, perfectly, with every name in it, and one more name that nobody can hear clearly. Pall +1. A Guest who goes down checks Dread 2.
Pall · Uneasy
Politely, Please Go
The elder comes to the Guests’ lodging with his hat in his hands and asks them, very politely, to leave. Things started when they arrived. He is sorry. He weeps a little. If the Guests go, the community’s next Turn is at −2. If they stay, Pall +1, and every Haggle in the village is Hard for the rest of the season.
Pall · Uneasy
The Widow’s Loaf
A widow who has lost everyone bakes for the whole street, and leaves a loaf on each step, and asks nothing. People eat it and cry and then come out of their doors and talk. Pall −1. Note her name. If she is ever lost to the Pull or to violence while the Guests are here, Pall +3.

Feverish (Pall 10–14)

Shared Seemings, witch-hunts, scapegoats. Contagion checks in the community are at Dread 3 and cults gain +2 to Hold. These are the cards of a place that has stopped trusting its own eyes.

Pall · Feverish
The Table in the Square
The whole street wakes at the second bell and goes to its windows, and sees a tall figure laying a long white cloth in the square, and a chair pulled out. At dawn there is nothing. Everybody saw it. Pall +1. Each Guest makes a Dread 2 check; on a failure at Fray 5+, they share the Seeming as a Derangement for a week.
Pall · Feverish
She Is Not My Wife
A man stands in the square and says his wife has been replaced. She eats differently, he says. She sleeps on the wrong side. By evening four husbands agree about their own. The women are locked in the chapel. Pall +2. The Guests must judge. Freeing the women: Pall −1, and the husbands now say the Guests are impostors too.
Pall · Feverish
The Scapegoat
The village chooses someone to blame: a Blank, a foreigner, the Seamer’s apprentice, one of the Guests. There is no evidence. There does not need to be. Pall +1 each week the scapegoat stays among them. If they are harmed, Pall +2. If a Guest takes their place, Pall −2, and that Guest is not safe here.
Pall · Feverish
They Came Out Singing
The preacher’s barn holds thirty now. They come out at dawn singing in thirds, arms linked, and do not stop for a day. Their children sing too. The cult gains Hold +1 on every household it has touched. Driving out its leader justly: Pall −2. Killing the leader: Pall +2, and a martyr.
Pall · Feverish
The Hat
The village begins drawing lots, at night, for something it will not name. Every household puts a name in a felt hat. One of the Guests’ names is in the hat; nobody will say who put it there. Pall +1. If the Guests do not learn what the lot is for within the week, the next card is drawn from the Broken band.
Pall · Feverish
For Their Own Good
A story arrives from the next village: a house burned with a family in it, for their own good, because the god was in them. On Tuesday someone here tries the same, and is stopped by the smell of oil in time. On Friday, someone else. Pall +2. Finding who poured the oil: Eye + Search, Grim 18.
Pall · Feverish
Chalk on the Lintel
The Guests come home to find a sign chalked on the lintel of their lodging: a plate with a bite out of it. By the next morning it is on every door they have visited. Pall +1. Every NPC in the village now treats the Guests at Hold 0 or worse. Washing the chalk off is taken as a confession.
Pall · Feverish
The Invented Punishment
A woman confesses in the square to eating her husband’s portion in Lack. The crowd invents a punishment on the spot: her hands are pressed to the bakehouse oven door, and held there, while she screams the grace. Pall +2. Witnesses check Dread 2. Intervening turns the crowd: a mob, Threat 2, Flesh 30.
Pall · Feverish
The Elder Has Been Spoken To
The village elder announces at the morning count that the god has spoken to him in the night, and it told him what it wants, and it was very reasonable. He will tell everyone on Sunday. Pall +2 unless the Guests expose him before then (Tongue + Persuade, Hard 14, against a crowd that wants him to be right).
Pall · Feverish
Grace Said Over the Miller
They find the miller at the crossroads at dawn, sitting at a trestle, his chest opened and his heart set on a plate in front of him, a fork laid straight beside it. Seven candles. Someone said grace. Pall +2. Dread 3 to see. The killers are the village’s most respected; learning it is Eye + Search, Grim 18. Exposing them justly: Pall −2.
Pall · Feverish
Dusk Mob
At dusk a crowd forms with no leader and no object, torches and cleavers, and walks one way and then the other, looking for something to happen to. Pall +1. A Guest who gives the mob an object decides what happens tonight. A Guest who sends it home (Tongue + Intimidate, Grim 18) lowers the Pall by 1.
Pall · Feverish
The Bell Rung for the Living
Someone rings the passing-bell at midnight, the long slow strokes for the dead, and keeps ringing: one stroke for each person in the village. Eighty-one strokes. The village has eighty. Pall +1. Everyone counts. Every Guest makes a Dread 2 check. Nobody can find the ringer. The rope is warm.

Broken (Pall 15–19)

Clusters of loss; the Pull goes through the streets. At Broken a card is drawn every week, even on a successful Turn. These are the cards of a community that is losing people to the god faster than it can mourn them. Run every one as tragedy.

Pall · Broken
Four Houses
The morning count goes unanswered on four houses. Their doors are open, their beds made, their bail-buckets and blink-books and ration-cloths set out neatly on the steps. Nobody saw them go. Pall +2. Dread 3, Dread 4 if the Guests knew them. Guests at Fray 5+ check Dread 2 or take the Pull as a shared Derangement.
Pall · Broken
The Hand That Let Go
A family answered the Pull together, holding hands and singing a nursery song. The eldest son, a man of twenty, let go of the hand and came back. He sits on his parents’ step and has not spoken since. Pall +2. Any Guest who sits with him a week: Pall −1, and 1 Fray to that Guest each day.
Pall · Broken
The Procession
The Celebrant leads a procession toward the god’s place, singing. Half the village follows. The other half has barricaded the road, and some of them are holding their own grown children back by the coat. The Guests choose a side. Holding the procession is a scene: use the Holding On rules for each of 2d6 people.
Pall · Broken
Please Feed the Cat
The midwife is gone, the one whose whole life was keeping people alive. A note in a careful hand on her table asks someone to feed the cat. Her bag is packed for a birth that is due tonight. Steadiness −1 permanently, unless a Guest with Stitching 2 or more takes her place for a season.
Pall · Broken
Dressed for Dinner
The graves are opened in the night, and the village dead are sat at a long table in the square, dressed in their best, their hands arranged on the cloth. Nobody will say who did it. Everybody’s hands are dirty. There is one more chair than dead. Pall +1. Dread 3. Reburial with a rite: Pall −1d3.
Pall · Broken
The Garland
The council votes, by the old law, to offer the god what it wants. A young woman volunteers. They walk her to the god’s place with a garland and a hymn. Next week nothing has changed. The god did not notice. Pall +3. Steadiness −1. Each Guest who did not try to stop it gains 1 Fray.
Pall · Broken
A Small Kind Gift
Someone the Guests liked, helped, perhaps saved, is gone in the night. On the Guests’ sill they left a gift: something small and kind and terrible, wrapped in a clean cloth. Dread 4. The Carver chooses the gift from that person’s life. Pall +1. Burying them without a body lowers it again.
Pall · Broken
Names at the Door
A rumour runs that the Guests can stop it. By morning a crowd stands at their door, begging, quietly, each with a name to give them: a son, a wife, a neighbour. Each name a Guest accepts is a promise. Each kept by the story’s end: Pall −1. Each broken: 1 Fray to that Guest, and the name comes back at a Visitation.
Pall · Broken
Not My Children
A mother insists all her children, grown and small, are impostors. Three neighbours agree about their own. They bring the children to the Guests in their coats with their bundles and ask them to take them away. Pall +1. Taking them: Pall −1, and the Guests now travel with 2d6 frightened children. Refusing: the Carver decides.
Pall · Broken
The Losers of the Vote
The surviving elders vote, solemnly and by the old law, to give the god what it wants. The vote is not unanimous. The eleven who voted against are locked in the chapel so they cannot leave. The key is with the Celebrant. Pall +2. Freeing them is theft under the village’s law. Leaving them is not forgiven.
Pall · Broken
A Quiet Week
Nothing happens. For a week, nothing at all. People are polite. Then a Cutwright arrives with a ledger and asks the Guests where they are going next, and writes it down. No change. The next village down the road begins at a Pall equal to half of this one’s.
Pall · Broken
The Rite for Everyone
The survivors decide, without the Celebrant, to hold one rite for all the named dead at once. It takes all night. Every name is said. Somebody has to say the names nobody else can. If the Guests help, Pall −1d3 and the next Turn cannot fail. If they do not, the rite falls apart at midnight: Pall +1.

The Tablenight Deck

Never answer a knock on a licked-clean night. Never answer it twice.
— Rim innkeepers’ rule

Tablenight is the longest night of Lack and the anniversary of the Gorging, and every land keeps it differently: the banquet the Kept cannot taste, the fast no Fatlands village has ever finished, the west door unbarred, the lamps put out for a minute, the doors propped wide, the twenty-four silent hours of the canyons, the Unfed standing outside with their backs to every door while the table is laid in every house, and on the Rim Road, at every inn, one extra chair set at the table and turned to face the wall. The Tablenight Deck is thirty cards that exist for this one night. It lives in its own box. It comes out at dusk and goes back at dawn, and between Tablenights nobody touches it.

The Night in Five Watches

Run Tablenight as a session of its own, or as the long middle of one. Divide the night into five watches: Dusk, First Dark, the Gorging Hour (midnight), the Small Hours, and Dawn’s Edge.

  • At Dusk, shuffle the deck and deal one card face-down in front of each Guest. This is their Place. Nobody looks at it yet. A player may turn their Place face-up at any moment of the night they choose, and must at Dawn’s Edge if they have not. The card then happens to that Guest, there and then.
  • At each of the four later watches, the Carver turns up one card from the top of the deck for the whole table, reads it aloud, and plays it.
  • Land cards describe one land’s custom. If the Guests are not in that land, someone of that land is with them (at the inn, in the company, in the Guests’ own number) keeping it, and the card happens to them, and through them to everyone in the room.
  • The night’s own rules hold throughout: on Tablenight a chair pulled out within reach is an Invitation check at Dire 22, the Rim inns’ gates are shut from dusk to dawn, and nobody in a house says come in to anyone for any reason.
  • At dawn, every card goes back in the box, face-down, whatever it said. Effects that last say so on the card. Everything else ends with the light, or at least stops.
Carver’s Advice: The Longest Night

This is the session in which the campaign’s hints are allowed to stand a little closer to the lamp. The extra chair, the extra plate, the grace with a gap in it, the frost-writing with a line left blank: let the players notice them, and let them ask, and do not answer. Nothing on these cards states what the empty place is for. The innkeepers do not know. The Hostwatch have stopped asking. The deck is built so that the Carver never has to say anything more than what is on the card, and the players will do the rest themselves, at three in the morning, with the lamp low, and they will be close.

My knees went at about the third hour. My neighbours held me up till dawn. You don’t fall on Tablenight. You’d fall forward, and forward is in.
a Thinwick widow
Tablenight
The Extra Chair
The innkeeper sets one chair more than there are guests, and turns it to face the wall. Nobody sits near it. It is for the one who isn’t coming, she says, and changes the subject. A Guest who turns it round finds it facing the wall again within the hour. Until dawn, that Guest’s Teeth bite back on a 1 or a 2.
Tablenight
Do Not Say Come In
A knock at the shut gate. A voice outside, cold, tired, belonging to someone a Guest knows and loves and who cannot possibly be here, asks to be let in out of the snow. It asks by name. Any Guest who says “come in,” for any reason, to anyone, tonight: the Carver writes it down, says nothing, and keeps the note.
Tablenight
The Gate After Dusk
A woman and an old man stand at the shut gate in the snow, too late, freezing. They do not ask to come in. Opening it without a word is allowed; the Carver rolls a d6 in secret and never says what a 6 means. Leave them, and at dawn there are footprints only one way.
Tablenight
The Banquet They Cannot Taste
The Sallowreach custom: the living cook a banquet for their Kept dead, who cannot taste it, and everyone pretends. A Kept grandmother turns to a Guest and asks what the goose tastes like. Tell her. Tongue + Persuade, Hard 14: success, she weeps for joy and everyone at the table removes 1 Fray. Failure: she knows. Dread 2.
Tablenight
Nobody Reaches Sundown
The Fatlands keep a one-day fast on Tablenight, in penance. No village has ever reached sundown. Somebody always breaks first, and is cheered, and everyone eats. Each Fatlander present rolls Caul + Resolve, Hard 14, at each watch, or eats. The first to break is the night’s hero. The last loses 1 Flesh and gains 2 Hunger at dawn.
Tablenight
The West Door
The Brinehollow custom: a bowl of seawater at the head of the table, and the west door unbarred until dawn, for whoever comes home. In the small hours, wet footprints cross the floor to the bowl, and stop. Dread 2. At dawn the bowl is empty and the cloth beneath it dry. Every Brinehollower present resists The West at Hard.
Tablenight
One Minute of Dark
The Vigil custom: every lamp put out for a single minute, everyone holding hands in the dark and counting aloud together to sixty. At fifty-eight there is one voice too many. At sixty it does not stop. Every Vigilant present makes a blink check at Hard. Everyone else makes a Dread 2 check. Light the lamps: count the hands.
Tablenight
Every Door Wide
The Cradlewrack custom: every door in the house propped open until dawn, so that nothing can be said to have broken in. At First Dark, something comes in. It has not broken anything. It is sitting in the kitchen. The Carver decides what it is. It must be let stay until dawn, by the custom. Dread 2 for anyone who goes to look.
Tablenight
The Silent Day
The Oathen custom: twenty-four hours without a sound, the only day the canyon-folk feel safe. Tonight, anything said aloud in the room is heard by everyone and witnessed by the god. Every word spoken aloud before dawn binds its speaker as a Weight 1 oath, read in its most literal sense.
Tablenight
Backs to Every Door
The Unfed custom: everyone stands outdoors from dusk to dawn, holding hands, backs to every door, while the table is laid in every house behind them. The smell makes people faint. You do not fall. Each watch, Gut + Endure, Hard 14, to stay standing. A Guest who falls falls forward, and makes an Invitation check at Dire 22.
Tablenight
Your Card
Beside your plate, a folded cream card, your name on it in brown ink the colour of dried gravy, in a hand that loved you. Spelled correctly. Unfed: Invitation check, Dire 22. Others: Caul + Resolve, Grim 18, or sit at the next table you see. Burning it does nothing.
Tablenight
The Old Grace
An old woman says the grace from before the Gorging, the one nobody knows. She names the Providers, seven of them. Then her lips move once more, on nothing, and she says amen. A Guest who listens for the missing word: Eye + Lore, Grim 18. Success: you hear it and lose it at once. 1 Fray. The Carver notes the date.
Tablenight
One Plate Too Many
At the Gorging Hour there is a plate in front of the chair that faces the wall. Clean. Polished. Nobody laid it. The innkeeper’s hands are shaking. Do not count the plates aloud. A Guest who counts them makes a Dread 3 check. A Guest who removes the plate finds it there again when they look back.
Tablenight
The Gorging Hour
At midnight, the hour the stories say the gods were eaten, every god in every blood on the Table turns over in its sleep at once. You feel yours roll toward the door. Every Guest with Cut 1 or more gains 1 Hunger. Every Unfed gains 1 Want. Every Blank, for one breath, hears seven heartbeats in the room that are not theirs.
Tablenight
Carried Bread
A stranger at the table, a Crumb-Runner by the look of her coat, takes a hard heel of bread from her own pack and breaks it and gives each Guest a piece, and says nothing. It was carried. It is safe. Each Guest who eats removes 2 Fray. An Unfed must refuse three times first, and does, and then accepts, and remembers.
Tablenight
The Chair Faces the Table
At Dawn’s Edge the extra chair is facing the table. Nobody turned it. It will not turn back: it is as if it were nailed to the floor, and it is not. The innkeeper sits down on the step and weeps. Nothing else happens. The Carver writes the inn’s name down. It matters later.
Tablenight
The Song Nobody Finishes
The inn sings the old feast-song of the longest night, the one with the ox and the barley in it. The last verse nobody knows. A traveller in the corner sings it, beautifully, in a voice like a warm kitchen. Everyone present removes 1 Fray. At dawn the traveller is gone. Nobody can remember the verse, or their face.
Tablenight
Frost on the Glass
In the small hours, writing appears in the frost on the inside of the window: the name of everyone in the room, in a fine round hand, one under another. Below the last name is a space the length of a name, and nothing in it. Dread 2. Wiping the window does nothing; it frosts again, the same.
Tablenight
The Eight-Sided Pin
A quiet couple at the next table wear the same small pin on their collars: a table, seen from above, with eight sides. They watch the extra chair all night with the expression of people waiting for a coach. Eye + Lore, Hard 14: you know it as the Second Table’s sign. They will answer one question, kindly, and then ask one.
Tablenight
The Night Is Hungry
Something in the long night wants your god to grow. If any Guest’s Hunger fills before dawn, they draw two Hunger cards instead of one and keep both, and their Regrowth still rises only by 1. The god took the long way round.
Tablenight
The Walker
Through the window, on the road, a figure in a nightshirt is walking west through the snow, barefoot, steady, singing under its breath. It is someone the Guests have met. Stopping them is a scene under the Holding On rules, in Lack, at night, outdoors. Letting them go: Dread 4 at dawn, when you know where they went.
Tablenight
The Turn at Dawn
If the Guests are in a community with a Pall, its Turn is rolled tonight, at dawn, whatever day of the week it is. On Tablenight a Grace lowers the Pall by 3 and a Lack raises it by 3. Draw from the Pall Deck as normal on a failure.
Tablenight
The Stall That Is Open
Every market on the Rim is shut tonight. One stall is open anyway: a clean white cloth, a smell of fresh bread, nobody behind it, and something on the cloth for each Guest. Taking it: draw a Market card for that Guest, and it is a Relic. Leaving it: it is in your pack at dawn.
Tablenight
The Dead Hear Better
On the longest night the dead are close. Every Oath on the Dead a Guest carries comes due a little. Each Guest with an unkept Oath on the Dead receives a Visitation before dawn, as the land’s rules describe. Any oath sworn on the dead tonight binds at +1 Weight.
Tablenight
The Last Red Ox
An old drover by the fire tells how his great-great-grandfather ate the last red ox on the ninth Tablenight and sang over it, and how his father wept, and how they all thought it was for the ox. Everyone who listens to the end removes 1 Fray. The drover asks the Guests, once, what they think it was really for.
Tablenight
Three, One, Three
