At the Gorging Hour, a knock on the inside of the wall: three, then one, then three. Then on the floor. Then on the underside of the table, under a Guest’s plate. Dread 2. A Cradlewracker present knows the knock and will not say what it means. Knocking back is a mistake, and the Carver may keep it.
Tablenight
The Longest Cold
The cold tonight is the cold of the ninth winter. The fire burns and gives nothing; the breath freezes on the blankets. Every Guest suffers −1 to all rolls until dawn unless they share warmth with someone. Those who do remove 1 Fray at dawn and are, for good or ill, closer.
Tablenight
A Lack Under the Plate
The Rim custom: a coin hidden under each plate, for luck in the year. Under yours is a lack that is wrong. It tastes of nothing and it is warm. Eye + Lore, Grim 18: it is Blank bone, and somebody was killed for it. Spending it is Dread 1. Keeping it brings you a dream of whose it was.
Tablenight
The Visitor at the Head of the Table
In the small hours, a Guest wakes and sees a tall shape at the head of the table, stooping under the beam, laying the cloth very gently so as not to wake anyone. It looks up. Invitation check, or Caul + Resolve for the non-Unfed, at Dire 22. Success: it apologises, and is gone. Failure: you are sitting down.
Tablenight
The Chair Turned to the Wall
Lay this card face-down at the empty side of the table, beside the extra chair. Nobody reads it again tonight. Nobody touches it. At dawn, look at it. If it is face-up, nobody turned it. Put it back in the box with the others.

The Market Deck

If it is cheap, it is false. If it is dear, it is false and you paid for the privilege.
— Lowmark Spur proverb

The Rim Market is the Table’s great leveller: every land’s money, every land’s goods, every land’s lies on one long road. The Rim Market chapter gives the rules for Availability, Counterfeit Goods, Taint and Relics. The Market Deck is what happens when those rules meet a purse. It holds thirty-six surprises in four suits: Counterfeit (twelve cards: the thing is not what it was sold as), Taint (eight: the thing is exactly what it was sold as, and something more), Relic (eight: the thing knows you), and Seller (eight: the problem is the person behind the counter).

Drawing

  • When to draw. The Carver draws one Market card, secretly, whenever a Guest buys from a stall nobody can vouch for: any stall on a Lack day, any black market, Cure-Sellers’ Lane at Gristmoot, anything behind the stockyards after Last Bell, any relic from any dealer. Draw also when a Haggle roll comes up a Lack, and once for the company on any Moot-day, whether or not they buy, because the market will find them.
  • Spotting it. Before money changes hands, a suspicious Guest may roll Eye + Craft (for goods) or Eye + Lore (for relics, coin and godflesh) against the item’s Availability difficulty, as the Counterfeit Goods rules say. On a success, the Carver shows the card: the Guest sees the trick and may walk away, and the card goes to the bottom of the deck. A Helping shows the card and who is behind it. Seller cards are spotted with Eye + Instinct instead.
  • Playing it. If the card is not spotted, the Carver keeps it face-down behind the screen, and plays it at once or, better, at the worst moment within the same story. Most counterfeits are discovered later. That is the point of them.
  • Not every card fits. If the drawn card cannot apply to what was bought, hold it and play it on the next purchase it does fit. If the Guests leave the market with a card unplayed, it follows them: the Carver may play it on anything they bought in that town.
  • The honest stall. One card in the deck is an honest stall. It is the cruellest card in the deck, in its way. Read it carefully.
Whose Bones?

Many Market cards concern coin. Remember that the lack is salt-cured bone, and that a character who has studied the grain (Grim 18 Eye + Lore, once in their life) knows which coins in their purse were people. Such a Guest makes a Dread 1 check the first time they pay for a meal with a coin they know was a person, and after that, as the Rim Market chapter says, they stop counting. Market cards that put a person’s bone in a Guest’s purse should remind the player of that, and then let them spend it. Everybody does.

Every fake on the Rim is real somewhere. That is how you can tell the good ones.
Mister Cutlery, closing his case

Counterfeit

Market · Counterfeit
Sweating Change
Your change is perfect: good weight, true bite. A week later the coins are greasy and grey, and your purse sweats, and smells faintly of the fen, and flies follow you. Kept bone. Spot it fresh: Eye + Reckoning, Hard 14. Pass it knowingly and the Company takes your thumb.
Market · Counterfeit
The Coin That Grows
One lack in your change is a hair thicker than it was. By next month it will not fit the string. It is Wrack bone, cut from a Part, and it is still growing, slowly, toward something. Spot it: Eye + Reckoning, Hard 14. Kept for a season, it grows a tiny knuckle. Nobody will take it.
Market · Counterfeit
Horn and Hoof
Half the coins you were paid are horn, pressed and dyed, too light in the hand. Touched with a hot needle they stink of a burnt stable. Spot it: Eye + Reckoning, Routine 10. Discovered at the next inn, the innkeeper calls the wardens before you can explain.
Market · Counterfeit
It Passed a Bite
Brine-soaked chalk, cut and cured until it tastes right. It passes a merchant’s bite. It fails a rain. The first shower turns your purse to white paste running down your leg. Lose the value. In Oathen, where it rains once a year, it buys you anything until it does.
Market · Counterfeit
A Fathom Short
The Netwatch night-rope is proved hemp, true knot, Ropewalk-stamped. It is also a fathom shorter than it says, measured with a Brinehollow wife’s forearm, which is shorter than a Netwatch man’s. The first night it is tied to something far off, it does not reach. The Calling roll that night is Hard regardless.
Market · Counterfeit
Sweet Water
The Purgation emetic, sealed with a brown thumbprint, is sugar-water with a pinch of mustard. It makes you retch a little and feel virtuous. It removes nothing. The Hunger from the Tainted meal you took it for stays. You learn this the next time you Partake.
Market · Counterfeit
The Note on a Dead Man
A sworn note, Tacit paper, backed by the issuer’s body, at a third of face value. The issuer died last Carving. The note is perfectly good. It can be redeemed for one thing: his body, which the bearer may claim from the Witnessing Vaults, and must then house, feed the candles of, and keep.
Market · Counterfeit
The Wax Is Tallow
The Unfed wax tin is tallow scented with pine, and in the warmth of a nostril it melts, and the smell of bread comes straight through it. The next Invitation check against a smell of baking is at +4 Difficulty. An Unfed who learns who sold it will walk a hundred miles to say so, three times.
Market · Counterfeit
A Thumb on the Scale
The seller weighs honestly, with an honest scale, and you watch him do it. His left thumb is a Kept thumb sewn on in Lastgate, and it rests on the pan, and it is heavier than it looks. Everything bought here was a fifth short. Eye + Search, Hard 14, to see the stitches. He is very sorry.
Market · Counterfeit
The Hollow Bit
The iron bit is iron only on the outside. Inside is soft pine. Your swearer’s jaw closes on it in the night with a crunch like a biscuit, and something is said, aloud, in the dark, before you reach the room. The Carver writes the oath. Weight 3. It binds.
Market · Counterfeit
Cut Lamp Oil
Lamp oil cut with fen-water. It burns well for an hour and then gutters and spits and goes out, without warning, at about the third bell. In the Vigil, everyone in the room makes a blink check at Hard when the light dies. Elsewhere, it is only dark.
Market · Counterfeit
Ossel’s Knucklebones
Sold as the god’s own knucklebones, wrapped in grey silk. They are a pig’s, boiled and greyed with lye. The Finishers who bought the last set found out on the threshold of a Hush. They do nothing. The Finishers want their money back from whoever holds them now.

Taint

Market · Taint
The Good Sausage
The best sausage you have ever eaten, sworn safe on the cook’s mother’s bones. It is Fatlands field-meat, boiled grey to hide the marbling. Taint 2 Hunger. You discover it when you cannot stop: Caul + Resolve, Hard 14, to leave the second one on the plate.
Market · Taint
Grandmother Honey
Dark honey in a stoneware crock, at a great price, taken from hives kept on the flank of a Brink-Laden grandmother in the Fold. It tastes of a long life ending. Taint 1 Regrowth (Ummer). Whoever eats it dreams of being a warm field, and of a hand feeding them, kneeling.
Market · Taint
Grey Salt
Fine grey salt, sold for curing, very cheap. It was boiled out of Brinehollow bail-water, coughed up at dawn by the Called. Your cured meat tastes of the deep. Taint 1 Regrowth (Dromm) per week of eating it. Those who eat it begin, at dusk, to face west.
Market · Taint
The Whimpering Candle
A fat yellow candle, beautifully made. When it is lit it gives a small sound, almost too low to hear, like someone trying not to cry in the next room. It is Kept tallow. Dread 2 to burn it, Dread 1 after the fifth night. A Sallowreacher knows whose it was.
Market · Taint
Wool That Grew in a Night
A red highland scarf, very warm, very soft, knitted from a fleece that grew in a single night. Wearing it, you leave doors open behind you and do not notice. Taint 1 Regrowth (Vey) each week worn. In the lining, a shearer’s hand has been sewn in, and in the cold it holds yours.
Market · Taint
Rouse, Cut With Lint
Strong rouse at a good price. The cutting agent is lint swept from the Dormitory floor, from under the rows. It keeps you awake. It also lets you see the long room, at the edge of your eye. Taint 1 Regrowth (Iss). Each dose, Dread 1: someone in the room is lying down who is not there.
Market · Taint
Slate Tea
A smoky canyon tea, brewed from a lichen scraped off the walls of the Witnessing Vaults. It settles the stomach. For a day afterward your words come back to you half a second late. Taint 1 Hunger (Tolm). Anything you promise while it is in you binds at Weight 1, whether you meant it or not.
Market · Taint
Warmer on Your Side
An ordinary Rim loaf from the Bakers’ Mile, still warm. It stays warm. It is warmer on the side facing you. Somewhere in the dough is a single crumb picked off a laid table. Dread 2 for an Unfed who handles it, and an Invitation check, Hard 14, to put it down.

Relic

Market · Relic
The Finger Points
In a jar on the back shelf, a grey nine-jointed Hand-line finger, still cold. As you pass, it turns in the brine, slowly, and points at you, and stays pointing. It was someone in your line. Buy it (1,200 lacks) and it closes one thing for you, once. Leave it and it is sold to someone who wants to know where you are.
Market · Relic
The Jar Says Your Name
A jar of Tenanted brine, sold as a curiosity. Hold it to your ear and it is talking, very slowly, like a hull settling. It is saying your name. It has been saying it since before the stall opened. Dread 2. Taint 3 Regrowth (Dromm) if bought. It knows where you were born, and the tide on that night.
Market · Relic
It Fits
On the bit-seller’s board, a silver bit dented with tooth-marks from the inside. Out of curiosity you set it to your mouth. It fits exactly. The tooth-marks are yours, chip and gap and all. Dread 2. The bit-seller will not say where he got it. He will not sell it to you either. He is afraid to.
Market · Relic
The Ear Comes Home
A jar in a Seamer’s booth: an ear, perfectly kept, with a Lying-In tag sewn to the lobe. The Tally number on the tag is yours. You were never told you surrendered anything. Dread 3 for a Cradlewracker. Bought, it hears for you through walls. It also hears you.
Market · Relic
In the Box of Oddments
A box of oddments, one lack the lot: buttons, a thimble, a bent spoon, and a small folded card in cream stock with your name on it in a fine round hand. A place card. It is not for sale; it was always yours. Invitation check, or Caul + Resolve for the non-Unfed, at Grim 18.
Market · Relic
Someone’s Teeth
A set of Granny Cracknel’s matched teeth, milled from toothed wheat, labelled with a name you know. Held in the mouth for a night, they give the last meal and last sight of the person they were matched to. Taint 1 Hunger, Dread 2. The last sight is your face.
Market · Relic
It Waves
A thief’s Kept hand on a cork board, still twitching, sold to pick locks. As you pass, it lifts and waves, the little two-finger wave of someone you knew in another town, who always waved like that. Dread 2. It picks locks at Threat 3. It does not want to be with anyone but you.
Market · Relic
The Pillow
A Dormitory pillow, smuggled down off the plateau, sold for sleepless nights. It smells of clean linen and, underneath, of someone you loved who is Counted. Sleeping on it removes all Weariness. You dream of their bed, and they are restless in it, and glad to see you.

Seller

Market · Seller
The Seller Is Not Alive
The old man behind the counter has not breathed all morning. His hand, when you take the change, is cold and soft as dough. His wife does the talking and works his arm. The licence is in his name. Say nothing and she weeps with gratitude. Say something and the Company seizes the stall, and her.
Market · Seller
In Your Coat
The pedlar is, unmistakably, you: your face, your walk, your scar, your coat. He pays exactly what you ask without haggling and walks away into the crowd. You are not wearing your coat. Eye + Instinct, Grim 18, to see which way he went. Nobody else noticed anything at all.
Market · Seller
Priced in Fathoms
The rope-wife is kind and cheerful and drives a fair bargain. Under her voice, a beat slow, a second voice is pricing everything in fathoms, and in names. She is Tenanted. She sells only to those heading west. If you buy, the second voice says thank you, and means something by it.
Market · Seller
The Face on the Mould
The pie-man’s newest mould is a face you know: the thin traveller who was weighed in at the gate just ahead of you yesterday. The pie-man says a man sells him moulds, behind the stockyards. Eye + Search, Hard 14, to find where. Dread 2. He winks and gives you a pie.
Market · Seller
The Steward Buys
A tall, stooping servant in a clean apron wants to buy something of yours. He pays in warm bread, the best you have ever smelled, and will not take no three times, only twice. Unfed: an Invitation check at Hard 14. Anyone who sells to him finds a place laid for them that night.
Market · Seller
For My Father
A girl, alone, very polite, has followed a thing you bought for a hundred miles. Her father was the one who sold it, or the one it was cut from. She has his eyes. She has his money. She would like it back. She offers twice what you paid. If you refuse, she waits outside your lodging, politely, every night.
Market · Seller
The Thumb-Jar
The factor’s clerk bites your coin and goes pale and calls the wardens. It is false, and you did not know, and the Company does not care. The thumb-jar for this year is nearly full. Talk your way clear: Tongue + Persuade, Grim 18. Fail, and it is ten times the face value and a thumb.
Market · Seller
The Honest Stall
Everything here is genuine, untainted, fairly weighed, and cheap. The seller is a quiet young woman with clear eyes who will not eat in front of you. She is a Blank. Buy anything at half price. Tomorrow the stall is empty and the Board’s bounty-men are asking who bought from her.
Who’s buying? Nobody’s buying. Who’s selling? Nobody’s selling. What’s it cost? Everything, love. Mind the gutter.
patter behind the rendering yards, Sated
Part Five
The Lexicon
Table-speech and its seven dialects, A to Z.
Chapter 11

The Lexicon of the Table

A–K
A word is a portion. Before you use it, ask which part of the meal it came from, and who was left with the bones.
— Oswy Larkspur, Cutwright, Keeper of the Word-Stacks at Quire, preface to the Ninth Recension of the Dictionary of Table-speech, 641 A.G.

On Table-speech

Every people on the Table speaks one tongue and swears it speaks seven. Both claims are true. Table-speech is older than the Gorging, older than the Lack, older than the carvings with the eighth place chiselled out; the tally-priests of the Bone Dole wrote their lists in it, and so, six centuries later, does the factor who chalks the price of rope at Gristmoot. A fen porter and a canyon notary can understand one another perfectly. It is only that one of them will take an hour to say what the other refuses to say at all.

The College has kept this dictionary since 140 A.G., when the first Copyists found that they could not trace a bloodline without first knowing what its grandmothers had meant by portion, board and company. It has been revised nine times. Each revision is longer, because the Regrowth makes words faster than the College can file them, and each is sadder, because a language is a record of what its speakers needed to say, and lately they have needed to say some terrible things. What follows is the first half of the Ninth Recension, abridged for the road. It gives Common usage first, then the dialects, then the cant of trades, thieves, children and the dying. Where a word is not printed, that is not an oversight.

Of the Root

Every student begins with orr-. From it come orren, to eat; orrel, to worship and also to give back; orrish, a shared meal; and Orrum, the Host, the one at whose board. In the oldest stratum of Table-speech there is no way to say I worship that does not also say I eat, nor any way to say I eat that does not admit you are at somebody’s table. Scholars insist the words always shared a root. The Purgation insists this is the whole problem. The College insists on nothing, in print, and notes only that the root turns up in places it has no business being, as the reader will find under abhorr, corrish and horror, and that it is pronounced at the back of the throat, rolled, the way a person clears the throat before saying grace.

How Oatheners Conjugate

The canyon dialect has the richest verb in the language and the fewest occasions to use it. Where Common has one present tense, Oathen has five moods, each a door out of the sentence. The Bare is the plain statement (I come), used aloud only by Sayers, by the dead in Testimony, and by fools once. The Exit adds -ra, rendered in Common as if able (I come-ra). The Intended adds -ent, rendered as I now intend. The Hearsay adds -sed, rendered I am told, and is the mood of all gossip and most prices. The Weathered adds -wed, rendered barring weather, and covers death, illness, flood and the late Rain. They stack, outermost exit first: a canyon child says cumerentwed, I come, if able, as I now intend, barring weather, before she can say mother. A sentence with no exit at all is called naked and is treated as Common treats an obscenity. Oathen has, in addition, a Niche tense for speaking of the dead, who Testify; it is the past tense with every verb turned into a question (Did she keep it? Did she not?), so that nothing said over a body can be held to be a claim. Handtalk has no tense and no mood whatever. That is one reason it was held not to bind.

How the Unfed Decline

The Fast dialect declines its nouns by distance from the mouth. A thing you carried yourself takes the Carried case, marked -own (breadown, my-own-bread, safe to eat). A thing held out to you takes the Offered case, which can only be spoken negated (nay-bread, the bread I am not taking). A thing laid by the Host takes no case at all: the Unfed drop the noun and point with the chin (there is a — on the sill), and children are slapped for supplying the missing word. The verb to accept has no first-person present. Come in cannot be conjugated, only uttered, and is classed by Unfed grammarians as a curse and not a phrase. And the Decline, the threefold No, thank you, works as grammar: the first no is a particle of politeness, the second an emphatic, the third a closing; an offer made a fourth time is answered in what the Fast calls, without smiling, the coat mood, after the proverb that the fourth no is a yes in a nicer coat.

The Seven Tells

A trained ear can place a speaker within a sentence. The fen drawl of Sallowreach never finishes a word: final consonants are left hanging, so that May you finish comes out May you finis’, a habit the College calls the open end. The Fatlander talks with a full mouth, literally and otherwise: vowels rounded by chewing, everything a diminutive (a little drop of gravy-kin), and praise always measured in weight. The Brinehollower’s voice is wet before the dawn bail and hoarse after it, and has a gargle in the back vowels called the salt-burr; the coast counts in fathoms even on dry land. The Vigilant speaks in long slurred runs between rouse-stammers and marks time in bells; to a Vigilant, a pause is a medical event. The highlander of Cradlewrack places a small catch, the knock, before any word beginning with a vowel, so as not to enter it unannounced. The Oathener is clipped, verbless where possible, and ends every sentence in an exit. The Unfed puts the negative first (No bread, thank you, none) and has no polite word for please, since asking is a form of accepting. And the Rim speaks Rimmish, a pidgin of all seven, which a factor can use to sell you rope in four dialects at once.

How to Read an Entry

Each entry gives the headword, its part of speech and where it is used (Common means everywhere on the Table), and then its sense, its story where it has one, and its use in a sentence, set in italics. Cross-references point to other headwords, some of which will be found in the second half of this dictionary, L to Z. The College has added a few notes for those who must use these words in company; where a word can get you killed, the entry says so. Where a word has a dangerous older form, the entry gives the newer. Use the new one.

There are two words for guest. Use the new one.
schoolroom correction, everywhere

The College keeps a short list of words that betray a speaker’s land at once, used by wardens, poachers, Reckoners and the Netwatch. A character passing as native of another land makes Tongue + Lore against Hard 14 whenever one comes up; a Lack means the slip is noticed by exactly the wrong person.

A

A.G. abbr., Common After Gorging: the count of years since the Night of Seven Tables, now standing at 641. The fen says it as one sound, ay-gee, and the canyons will not say it at all, since a date is a kind of claim. Before 0 A.G. there are no numbered years, only the nine of the Lack, which are counted backward and named for what failed in them. Born in four hundred A.G., dead in four hundred A.G., and still on the stoop. See Lack, the Long and Gorging.

abed adv., Vigil, obscene Lying down. In every other dialect abed means asleep or ill; on the Lid it is too filthy for the bell-sheets, and the Ordinances spell it a—d. Lovers whisper it. Wakers write it on charge sheets in red. Caught abed is the Vigil’s equivalent of caught in the act, and covers the same territory, and worse.

abhorr v., Common (old), Fast To refuse a meal that has been offered to you; to turn from the board. From ab-, away, and orr-, the board. In the Fast it is a verb of praise (she abhorred three times, and on the fourth they wed), and in every other land it has slid into meaning to loathe, which the Unfed take as proof that the Godeaters cannot tell disgust from good manners. The College’s etymology is disputed by the College. See Decline, the.

Abide n., Fast An Unfed given name, from the Refusal, meaning to wait without eating. Like all such names it is given on the day the infant first refuses something, usually the breast, which is why many Abides are three months old before they are anybody. Diminutive Abby, considered a little soft. See Abstain and Forbear.

Abstain n., Fast The commonest girl’s name in the Fast and the commonest insult in the Fatlands, where a right Abstain is any woman who leaves food on her plate. In the Fast the name is held by roughly one girl in nine, so that at any meeting of the Abstinent someone must specify Abstain-of-the-Lean-End or Abstain-who-wept. Get your elbows off the table, Abstain, there is no table.

Abstinent, the n., Fast The council of elders at Wanting who hold the Pantry and decide, by the simple act of leaving a name off a list, who will eat this winter. Members are addressed as Elder and never thanked, since thanks imply a gift. To be abstinented is Rim slang for being quietly starved by a committee, and is applied with relish to anyone denied a Company pension. See omission and Pantry.

abundance n., Fatlands A word the south uses for a field in which somebody’s grandmother has been Seated, since the crop is always heavy there. We’ve an abundance on the north slope means the family has lost its matriarch to the ground and gained a very good acre. The proper response is congratulation, and a small cake.

Admiralty n., Brinehollow The Tidal Admiralty: the navy that became a government, commanding four hundred warships standing on props in the mud. Hence admiralty (adj., Rim), describing any institution that drills daily for a world that has left it: the Court is very admiralty about the Hushes. A Brinehollow joke asks how many Admiralty captains it takes to sail a ship; the answer is all of them, and they are waiting.

afters n., Brinehollow, rude The Tenanted; what comes back after the sea has had its meal. Said in the Chapel Reach rouse-houses and never on the Mile in daylight, because the afters hear very well and are perfectly courteous about it, which is worse than if they were not. Her husband? He’s afters now. Brings her tea. See Tenanted, Passenger and Wreckwife.

aftertaste n., Common The memory a family keeps of the Kitchen Year; the thing in the house nobody mentions. Every old family has an aftertaste, and the Cutwrights can usually tell you what it is. They’re good people, the Strakes, but there’s an aftertaste. A family that has lost its aftertaste has forgotten what it did, and is held to be in danger of doing it again. See trading tables and Kitchen Year.

aftward adv., Sallowreach In the fen, after death, used of the Kept as other dialects use later in life: He took up the fiddle aftward and has been learning it two hundred years. A fen child asked what she wants to be aftward is being asked what trade she will follow once she has stopped breathing, which is the longer career by some centuries.

ague-salt n., Brinehollow Salt boiled from the bail-water of the Called on their last night ashore, believed to carry the pull and sold to the lovesick to make a sweetheart follow them. It does not make a sweetheart follow. It makes them stand at a west window. Illegal, cheap, and found in most wedding chests on the Mile.

aleuse n., Sallowreach (Pronounced ALE-yoos.) The interval in a fen tavern when the Kept patrons, who cannot drink, are brought a cup to hold for the sake of company and the living drink it for them. The custom is fond. The cups are refilled. The aleuse can last until morning, and a Kept regular in Weir Row has been holding the same pewter mug since 377.

aleway n., Rim The gutter that runs down the middle of the floor of the Groaning Board and every Fatlands-style common room, carrying grease, spilt gravy and worse to the drain. Gone down the aleway means wasted, ruined, or rolled out of the inn at closing by six men. See Groaning Board.

Already Counted adj. phr., Vigil Written off; as good as asleep. Originally said of a Vigilant who has been found lying down and carried to the Dormitory before their bed number is assigned; now said of any cause, love affair or ward of the Slope that has gone beyond help. Don’t bother nudging that one, he’s Already Counted. Said to a person’s face, it is the cruellest thing on the Lid short of sleep well. See Counted, the.

Ambrose’s beard n., Cradlewrack Anything that should get smaller and will not, or anything that is getting smaller and should not; from Ambrose, the Eldest Infant, born twelve years ago with a white beard and growing younger. The interval is Ambrose’s beard means that the pangs are shortening. Highland mothers say it, gently, of a child who is learning too fast.

anchor v. and n., Brinehollow To sleep tied, chained or weighted to the bed so that the Calling cannot walk you to the sea; the rope, chain or weight itself. Children are anchored to a parent’s wrist until seven. The great domestic tragedy of the coast is a rope cut in the night, and the great domestic comedy is the husband who comes home late and has to be anchored by a wife who is still angry. Anchor tight, love, and I’ll see you at the count. See Anchorite and rope, to take the.

Anchorite n., Brinehollow One of the order who chain themselves permanently to the cliff of the Hanging Abbey, so that the Calling can never take them. The Deepening calls them nails. Fishwives call any immovable old man an anchorite, especially at a dinner he will not leave. Father Ebb has held fifty-one years on the same rock, and says it is not the chain that holds him.

and let it stay phr., Cradlewrack The highland half of the common grace, said after Lack keep away over every meal, and by the crowd at the Tally-steps when a birth is read out as stays. It is the most hopeful phrase in the red hills and the most frequently disappointed. See Lack keep away and Questions, the Two.

ankle-biter n., Cradlewrack, children’s A Part, especially a hand, that has got loose and crawls along the floor of a house at night, gripping whatever it finds. Highland children say it as other children say bogey; highland parents do not correct them, because it is accurate. Feet up on the bench, there’s an ankle-biter in the Gorses’ scullery and it hasn’t been found. See Part and Gathered.

Annalow v., Rim, Fatlands To stop a thing with one word, completely, and in a way that suggests you know what was inside it. From Mistress Brisket Annalow of the Renderers’ Union, who can halt every barrel on the Rim Road by saying so. The factor tried to raise the toll and the drovers annalowed him. A barrel that has been annalowed is one nobody will now open, at any price. See Chute.

annex v., Oathen To put a terrible fact where nobody will be required to read it aloud. From the Clausewrights’ practice of placing awkward provisions in an annexed opinion, page thirty-eight or so, which the parties swear they have read and need not recite. The bride’s mother wanted the word “living” in the bed clause; the drafter annexed his reasons. In the Galleries, to say a family keeps an annex is to say it has a cellar.

Appetite, the n., Common The second stage of the Regrowth, between the Taste and the Course: the stage at which the body begins to want what the god wants and to do it without asking. In the fen it is the closing of lids; in the south, the eating of soil and hair; on the coast, the walking west; in the Vigil, the blink; in the highlands, the false labour; in the canyons, the compulsion to swear. She’s into her Appetite is said of anyone with a new and embarrassing habit, and a bit of Appetite of anyone in love. See Taste, the, Course, the and Want.

appleskin n., Fatlands The fine outer skin of an orchard fruit from the Bleeding Orchards, beneath which lies a layer of fat and, at the centre, a pit very like bone. As an endearment, a lover’s skin: my little appleskin. As an insult, someone who is thin on the outside and fat within, that is, a hypocrite of the Thin. Orchard-keepers peel appleskins with their teeth and do not, as a rule, look at the pit.

apron n., Cradlewrack A midwife of the Attendance, by the white apron of her office; also the Attendance as a whole. Send for the apron means that a birth has begun, or that someone is about to be judged, which in the highlands is the same summons. An apron without a knife is a midwife of the Late-faction. Children who see an apron in the lane go quiet and stand against the wall until it has passed. See Opinion, Second and Attendance.

Archprovost n., College The head of the Cutwrights’ College, keeper of the Master Concordance at Quire; there is only one, and she bears no mark of office because she is known. The present Archprovost has had the extra chair removed from every room in Quire, which junior Copyists are forbidden to remark upon and remark upon constantly.

Ardent n., Fast, shameful An old Unfed surname, once one of Orrum’s names, and now borne by families that would rather it were not. Welcome Ardent, who walks a mile ahead of the Host laying its tables, is the reason. To call an Unfed ardent in the adjectival sense, eager, is a deadly insult. Compare Blythe and Welcome.

arithmetic, the n., Brinehollow The Salt Assay’s forbidden finding that the volume of sea lost each year matches the number of the Tenanted. Doing the arithmetic on the Mile means drawing a conclusion the Admiralty has made illegal, and the phrase is said with a glance at the door. I’m not saying, I’m just doing the arithmetic. A clerk heard doing it aloud in an Admiralty office is reassigned to the far end of the pier.

arrears n. pl., Sallowreach The parts of a Kept relative that have come off and have not yet been restitched, pickled or sunk: a finger in the button-box, an ear in the vinegar crock, a jaw on the mantel awaiting the Seamer’s spring visit. Every fen house has its arrears and every fen landlord asks about them before letting a room. Gran’s arrears are in the hatbox, mind you don’t sit on them. See Keeping and Seamer.

as I now intend phr., Oathen The second of the canyon exits, rendered in grammar as the Intended mood: a promise that binds only what the speaker means at the moment of speaking, so that a change of heart is not a Breaking. It does not protect against the god’s reading of what one now intended, which is always more than one admits. I will love you, as I now intend is the canyon marriage vow in short, and the long form runs to forty pages. See exit and If able.

Ashby n., Fast An old Unfed surname from before the Gorging, meaning the farm by the ash trees, and now, after Lent Ashby rose from the Host’s table, a verb in the Hostwatch: to ashby, to get up from somewhere nobody gets up from. It is said of the impossible and never of anything good. He ashbied out of the Lean House, and now there’s a table laid wherever he sleeps.

ashmouth n., Fatlands, Common A member of the Thin, the outlawed fasters of the south, from their diet of water and ash. Fatland children are told that an ashmouth will kiss them and take their appetite away, and some of them wish one would. Lock the larder, there’s ashmouths in the hedge. The Thin, who have no fondness for jokes, use the word of themselves with a certain bony pride.

Ask me again phr., Fast The whole of an Unfed proposal of marriage, repeated over months by the proposer and answered by the beloved’s threefold No, thank you, until the fourth asking is made and taken. Children play at it in the Cold Yards with pebbles. Used elsewhere on the Rim for any courtship that goes on too long: Still at Ask-me-again with the cooper’s widow, are you? See Decline, the and coat mood.

Aspic, in phr., Fatlands, Rim Displayed, preserved, humiliated and still blinking. From Lady Aspic Dellamore’s gallery of rivals, set in clear jelly, garnished, and awake. The Board has the old Chairman’s son in aspic: a title, a window seat, and nobody listening. A Sated hostess who seats you facing the room where everyone can see you eat has put you in aspic.

Assay, the Salt n., Brinehollow The Admiralty office that measures the falling sea, whose figures are a state secret. To take the assay of something, on the coast, is to measure exactly how bad it is and then not say. A man who visits a doctor and comes home silent has taken his assay. See arithmetic, the.

Assembler n., Cradlewrack A member of the sect that collects Parts from every family in the highlands and joins them into one figure, eleven feet long, lying in a barn near Rudge. Their slogan, chalked on walls, is Every hand in the crock is somebody’s baby. To assemble a thing, in highland slang, is to make a whole of what should have been left in pieces: a marriage, an argument, a story. Don’t assemble it, Nan, let it lie. See Barn, the and Gathered.

assent-bone n., Oathen A knucklebone carried by the canyon poor and laid on a table in place of saying yes to a bargain, since a bone set down is held not to bind. Merchants of the Felt Market accept it. The Bench has never ruled on it, and since handtalk began to break, the price of a good assent-bone has doubled.

at the window phr., Vigil Gone somewhere that is not the room and not the street, for a whole watch, upright, eyes open, pinching one’s own wrist in a steady rhythm; returned with nothing but the bruise and a smell of clean linen. It is not sleep. The Wakers call it malingering; the Hourkeeper believes it is where the lengthening hours are going. Where’s Mam? At the window again. See blink and Seeming.

Attend v., Cradlewrack To be present at a birth as a midwife of the Attendance, with the right and duty of asking the Two Questions. The Attendance’s single vow is I will go into the room; nobody has been known to break it, though many have died keeping it. To attend a matter is to settle it finally and without appeal. I’ll attend to your brother is a threat in the red hills, and is meant as one. See apron.

Attendance, the n., Cradlewrack The order of midwives who rule the highlands: judges, physicians, priests and executioners in one apron. The Attendance has never called itself a government, which is why it has never fallen. See Attend, Opinion, Second and Lying.

Aubrey’s kick n., Cradlewrack A decision made by someone who cannot be seen, interpreted by someone who is tired. From Queen Dowager Sibyl Aubrey, who has carried the King Within for forty-four years and reports his kicks to the court: one for yes. Any order from on high whose source is doubtful: Is that the Attendance’s ruling, or is it Aubrey’s kick?

auditor n., Rim A Company assessor sent to price a loss. To be audited, in Bonded Hands’ slang, is to be costed by the Company and found more valuable as something else: a Bonded Hand who stole a platter and was audited is now on display at Treaty Stair. Reeve Calder Stokes, sent to price Brinehollow, is the Rim’s best-known auditor; the coast has begun to say he is being audited himself, since he tasted salt.

awake-and-sworn adj. phr., Vigil The formula with which every Vigil contract opens, certifying that the party was not in a blink when they signed. Contracts lacking it may be voided by anyone who can produce a blink-book entry for that bell. Hence, in common speech, genuinely meant: I love you, awake-and-sworn. See blink-book.

axe-morning n., Fast The dawn after Tablenight, when every Unfed household turns from the long cold standing, goes in, and breaks the table that has been laid in the house overnight. Every Unfed house owns an axe for no other purpose; it hangs by the door. Axe-morning is a day of quiet exhaustion and sweeping, of carrying out the splinters and the untouched food, and of counting who is not standing in the yard. Those not standing are usually found indoors, at the table, very happy.

aye-cough n., Brinehollow A short dry cough given in place of an answer at the morning count, when a neighbour calls a name through the wall and the one called has not yet bailed. It means still here, can’t speak. Silence means someone was Called. Two coughs means still here, but come round. A widow on the Mile can tell her whole street’s health by its aye-coughs. See count, the.

The College is sometimes asked why a dictionary needs nine recensions. Because every time we finish one, someone finds a new way to say they are hungry.
Oswy Larkspur, at the Inkhorn, Quire

B

bad day’s wage n. phr., Rim A human thigh-bone, among the coin-cutters of the Cure-House at Saltbridge, who get nineteen lacks from a good one. The phrase has crept out of the sheds into Rim speech for any profit that came out of someone: He inherited the farm, poor lad, a bad day’s wage. See bone-grain and shut-mouth.

bail v. and n., Brinehollow To cough up, at dawn and dusk, the salt water that fills a Brinehollower’s lungs from nowhere; the act and the water both. Children are taught to bail before they read. A good bail is a long wet heave over the bucket followed by a ragged first breath that tastes of the open sea. Bail first, talk after is the coast’s answer to every question asked before sunrise. Figuratively, to confess: Go on, bail it, what did you do? See bail-bucket, dry man and land-drowned.

bail-bucket n., Brinehollow The small tin or tarred-leather pail every Brinehollower carries at the waist-rope for bailing. Losing one is like losing your shoes. Sweethearts exchange them; to give a girl your bucket is to propose, and to take it back is the end. Bucketing, the confiscation of an offender’s bucket for a day and a night, is the coast’s punishment for slander, and a bucketed woman crawling door to door at dusk, gargling, with her hands out, is a sight every child on the Mile has seen.

bail-token n., Brinehollow A lead disc stamped with a bucket, given by the parishes to those who bail the infirm, good for a cup of sweet water at an Admiralty cistern. Small change on the coast. Not worth a bail-token is said of a man who will not get out of bed to help his neighbour cough.

Bait, the n., Common The third and illegal doctrine: that the gods wanted to be eaten, that the Lack was theirs, and that this is how gods breed, by being swallowed by a people and growing back through ten thousand bodies instead of one. Outlawed in four lands and gaining ground in all seven. On the coast it is called the Spawning. Its believers are Baiters to their enemies and nothing at all to themselves. See Theft, the and Gift, the.

Baiter n., Common, rude A believer in the Bait. Also, in Fatlands kitchens, a cook who seasons too well, as if to make the eater want more than is good for them. The College, which is dominated by quiet Baiters, does not include itself in the definition. Don’t let the Baiters at the Weeping Post hear you say “seed.”

bark soup n., archaic The food of the fifth and sixth years of the Lack, made of boiled inner bark, leather and belt. In the oldest songs it is the dish that grandmothers pushed across the table to the youngest child before they died. To push the bark soup means to give up one’s share so that someone younger may live, and is said in four lands with a particular grief. See Kitchen Year and eldest, to walk the.

Barn, the n., Cradlewrack The Assemblers’ Barn near Rudge: guarded, lamplit, warm, and long, where four hundred Parts from four hundred families have been fitted into one figure that breathes. Visitors are not shown the far end. The far end of the barn is highland slang for the place in any story that the teller will not go. What happened to your first husband, Marta? Far end of the barn. See Assembler.

Barren n., Cradlewrack A member of the Barren Order, who have had themselves cut so they can bear nothing, and preach that the kindest thing a person can do is start nothing. Their numbers grow with every pang. To go Barren is to give up on a project, a love affair or a grudge before it can begin. Highland mothers say a quiet child has a Barren look, and mean it fondly, and are frightened.

Barrows, the n., Fast The long chalk mounds on the hill at Hallowboard where those who starved at the Refusal lie, nine in ten of a whole people. The Unfed swear on them: By the ones who stood. A serious oath is sworn barefoot, standing in one’s own ancestor’s footprint in the trench. See ones who stood, by the.

Bed One n., Vigil The first bed in the Dormitory, in which Aveline Morne, a baker’s daughter, lay down on the First Night of 341 and did not rise, and whose lips have lately begun to shape words. Since Bed One means forever on the Lid, and to be Bed One is to be the first to fall in any disaster. Who’ll be Bed One? is the question asked at the start of a hard night shift, half joke. See Counted, the and Dormitory.

Bedded, the n., Vigil The heretics who preach that sleep is a homecoming, that the eye in the long room is kind, and that the city is three hundred years late. Their prophet looks rested, which on the Lid is the most suspicious thing a face can do. Don’t talk Bedded at me means don’t tell me it’ll be all right. See Lullaby, the.

Belch, the n., Fatlands The hot wind of Plenty that comes up from the south smelling of rendering. Belch days are good for curing and bad for marriages. A Fatland child born on a Belch day is said to be Belch-born: loud, hungry and impossible to embarrass. See Marbling and drip.

bell n., Vigil The Vigil’s unit of time, a quarter-hour struck by the city’s bells to keep it awake, and by extension any measure of a life on the Lid. Slope children are named for the bell they were born at: Pip Eleven-Bell, Rook Quarter-Bell. Which bell were you born at? is the first question at a Vigil hiring, since the Ward-Sergeants hold that it tells you how tired a person will be. What bell? is the Vigil’s what time is it, and the shibboleth that betrays a Vigilant abroad. See bell-sheet and long bell.

bell-sheet n., Vigil The printed news of the Vigil, run off at every first bell and posted at the Bonfires: entered Seemings, Dormitory admissions, rouse prices, Breakings of the Waking Laws. A Vigilant who says it was in the bell-sheet means that it is officially true, whether or not it happened. See Seeming and struck book.

bellyful n., Fatlands A unit of time, the interval between two of the five lawful meals, roughly a fifth of the waking day. I’ll be a bellyful means I’ll be back before the next meal, and two bellyfuls late is very late indeed. A Fatland prisoner’s sentence is reckoned in bellyfuls. Abroad, Fatlanders get hopelessly lost in other lands’ clocks, since nowhere else is anyone hungry on schedule.

Bench n., Oathen, Brinehollow In the canyons, the Bench of Clauses, the council of Clausewrights that rules in practice under the Mute King, and whose members are Benchers. On the coast, the Drowned Bench, the judges of the Tenanted, whose verdicts are final and whose loyalty nobody questions aloud. To go before the Bench means a reckoning in either land, and in the Rim’s mouth it means a lawsuit you will lose to someone who is not entirely human. See Clausewright and Tenanted.

bench, honest n., Rim The long bench nearest the fire in every Company common room, where strangers of different lands are seated together by the factor’s choice and not their own. It is a Rim saying that more marriages, partnerships and murders have begun on the honest bench than anywhere else on the Table. We met on the honest bench is how half the Rim’s mixed couples explain themselves, and how most of its poisonings are explained in court.

Bill, the n., Common What comes after the Long Grace: the reckoning, the gods grown back, the meal paid for. Priests of every doctrine use it; the poor use it as a shrug. We’ll all be at the Bill means we’ll all die, and put it on the Bill means don’t worry about it, it hardly matters now. The Company, which owns all the other bills on the Table, does not care for the expression. See Grace, the Long.

bit n., Oathen, Cradlewrack (1) In Oathen, the soft leather muzzle worn by every child from the first tooth until twelve, decorated with beads, ribbons and family marks; also the iron bit of the Appetite-struck and the gold bit of a Sayer. Old family bits, worn by six generations, taste of all of them. Better bitted than broken. (2) In Cradlewrack, a pet word for an unnamed infant, along with small and keep, used through the naming-year so as not to love the thing too much before it is known what it is. See Unbitting and naming-year.

bit back v. phr., Common Of the god in the blood: to cost more than was meant. Said of Partaking when the Tooth comes up a single pip and the hunger rises twice. I called on her and she bit back. At the table, a Tooth showing 1 adds a further point of Hunger. Among the poor it has become a phrase for any help that costs more than it saves: The moneylender bit back. See Tooth, the and Partake.

bite of the house n. phr., Rim What a guest at a Company inn takes when they leave without returning the crumb they were given at the gate with their pinch of salt. A guest who has taken a bite of the house is not let in again, at that house or, by gossip, at any other on the Rim. Figuratively, any small ingratitude that ruins a reputation for good.

Bitterhouse n., Vigil The Apothecary-General’s works where rouse is compounded; hence Bitterhouse black, the sealed state cake, and bitterhouse as an adjective for anything harsh and necessary. She’s very bitterhouse with the children, but they’re all still up.

Black Draught n., Common The emetic of the Purgation, administered at their altars to Penitents and retched up before the congregation; whatever comes up is held to the lamps and judged. It purges nothing of the god and everything else. To take the Draught is Rim slang for a public humiliation endured on purpose, such as a confession in a tavern or a marriage to a Fatlands heiress.

Black Noon n., Sallowreach A front of flies thick enough to put out lamps, darkening the fen in the middle of the day. Fen almanacs predict them by counting flies on the inside of a windowpane at dawn. Black Noon on Needle Street means a crowd so dense you cannot see your hand. Kept elders are brought in off the stoops before a Black Noon, since the green-bottles favour the newly lacquered. See Breath, the and weep.

blade-man n., Rim A thief of Company platters, so called from the shoulder blade from which each platter is cut. Blade-men are hanged at the post like murderers, since the Company regards a stolen platter as a stolen oath. Watch him, he has a blade-man’s hands: long fingers, a scarred thumb, and an eye always on the wax.

Blank n., Common A person born with no godsign at all: Cut 0, a mouthful of nothing. Hunted in every land as saints, specimens or spare parts. A Blank’s organs fetch a noble’s ransom and their blood is said to quiet any Regrowth for a season; neither claim has been shown, and neither has slowed the trade. Blank is also a child’s taunt for a slow learner, and a poacher’s word for a good night’s work. See blank bone, Unfed and Seasoning.

blank bone n., Rim Bone coin cut from the skeletons of Blanks or the Unfed: the only lacks with no god in them at all. Collectors pay twenty times face value. They are almost always proof that someone was killed for their bones. A blank-bone price is an obscene price for something nobody should have sold.

blessing n., archaic Godsign, in the first generations after the Gorging, when it still looked like a gift: the fen elder who could not die, the Fatland field that rose in a week. The word survives in the Upper Boards and the Gut-lines as a polite term for the Course. His lordship’s blessing has reached his knees. The poor have stopped using it. See godsign.

blink n. and v., Vigil A sleep of a second or two, on one’s feet, mid-sentence, the mark of the Appetite in the Vigil; during a blink the sleeper is in the long room with the eye for exactly as long as they are out, and comes back having moved. I blinked is the Vigil’s most frightening confession and its most common lie. In a blink means not quickly but dangerously. See blink-book, blink-murder and room, the.

blink-book n., Vigil The small book in which a nudger records every blink of their charge, by bell, in their best hand; required by law in contracts of nudging and by the Registrar of the Seeming for every witness. A clean blink-book is the Vigil’s certificate of good character. Forged ones are sold on the Slope at a crumb a page. His blink-book’s longer than his arm is said of a man who is going down.

blink-murder n., Vigil A killing done by an ordinary person during a two-second sleep, with no memory after. The Wakers have forty such cases on file and the method is the same in each. The word is never used in front of the families. Ordinary Vigilants say instead that the killer went to the window with a knife. See at the window.

Blue in the bucket phr., Brinehollow Half a proverb, blue in the bucket, rope on the bed: when a person’s bail-water comes up tinged with blue, tie them tight tonight, because the Calling is near. Bailer-boys read the colour of the water at every door they bail. A man told his water is blue is being told, kindly, to say his goodbyes. See Called, the.

Blythe n., Fast An old surname of the heartland, once one of Orrum’s names, now a family shame like Ardent, Welcome and Mercy. Osanna Blythe, who leads three hundred starving Fatlanders into the Fast to find the Host and sit down, has made the shame worse. To be blythe, in the Fast, is not to be cheerful; it is to be ready to say yes.

Board n., Common, Fatlands (1) In Old Table-speech, a table, especially the table of a Provider; cognate with orr-, the root of eating and worship. The phrase at whose board gives the Host his name. (2) In the Fatlands, the Board of Plenty, the government at Sated, whose members’ votes are weighed. The Board’s appetite is the south’s phrase for taxation. Compare Hallowboard and Groaning Board.

Boarding n., Vigil The Vigil’s death rite: the one day a corpse is permitted to lie down, flat on a board in the public way, under a Boarding Licence, so that the neighbours may come and touch its closed eyes and envy it. Don’t board me yet is said by any Vigilant accused of looking tired. To board-envy is to look too long at someone else’s ease. See licence and lie down, to.

boardless adj., Fast, Common Without a table. In the Fast, the proper condition of every decent home, where the centre of the floor is left bare and worn smooth in a ring by people walking round it. On the Rim, boardless means homeless and is said with pity, which the Unfed find hilarious in their own unsmiling way. A good boardless house, swept every morning.

boiling n., Cradlewrack One of the born-grown who walks out of the steam of the Coppers, the great laundries of Kest, naked and new, having been born of a vat in the night. The laundresses’ rule: give it an apron and walk it to the Crèche. A boiling is also highland slang for any grown man who behaves like he arrived last week, and for any idea nobody remembers having. See born-grown and without bearer.

Bone Dole n., Common The seventh year of the Long Lack, when the governments of every land collected the dead and rendered them in public kitchens and gave out the meat by ration, and the first bone ration-discs were cut. It was the most orderly year of the famine. The College was born at a vat-side with a pen. As fair as the Bone Dole means scrupulously fair and utterly monstrous. See lack and tally-priest.

bone-cough n., Rim The dry, gritty cough of the old coin-cutters of Saltbridge, whose lungs are full of the fine grey flour of sawn bone. The cutters say you can tell what a man cut by what he coughs. Grandad’s got the bone-cough explains a family’s comfortable circumstances and its silence on certain subjects.

bone-grain n., Rim The texture of a lack’s face under a lamp, from which an expert can tell a cattle coin from a person coin. Learning to read it is a Grim 18 matter of Eye and Lore, and afterward the reader knows which coins in their purse were people, and spends them anyway. I know the bone-grain on that one means I know where that money came from.

bone-lifting n., Oathen The theft of a witness from its niche in the Witnessing Vaults, by an oathbreaker who hopes a dead one removed can no longer Testify. It does not work. The bones Testify from wherever they are taken. The Keeners hate bone-lifters above all criminals. See eating the witness and Keener.

Bonfire n., Vigil One of the great fires burning in the squares of the Vigil, around which the city gathers to hear the bell-sheets read, to marry, and to stand together through the long watches. Bonfire weddings are loud, bright and short. To have it read at the Bonfire is to make something public beyond retraction. See Pinching, the.

born-grown adj. and n., Cradlewrack Born as an adult, sometimes mid-stride, with no childhood and nobody to claim them; the stuff of the Foundling Companies, the state’s only army. General Tibb was born six years ago as a man of thirty and has a private terror of the day he turns seven. Born-grown is said of any foreigner who seems to have come out of nowhere, fully opinionated. Abbreviated g. in the Tally. See boiling and Foundling.

bottle-sea n., Rim, Vigil Brinehollow bail-water bottled and sold inland as a tonic, chiefly by Dry Jonah Skerry, and cut into Vigil rouse on the Slope as sea-cut, because it holds longest. Its customers stay awake. They have also started walking west, four hundred miles from any coast. Bottle-sea in the blood is the Vigil’s newest phrase for a neighbour who stands at the window facing the wrong way.

bowshot n., Rim The width of the Company’s jurisdiction on either side of the Rim Road, as granted by the Ring Charter of 71: within a bowshot of the road, no land’s law runs, only the Company’s three articles. Within a bowshot means on neutral ground; a bowshot off means anything goes. The Ditch Toll is charged on anyone sleeping within a bowshot, two crumbs a night, collected at dawn by whoever finds you.

bread without salt n. phr., Common A fool; someone with nothing in them to give a taste. The commonest insult on the Table after the omission of the grace. In Brinehollow it is softened to dry bread, since everything there is salted whether it likes it or not.

bread-cousin n., archaic, Fatlands A child one was traded with in the Kitchen Year: the cousin who walked across the village one way while you walked the other, holding a stranger’s hand, and passed you in the lane, and did not look up. The word survives only in the oldest Fatlands families, where it means a relative one is bound to by a debt that cannot be named. The Strakes and the Hesks are bread-cousins explains why two great houses never quarrel and never dine together. See trading tables.

Breakdowns, the n., Oathen The low canyon slum on the floor of the gorge at Tacit where the Forsworn live, organized, angry and with very little left to lose. Breakdown talk is plain speech, without exits, of the kind only those with nothing left to break can afford. He talks like the Breakdowns is said of an honest man by people who mean it as a warning. See Forsworn and Unread.

Breaking n., Oathen The physical result of a broken promise in Oathen: the body breaks to match the oath, at once, with a sound, aptly and never fatally. A man who swore to stand by his brother and ran had both legs fold under him; a faithless wife’s chest opened like a cupboard. The Breakings are the cases tried before Judge Thane Urrow, where the accused simply repeats the promise aloud and the court watches. See Forsworn and Weight.

breath n., Sallowreach The smallest money of the north: a twelfth of a minute of Closing, about five lacks, issued as a stamped lead slip by the Mortuary Court. Families save breaths in a slotted crock under the hearth-board for the day they can afford to finish a grandmother. Not worth a breath means worthless in the strictest sense. See licence, death- and minute.

Breath Toll n., Rim Five lacks a post, charged on any traveller showing godsign at the Course, since a Gut-line rooted in the road near the Chute in 604 and had to be dug around. Waived for Company officers. Paying breath is Rim slang for being visibly far gone, and is said of nobles behind their backs at every inn.

Breath, the n., Sallowreach The fog over the fens, which has not lifted in living or unliving memory; warm, wet and sweet in the wrong way. A long dry wind off the southern road, a sigh, clears it for an hour and shows a white sky. Lost in the Breath means forgotten, or gone into the deep fen and still moving there a little. See weep and dew-rot.

brick n. and v., Cradlewrack The brick that seals a dead kinsman’s niche in a Stillyard wall, stamped with the family mark; also, to mortar a person into a room for the night, or into the Debt Wall for life. Oaths are sworn with a hand on a kinsman’s brick. Bricked is the only shut. A bricked couple on their wedding night are broken out at dawn, which is lucky, since nothing came in. Who’s in the Brick? is a lane game. See Debt Wall, shut door, by the and Unbricking.

Brink, the n., Common The penultimate stage of Regrowth, between the Course and the Seating, when the god is close enough to touch and the person is a thin skin over it. On the Brink is said of anyone at the end of their tether, and Brink-mad of those whose godsign has driven them past help. Canyon mothers of Brink-mad sons keep a stone by the door of the room, not for the door. See Seating, the.

Brisket’s word n. phr., Fatlands A word that stops a trade. See Annalow. In the Renderers’ yards it also means a secret everybody in the Union knows and nobody repeats: What’s in the notched barrels? Brisket’s word.

bucket-kiss n., Brinehollow The exchange of bail-buckets between sweethearts; a betrothal. They’ve bucket-kissed means they’re engaged. A bucket-kiss refused is a public humiliation, and a girl who keeps two buckets on her rope is talked about on the Mile.

Bucketing n., Brinehollow See bail-bucket. The punishment of the bucketless: a day and a night begging every neighbour to bail you, door to door, gargling. Used figuratively of any public begging: The Admiralty went bucketing to the Company for timber.

burr-cloth n., Vigil Coarse wool woven with dried thistle-heads, worn on the Lid so that every movement pricks. The rich wear galled silk, laced with fine wire. Soft as burr-cloth is a Vigil joke, and a burr-cloth welcome is a hospitable one, with a pin offered at the door.

Burying, the n., Fast The first of Grace in the Fast, when families walk to the Barrows and cut the grass on them once, with knives, kneeling. It is the nearest thing the Unfed have to a festival of the dead, and nothing is eaten on the hill. See Barrows, the.

butcher’s grace n., Fatlands The apology a butcher says to each joint as it comes off the carcass, after the habit of Hob Gristle, the Honest Butcher, who can taste what a cut used to be, down to the name. Most butchers say it as a joke. In Sated, lately, fewer of them are laughing. Say the butcher’s grace over that, will you is said of any meal of uncertain origin.

by my mother’s meat oath, Fatlands The binding oath of the south, sworn with a mouthful of a dead relative’s flesh held on the tongue: By my mother’s meat, which is in me. To break it is to have eaten your mother for nothing. Families keep a little dried meat of their elders in a salt-box under the marriage bed against the day they must swear. An oath-breaker is set an empty plate at every meal for life. See salt-box.

by the line that did not hold oath, Brinehollow The coast’s binding oath, sworn with a piece of a Called person’s rope held in the fist. To break it is to invite the Called one to come back for you, which people believe literally, and sometimes they are right: the Saltwick salt-merchant found drowned in two inches of cellar water, his brother’s rope round his wrist, wet footprints going down the drain. See name-rope.

A foreigner asked me the fen word for widow. I told him we have one, but it is in the Lofts, on a shelf, and it still whispers.
a Lastgate ferryman, to a Lineman collecting dialect

C

Cage Toll n., Rim Three lacks a post on live cargo in a closed cart, no questions asked; introduced in 301, the year of the first recorded poaching out of the Fast. The most profitable toll on the Rim and the one the Company least likes discussed. Envoy Prudence Lowell reads it aloud at every Company congress, slowly, and stops. Paid the cage is poachers’ slang for a successful run. See poacher and Blank.

Called, the n., Brinehollow Those whom the tide has pulled from their beds to walk to the shore and keep walking. Most are never seen again. Some come back weeks later, heavier, calm and courteous, and are the Tenanted. She was Called is the coast’s whole funeral sentence; the rest is rope. It is rude to ask a returned person where they went. Called is also the children’s game in which one child walks blindfold toward a wall while the others try to drag them back. See anchor, Blue in the bucket and Tenanted.

Calling n., Common (1) The coast’s word for the pull of the sea. (2) Everywhere else, a person’s trade or station in life, as a Seamer, a Netwatch hooker, a Crumb-Runner; the College asks every applicant for a certificate their Calling, their land and their mother, in that order. Brinehollowers dislike the second sense and say trade instead. What’s your Calling? On the coast we don’t ask.

candlekin n., Sallowreach One of Wick Tallow’s candles, rendered from the unclaimed dead, which feel themselves burn and give a very steady light. Reading by candlekin means reading by the light of somebody you used to know, which half of Lastgate does. Fen children say a candlekin flame bends toward the person it loved. The Chandlers deny this. The children are right.

Carried case n., Fast grammar The case of a noun one has carried oneself and may safely eat, marked -own: breadown, waterown. The Unfed hold it to be the only honest case in the language. Carry your own is both the proverb and the grammar lesson. See Offered case in the second half of this dictionary.

Carrier n., Fast The lowest rank of a Reckoner band: the one who bears the band’s food and water on a raid, in a pack nobody else may open. The Carrier eats a full measure, which is more than anyone at home, and is resented accordingly. To carry for someone, in Wanting, is to do the unglamorous work of their crimes.

Carver n., Common A butcher who cuts at table; in the Second Table, the fourth rank, who leads a chapter in a land and keeps its knife of grey bone with a course-name on the handle. Who’s carving? is a host’s question in every land and, in the mouths of the poor, an accusation: who decided this, and what did they keep for themselves?

Carving n., Common (1) The third season, autumn, the season of slaughter, the Reaping and the Weighing. (2) In the trade in leavings, the cutting of a relic from a god-touched body, place or person, which the College classes as surgery, butchery or desecration depending on who is paying. (3) The Second Table’s word for its rite. Carving weather is cold, clear and smells of iron. She’s in her Carving means a woman of middle age, handsome and dangerous.

caul n., Cradlewrack The membrane over the head of a newborn; in the highlands, the mark of the Caul-lines, who ate Vey’s caul and are born veiled in a membrane that in the highest houses never comes off. They live behind it, speak through it, see the future through it, blurred. The caul of a Caul-line child is eaten raw from a silver dish at its naming. Caul-mouthed means speaking prophecy, or speaking nonsense very slowly. See keep the veil.

certain adj., Oathen The second-worst thing you can call an Oathener, after talkative. A certain person is one who speaks without exits and therefore lives without spare limbs. Don’t be certain, love, you’ve only the two hands. In the Breakdowns the word is reclaimed: Brakk is the most certain man in the canyon.

chair, pulled out n. phr., Common The sign of an Orrum table: a chair drawn back for you. The Fifth Rule of the Fast says not to thank it. On the Rim, a chair pulled out means an offer too good to be honest. That job had a chair pulled out. On Tablenight the Company sets an extra chair at every table and turns it to face the wall. See count the chairs and head of the table.

Chairman’s feet n. phr., Fatlands A thing everybody can see and has agreed not to notice. From Chairman Obb Tullow, nineteen hundred pounds, whose feet rooted through the floor of his cart last spring, a matter on which the Board voted not to remark. The Chute’s barrels are the Chairman’s feet says in five words what would get a man dusk-shifted in fifty.

cherish v., Oathen In the canyon marriage contract: to wish the other well, and to act where able for the other’s good, and to speak no ill of them before a third person save in a court, a sickroom or the Vaults. The standard contract adds that cherish does not require any feeling at any particular hour, since feeling is weather. A canyon husband who says I cherish you has said something enforceable and nothing romantic, and his wife will be moved to tears by it.

Chewing-time n., Fatlands, children’s The Reaping, as small children of Low Tilth call it: the Carving dusks when people go missing from the fields. Don’t go out at Chewing-time. They all do, once, on a dare. Grown Fatlanders do not use the word, but they do not correct it either. See Reaping in the second half of this dictionary.

chin, to point with the v. phr., Fast To indicate a thing laid by the Host without naming it, since such things take no case in the Fast grammar. There’s a — on the step, with a jerk of the chin, is the Unfed alarm. Children who say the word cake aloud at such a moment are slapped. Rim folk who have travelled in the Fast point with their chins for the rest of their lives, at anything they would rather not name.

Chute, the n., Fatlands The Renderers’ Union’s export depot on the Rim, where meat goes out by the thousand barrels a day with the origin stamped over twice. Down the Chute means sold abroad and never asked about. Stamped twice means of doubtful origin: a stamped-twice alibi, a stamped-twice grandfather. The bone of the Table’s coin begins here, in carts marked BONE: MIXED. See notch and Annalow.

cistern-husband n., Brinehollow A Tenanted spouse who sleeps in the house cistern, as the returned do, while the living spouse sleeps in the bed. The phrase is neutral on the Mile and obscene inland. She keeps a cistern-husband and a bed-husband and ties herself between them, and nobody asks whose line holds whose. See Wreckwife.

clatter-roof n., Vigil A roof of loose tin built so that rain clatters on it instead of soothing, as rain on a sound roof is too restful for the Lid. Living under a clatter-roof means living with a nag, and is said fondly. A quiet roof is a scandal, reported to the Wakers by neighbours.

Clausewright n., Oathen A lawyer-priest of the Bench of Clauses, trained twenty years in drafting promises that can survive contact with reality. A Clausewright may speak a whole day without committing to anything, and is examined for rank by being questioned for a full day without a binding misstep. Never clause-writer, which is a clerk. Get a Clausewright is the canyon’s answer to any proposal, including of marriage. See exit and naked.

clean adj., Fast, Common In the Fast, empty: Empty plate, clean soul. An Unfed who has eaten nothing that was offered is clean; one who has accepted is not, forever. On the Rim, clean means free of godsign, especially of a corpse sold for parts, and the poachers’ price-lists say clean where a butcher’s would say fresh. Clean Through is the Unfed’s Knack of enduring hunger.

Clean the Plate n. phr., Fatlands The Fatlands’ Sop, eating until the god in the gut is quiet for a while; the hunger always comes back. As a curse, May your plate be clean, it is the worst thing one Fatlander can say to another: may you have nothing left, may your table be bare, may you be in the Fast. See Sop.

cleared adj., Common Dead; the plate taken away. Being cleared is death in most dialects. In Sallowreach, where nobody is cleared, it is said wistfully of the dead of other lands, and in the Fatlands, where the dead are served, it has a second and literal meaning which the Fatlands enjoy explaining to foreigners at dinner.

close the book v. phr., Sallowreach To end an argument by force, or by a Closer’s touch. From the Appetite of the Hand-lines, who close books, lids, shutters and eyes compulsively. The Court closed the book on him means a licensed death; I’ll close your book is a fen threat that most of the people saying it cannot carry out. See Closing.

Closed Hand n., Oathen, children’s A game of bitted children in which the loser is the first to answer a question. It is played in handtalk, at great speed, and children who are good at it grow up to be Clausewrights. She’s playing Closed Hand is said of an adult who will not give a straight answer.

closed week n., Cradlewrack The days around each pang during which highland couples abstain, in the belief that whatever begins in pang-week begins wrong. With the interval now nine days, the closed week takes up the better part of the calendar, which the Barren Order considers a great evangelical success. See pang.

Closer n., Sallowreach A Hand-line noble who sells death by touch, under licence of the Mortuary Court; the Left Hand of the Court, Lady Corrow Vane, has finished eleven thousand. Closers wear black kid gloves sewn at the wrist. Never offer to shake a Sallowreacher’s hand. In fen speech any expensive professional who ends a matter is a closer: a good divorce advocate, a hired fist, a priest who can finish a sermon.

Closing n., Sallowreach A licensed death by a Closer’s touch, costing about four thousand lacks and rising: the only death available in the fen, and the most valuable thing a family can save for. Saving for Gran’s Closing is the fen’s equivalent of a dowry, a pension and a mortgage at once. See licence, death-, breath and domestic license.

coat mood n., Fast grammar The form in which an Unfed accepts an offer made a fourth time, after three proper refusals; after the proverb The fourth no is a yes in a nicer coat. Spoken lowered, with the eyes on the ground. Orrum, the Hostwatch note, has made hundreds of thousands of first, second and third offers in six centuries and has never once been known to make a fourth. See Decline, the.

Cold Yards n., Fast The walled squares of beaten earth at the edge of Wanting where the Unfed cook, on bare ground under the open sky, putting the fire out the moment the pot is warm. Cold Yard manners: eating facing a wall, without expression or sound. To meet in the Cold Yards is to court.

coldbed n., Sallowreach, rude A marriage carried on between the living and the Kept, and what passes between them behind the shutters, which the Court does not regulate and nobody discusses. Said only by the rude, and always in a lowered voice, and usually of a neighbour whose curtains are drawn in the afternoon. The polite fen has no word for it at all. See setting-apart.

come in phr., Fast The worst thing that can be said in the Fast, ranked by Unfed grammarians not as a phrase but as a curse; it cannot be conjugated, only uttered. The Second Rule says never to answer it. It is never punished, because it never needs to be: the Unfed will not cross the threshold of anyone who has said it, ever again. On the Rim, on Tablenight, nobody says come in to anyone until dawn. As a Fast curse it is complete in itself. Come in, said to an enemy, means may you sit down at a table and never rise.

Coming-Heavy, the n., Vigil The age, about four, at which a Vigil child born awake first yawns, rubs its eyes and asks in a small cross voice why it cannot lie down. That is when the Vigil loses its children. A wing of the Dormitory called the Small Rows holds those it lost. The word is said quietly, and only of other people’s children. See starer.

company n., Fast (1) A warm front: the ground left warm where the Host has walked, by which the Unfed track it in the melted frost. Company in the east field this morning. (2) Elsewhere on the Table, guests at a meal. The Unfed find it both funny and frightening that the rest of the world uses their word for the god’s footprints to mean friends at dinner. In the Kitchen Year, company had a third sense, which the College records and does not define.

Concordance, Master n., College The genealogical ledger of every bloodline on the Table, from the Meal to the present, kept in a vault under the library at Quire, cool with spring water. A new Copyist’s first task is to copy their own line from it, by hand, back to the Meal, alone, which takes three days. Some weep. Some are sick into the channel. It’s in the Concordance means you cannot escape what your family did.

Confessor n., Common A priest of the Theft doctrine, who hears penitents ask forgiveness for the Meal, most famously at the Weeping Post, where travellers of two lands kneel in brown water. To confess the Meal is to apologize for something that happened before you were born and for which you are still, somehow, responsible: a family debt, a national border, a nose.

Coppers, the n., Cradlewrack The great laundries of Kest, where the aprons of the Attendance are boiled three times and the third water poured on the hill, and from whose steam the born-grown sometimes walk at night. Out of the Coppers means unexpectedly arrived and in need of clothes. See boiling.

Copyist n., College The lowest rank of the College: grey gown, board at Quire, access to the open stacks, and an ink-black right thumb that never washes clean. Inkthumb is Rim slang for any clerk of the College. Copyists are taken young or by examination, and each gives a pint of blood on entering, which is tasted, graded and entered, so that the College knows exactly what they are, and how fast they are going.

corrish n., Old Table-speech A shared grave, literally with-the-board; the pit into which a household that had eaten together was laid together. The word dropped out of use after the Kitchen Year, when it acquired an ambiguity nobody could bear, and survives only in the oldest carvings and in the College’s etymologies, where it is listed under orr- with a small mark meaning do not read aloud to students under twelve.

count the chairs v. phr., Rim, Common To ask the forbidden question: how many gods, how many peoples, and who is missing. Every land has at some time made it a crime. Don’t count the chairs means leave it alone, and is said to scholars, to children, and to anyone at a long table who seems to be counting. The Unfed proverb Count your chairs means the opposite: notice how many places are laid, and get out. See Eighth, the.

count, the n., Brinehollow, Vigil, Rim (1) In Brinehollow, the morning ritual of calling names through the wall to one’s neighbours; silence means someone was Called. (2) In the Vigil, the Count of 401, when a diver brought back the number of sleepers at which the eye opens, said it once to three officials, and was added to it. (3) On the Rim, the Night Count of heads at dusk and dawn in every inn; if the dawn count is higher, nobody calls the wardens, the extra place at breakfast is set and left empty, and the page is burned at noon. See aye-cough and Counted, the.

Counted, the n., Vigil The sleepers of the Dormitory, sixty thousand in numbered beds, breathing in time, who cannot be roused and do not age. Called the Counted because there is a number of them at which the eye in the dream opens, and the number is a state secret, and the beds are nearly full. By my mother’s bed-rail, with the hand on a Counted kinsman’s bed, is the Vigil’s oath on the dead. To be counted is to fall asleep for good. See Bed One and Already Counted.
