Iron Belly n., Fatlands The Taste of the Regrowth in the south: a stomach that can take anything, soil, tallow, leather, and does. Iron-bellied is a compliment to a child and an accusation against a merchant. The children who have it chew their sleeves.

Iss n., Vigil The Lidded, god of sleep, eaten with its eyes still shut; it did not wake while they did it, a detail that has never stopped bothering the Vigil. Its name is said quietly and never near a sleeper. By Iss is a Vigil oath of extreme seriousness, sworn with eyes held open by the fingers. Vigil children are told that if they say the name three times with their eyes shut, the lid will lift.

It worked once phr., Common The creed of the Second Table, engraved inside the band of a Trencherman’s signet: when the gods finish regrowing, eat them again. In the mouths of the poor it has become a sneer at any scheme of the rich: Another war? Well, it worked once.

In the canyons I said if able to a Clausewright and he smiled at me as if I’d handed him a knife and turned my back.
a Rim factor, on his first season at Quillhouse

J

Jack, to v., Sallowreach, Rim To steal a part from a living or Kept body while it shelves or sleeps; from Marrow Jack, the part-thief of Lastgate, whose victims wake able to feel what their missing hands are being used for. Jacked means robbed of something you will feel the absence of forever. Fen mothers tell children who leave their arms outside the blanket that Marrow Jack will have them.

jangle n., Fast The ringing of a Hostwatch bell at the belt, which means the Host is near. I heard a jangle at the Rim inn is a new and frightening sentence. Jangle-sick means nervous of every bell, and is common among Hostwatch widows.

Jar Room n., Sallowreach The Court’s prison: one shelf, very long. On quiet nights the low shelf ticks and taps like a roomful of people waiting. Off to the Jar Room is a fen parent’s threat, not meant, and children who have been there on a school visit never need it said twice.

jar, to v., Sallowreach To sentence a criminal to be Kept forever, in pieces, in a jar, on the long shelf of the Jar Room; the Court’s ultimate punishment. The heads float in amber pickle with their hair drifting upward; the hands are jarred separately, a pair to a jar, and are the busy ones, drumming. Jarred is the fen’s word for any sentence without end. A Sallowreacher who says I’d sooner be jarred means never. Ned Scurl asked to be jarred near a window.

jaw-click n., Sallowreach The speech of the Kept far gone, whose throats no longer work, conducted by clicks of the jaw and translated by hired interpreters; an argument begun in 212 is still being conducted this way, in a room in Lastgate. Jaw-click lawyer is a fen insult for a pettifogger. I could hear his jaw clicking means a man was furious and could not say so.

jaw-wire n., Sallowreach The wire with which the oldest Kept jaws in Lastgate are bound shut until a promise falls due, under the oath sworn with a hand in a Kept parent’s mouth; when the debt is broken, the wire is cut, and the parent may close their jaw. Cut the jaw-wire means call in the debt. See oath on the dead in the second half of this dictionary.

jelly n., Fatlands Aspic; in the mouths of Sated’s gossips, the display of a rival. See Aspic, in. Jellied means trapped in a situation where everyone can see you and nobody will help.

Jessamy’s word n., Rim The witness on which every Company contract rests: Jessamy Quill, Notary of the Rim Road. If she dies or breaks, half the trade of the Table comes unbound in an afternoon. As good as Jessamy’s word is the Rim’s highest guarantee. When Jessamy goes is how factors say at the end of the world.

Joining, the n., Cradlewrack The Assemblers’ rite of fitting a new Part to the figure in the Barn. A Joining is also a highland wedding between families who had previously quarrelled over a Part, and the guests do not look too closely at the bride’s sleeves.

joint v., Fatlands To cut a carcass into its parts, a skill every Fatland child learns: how to joint a pig, a sheep and a person, and that the order is the same. Joint it means break it down into manageable pieces, and is said of tasks, problems and arguments. Out of joint, in the south, means badly butchered.

Jointer n., Fatlands A slaughterman of the Renderers’ Union who works the wake-tables of families who cannot afford to carve their own dead. Respected, sad and well-fed. A Jointer’s grace is a few kind words over the body before the knife.

jolt n., Vigil A dose of rouse taken in a hurry, dry, against the gum, when a blink has been felt coming. Jolt-mouth is the black, toothless smile of a Vigilant over forty. I need a jolt is the Vigil’s I need a drink. See rouse in the second half of this dictionary.

Jonah, Dry n., Brinehollow Captain Jonah Skerry, smuggler of bottled bail-water. A dry Jonah is any man who profits from a trouble that does not touch him. Jonah’s tonic is bottle-sea. The Vigil has begun to dream about him, and does not know why. See bottle-sea.

Jude’s hour n., Oathen The hour Jude Crake, the Breaker, spends talking pleasantly with the condemned until they promise him something small; it has never taken longer. Jude’s hour is any conversation in which someone is being drawn to their ruin by charm. See Crake, to.

Judge’s buzz n., Sallowreach See Honorable Maggot. The buzzing in which Justice Lathe’s verdicts are delivered. I got the Judge’s buzz means I got an answer I couldn’t understand and must obey.

jug-gran n., Sallowreach, children’s A Kept relative so far gone that she is kept in a stoneware jug on the shelf and taken down on feast days to be read to. Fen children love their jug-grans, who are always pleased to see them and cannot stop them from eating sweets. See Setting Aside in the second half of this dictionary.

I wish it would stop.
the first words of the First Sayer, 598 A.G., during a storm; it stopped, and so did everything else in the valley

K

Keener n., Oathen A keeper of the Witnessing Vaults, where the canyon dead are entombed upright, faces outward, to witness the oaths of the living. Before a body is set in its niche the Keener asks the corpse, formally, whether each promise made to it in life was kept. The dead do not answer. Usually. Keeners hate bone-lifters above all criminals. To keen in the canyons does not mean to wail; it means to ask the dead a question and wait. See Testify in the second half of this dictionary.

keep v., Sallowreach To go on existing after death, as all the fen does; to look after one’s dead. Keeping is the family duty of holding the Kept together: six or seven generations share a house, grandmothers are restitched each spring, and the quarrel over whose turn it is to keep great-great-grandfather is the standard subject of fen comedy. He’ll keep means a problem can wait forever. Keep well is not a fen blessing. See Kept, the.

Keep n., Fast An Unfed given name, from the Refusal, meaning to hold back. Marshal Keep Aldane holds the border against poachers and pilgrims. Fen travellers in the Fast find the name very funny once, and then never again, after someone explains.

keep dry phr., Brinehollow The coast’s greeting and farewell, in place of good morning, since mornings on the coast are wet by definition. Keep dry to a Brinehollower betrays a foreigner who has learned the phrase; keep you dry is the grace’s coastal ending. A coast mother says it to a child going out the door the way other mothers say be careful, and means come back.

keep the veil v. phr., Cradlewrack To marry within the house, as the Caul-lines do, so that the caul stays thick; the thicker the caul, the higher the line. The Cutwrights record these unions in a locked volume in a private shorthand whose key the College does not lend. In the lanes of Kest, keeping the veil is said, low, of any family that does not marry out, and of what that implies, and nothing more is said.

Keep-salt n., Rim Salt from Mother Gall’s pickling brine in the fen, said to keep a body sound and the soul in it; sold in the cure trade as a remedy for dying abroad. Mother Gall’s cellar holds four hundred customers in barrels, paid up in advance, all wide awake. Keep-salted means preserved and conscious, and is how the fen describes a long, unhappy marriage.

Keeper n., Fast One of the party of the Abstinent who hold that the Unfed’s duty is to refuse, endure and stay clean; opposed to the Reckoners, who carry the Refusal across the Rim on a blade. A Keeper’s patience is the endurance of someone who will starve rather than act. Reckoners use it as an insult.

keeper-awake n., Vigil A wake-valet: a professional who keeps the rich awake by an artistry of tolerable pain. Jack Tenterhook, the best of them, was a torturer before, and says the only difference is the tipping. She’s had a keeper-awake since she was six explains a Height lady’s beautiful manners and the scars on her wrists.

keepings n. pl., Cradlewrack Births that do not leave the body: a small perfect hand growing from the inside of an elbow, a cluster of fingers at the base of a spine, an ear opening in the side of a neck which hears, and which the bearer hears with. The Book of Questions has three hundred pages of cases. The Attendance may cut a keeping free, and it then becomes a Part, crawling, hungry, drawn to the others; and the place it was cut from remembers. She has a keeping is said in a lowered voice.

keepsake-strip n., Fatlands The strip of a husband’s wake-meat, dried hard as leather, kept in a little bone box by widows of the Leanings, to put on the tongue at night when they cannot sleep. She’s got him in a box is said of a widow, fondly. To steal a keepsake-strip is considered, in the south, worse than murder, since murder only takes the living.

Kelp, the n., Brinehollow Brenna Kelp, Salt Assayer, keeper of the falling number, who hid three copies of the arithmetic. Doing a Kelp means hiding the truth in three places so that the state cannot burn it all at once. See arithmetic, the.

kelp-stair n., Brinehollow A cellar stair on the coast, slick with the weed the indoor tide leaves twice a day. Mind the kelp-stair is the coast’s watch your step, and is said to anyone going down into a matter better left alone.

Kept bone n., Rim Lack cut from the bones of the Kept, perfect in every respect except that it never stops decaying: in a few weeks it goes greasy and grey and smells faintly of the fen, and a purse of it sweats and draws flies. Kept-bone money is income that will rot. Fen counterfeiters swear the coin is untraceable. The flies trace it.

Kept man’s wage n. phr., Sallowreach Nothing at all; the wage of Kept labour, who do not need to eat and therefore, the fen employers argue, do not need to be paid. Working for a Kept man’s wage is how the living poor of Lastgate describe their own pay, and why they hate the Unvacated.

Kept Rain n., Oathen The rain Tolm promised the canyons on the first day of Grace before it died, which has fallen on that day for six hundred and forty years because a god’s word outlives the god; this year it came three days late. As sure as the Kept Rain was the canyon’s strongest guarantee. It is not said any longer. Yusra Thole, the Rainwarden, has said nothing at all for a month.

Kept, the n., Sallowreach Those who have died in the fen and carried on, who outnumber the breathing nine to one: the mind stays, the pain stays, and the body goes on coming apart for centuries. A Kept person who steps across the border drops, finished, at once. Kept is the fen’s neutral word for the dead and its tender word for the old. Long kept is a compliment. Badly kept is a reproach to a family. See keep, arrears and Drop, the.

Kept-breath n., Rim The bottled exhalation of a Kept elder, sold in the cure trade to the sleepless of the Vigil as a draught of deathless rest. It is fen air, warm, sweet in the wrong way, and smells faintly of the person. Selling Kept-breath means selling a dead man’s promise.

kerb-hour n., Vigil The one hour Vigil mourners are permitted to sit on the kerb beside a boarded corpse; the only lawful sitting in the city outside the Watch’s benches. She took her kerb-hour means she grieved properly. A kerb-hour friend is one who sits with you in sorrow and stands at the bell. See Boarding.

kerchief-bit n., Oathen A bit made of a folded kerchief, tied over the mouth of a foreigner at Mumchance who has been seen to be talkative; offered politely, with a card of safe phrases. Take the kerchief means shut up before you break something. Every year somebody refuses it and leaves on a stretcher.

Kest n., Cradlewrack The highland capital and seat of the Attendance: a city of round red buildings without a single door that locks. Pronounced with the knock: ’Kest. A Kest door is one that does not shut, and Kest-shut means not shut at all. A Kest child is said to be born knocking. See knock.

Kettle Furrow n., Fatlands A village of the Leanings whose barn wall bears the oldest copy of Hogget’s tally, kept in strokes since the Long Count began. She’s from Kettle Furrow explains a Fatland exile’s homesickness, since her mother is a slope near it. Kettle Furrow sums are counts that only go up.

keystone-mother n., Cradlewrack The eldest bearer in a household, through whom the whole Tally line runs; the most important person in any highland family. She’s the keystone means everything depends on her. When a keystone-mother dies, the household is said to be unhinged for a year, whether or not the parish takes the doors. See unhinging in the second half of this dictionary.

kick n., Cradlewrack The King Within’s means of government: one kick for yes, felt by the Queen Dowager, who has carried him forty-four years and reports to the court. The Book of Kicks records them. Kick for it means vote. She is ninety and very tired, and lately he has begun to answer questions nobody asked. See Aubrey’s kick.

Kicker n., Cradlewrack, rude A courtier who claims special insight into what the King Within wants. The Kickers say he’s for the war. Sneered at by everyone who is not one. Compare Aubrey’s kick.

kin-knife n., Fast A killing within an Unfed family for a reason the Fast’s own creed supplies: a son back from the Rim with buttoned sleeves, a sister who craves tallow, a cousin found to carry High Cut blood. The Abstinent will not omit for godsign. Families have sometimes decided that the Five Rules were not enough. The kin-knife came out at the Danners’ is said, and nothing more. See Standing in the second half of this dictionary.

kin-name n., Cradlewrack The line of descent recorded in the Tally, which runs through whoever bore you; in many cases this requires a footnote. What’s your kin-name? means who carried you?, and the answer may be a woman, a man, a grandfather, a well, a hill, or without bearer. Descent-fraud, claiming a bearer who did not bear you, is a great crime.

Kin-Reader n., Fast The third rank of a Reckoner band: the one who holds the stolen genealogies and plans which beds, in what order; marked by a stolen College quire. A kin-reader among the Unfed is also any gossip who knows too much about who married whom on the Rim. The College regards the title as theft and the work as excellent.

kindly adj., Brinehollow Of a returned spouse: changed for the better, in the way that frightens. He came back kinder is the coast’s most chilling sentence. A Wreckwife who says her husband is very kindly now is asking for help without asking. Sennet Gull keeps hers in the cistern, brings him his dinner, and has started to prefer him. See Tenanted and afters.

King Within n., Cradlewrack The rightful king of the highlands, in the womb of the Queen Dowager for forty-four years, consulted on matters of state by kicks. Rule like the King Within means govern from somewhere nobody can see, by signs nobody can read, and a King Within is any heir who refuses to arrive.

kinsale n., Rim, poachers’ cant The sale of one relative by another to a poacher or a parts-surgeon, which happens more often than the Rim admits, especially at the end of a long Lack. Kinsale price is the lowest price for anything, since the seller only wants it gone. Dr. Mercy Thrane has traced three kinsales to the same surgery. See Cage Toll and Blank.

Kitchen Year n., Common The sixth year of the Long Lack, the year the songs leave out, when the dead were kept at home and the pot was put on, and then the lots were drawn, and children were sent across the village to cousins so that no one would have to eat their own. Kitchen Year is never said at a table. That was before the Kitchen Year means before we were all guilty. The College publishes its account only in cipher. See trading tables, aftertaste and bread-cousin.

kitchen, to v., archaic, Common To eat a dead kinsman at home in the sixth year of the Lack, before the Bone Dole made it a matter for the state; preserved in old depositions and in one Fatlands curse, may your children kitchen you, which is the worst thing anyone in the south has ever been heard to say, and is said perhaps once a generation, at a deathbed, by someone who has been wronged beyond bearing.

kitchen-bones n. pl., Common Bones of the Kitchen Year found by builders under hearthstones, cracked lengthwise for the marrow; a skull in a chimney-breast wrapped in a christening gown; a pot in a bricked canyon cupboard with a spoon still standing in it. Such finds are not reported. They are wrapped in clean cloth, by custom, and carried at night to the nearest crossroads and left. Taking them to the crossroads means burying an old shame without a word.

knacker n., Fatlands A worker of the Renderers’ Union who deals in the parts of a beast that cannot be sold as meat: hoof, horn, bone, and the long bones that go north in carts marked BONE: MIXED. Knacker’s arithmetic is the reckoning that always comes out in the Union’s favour. See Chute.

knee, of the adj. phr., Oathen, Rim Of a canyon courier: died of a Breaking by arriving late, the knee reversing on a sworn delivery; the Fogmouth register of 641 records an Oathen courier dead of the knee, having arrived. Of the knee is used on the Rim for any death by duty. The Seal Toll is waived for couriers under an Oathen oath, since the Company will not delay a sworn word.

kneel-water n., Rim The tea-brown pool at the Weeping Post where travellers of two lands kneel and ask forgiveness for the Meal. To go to the kneel-water is to apologize for something you did not personally do, at great length, in public. See Confessor.

Knife n., Fast, Cradlewrack (1) The second rank of a Reckoner band: the one who enters the house, bearing the black-iron blade, unadorned. (2) In the highlands, the Second Opinion, the midwife’s knife; the Knife-faction of the Attendance holds that it has kept the country together for six centuries. Under the knife, in either land, means judged and found unfit to continue. See Opinion, Second in the second half of this dictionary.

Knife-and-Ear n., Oathen, children’s A counting game of bitted canyon children, played in handtalk, in which one child is the Ear and listens while the others sign promises, and the Knife points at the one whose fingers flinch. Mothers beat it out of their children, silently, in doorways, since a game about promises is no longer a game. See Closed Hand.

knife-apron n., Cradlewrack The white apron of an Attendance midwife with the knife-case at the hip that nobody looks at directly; boiled three times in the Coppers, the third water poured on the hill. She’s put on the knife-apron means a woman has taken up a terrible responsibility. Opinions develop a callus on the inside of the ring finger where the hook of the knife rests, and wear it like a brand.

Knife-faction n., Cradlewrack The party within the Attendance led by Midwife-Paramount Orla Kest, holding that the Second Opinion has kept the country together for six centuries and must stay steady until the interval closes. Opposed by the Late-faction, who whisper that the knife was six centuries too late. Knife-faction talk is any argument that the old cruelty is the only safety.

knock n. and v., Cradlewrack (1) The gravest courtesy of the highlands: one knocks before opening any door, to warn whatever is on the other side. Knock first. It’s not for your sake. A greeting is three knocks. (2) The small catch in the throat with which highlanders begin any word that starts with a vowel, so as not to enter it unannounced; the tell of the dialect. (3) Mourners knock three times on a new brick in the Stillyard and do not wait for an answer. She knocks four is said of a dead woman who has begun to answer. See brick and Knocking Gate.

knock-four n., Cradlewrack A dead kinsman in a Stillyard wall who knocks back four times after a pang instead of the mourners’ three: the beginning of a haunting, a birth, or both. Hobb Marl of Mortar Rise, on the Debt Wall for his brother’s death, says his mother still knocks four, every pang. Knock-four is said of anything that should be finished and is not.

knock-shy adj., Cradlewrack Afraid to knock at a door for fear of what will answer; a condition of highland children after a pang, and of highland adults after a funeral. Don’t be knock-shy is what an apprentice midwife is told on her first night, and then she goes into the room.

Knocking Gate n., Rim The Company station at the Cradlewrack border where Marshal Gideon Breech’s men check every traveller for signs of carrying. Its inn, the Open Door, has no doors at all, only curtains, so that nothing can be accused of breaking in; visitors knock on the frames out of politeness, and occasionally something knocks back from inside an empty room. Through Knocking Gate means got away, and the highland proverb answers: the country goes with you.

knot n., Brinehollow The coast’s whole morality. Tie your own knot means take care of yourself and trust no one else’s rope. A loose knot is a crime, punishable by bucketing. A Sounder of the ninth knot had dived nine fathoms past the bursting of the eardrums. A Rim inn near the coast charges a crumb a knot for tying a guest to the bed. Knot-week is the first week of a coast marriage, when the couple sleep roped to each other and nobody else.

Knot Canyon n., Oathen A gorge of the back canyons, with lime-pits where bone-lifters dump the stolen dead; the bones Testify from there all the same. Thrown in Knot Canyon means hidden somewhere it will be found out anyway.

knucklebones n. pl., Common The sheep’s ankle-bones every house on the Table owns, for games and for drawing lots; in the Kitchen Year, the lots for the pot were drawn with them, because every house had a set and a knucklebone does not lie. The College holds a set from a Brinehollow cottage, yellow with handling, five bones and a sixth, smaller, separate, which is not a sheep’s. To throw the knucklebones means to leave a hard choice to chance. Children play the game everywhere still, and say the old rhyme, and do not know what it means. See Who’s for the pot in the second half of this dictionary.

The College has nothing further to print under this head.
the whole of an entry in the Ninth Recension, between guest and Gullet, struck from the abridged edition by order of the Archprovost
Chapter 12

The Lexicon of the Table

L–Z
A word is a mouthful you have agreed to share. Chew it before you swallow it, and know whose it was.
— preface to the Quire Word-Book, second half, fourth recension (641 A.G.)

The second half of the College’s word-book picks up where the first left off, at the letter that begins Lack, which is as good a place as any to begin a description of the Table. Like its sister volume, it was compiled by Copyists and Linemen of the Cutwrights’ College on their rounds, from the mouths of innkeepers, Seamers, nudgers, Renderers, Clausewrights, Crumb-Runners, children at doorsteps and the dead on their shelves, and corrected (where the Compiler could bear to) against the College’s own ledgers. It is a working book. The College wants to know what people call things, because what people call a thing is what they are afraid it is.

The Compiler is a Cutwright of the Chapter-House at Quire, and has asked that her name be left off the title page, on the grounds that several of the words below are about people who would recognise it. Her marginal notes are kept, set off in brackets, because the Archprovost found them useful and because she would not let them be cut.

How to Read an Entry

Each entry gives the word, its kind (n. noun, v. verb, adj. adjective, interj. interjection, phr. phrase, prov. proverb, excl. oath or curse, title, child. nursery word, cant thieves’ or trade jargon), the land or road where it is heard (common means everywhere on the Table), and a definition, often with an example in italics as it was overheard. Bold names point to another entry, in this half or the first. Words marked cant should not be used in front of the people they describe. Words marked child. should not be used in front of their mothers.

I have written down every word they would say to me. The ones they would not, I have written down too, from behind doors.
the Compiler, in the margin of the L proofs
Using the Lexicon at the Table

The Lexicon is a prop and a toolbox. Read an entry aloud as an NPC’s line; hand a player the insult their character would know; let a Guest who speaks a word correctly in the right land take +1 to a Persuade or Deceive roll there, and let a Guest who uses one wrongly (calling an Oathener talkative, wishing a fen-widow long life) face a Hard 14 Tongue + Persuade roll to undo it. Every few entries carries a hook: a name, a place, a rumor. Where an entry gives a rule, it uses the standard numbers.

L

Lack n., common 1. The nine-year famine before the Gorging, the Long Lack. 2. Winter, the fourth season. 3. Poverty, hunger and bad luck, which on the Table are one condition and need only one word. 4. On the dice, a failed roll showing doubles, the worst plausible complication. Lack sat down at our table in my grandmother’s time and never got up (a Rim way of saying a family has always been poor). See also lack, Licked Clean.

lack n., common The bone coin: a salt-cured disc the width of a thumb-joint, pierced for the string, stamped with the Plate on one face and an empty circle on the other, worth a day’s bread. Ten crumbs to the lack, twenty lacks to the platter. Struck at Saltbridge since 212 A.G. from bone the Company calls cattle. The lack is thin this year means bread is dear. (Compiler: the empty circle is either “the bread to be bought” or a chair seen from above. I have looked at it from above. I recommend not doing so.)

lack-bitten adj., Rim Of a coin: clipped at the edge by someone shaving bone dust to sell as tooth-powder. Of a person: thin in a way that shows at the wrists and the temples. Lack-bitten lacks for lack-bitten folk (said of the change in a Thimble Cross tavern).

Lack keep away phr., common The grace said before eating with strangers, everywhere on the Table, and the oldest sentence anyone still uses. Omitting it is the universal insult, worse than a blow, and in some inns a cause for the bill to be doubled. Said fast in the Fatlands, signed in Oathen, mouthed in the Vigil, and in the Fast followed by and keep the Host away, under the breath. See grace.

lackling n., Rim, cant A child born in the Lack season, held unlucky on the Rim and lucky in the Fast. Crumb-Runners prefer lacklings as carriers, because they are used to cold and expect nothing.

ladder-hand n., Sallowreach The lowest Loft-Warden: one lamp, one key to one hall, and a list of the Set-Aside to be read aloud to. Ladder-hands are mostly orphans and the very old. Their wage is three lacks a week and whatever the shelves whisper.

Laden n. and title, Fatlands 1. Ummer, the eaten god, the Laden. 2. A Fatlander at the Course, swollen past proportion, feet rooting, skin gone soft and loamy. Among the Gut-lines it is a title, used on letters: To the Laden Dame Marrable, at table. Among Scraplings it is said with the hand over the mouth, as you might say dying. A Laden person who roots becomes a hill; see Dowager Hills, Seating.

ladle n., Fatlands 1. A Bailiff’s badge of office, the lowest rank of the Board’s men, carried at the belt. 2. v. To force-feed under the Feasting Laws, gently or otherwise. They ladled him at the crossroads and he thanked them for it after; he had no choice, his mouth was full. See Gavage.

Lain Book n., Vigil The ledger kept by Teodor Rell of the Slope, in which the notes the Lain-Down leave behind are copied out and sent with them to the Dormitory. It is the saddest book on the Table and the Watch has twice tried to have it burned. People queue on the Slope to read a page aloud, so that the note will have been heard once.

Lain-Down n., Vigil A Vigilant who lay down on purpose. The law says voluntary rest and fines the nudger; the city says went to the room and does not discuss it. Those left go and stand at the foot of the bed, which has a number and no grave, for the rest of their lives. My brother is Lain-Down. No, he is well. He is at bed fifty-eight thousand. He looks very well. See Lain Book.

Lain Lane n., Vigil Any street where a Lying-Down has happened; specifically the lane behind Gallow Street, where the neighbourhood walks the long way round by Thimble rather than pass it. Don’t go by the Lain Lane, love; take the stair.

lamp-friend n., Vigil A stranger you have stood beside under the same lamp for long enough to have seen the same Seeming. A lamp-friend has a claim on you for one favour. Lovers on the Slope begin as lamp-friends; the phrase is also used, bitterly, for people who only know each other through shared hallucination.

lamp-meat n., Vigil, cant The tallow in the lamps of the Row and the poorer streets, which the Lamplighters’ Guild buys from wherever it can. Smell that? Lamp-meat. Somebody’s uncle is lighting the corner. (Compiler: the Guild calls it economy. Wick Tallow calls it a partnership.)

Lancing n., Rim A massacre carried out by the Purgation against a high-Cut family, named for the lancet and the lancing-spear. Lancings are announced the night before by a pewter bowl left upturned on the doorstep. The family usually knows what the bowl means. The neighbours always do. The word is also used for any act of violence done for someone’s own good, and the Vigil’s Wakers have adopted it with pride.

land-drowned adj., Brinehollow Drowned in bed for want of bailing, the lungs filled from the inside with sea that came from nowhere. The body is easy to know: the lips are white with salt and there is kelp in the throat. Land-drowned is the coast’s commonest death and its least spoken of, because someone was supposed to wake them.

lardlord n., Fatlands, insult A Gut-line landowner, heavy with rent and fat, who will not leave his bed to see the land he owns and could not if he wished. Said by tenant-farmers behind the hand, and once, in 455, through a speaking-trumpet in the square at Sated, after which the speaker was fed until he stopped.

Last Bell n., Rim The dusk bell that closes the lawful market at Gristmoot and other Company towns. What is sold after it is sold in the pens behind the stockyards, a bowshot and a half from Company law. After Last Bell is Rim slang for anything you do not want written down.

Last Cake n., Rim The final thing a Crumb-Runner eats at Wanting Post before crossing inward with the grain, bought from the Company counter and never finished; the half left on the plate is for luck. Innkeepers at the Post keep the half-cakes on a shelf, by name, and throw them out only when the Runner comes back.

Lastgate n., Sallowreach The capital of the fens, on pilings, where the border road ends. Its lower storeys have been sinking for centuries and are inhabited all the way down. Lastgate manners: courtesy so slow that it takes a century to deliver an insult, and does.

Lasting n., Sallowreach The dread of a living fen-child that she will never be allowed to finish. Mothers whisper no Lasting for you over cradles, as an Oathener would whisper if able. See Long life.

Last Verse n., Sallowreach The final verse of a song, which in the fens does not exist, since nothing there can finish. Bram Hollin, the Last Mourner, knows the old funeral rite with its Last Verse, and is the only man alive who does. To sing someone the Last Verse is to Close them, or to wish it. A Last Verse heard sung aloud in Lastgate is a Dread 1 event; people weep in the street.

Lean n. and title, Fatlands The second rank of the Thin: one who has been taught where the safe barns are and been given a share of the ash-bread. Also the Board’s word for any fasting rebel, used in warrants. Wanted: one Lean, sex uncertain, weight unrecorded, believed to be eating nothing in the Bleeding Orchards.

Lean House n., Fast The building at the edge of Wanting where the omitted go when their names are left off the Pantry list, to lie down among others in the same case and wait, with dignity, in clean linen. It has never been full and never been empty. She walked to the Lean House is the Fast’s commonest obituary.

Lean Levy n., Fatlands A tax on the thin, assessed on the bones that can be counted from across a room. The Board calls it a tax on the withheld portion; the Thin call it a bounty on ribs. Levy-men carry callipers. He paid the Lean Levy and still had money left; he couldn’t have been very thin.

Leathering n., Sallowreach The stage of the long rot at which a Kept body has dried, darkened and toughened like an old saddle, around the second century of being upright. Leathered grandmothers are sharp as vinegar and hard to restitch, because the needle will not go through. She’s at the Leathering means she is old, proud and impossible.

Leavings n., common Any part of a high-Cut body, a Seated place or a god-touched thing that still holds some of the god, and is cut, kept, traded and used: a ninth joint, a Laden pear, a Tenanted tear. The trade has its own book (Seven Tables, The Carving Knife). On the Rim the word also means simply what is left on the plate. Leavings to the dogs and the dogs to the Board.

On the Rim, three words in five are about food, and the other two are about who is going to pay for it.
the Compiler

Ledger, the n., Oathen The cliff face at Tacit into which every vow of public record has been carved: four miles long and growing by a yard a week. Scribes cut it by lamplight in the season of Carving. To be on the Ledger is to have made a public promise. To be off the Ledger is to be a child, a foreigner or a liar. A miscut on the Ledger in 640 broke a man who had kept his word perfectly, and nobody has explained it.

Left Hand, the title, Sallowreach The chief Closer of the Mortuary Court, at present Lady Corrow Vane, whose gloves are sewn on. Gone to the Left Hand is a polite way of saying someone has bought a Closing and is, at last, about to be properly dead. Children play Left Hand, Right Hand, a touching game in which the one who is touched has to lie down and not get up until the next round.

Lending, the n., Brinehollow The coast’s name for the doctrine of the Gift: Dromm lent itself to the hungry, and the sea is coming back to collect what was lent. Lending-folk are gentle with the Tenanted. It’s not stealing if it was lent is what Lending-folk say of the Calling, and what nobody else on the coast can bear to hear.

lending a light phr., Vigil Keeping a stranger awake for a while, unpaid, as a kindness: walking beside them, pinching them, talking. Lend us a light, mister, my nudger’s gone. It is the commonest beggar’s line on the Slope and the commonest way robbers open a conversation.

Lessening, the n., Vigil The quiet party in the Watch of Watches that would like the number of the Counted to be reduced. Its members never say how. Its badge, never worn openly, is a pillow embroidered with a single stitch. A Lessening sort of man is a man you would not leave alone at a bedside.

Licenser title, Sallowreach A clerk of the Mortuary Court who drafts and seals Closing licenses, and may move one name a season up the waiting list. Licensers are the most bribed people in the north and the most hated, after the dead.

Licked Clean adj. and n., common 1. A new moon, the Plate empty; nobody sets out on a licked-clean night, doors are barred, plates are not counted. 2. On the dice, double ones: automatic failure and a Lack. 3. Utterly ruined, with nothing left on the bone. We came back licked clean: no mules, no coin, and Harrow’s left hand.

licker n., common, insult A Scrapling, in the mouths of the high: one descended from those who licked the bones. Among Scraplings, the word is a boast at harvest and a fighting word in the mouth of anyone else. Licker’s luck: little god, little to lose.

Lid, the n., Vigil 1. The plateau on which the city stands. 2. The great closed eye at the far end of the long dim room in the sleepers’ dream. Under the Lid means asleep, gone. Over the Lid means abroad, anywhere but the Vigil. Divers who have come within thirty paces of the Lid say it is not quite shut.

lid-salt n., Vigil The salt crust that forms on lidless eyes between wettings, scraped off by the Eye-Wetters and sold as a love-charm on the Slope. Real lid-salt from a noble eye fetches a lack a pinch. Most of it is scraped from the corners of beggars. See tear-salt.

Listener n., several lands A rank, or an office, in at least four orders: the Wreckwives (who listen at the wall for a Tenanted spouse’s second voice), the Dream-Divers (who sit at the top of the tether and hear the diver’s breath), the Barren Order, and the Echo-Wardens of Oathen. All four kinds of Listener go deaf in the end, in different ways.

listen twice phr., Oathen Advice to anyone in the canyons: a thing you hear once may be a person; a thing you hear twice is an echo, and binds. Listen twice before you nod.

Lists, the n., Fatlands The reading of the Reaping’s missing in every village square on Carving afternoons. Not a holy day; everyone attends. The reader is chosen by lot and may not stop to weep. She went off the Lists means she was found, which happens about once a decade, and was not glad of it.

Lofts, the n., Sallowreach The warehouses of the Set-Aside in Lastgate: nine storeys of shelving, forty thousand of the too-far-gone wrapped and labelled and awake, whispering. The sound is audible from the street. Shelf-talk is what the Lofts say; Loft-wise is what you are after a week of listening to it. Lately the whole building says one word. See whisper-book.

Long Count, the n., Fatlands Pell Hogget’s tally of the Reaping, begun in Low Tilth and copied now in two hundred villages, on notched staves, on barn doors, in the backs of Feasting Law primers. The numbers rise every year. Keep the Long Count is a Thin blessing and a Board offence.

Long Grace, the n., common The age itself: the six hundred and forty-one years between the meal and the bill, a long pause like a grace said before eating, before the gods finish growing back. The Grace is ending is said at every bad harvest, late rain, odd birth and new Hush, and is said more often every year.

Long Lack, the n., common The nine years of famine before the Gorging, numbered backward by scholars (Lack 1 to Lack 9) and by nobody else at all. Each year has a name: the Thin Harvest, the Empty Nets, the Barren Stalls, the Ash Bread, the Leather Winter, the Kitchen Year, the Bone Dole, the Eldest Walk, the Turning. As long as the Lack means forever.

long life excl., Sallowreach The worst curse in the fens, and the most dangerous thing a foreigner can say there by accident. Said to a Kept person it is a slap; said to a living one it is a threat. Fen children who quarrel say it to each other and are whipped. The proper wish is May you finish.

Long Table, the n., Fast The valley road where six hundred years of the Seated sit at one continuous table, nine miles end to end, lifting empty forks together. The sound of them chewing is like a herd grazing. Gone to the Long Table means lost to the Host. Do not look for anyone there for long. People who look for long enough find a chair.

loose adj., Sallowreach Of the Kept: coming apart at a seam, in public. Falling loose has been a fineable offence since the Stitching Laws of 130 A.G. He’s gone loose at the jaw again, poor soul; fetch the Seamer and a cloth. A loose-parts man is a part-thief or a back-alley seamer; see Marrow Jack.

lose the bottom phr., Brinehollow Originally a pilot’s phrase, when the sounding-lead finds nothing. Now: to sense the pull, to stand too long at a west-facing window, to be on the way to being Called. Hask Tarn will not go near the places where he once lost the bottom, though they are dry land now.

lowing n., Fatlands, cant Drovers’ word for the sound Sal Trotter’s herds make on the road at night, which is not quite the sound cattle make. They were lowing in words again by the river.

Lowmark n., Brinehollow The capital: a pier-city nineteen miles long built out across the dry seabed after the retreating sea, a mile a year. Its quarters are called Miles, numbered from the old shore. Living on the Twelfth Mile is living in the slums; living on the First is living on the old money and the old smell.

Low Water n., Brinehollow The lowest tide of the year, in late Carving, when the Tenanted gather on the Uncovered and sing, and families watch from the rail of the Mile. She sings at Low Water means she is Tenanted. Ilse Marl’s transcriptions of the singing, laid end to end, make a chart.

Lullaby, the n., Vigil The Vigil’s name for the doctrine of the Gift: Iss gave its sleep so that the city could be awake, and the room is where it keeps what it was given. The faith of most ordinary Vigilants, and the one hymn the Wakers allow to be hummed, never sung.

Lung-lines n., Brinehollow The noble houses descended from those who ate Dromm’s lungs, chief among them the Vashts. They cannot breathe air for long, and hold court from glass tanks. Lung-proud means vain, and the poor of the Mile use it of anyone who holds their breath to look important.

lying-in n., Cradlewrack Any confinement at all, of anyone, of any sex or age, for any reason, since in the highlands anyone may come to bear. The Lying-In, capitalised, is the Attendance’s fortress hospital, where the births nobody speaks about are taken. She’s gone to the Lying-In is said of a woman who will not be seen again, and of her child, and of whatever it was.

M

maggot-wise adj., Sallowreach Wise in the way of the very old dead: slow, cold, entirely right and of no use to anyone living. From Justice Ever Lathe, the Honorable Maggot, whose rulings are buzzed and translated. Maggot-wise counsel is advice that will be correct in a century.

make them last phr., Fast What Unfed mothers say when they hand children a crust. Also the motto over the Pantry door. In the Vigil the same phrase is said of rouse-tabs, bitterly.

Making Good n., Fast The Unfed rite by which an omitted household that has survived a winter without the Pantry is put back on the list, and must thank the Abstinent who left them off, by name, aloud, at the Pantry window. She made good last Grace and has not spoken to Elder Wend since, except to say thank you.

Mangling n., common The table of Injuries the body takes at Ruin. Physicians’ slang: a Mangling is any wound bad enough that the surgeon reaches for the saw before the needle. Mangled in the fens is a compliment to a Seamer’s work: so ruined that only a master could have made it stand.

Marbling n., Fatlands The first frost, when the fat in the soil whitens and the plains look like a cut of meat from horizon to horizon. On Marbling Morning children run barefoot on the white veins. Some years the veins form shapes. Marbled means rich and also means very old.

mardy adj., child., Fatlands Sulky from hunger, which in the south is the only kind of sulk there is. Don’t be mardy, there’s a fifth meal coming. Fatland grandmothers say a mardy child has the field in its belly, and give it a heel of bread to chew while it cries.

marrow-jack n., Sallowreach, cant Any part-thief: one who takes limbs from the Kept while they shelve or sleep and sells them to back-alley seamers. From the most notorious, whose victims wake able to feel what their missing hands are being used for. Marrow-jacked: missing a piece, and aware of it.

marrow-mouth n., Fatlands, insult A greedy person, one who cracks the bones at the wake before the family has had the joints. Also used, approvingly, of babies.

marrying the water phr., Brinehollow Being Called. A gentle phrase, said by the Deepening and by grandmothers. She married the water in her sixtieth year and we think she was happy. The Netwatch use it with contempt.

Matron title, Vigil The Keeper of the Dormitory, at present Cecily Dorm, the only living person who knows the number. Matron’s count is any total you are not allowed to hear. Matron’s pillow: an act of mercy that the law calls murder. Nobody says the second phrase above a whisper.

May you finish phr., Sallowreach The polite greeting and farewell of the fens. Said to the Kept with feeling, to the living with affection, to the Hand-lines with care, since from them it can sound like a request. The reply is In time. See long life.

meal-mouthed adj., Rim Speaking of horror only in food-words, so as never to say it plainly: she was cleared, he’s been served, they were picked. The Compiler is told she is meal-mouthed herself. The whole Table is. The first line of every history says it plainly, and then nobody does again.

Measure n., Fast The Pantry ration: one oatcake, a handful of grain, sometimes a strip of dried Rim fish, weighed out by Mother Stint Avery’s clerks. Short measure is the worst thing that can happen in a winter. Full measure, said of a person, means honest. An Orrum table sometimes lays out a Measure, but whole, and hot, and buttered to the edges, the measure as it should have been.

Measure-Bearer title, Fast The lowest servant of the Pantry, who carries the day’s rations to the window and is searched on the way in and the way out, by two clerks, every day of their life. Honest as a Measure-Bearer: honest because watched.

meat scrip n., Fatlands The Board’s money: greased paper slips redeemable for a weight of meat at any Board store (the pound, the stone, the side). Its value falls every Carving with the Reaping, and Pell Hogget’s tally-keepers chart the two together. Scrip-fat: rich on paper. Paid in scrip: paid in somebody.

Member title, Fatlands One who holds a vote on the Board of Plenty by weight. A Member is immune from the dusk shift. He’s Member size is a compliment. He’s lost his seat means he has lost forty pounds, or died, which in the Fatlands are about equally shameful.

Mercy n., Rim 1. A Fast name, given to girls born in a hard winter. 2. In Purgation cant, the Black Draught, the emetic given free on Retching Day at the Weeping Post. Take your Mercy means drink and bring it up. Dr. Mercy Thrane, who is from the Fast, does not find this funny.

mercy-pinch n., Vigil A pinch given to a child who has begun to blink, hard enough to bruise, by a stranger in the street. Mothers thank the stranger. The bruise is called a kiss.

mere-light n., Sallowreach The glow on the fen at night from Wick Tallow’s candles drifting on cork, upright and lit, leaning their flames toward passing punts. Following a mere-light is a fen child’s dare. Children who follow it come home in the morning and say the candle told them its name.

Middle Plate n., common The second month of any season, named for the moon. Dates are given the ninth of Middle Plenty. Middle-plated is Rim slang for a person of no particular class, neither Scrapling nor Prime, a common Cut 2. See Appendix, Numbers, Measures and Time.

Midwife title, Cradlewrack A member of the Attendance, judge, physician, priest and executioner in one apron, who asks the Two Questions at every birth and answers them herself. The Midwife’s Two Questions: What is it? Does it stay? Highland children play Midwife with dolls, and the dolls do not always stay.

Fen children learn three words before they learn their names: shut, stitch, and finish. In that order, says Mother Gall, if they’re lucky.
the Compiler

Mile n., Brinehollow One of the numbered sections of Lowmark’s pier-city. Each Mile has its own bell, its own netwatch post and its own reputation. A Mile-cart is the long rail-trolley that runs the length of the pier; riding the Mile is commuting, and also being slowly drawn west.

Mile-mad adj., Brinehollow Restless in the way of the poor of the far Miles: walking out to the pier’s end at night to watch the water, which is always a little further off. Mile-madness is the Appetite of the coast, in the mouths of people who will not say the pull.

mither v., Brinehollow To fuss over someone’s bail-bucket: to check its rope, its rim, its smell, the colour of what is in it. Mothers mither. Sweethearts who have exchanged buckets mither each other. Stop mithering, I coughed clean this morning.

mittens n., Sallowreach Worn by sufferers at the Appetite, to stop the compulsive closing of lids, books, shutters and the eyes of strangers. Wool for the Taste, leather for the Appetite, lead for the Course. He’s in his mittens means he is not to be trusted near the infirm. Osric Vane’s are lead and locked.

Moot n., Rim A Company market town, especially Gristmoot, where every stall-keeper on the road comes at last, and the Grace Bell at noon stops three miles of stalls so everyone can turn to the nearest stranger and say the grace. Moot-honest: honest only within earshot of the Weighhouse bell.

morning count n., Brinehollow The dawn calling of names through the party wall, house to house, the length of a street, so that silence will show who was Called in the night. Missed the count means dead or gone. In every party wall there is a worn place, sometimes carved as an ear, where the names are called. See plank-ear.

Mortuary Court n., Sallowreach The council of the Hand-lines under the Unvacated Regent, sellers and hoarders of death. To have friends at the Court is to be expected to die on time. Court-dead: Closed by license, as opposed to Hush-dead or foreign-dead.

mothered adj., Cradlewrack Descended from a particular bearer, who may not have been a woman, or a person. I am mothered of Hessa Gorse, and through her of the well at Rudge is a respectable pedigree in the highlands, with a footnote.

Mother of Cords title, Cradlewrack The eldest of the Uncut, whose cord has grown down into the red clay and become a Root; through it she feels the pulse of the land, and says it has two beats now. By the Mother of Cords is an Uncut oath; it is taken holding someone else’s cord.

Mother of the Water title, Brinehollow The head of the Deepening, at present Mother Limpet, who has walked two thousand into the sea at night with lanterns and says she will follow when the last is safely under. Mother-of-the-Water patience: the patience of someone who is going to win.

moth-wife n., Vigil A Seeming that walks: a woman made of moths, who comes down the lane dimming each lamp she passes and smelling of flour. Several districts have entered her in the public record. She is said to stop in front of people who are about to blink for the last time.

mourner n., Sallowreach A trade six centuries extinct: one paid to weep at a death, back when there were deaths. Bram Hollin is the last, and in demand now the Hushes have come. Hire a mourner is fen slang for make a fuss, and has suddenly stopped being a joke.

mouth, the n., Fatlands The opening a Seated Laden hill sometimes keeps: a warm damp crack in the turf that exhales and, on consultation days, speaks. Going to the mouth is asking a family hill for advice on a marriage. The advice is always right. The hill is always hungry. Bring something.

mouthful n., common 1. A unit of time: as long as it takes to chew and swallow one mouthful, about a count of twenty. 2. A unit of speech in Oathen: the most one may say at once without a Clausewright, by custom about nine words. Say it in a mouthful or not at all. See Appendix.

mouthless adj., Fatlands Of a Seated Laden hill: one that kept no mouth. The courts have ruled that a mouthless hill still holds title. Mouthless matriarchs are consulted by the laying-on of hands on warm turf, and their heirs report what they felt, which is convenient for the heirs.

muck-sworn adj., Oathen, cant Of an oath: made in the Breakdowns, by somebody already broken, and therefore cheap, since the swearer has little left to lose. I’ll take your muck-sworn word for it, Splint, and your other kneecap if it fails.

mumble-sworn adj., Oathen Bound by an oath you did not hear yourself make, as by an echo, a sleep-talk, or a Sayer’s careless sentence. Mumble-sworn oaths are the commonest cause of Breakings among the poor, who sleep in shared galleries where the walls carry. The Bench has no remedy.

Mumchance n., Rim 1. The quietest inn in the world, where the Rim enters Oathen; orders on slates, the bill in chalk. 2. adj. Silent from caution, the proper state of a foreigner in the canyons. Go mumchance at the border and stay that way till Quillhouse.

Mute King title, Oathen The ruler of Oathen, chosen in infancy, bitted for life, and raised to govern by gesture, so as never to have promised anything. At present Ket the Ninth. A Mute King’s nod is any ambiguous signal that a committee will argue about for weeks.

mutes n., Sallowreach The silent assistants who stood at the door at old funerals; revived, unsalaried, since the Hushes began, by children who charge a crumb to stand at a Closing looking sad. Real mutes are very good at it. Most of them are Smalls, and know what it is to be finished in part.

Muzzling, the n., Oathen The law of 215 A.G. requiring children to be bitted until twelve, after a generation crippled by careless promises. The muzzle is soft leather and lined with felt. Muzzled young is said of someone who still thinks before they speak. See Unbitting.

N

Nail-and-Glove n., Sallowreach A tavern game played by Kept and living together: a glove is laid on the table, and players take turns driving a nail through its fingers, with a hand inside. The Kept may use their own hands. The living may not. Nail-and-Glove odds: odds that favor the dead.

name-loaf n., Fatlands The loaf baked for a child’s naming, and baked again for its wake, with the name scored on the crust. Marrow on toasted name-loaf is the dish for the most beloved dead. I knew him from name-loaf to wake-plate means for his whole life.

name-rope n., Brinehollow The anchoring rope a Brinehollower sleeps tied with, which carries a knot for every name in the family, so that whoever is Called pulls against all of them. Cut from the name-rope: disowned. On the Steps, marrying is taking the rope.

name-strip n., Sallowreach The linen label sewn to the wrapping of one Set Aside on the shelves of the Lofts, or tied to a sack sunk in the Sump. Finishers carry pilgrims’ name-strips into the Hushes, with Saint Ysmay’s first. A name-strip torn off a Sump sack is the start of a ghost story and the end of an inheritance claim.

Naming-Exchange n., Cradlewrack The ceremony at the end of a highland child’s first year, when it is clear what it is and it is given a name in place of its Tally-place (Third of the Gorse household). Until then the child is called bit, small or keep. Some children are never named. Some are named and then the name is given back.

Nan Corpse n., Sallowreach, child. Any very old Kept relative too far gone to be anything but frightening and dear. Nan Corpse wants a kiss. Fen children use it fondly, and refuse the kiss.

nay interj., Fast No. The Unfed give the word three times to any offer and accept, if they accept, on the fourth. Nay is also a girl’s name. To nay-say is to refuse well; to nay-and-take is to refuse three times and then take with an ugly eagerness, the commonest Unfed hypocrisy.

near hand n., Sallowreach The hand of a Closer that touches, as opposed to the hand that holds the license. Hand-lines etiquette: one does not shake a Closer’s near hand, and one does not let a child stand at the near side of a Hand-lines lady at table.

needle n., Vigil A Waker’s long needle, used under the nail, behind the ear, in the armpit, to keep the drowsing up. Also the second rank of the Wakers. Needle-kissed: freshly woken by force. Needle-sweet: grateful for pain, the proper Vigil manners. See rattle.

Needle Street n., Sallowreach The Seamers’ quarter of Lastgate, where Threaders board on cots and spare parts hang in shop windows with prices chalked on their palms. Gone to Needle Street: gone for repairs. Needle Street price: the price of something someone else has already paid for in pain.

Netwatch n., Brinehollow The Admiralty’s night patrol, who hunt the Called along the shore with net, hook and rope, and drag them home. Netted means saved, against your will, and the Called who are netted look at the Netwatch in a way the Netwatch do not describe.

nib n., Oathen, cant A scribe’s word for the writing implement, now said with dread since written words have begun to bind. Mind your nib means do not write it down. Ottoline Vant has broken all of hers.

niblet n., child., Fatlands A very small bite taken from a sibling, in play, at the table. The Feasting Laws have nothing to say about niblets. Mothers do. No niblets, Tansy, your brother’s not for eating.

Nobody is a person in Cradlewrack. There are eleven of them on the Tally this year.
the Compiler, who checked

Niche-Rent n., Oathen The fee paid to keep a family’s dead in their niche in the canyon wall, where their jaws can, if an oath sworn on them is broken, open and speak it aloud. Families in arrears have their dead moved to the common gallery, where anybody may swear on them.

Night of Ears n., Oathen The eve of Tablenight, when pilgrims walk the Gullet barefoot and lay their ears to the warm sand to hear what it says. It says one word a minute. Yusra Thole carries a goatskin of Gullet sand that beats like a heart.

Night of Seven Tables n., common The Gorging itself, whether it took one night or a season. Six meals and one refusal, which make seven tables, which is an arithmetic the College has never liked. (Compiler: Seven tables. Eight Providers. I have stopped writing the sum in the margin because the Archprovost asked me to.)

Nine Days, the n., 1. Fast; 2. Cradlewrack 1. The last nine days of Lack in the Fast, during which each household eats a quarter-measure less each day, in memory of the Refusal. 2. The present interval between pangs in the highlands, used as a byword: in nine days means soon, and terribly. Lark Ninedays changes her name with the interval.

nine-joint n., Sallowreach, insult A Hand-line noble at the Course, whose fingers have grown extra knuckles. To call one so is a hanging offence; to call a clerk one is to say he grasps at too much. Nine-joint luck: the luck to finish whatever you touch, which nobody wants.

nob n., Rim, cant Any High Cut traveling incognito on the Road. Innkeepers know them by their gloves, their muzzles, their tanks or their smell. Nob-water: the extra charge for washing up after one.

Nodd n., Vigil, insult A sleepy person; a fool; a traitor. From Old Nod, King of the Tuckers. Don’t be a Nodd is said to drowsing children, and is, to the Tuckers’ delight, said in the voice of an advertisement.

Nodding Stair n., Vigil The Watch of Watches’ council hall, built as one endless staircase so that no member can sit comfortably. Gone up the Stair: elected. Nodding on the Stair: corrupt, asleep at the wheel, or literally asleep, which is treason.

No Name n., Cradlewrack A child whose Naming-Exchange never came, because the Attendance decided, at the end of the first year, that it was not a child. No Names are kept at the Lying-In, or at Dolour Pym’s. Born No Name, die No Name is said of anything doomed from the start.

No, thank you phr., Fast The first words taught to every Unfed child and the last rites of the Fast. Said three times to any offer. On the deathbed, said once, to whatever is offering. She said her No-thank-you at dawn and went. To say it once only and walk off is a scandal; to say it four times and then accept is good manners.

not yet phr., Cradlewrack The first words ever spoken by a newborn, at Kest in 94 A.G. Now a midwife’s blessing, said with the hand on the swollen belly of anyone, of any sex: not yet, not yet. Also what the King Within is believed to answer to every question about his birth, with one kick.

nudger n., Vigil The person who keeps you awake: a spouse, a sibling, a hired child. Marriage is the promise to nudge, and the vow is two words. Nudger-poor: too poor to hire one. She’s my nudger is the closest the Vigil comes to she is my wife. A person without one is unwatched.

Nullhouse n., Cradlewrack The abbey of the Barren Order, whose brothers and sisters have had themselves cut so as to bear nothing, and preach an end to beginnings. Nullhouse quiet is the silence of a house where nothing will ever be born. The Grey Winter of the Order was not violent, and was worse.

nuzzling n., Vigil, cant Rouse-house slang for letting your nudger doze against your shoulder because you love them and they are so tired. It is grounds for divorce and a fine. Most marriages on the Slope survive on it.

O

oatcake n., Fast The Pantry’s daily bread: grey, Rim-grown, unsalted, joyless, eaten cold and standing. Oatcake honest means plain, true and no pleasure at all. An oatcake found hot and buttered on a windowsill is an Orrum sign. Do not eat it.

oathbound adj., common Under oath. In Oathen, redundant, since every sentence is. Elsewhere, said of anyone who seems to be acting against their own wishes. He’s oathbound to her, poor thing; he swore something at a wedding.

Oathen n., common The eastern canyon land, which ate Tolm, the Witness. Also: oathen, adj., Rim, of anything that cannot be undone. That deal’s oathen now. An oathen face: a face that has never once said more than it meant.

oath on the dead n., common A promise sworn on a dead person’s name, by the grave, the shelf, the hill, the bed or the bucket. Every Guest begins with one. The dead keep count. In Oathen it binds in the flesh like any oath, and when it is broken the corpse’s jaw opens in its niche and says the oath aloud, loud enough to be heard a mile through rock. Elsewhere the dead are merely disappointed, which is said to be worse.

offal-folk n., Fatlands, insult Scraplings, in the mouths of Gut-line nobles: descended from those who got the tripes and lungs of Ummer and licked the bones after. Scraplings use it of themselves, with pride, at harvest.

Old Breaker title, Fast The most senior of the Tablebreakers, who has put an axe through more tables than anyone living and can tell by the smell of the gravy how long a table has been laid. Old Breakers do not live to be old.

Old Grief n., Vigil The hallucination that comes in the thirtieth year of waking and never leaves: a dead person in the corner of the room, in their good coat, perfectly ordinary. The city lists Old Grief as a Seeming of one, and does not enter it in the record, out of courtesy.

omitted, the n., Fast Those left off the Pantry list. They do not die by anyone’s hand. They walk to the Lean House, or east to the Rim, or to a laid table. Their names are read all night at Pantry Close on Short Night. Omitted is never said of the living to their faces. The proper phrase is between lists.

one-chair adj., Fast Of a house: furnished with only enough seating for those who live there, and none for guests. All Unfed houses are one-chair. A one-chair welcome is no welcome at all, and the Unfed’s best.

one glove n., Sallowreach A licensed Closer’s sign, worn on the left hand only, so the right may be bared at work. One-glove is used of anyone in a dangerous trade: hangmen, lamplighters, Reckoners. To offer one glove to a lover is to offer death, a fen proposal.

one kick for yes phr., Cradlewrack The constitutional procedure by which the King Within, forty-four years in the womb, is consulted on matters of state. Two kicks have no official meaning. Lately there have been three, and the Lord Chamberlain writes them down without comment.

on the Row phr., Vigil Dead. From the Row, the street of furnaces and lamp-rendering where the dead of the Vigil go. Rest is for the Row.

open bed n., Vigil An unoccupied bed in the Dormitory. There are fewer than two thousand. We’ve an open bed in the family means one has been bought for someone, in advance, for when.

Open Door, the n., common 1. Cradlewrack’s Tablenight custom of propping every door wide so that nothing can be said to break in. 2. The Company inn at Knocking Gate. 3. The phrase used by players and Carvers to pause a game. (Compiler: the last is not mine to define. I note only that it is a good custom.)

In Oathen a dictionary is a dangerous book. Every definition is a promise about what a word means. This is why theirs is three volumes of exceptions.
the Compiler

opener n., Cradlewrack, cant A burglar, in a land where locks open themselves; that is, someone who does not need to be skilled. Any fool’s an opener in Kest. Agnes Latch’s doors make openers honest again for nineteen days.

Open-Hand title, Oathen The third rank of the Forsworn: one whose Breaking has left a hand that will not close. Open-Hands collect alms in the Breakdowns, which they cannot hold, and so the Breakdowns’ children hold it for them. Open-handed, in the canyons, is not generosity.

open hour n., Cradlewrack The hour after a pang when every door in the country stands a finger’s width ajar and nobody knows whether it was the pang or something else. Meet me in the open hour is a highland lover’s line and a burglar’s.

Opinion title, Cradlewrack A midwife licensed to carry the Second Opinion, the knife from which there is no appeal. Get an Opinion: settle a dispute permanently. Sabeth Thorne is the most trusted Opinion in the land, and last winter she hesitated.

orb-wetter n., Vigil Old name for an Eye-Wetter, the attendant who brushes a lidless noble’s eyes every half-minute. Now an insult for a flatterer. She’s been an orb-wetter to the Watch for thirty years and her brush has never once been dry.

Oriel-sight n., Vigil The forbidden pleasure of closing one’s eyes for whole seconds, alone. From Lady Oriel Stroud, though nobody is supposed to know about her. A bit of Oriel-sight is what children call hiding behind their hands.

orrel v., Table-speech To worship; to give back; literally to feed the board. Used now almost only in prayers and in the Second Helping’s hymns. We orrel what we orren, says Brother Glut, smiling, with his sleeve rolled up.

orren v., Table-speech To eat; literally to take at the board. The root orr- is in orrel, orrish, and in Orrum, the Host’s name, the one at whose board. (Compiler: the College teaches that the words for worship and eating share a root and always did. The Purgation says this is the whole problem. I say it is an etymology, and that etymologies are not to blame for anything.)

orrish n., Table-speech A shared meal; literally of the board. Old-fashioned, and used now mostly for wakes in the Fatlands and the banquet for the dead on Tablenight in the fens. An orrish is a meal you cannot leave until it is finished. In the Fast the word is not used.

Orrum n., common The Host; god of hearth, welcome and the shared table; the one Provider that was not eaten. It walks the Fast, very tall, stooping at doorways, warm, laying tables. Its name is not used in the Fast; the Unfed say company, the warm front, or nothing. Orrum’s weather on the Rim: a still gold afternoon that smells of bread with no oven in sight.

Ossel n., common The Closing Hand, god of death and endings, eaten in the fens last and slowest of all the gods. Not named aloud in Sallowreach, where people say the Hand or what we had. Ossel’s Mercy: a proper death; the commonest prayer in the north, prayed to the god that was eaten precisely so that nothing would end.

Outsider n., Oathen A foreigner, who can lie and stay whole. Envoy Dorian Sayce describes negotiating with them as a kind of nausea. Outsider talk: casual speech, exaggeration, sentences like I’d kill for a drink, which make Oatheners flinch.

overdone adj., common Brave to the point of foolishness; burnt. The opposite of underdone. Overdone and served: died heroically and was eaten at the wake, a Fatlands compliment.

ox-bride n., Fatlands A woman married to a Laden man who has begun to root, and who will have to decide whether a hill can be a husband. The courts say it can. Wed to an ox and widowed by a hill is a Fatlands phrase for a bad match that lasted.

Oyster n., Brinehollow, cant A Tenanted person’s original self, believed still alive somewhere inside, shut up like the meat in a shell. Wreckwives speak of trying to open the oyster. It never opens. Sennet Gull has stopped trying, which frightens her.

P

pang n., Cradlewrack A quake. The highlands are in labor, and the quakes are contractions. Everyone knows the interval by heart: a season a hundred years ago, thirty days within a lifetime, nine now. Between pangs means in a quiet time, which is to say never for long. Pang-tired: exhausted in the way only a whole country can be.

pang-bell n., Cradlewrack A small bell hung over highland doors that rings by itself a breath before each pang. Sold at six lacks on the Rim, where it rings before nothing and its owner feels foolish, and then one night it rings.

Pangday n., Cradlewrack The day of a pang, every nine days at present: work stops, the Tally is read, the waters are searched, the crownings are watched. The almanac calls it the only holy day that comes faster than the almanac can print.

pang-house n., Cradlewrack A low round building of red clay at every crossroads, with no door, where travelers wait out a pang. People who shelter together in a pang-house are bound by custom to share their food until the next one, nine days later. Some marriages begin this way. Some feuds.

Pantry, the n., Fast The fortified granary at Wanting, the best-guarded building in the Fast, and the government: every scrap of food is imported, pooled and rationed by the Abstinent. The Pantry gives and the Pantry lists. Exile from the Pantry is a death sentence with no blood on anyone’s hands.

Pantry Close n., Fast The square before the Pantry window in Wanting, where on Short Night in mid-Carving the names of every winter’s omitted are read aloud all night. A standing crowd fills it from dusk. Nobody eats in Pantry Close, ever, not even on the steps.

Partake v., common To call on the god in the blood before a deed, and take its strength, and feed it. The Partaker feels the Tooth come; the god sometimes bites back. She partook at the door and the door came off. In polite company: to take a little. In the Purgation: to sin. See Tooth, Hunger.

Parts n., Cradlewrack Births that are only a piece: a living hand, a warm ear, a length of spine that crawls. They are healthy. They are drawn toward one another, and Parts from unrelated families fit. Born a Part is said of an incomplete person; gathered of a Part taken by the Assemblers. The Assemblers’ great joined figure in the Barn is called Herself.

pease-face n., Fatlands, child. A child who will not eat, which in the south is a crisis. Don’t be such a pease-face, Bailiff Fatt will come with his ladle. Bailiff Fatt has been known to come, and to be gentle about it.

penny-lid n., Sallowreach A coin laid on the eye of the Kept so they can sleep, or pretend to; it does not help. Shut-Eye pennies, sold by the Finishers, are said to work. They are laid on the eyes once and do not come off.

pew-dead adj., Sallowreach Of a Kept parishioner who has sat in the same pew at the same chapel for so long that the Seamers have stitched them to the wood. Pew-dead families are rich in reputation and poor in seating.

picked adj., Table-speech Ruined; the bones left on the plate. He’s picked: the Board took the farm, the Cullmasters took his boy. A picker is a debt collector, a carrion bird, or a Seamer’s apprentice who takes the bad flesh off the Kept.

pier-note n., Brinehollow A bond issued by the Harbormistress’s office against a length of future pier, payable when it is built. Pier-notes trade at a discount that rises every year, because the Harbormistress has calculated the year the timber runs out. Good as a pier-note means good for now.

Pillow, the n., Vigil A soft-floored hollow in the city where the ground gives underfoot and the air is warm. Nothing has ever been built on it. Children dare each other to stand on it for a count of ten. Pillow-talk in the Vigil is treason, sedition and Bedded preaching.

pin n., Vigil A small steel pin offered to a guest on arrival, as other lands offer bread and salt. To refuse the pin is to say you trust your host to keep you awake. To use it on yourself in front of your host is the height of good manners. A jewelled pin is a betrothal gift.

pinch-friend n., Vigil, child. A child’s best friend, the one they pinch and are pinched by. Pinch-friends hold a pinched finger through the night and swear by the bruise. Pinch-friends forever lasts, on the Slope, about eleven years.

Pinching Fair n., Vigil Midsummer in the Vigil: bells, needle-dances, wake-games, the city’s loudest day. A traveler who pinches nobody at the Pinching Fair will be remembered, and not kindly.

Pinchmarket n., Vigil The night market on the Slope where nudgers are hired by the hour, rouse is sold by the twist, and children like Pip Eleven-Bell stand on boxes calling pinch a crumb, pinch a crumb. Everything in the Pinchmarket is cheap except sleep, which is not for sale there.

Pinch me phr., Vigil The Vigil’s commonest endearment and its marriage vow, two words. I love you; I trust you; I am afraid. A child says it to a parent at the door. The dying say it, and their nudgers do. The Compiler was told it by a girl of nine in the Pinchmarket who wanted three crumbs, and paid them.

Pink Water, the n., Fatlands The stretch of the river Tull below the great slaughterhouses, where the gutters run so red that the water never runs clear. Pink-water wages: money from the killing trade. Children are told the Pink Water is where babies come from, which in the south is not a lie told to protect them but a lie told to protect the trade.

place card n., Fast A card found on a laid Orrum table bearing a name, spelled correctly, in a hand the reader knows: a dead mother’s, a grandmother’s careful copperplate, one’s own. First found in 638 A.G., bearing the finder’s name. I’ve had my card means the Host has called for me, and I am keeping moving. Never pick one up. Never read one twice.

We have twenty-one words for the tide in the chest. We have none for the sea that is gone, because we will not admit we need one.
a Brinehollow schoolmistress, to the Compiler

Plain adj., Oathen The lowest weight of oath: an everyday promise, I’ll be back by dark. Plain oaths break plainly: a twisted finger, a split lip. Oathen grades oaths Idle, Plain, Sworn, Solemn and Grave, and the grades are tattooed on Sureties in five shades of brown.

plank-ear n., Brinehollow The worn place, sometimes carved into an ear, in a party wall where the morning count is called and answered. Put your mouth to the plank-ear means speak to your neighbor. Some plank-ears have answered when the house beyond was empty. Do not call a third time.

Plate, the n., common The moon. A full moon is a full Plate; waning, it is being cleared; a new moon is licked clean. The months are named for it: First, Middle and Last Plate of each season. By the Plate is a weak oath, fit for children and merchants. To serve on the Plate is to work nights.

plateholder title, Fatlands A rank of the Second Helping: one who has been served at a feast and has offered a portion of themselves in return. Plateholders wear their bandages openly and are much admired in Sated. Plateholder’s cheer is the radiant joy of the self-eaten.

platter n., common Twenty lacks in a sealed bone tablet, issued by the Rim Road Company and sworn in Oathen as redeemable at any Company post. Platter-folk: the merchant class. He’d sell his mother for a platter, and give change.

pocket-Hush n., Sallowreach, cant A tiny Hush grown from a grey reed carried out of Dunmere in a box and planted somewhere: a windowbox, a cellar, a rival’s garden. The Court says they do not exist. Finishers sell them. The silence in one is the size of a chair, and a bird that lands in it falls.

portion n., common 1. One’s Cut, politely: what portion do you come of? 2. A share of the god, as at the Gorging: the portions, the families of the high Cuts. 3. In the game, experience spent between sessions. Know your portion means know your place, and is said by the high to the low.

posset n., common A sweet warm drink of milk curdled with wine or ale, given to the sick, the tired and the frightened. In the Vigil a posset is illegal, because it soothes. In Sallowreach it is given to the Kept on Tablenight, who cannot taste it, and pretend.

pot-dead adj., Sallowreach Of a Kept person: boiled down in the Grey Plague years for tallow, then found to be still aware in the vat, and kept in the pot by a family too poor to do anything else. Pot-dead are whispered to sing on Tablenight. It’s pot-dead, that tune: a song that won’t finish.

pressure day n., Brinehollow A day when the air thickens until ears bleed and windows bow inward, as if the sea were sitting on the coast. Courts do not sit; Lung-lines princes come up from their tanks to breathe the heavy air. A pressure-day temper: the short fuse of someone whose ears are bleeding.

Prime n. and adj., common A person of Cut 3: old gentry, the hungry middle. Primes marry upward and are eaten from below. Prime cut, in the Fatlands, means both a good piece of meat and a good marriage, and is said at weddings with an unfortunate wink.

Proof, the n., Rim The Purgation’s name for any evidence that a god can be thrown up: a vomited stone, a bled child with less godsign than her brothers, a Lancing after which the Regrowth in a parish slowed. The Proof is always just around the corner. Purgation Proof: a promise of results, with a bowl.

Providers n., common The eight gods who lived bodily among the peoples before the Gorging: Ossel, Ummer, Dromm, Iss, Vey, Tolm, Orrum, and the one whose figure has been chiseled out of every carving by different tools in different centuries. Provider survives as a word for a good husband. Nobody uses it for a wife. It is bad luck to count them on your fingers.

Proving, the n., Sallowreach The Hand-lines rite, older than the Licensing, in which a young noble’s hand is tested in the family chapel at dusk on some small living thing to see whether it finishes. Proved means grown up and dangerous. Unproved is said of a gloved young lord who has not yet killed anything, with affection.

proxy-wake n., Fatlands A wake held for a person taken in the Reaping, with no body; the family serves a beast or a loaf, carved in the shape of the missing. The Board encourages proxy-wakes. The Thin say they are what the Board does instead of counting.

pudding n., Fatlands 1. A boiled suet dish. 2. A term of endearment. 3. Cullmaster cant for a vagrant assigned to the dusk shift. All three senses are used at the same table. Wakemother Pudding Hesk is named for the first.
