puddle-deep adj., Brinehollow Deeper than it looks, said of a person or a puddle; from the puddles that follow Old Wet Tom down corridors, into which children say you can look a long way. Don’t trust a puddle-deep man.

pull, the n., Brinehollow The god’s tide in a person: standing at west-facing windows, sleepwalking to wells and washbasins, the Appetite of the coast. She’s got the pull is said low, the way other lands say she’s got the cough. Wardens at Lowmark Spur watch travelers for it.

Pull-rope n., Brinehollow The rope hung from every bedhead on the coast, tied at night to wrist or ankle. She cut her pull-rope means she went into the sea willingly. A child found holding a cut pull-rope on a doorstep, waiting for someone to tie it again, is the coast’s most common Dread 2 sight.

Purgation n., common The cross-border movement that believes the gods can be thrown back up, by fasting, bleeding, emetic and, at the far end, by massacre of high-Cut families. Purge-hall: one of their soup kitchens. Purged: vomited, emptied, or killed in a Lancing, depending on who says it.

purse-tooth n., Rim A false tooth, hollow, in which a traveler keeps a platter rolled thin. Purse-tooth thieves work the Rim with pliers and a kind voice. Pull a purse-tooth: to rob someone who thought they were clever.

Q

quaff-wake n., Fatlands A wake at which the dead are drunk rather than eaten: the dead rendered into a broth, for those who died too thin to carve. It is considered shameful to the family and kind to the dead.

quarter-measure n., Fast One quarter of a Pantry Measure, the amount by which each household’s ration falls each day in the Nine Days. To live on quarter-measure is to be dying respectably.

Queen of the Smalls title, Sallowreach Little Nell Ash, who died at seven two hundred years ago and rules the child-dead of Lastgate’s undercity with a two-century mind and a seven-year-old’s idea of fairness. A Queen-of-the-Smalls ruling: a judgement that is completely fair and completely unreasonable.

Question, the n., Cradlewrack The second of the Midwife’s Two Questions, Does it stay?, which is the only one that matters. Put the Question means decide whether something shall live, and is used of business, marriages and puppies, by people who have never seen it put at a bedside.

quick adj., Vigil Awake; alive, in the Vigil’s sense. The quick and the Counted. The Inquisitor of the Quick is the Wakers’ officer who decides whether a sleeper was truly asleep or only resting their eyes. Quick-proof: a pin through the palm, offered in court.

quick-loaf n., Rim Bread baked fast and badly at waystations for travelers, sold hot so that you eat it at the door before you notice. Quick-loaf manners: eating with strangers without saying the grace, because you were hungry. It is still an insult.

Quiet, the n., Oathen An ascetic order that has given up speech, some by vow and some by knife. Its ranks run Hushed, Sealed, Tongueless, Stillmind, and the Abbess. Sister Verity Amn teaches that for the highest bloodlines, a promise made only in thought now binds. Gone to the Quiet is said of someone who will never be heard again, and is no longer always a joke.

quiet-keeper n., Oathen A household servant whose job is to sit with the children before the Unbitting and stop them making promises with their hands. Quiet-keepers are fierce, devoted and often Forsworn themselves, and some of them have lost fingers to save a child’s.

Quiet Supper n., Oathen Any meal eaten in total silence, as on Tablenight and at the old Silent Supper of the Gorging. Oathen families hold a Quiet Supper to mark a death, a birth or a breaking. Guests who speak at one are asked to leave and to swear, in writing, that they will not come again.

Quillhouse n., Rim The Company’s eastern waystation on the high causeway across north Oathen: felted bridges, slates at every door, and the place where foreigners first learn to keep their mouths shut. A Quillhouse silence is the silence of someone who has just realized what they almost said.

quillon n., Oathen, cant The small cross-stroke a Clausewright adds beneath a written conditional to show it is meant as a door out of the sentence. Since writing began to bind, the quillon has been added to letters, shop signs and graffiti. Breakdowns wits write only quillons, and nothing above them.

quilting n., Sallowreach The patching of a Kept body with squares of other skin, bought from Needle Street, sewn in a pattern. A quilted grandmother is a family’s pride. She’s more quilt than Gran is said of the very old, kindly.

quire n., Rim A ledger of the Cutwrights’ College, bound in grey, recording a land’s or a parish’s Cuts across six centuries. A stolen quire is a Reckoner’s target list. Quired means recorded, known, measured: she’s quired to the fourth decimal. To burn the quire is to destroy the evidence of a bloodline.

Quire n., Rim The College’s walled town of grey stone on a green hill on the northeastern Rim, holding the Master Concordance. Quire-clever: precise and unkind. (Compiler: I am from Quire. I contest only the second half of this.)

R

ration chit n., Fast A square of unbleached cloth stamped with an empty bowl, entitling the bearer to one day’s ration at the Pantry window. Issued by household, by name, by list. Cannot lawfully be sold and is sold constantly, at three lacks in Lack season. Chit-sold: a family that has sold its future to eat now.

rattle n., Vigil 1. The wooden rattle every Waker carries, swung under the ear of the drowsing. 2. The lowest rank of the Wakers. 3. The sound of tin roofs in rain, built loose on purpose so that rain will not soothe anyone. Rattle-rich: wealthy enough to afford a tin roof that is really loud.

rattle-baby n., Vigil A baby born to a Waker family, given a rattle instead of a lullaby and pinched in the cradle. Rattle-babies grow up to be Wakers or to run away to the Slope. Rattle-baby manners: rough, efficient, rather kind.

Rattlehouse n., Vigil The Wakers’ barracks and training-house, where recruits learn the precisely tolerable pain. Its walls are hung with needles, the way a smithy is hung with tongs. Sent to the Rattlehouse: arrested for dozing.

reading, the n., Oathen The Forsworn custom of interpreting another person’s Breakings, from across a street, as a moral biography: a wrist bent so, a jaw wired thus, a spine hooked. I’ve read him means I know exactly what he has broken. The Breakdowns teach children to read before they teach them letters.

Reaping, the n., Fatlands The yearly vanishing, each Carving, of people who are out in the far field at dusk and are not back by morning. The official explanation is wolves. There are no wolves in the Fatlands. Reaped is said of the missing. Reaping weather: a warm, still evening in Carving with the fields breathing. See Long Count, Cullmaster.

Reckoner n., common A raider out of the Fast who crosses the Rim to kill the highest bloodlines of the Godeaters in their beds. Ranks: Carrier, Knife, Kin-Reader, Band-Captain, Reckoner-Captain. A Reckoner’s welcome: a black-iron knife in the night. To reckon in the high Cuts’ houses has stopped meaning to count.

red ledger n., Rim Any record of deaths kept by someone who was not supposed to keep it: Pell Hogget’s staves, Teodor Rell’s Lain Book, the Assay’s figures, Mercy Thrane’s list of surgeries. Keeping a red ledger is dangerous everywhere and a crime in four lands.

Regrowth n., common The return of an eaten god through its eaters, in stages: the Taste, the Appetite, the Course, the Brink, the Seating. Its marks are godsign. Regrowth is formal, used in the College and in sermons. People say it’s coming on her, she’s turning, she’s growing back.

relict n., Fast The survivor of a family whose other members are Seated. Relicts visit the Long Table on feast days, from the verge. A relict’s portion: the food of a family that has fewer mouths than it used to, carried home uneaten.

Renderers n., Fatlands The slaughter, salting and shipping trades, organized in a Union whose ranks run Hook, Jointer, Yardmaster, Stamper and Mistress. They know what is in every barrel that leaves the Chute. Going through the joint is their phrase for a killing done in a dispute.

rendering n., Fatlands The boiling of fat from carcasses for tallow, soap and lamp-oil; the trade of the Renderers’ Union. Rendered means melted down, and also means explained in public to the point of ruin. Rendering-house: a slaughterhouse; and in Board cant, the Weighhouse cellars.

rest n., Vigil A forbidden word in polite company, as obscene as any curse. Voluntary rest is the law’s term for the Lain-Down. Rest well is the Vigil’s worst insult, a wish of death. Foreigners who say it on leaving an inn are stared at.

Restitching n., Sallowreach The annual repair of the Kept at home in early Grace, the one joyful mass of the fen year. Families sit their grandmothers at the kitchen table, lay out thread, and sing. Restitching Week is when Seamers raise their prices and children learn to thread a needle.

Retching Day n., Rim The anniversary of the Purgation’s founding, when the halls give the Black Draught free at the Weeping Post and the road there is lined with the kneeling. Retching Day promises: resolutions made in a moment of physical misery and abandoned.

returning n., Cradlewrack The great dread of highland parents: a child who grows younger, like Ambrose the Eldest Infant, back toward the cradle and through it. She’s returning is said of a child whose teeth are coming out the wrong way.

Ribwalker n., Brinehollow A thing on the Uncovered with too many ribs, the size of an ox, dragging itself toward the far water on fins of rotting leather. Salvagers name them; Ribwalker bellows are a Leaving. A Ribwalker of a man: someone long past dying who will not stop.

Ridden adj., several lands Possessed: of a Tenanted Brinehollower, of a Seemer seeing through someone else’s eyes, of a Fatlander with the god’s appetite in charge. Polite people say occupied. The Compiler has heard ridden said, of a lord, by his own groom.

The sentence I heard most often on the Rim was I’m sorry, we don’t say that here. I heard it in seven lands, about seven different words.
the Compiler

Rim, the n., common The Rim Road, the ring of highway around the Fast’s border along which all trade moves; and the inns, tolls and towns along it; and the Company that owns them. On the Rim: abroad, homeless, in trade. Rim-born: belonging to no land and every inn.

Rim-fever n., Rim The restless conviction, on long journeys, that the cure for your land is in the next one. Every land has it. Nothing has ever worked. Rim-fever is also the trade in cures itself, and the innkeepers’ word for the travelers who keep it going.

rind n., Fatlands The tough outer skin of the Laden in the Course, rough as bark, which their servants oil daily. Old Mother Rind is a Seated hill-woman whose advice is always right. To rind is to grow hard and old; rinded is used, admiringly, of a matriarch.

ring-closer n., Vigil A Slope widow or widower who takes a dead nudger’s place in a household’s ring of watchers for the rest of their life, watched by whoever watched the dead. Said quietly, with a respect close to fear. See closing the ring.

Rising, the n., Fast The day after the Nine Days, the anniversary of the day Orrum got up from Hallowboard. Nobody speaks above a whisper and nobody looks west. A traveler who answers come in on the Rising will be remembered.

rook v., Vigil, cant To cut rouse with something that works, especially bottled Brinehollow brine, after Rook Quarter-Bell. Rooked rouse keeps you awake. It also sets you walking west. Rooked to the eyebrows means awake, wet-lunged and heading for the coast.

Root n., Cradlewrack An Uncut elder whose cord has grown down into the clay. The long houses feel the land’s pulse through their Roots. To put down a Root is to settle forever; the Fatlands say the same, and mean something worse.

rootkin n., Fatlands Living things grown from the buried or Seated dead: roots with birthmarks, tubers with fingernails. Tansy Lard waters one behind her house. Rootkin sap is bottled and sold as a tonic for grief; it tastes of the person.

rope funeral n., Brinehollow The rite for the Called who do not come back: the name-rope is cut, coiled, and burned on the Chapel Reach, and the knot that was theirs is kept by the eldest. She had a rope funeral means no body. She had two means she came back Tenanted and was buried twice.

Rope-Holder title, Fast The Tablebreaker who holds the rope tied round the Axe’s waist, to pull them back if they begin to sit. To hold someone’s rope is to be the one person they trust not to let them sit down, and is the Fast’s word for marriage, though nobody says so.

round-house n., Cradlewrack The common highland dwelling: round, red clay, with no corners for anything to wait in and no door that locks. Round-house honest: hiding nothing, because nothing can be hidden.

rouse n., Vigil The bitter black stimulant taken hourly. Teeth go first, then the heart. The dose has risen every decade since the Patent of 390 A.G. and the Apothecary-General knows where the curve ends. Rouse-mouth: black-stained teeth. Rouse-poor: unable to afford enough to stay awake, which is a death sentence by bed.

rouse-tab n., Vigil The Vigil’s small money: a pressed lozenge of rouse stamped with an open eye, nominally an hour awake and worth three crumbs. The only currency on the Table that suffers inflation of the body: the stamped eye gets smaller every season. Paid in tabs means paid in time.

Row, the n., Vigil The street of furnaces and lamp-rendering where the dead of the Vigil are taken and, it is said quietly, put to use. He’s on the Row: he is dead. Rest is for the Row: a proverb said to anyone who complains of tiredness.

rue-child n., Oathen A person held at an age by their own childhood promise, like Little Rue, sixty-three in a child’s body. Rue-children are rare, sad and much consulted, because they remember everything. Don’t make a rue-child of him is said to parents who extract promises from toddlers.

Ruin n., common What happens to a body when its Flesh runs out: an Injury from the Mangling and collapse. Ruined in common speech is a lady’s word for having lost a limb. She’s in ruin: she is down, still breathing, and the next blow kills, except in the fens, where nothing does.

Runner n., Fast A Crumb-Runner: a smuggler who brings food in from the Rim. Despised, spat upon in the street, and the only reason anyone in the Fast is alive. The Runners call their trade by the insult, the way a scarred man calls himself Scar.

rust-hand n., Sallowreach, insult A Seamer who uses cheap iron wire that rusts, staining the Kept a brown that never comes out. Rust-handed work is any shoddy job, especially one on a person.

S

Sallowreach n., common The northern fen land, which ate Ossel, the Closing Hand, and where nothing dies. Sallow is fen-grey, the colour of a Kept cheek. Sallowreach weather: warm, wet, sweet in the wrong way, with flies.

Saltbridge n., Rim The Company’s Cure-House, the only lawful mint on the Table since 212 A.G., where Fatlands bone is cured in salt boiled from Brinehollow bail-water. Saltbridge-new: freshly minted, or freshly dead.

salt-gift n., Brinehollow A pinch of salt from a bail-bucket, given to a departing traveler for luck. Refusing it is unkind. Accepting it is unwise, since it is, after all, a little of the sea, and the sea is going somewhere.

salt manners n., Brinehollow The coast’s courtesy: do not mention how anyone sounds when they breathe, and do not ask a returned person where they went. She has no salt manners means she is a foreigner or a child. The Compiler was corrected four times in one morning.

Sated n., Fatlands The capital: wide doors, reinforced floors, ramps instead of stairs, and the smell of gravy from every drain. Sated is never used to mean full, since no one in the south has ever been full. Sated-shaped: enormous; a compliment.

Sayer n., Oathen A Tongue-line at the Seating, who does not describe the world. What they say, is. The few alive are kept bitted in gold in the Gilded Cells. Sayer-sure: absolutely certain; and a Sayer’s sentence is any decision that cannot be undone. Lady Imre Dath is the one the Table means.

scarecrow-sure adj., Fatlands Surely coming, slowly. From the Scarecrow of Low Tilth, which stands in the far field with its back to the village, a few furrows closer each Carving. Last year someone saw it turn around. Scarecrow-sure is said of debts, death and the Board.

Scrapling n., common A descendant of those who got the scraps and licked the bones at the Gorging; Cut 1; the least changed people alive, and the poor of every land. Scraplings use the word of themselves without shame. Scrap-luck is the luck of having little god in you, which is the only luck the poor have.

Seamer n., Sallowreach A stitcher, embalmer and wire-worker of the Guild that holds the population together. Ranks run Threader, Journeyman, Seamer, Master of the Seam, Master Seamer. A Seamers’ strike would be national collapse within a month. Seamer’s patience is infinite, slow and paid by the hour.

Seated, the n., Fast Those who sat at Orrum’s tables, and do not get up. They remain for decades eating from empty plates, smiling, wasting, praising the food, and invite you to join them, and mean it kindly. Seated is never used in the Fast to mean sitting down. The Unfed say they took a chair for that, if they say it at all.

Seating n., common The last stage of the Regrowth, at which the god is in some real portion present again, wearing a person or a place: a Hush, a hill, a Tenant, a moving sleeper, a land in labor, a Sayer. The Seating in sermons; the end in kitchens. No land has reached a full one. Three are close.

Second Face n., Brinehollow The other self that looks out through a Tenanted person’s eyes: courteous, calm, very old. Wreckwives can see it in the half-second after a laugh. I saw her Second Face at supper is how a wife says she knows.

Second Helping n., common 1. On the dice, double tens: an automatic success with a Grace. 2. A second chance, usually an unwise one. 3. the Second Helping, a joyous Fatlands cult of the Bait doctrine, who preach that the god wants to feed and be fed, and volunteer portions of themselves at table.

Second Opinion n., Cradlewrack The Attendance’s knife, and any midwife who carries it. There is no appeal from it. Getting a second opinion in the highlands is not advice-seeking. It is an end.

Second Table n., common A hidden cult, mostly of nobles, whose one idea is: it worked once. When the gods finish regrowing, eat them again. Ranks: Scullion, Taster, Trencherman, Carver, and the Head of the Table, who presides from an empty chair. Second-table talk: any dinner conversation that suddenly becomes about appetite.

Seeming, the n., Vigil The hallucinations that come after enough waking, made a civic sense: when a whole street sees the same thing it is entered in the public record as news. Seemer: an official who reads and records them, like Mirela Sconce. This month eleven districts separately saw a tall figure laying a table in the street. It is entered.

Set-Aside, the n., Sallowreach The Kept who are too far gone to stand, wrapped, labelled and shelved in the Lofts, still aware. Setting Aside is the nearest thing to a funeral. Families visit on feast days and read aloud. Forty thousand of them whisper, and lately they all whisper the same word.

shelf-talk n., Sallowreach What the Set-Aside say to the Loft-Wardens: recipes nobody has cooked in four hundred years, the true names of grandmothers, forgiveness, directions to doors. Shelf-talk is also what fen folk call gossip that has gone on so long it has become history.

shoes to the door phr., Vigil The Lain-Down leave their shoes side by side, toes to the door, before they lie down. Shoes to the door is said of anyone who has given up, and is never said in front of their family. Vigilant children are taught to kick shoes over when they see them set so, and then to run for a Waker.

Short Night n., Fast Mid-Carving, when the names of every winter’s omitted are read in Pantry Close from dusk to dawn. Called short because it never feels long enough to finish the list. It does not finish. The readers stop at dawn and begin there the next year.

Shut Eye title, Sallowreach A senior Finisher, told where new Hushes form; the High Shut Eye is Sister Lorn, who has led nine hundred pilgrims into the silence and stayed outside every time. Shut-Eye pennies are laid on the eyes of the Kept and do not come off.

shut-mouth n. and adj., Oathen A person of discretion; the highest compliment in the canyons. A shut-mouth woman, may she live long and say little. Its opposite is talkative, the worst insult in Oathen.

Shutter Days n., Sallowreach The days of high Plenty when the Kept stay indoors while the flies breed, and smudge-pots burn in every street. A Shutter-Day lover: a sweetheart you see only when the dead are locked in.

Sill, the n., Cradlewrack A hilltop where a single door stands in its frame with no wall around it, ajar since the Gorging, a finger’s width wider each year. Old Hinge tends it. To stand at the Sill is to be on the verge of anything. Nobody has looked through.

Sinks, the n., Sallowreach The lowest inhabited storeys of Lastgate, sunk below the fen, where the Heirs keep safehouses and the water comes in at the ankle. Sink-born: poor, damp and very hard to frighten.

Sister of the Lid title, Vigil A senior of the Bedded, who preach that sleep is a homecoming. Sisters of the Lid look rested. Nobody can explain it. Lidsister, on the Slope, means a woman who has helped someone lie down.

sitter n., Fast One who has taken a chair at a laid table, before they are known to be Seated: the first hours, when the family still believes they will get up. Sitter’s hope is a hope everyone else has already given up.

skim n., Fatlands The film that the drip-rain leaves on standing water, which cooks skim off and use. Skimmed means robbed of the best part. Skim-fed: poor.

Slate-Clerk title, Oathen The lowest Clausewright, who takes down conditions in chalk on a slate so that they can be wiped away before they bind. Slate-promise: a provisional undertaking. Since written words began to bind, Slate-Clerks have begun losing fingers, and the Bench has ordered softer chalk.

sleep-cheat n., Vigil, cant One who buys a minute from the Tuckers and comes back. The Tuckers’ word for a satisfied customer, and the Wakers’ word for a criminal. A sleep-cheat’s face: the look of someone who has seen the long room and the eye at the end of it, and will go back.

The fen word for kindness and the fen word for thread are the same word. The Seamers say this is no coincidence. The Heirs say that is what they would say.
the Compiler

Slope, the n., Vigil The slum quarter where rouse is cut thin, nudgers are cheap, and whole families go down in an afternoon. Slope-tired: past saving. She’s from the Slope means she can stay awake on spite.

Smalls, the n., Sallowreach The child-dead of Lastgate’s undercity, ruled by Little Nell Ash, who calls all four hundred of their names every morning. Small-wise: old and young at once. The Smalls are not to be pitied to their faces, which they find patronising, and they bite.

smudge n., Sallowreach The smoke from the smudge-pots burnt in every street during the Shutter Days of high Plenty, when the Kept are shut in while the flies breed. Smudge-faced: poor, since the rich smell of cedar and the poor of themselves and smoke.

Sniffer title, Fast The lowest Tablebreaker, a child or a light old woman sent ahead to smell for bread on the wind and turn into it, which is the one time in an Unfed life when walking toward the smell is right. Sniffers are lost more often than Axes. Sniffer’s nose: the gift of knowing where the trouble is laid.

sold adj., Oathen Of a principal who has knowingly defaulted on a Surety, so that another body broke in their place: no Surety in the land will stand for them again. The sold drift west along the Rim, where nobody can read the bruise-script on the people they broke.

Sop n., common The act that quiets the god in the blood for a time and feeds the habit: closing, eating, bailing, staying awake, opening, swearing, refusing. Taking a sop is a confession; sop-sick is the state of one who sops too often and cannot stop.

sounding n., Brinehollow Taking the depth of a person: a physician’s old practice of tapping a Brinehollower’s chest to hear how much sea is in it. She’s sounding deep means she is close to the Course. Dr. Isolde Reave’s soundings have found current, and shells.

spare n. and adj., Fast 1. A name for a child: Spare Tolland. 2. Thin, the proper Unfed body. 3. Poachers’ cant for a captured Unfed sold for parts: a spare, spares. The three meanings are known to everyone in the Fast and Spare Tolland has stopped introducing himself.

Spawning, the n., Brinehollow The coast’s name for the doctrine of the Bait: Dromm let itself be eaten as a fish lets itself be scattered, to breed. Illegal on the coast. Spawny talk: heresy, and also any argument that makes a horror sound like a plan.

speaking-trumpet n., Oathen A brass trumpet used by the Forsworn of the Breakdowns, who have nothing left to break, to shout across the canyon to the Bench. Trumpet-honest: truthful at great volume, from Brakk’s habit.

Splint title, Oathen The fourth rank of the Forsworn: one so broken that they are held together by splints and boards, and lead a district of the Breakdowns. Splint-proud is said of anyone who wears their failures openly.

Spoke title, Rim One of the seven on the Wheel, the Rim Road Company’s ruling council, who wear a gold spoke at the throat. Spoked means bribed at the highest level. There are seven Spokes and one hub, says the Company, and does not say who sits at the hub.

spoon-fork n., Rim The two-tined enamel fork carried inside the coat by a Second Table Taster. Rim innkeepers who see one turn their own cutlery face down. Spoon-fork smile: the smile of a person who is about to ask what you are made of.

spoon-reader n., Rim A fortune-teller who reads the scratches on a used spoon to tell what the eater wants. Every inn on the Rim has one. Most are frauds. The ones at Thimble Cross are not, and they have started refusing spoons with a certain pattern of wear, and will not say why.

Stair-Clerk title, Vigil The lowest officer of the Watch of Watches, who carries papers up and down the Nodding Stair for eighteen hours a shift. Stair-legs: the thick calves of a Vigil civil servant.

starers n., Vigil Infants born lidless, paraded in open baskets on Starers’ Day in early Grace with bells thrown in. Vigilants consider them a mercy of the god. Their mothers lean over the baskets and weep, and the weeping is described in the almanac as joy.

Starved Saint n., Fast An ascetic who eats nothing at all. A few have kept it up far longer than a body can. Sister Nay Corliss has not eaten in three years and wakes each morning with crumbs on her lips. Saint-thin is said of the very holy and of the dying, who are, in the Fast, often the same.

Steward, the title, Fast Welcome Ardent, who walks a mile ahead of Orrum laying the tables: the first of the Unfed ever to accept, six hundred years ago, and the only guest offered a position. Polite, exhausted, and very much in want of relief. To be offered stewardship is a Rim euphemism for a promotion nobody can refuse or survive.

still-born to the deep phr., Brinehollow Of a child who drowned in the womb from its mother’s tide, and was given to the sea unnamed. The household calls them so, and the tide-post of Fathomhouse carries their names in a column with no dates.

stitching-tithe n., Sallowreach The tax a family pays to the Seamers’ Guild for the upkeep of its dead, assessed per body per year. A household with seven generations upright may owe more than it earns. Tithed to the thread: bankrupted by grandparents.

Stopping, the n., Oathen What happened in 598 A.G. when the First Sayer said I wish it would stop during a storm. The storm stopped. So did everything else in the valley. A Stopping is any calamity caused by a careless word, and the valley is still there, stopped, and posted.

stranded adj., Brinehollow The word High Admiral Corvin Sund will hang any officer for saying: of the fleet, on its props, fully crewed, four hundred ships on dry ground. Said everywhere else on the coast, of everything. Don’t call it stranded, call it waiting.

Stranger’s Loaf n., Rim A hot loaf given to every guest at the inn door in Company towns, especially at Gristmoot. The whole street watches to see whether you eat it, and whether you say the grace first. In the Fast, a stranger’s loaf is something you must never eat, because you did not carry it.

stuffed adj., Fatlands The Gut-lines’ word for a Laden noble so swollen they can no longer leave the bed. Not an insult in the south. Elsewhere, a stuffed lord is a joke. In the Fatlands, it is a rank, and a stuffed lord’s word outweighs a walking one’s by law.

Sump, the n., Sallowreach The deep fen where those beyond stitching are sunk in weighted sacks. Bubbles rise in patterns. Sump-talk: the bubbling sound a too-far-gone Kept makes. Sent to the Sump is the fen’s word for abandoned, and its cruelest.

Surety n., Oathen One who takes on another’s oath for a fee and carries the risk in their own body, tattooed from collarbone to ankle in brown script. I stand for this word. A Surety twenty years in the trade is rich and a ruin. Surety-sure: as certain as a debt someone else will pay in bone.

Swab title, Brinehollow The lowest rank of the Tidal Admiralty, who scrapes the hulls of the dry fleet of barnacles that are not there. Swab’s errand: pointless labor, faithfully done.

Sweating Night n., Fatlands The hottest night of Plenty, when villages sleep out in the warm fields. Couples conceive, and the children are called field-gotten and thought lucky. Some sleepers do not wake, and are found smiling. The Board does not count them in the Reaping.

sweet water n., Brinehollow Fresh water, rain or well, as opposed to bail-water. Sweet-water folk: inlanders, foreigners. To give sweet water to a coughing stranger is a courtesy and an old charm against the pull.

Sworn Gorge n., Oathen A sealed ravine where an oath shouted in 419 A.G. has never stopped echoing. Anyone who hears it is bound by it. Nobody knows what it says. Halvar Stane has made out two words, and will not repeat them. Sworn-Gorge debt: an obligation whose terms nobody can remember.

sworn note n., Oathen A promissory note sworn aloud before a Clausewright and backed by the issuer’s own body, named in the clause: let my left hand answer. The paper money of the eastern Table. A default snaps the named part wherever the issuer stands, and the bearer hears the snap at the back of the skull. See dry paper.

T

Table, the n., common 1. The known world, one round continent with a dead heartland. 2. Any table where strangers eat, which is why the word is said carefully. All round the Table: everywhere. Under the Table: dead, eaten, or a Second Table member, depending on the wink. (Compiler: In the oldest carvings the world and the board are drawn with one line. I have stopped asking which was drawn first.)

Tablebread n., Fast, child. Bread found on a laid table. Unfed children are taught a rhyme about it: Tablebread, Tablebread, warm as a bed, eat it and stay, and never be fed. Abby Rooke leaves a crust on the windowsill and finds something better there in the morning.

Tablebreaker n., Fast One of the bands who hunt Orrum’s tables and smash them with axes before anyone can sit. Ranks: Sniffer, Axe, Rope-Holder, Breaker, Old Breaker. Dangerous, honored work. A Tablebreaker’s supper: whatever you ate before you went out, cold, from the hand, quickly.

Tablenight n., common The anniversary of the Gorging, the longest night of Lack, kept by every land differently: a banquet for the dead in the fens, a failed fast in the south, a bowl of seawater on the coast, a minute of darkness in the Vigil, open doors in the highlands, silence in the canyons, and the Fast standing outdoors with its back to every door. On the Rim, one extra chair is set at every table, turned to face the wall.

Tablenight chair n., Rim The extra chair set at every Rim table on Tablenight, turned to face the wall, for the one who isn’t coming. Travelers who turn it round in the night find it turned to the wall again by morning. Do not ask the innkeeper. Do not count the chairs.

Table-speech n., common The common tongue, older than the Gorging, spoken in every land: drawled and wet in the fens, clipped to almost nothing in Oathen, stretched and slurred in the Vigil. Rich in food-words used for everything. There are two words for guest in it. Everyone uses the newer.

take a chair phr., Fast To sit at one of Orrum’s tables, and therefore to be lost. The Unfed never say sit down; they say rest your legs, or squat, and they mean the ground. She took a chair is the Fast’s way of saying a person is gone to the Host.

talkative adj., Oathen The worst thing you can call someone in the canyons. Worse than liar, which in Oathen is a technical term. Foreigners who say you’re very quiet as a compliment have been punched.

tallow-saint n., Sallowreach One of Wick Tallow’s candles, made of the unclaimed dead, which feels itself burn and gives a very steady light. Half of Lastgate reads by people it used to know. Reading by grandmother: reading by a candle made from someone you knew. Some families sell their own.

Tally, the n., Cradlewrack The public ledger of every birth of every kind, read aloud each evening as the news. Rufus Ochre keeps it, and by his figures eleven hundred more were born last year than were carried by anyone or anything. On the Tally: alive and accounted for. Off the Tally: unaccounted for, which in the highlands is worse than dead.

Taste, the n., common The first stage of the Regrowth: small wrongnesses, dreams, cravings, a tell in the body. She’s got the Taste is said of children who will not sleep with the door ajar, chew their sleeves, wake with salt on the lip, yawn too much, leave doors open, hear their words echo. Everyone has it a little. It is the season of the Taste on the whole Table.

Taster title, Rim The second rank of the Second Table: one admitted to a practice dinner and permitted to eat what is served. Carries the two-tined fork. A Taster’s smile is a smile with a question behind it about what you are made of.

tear-salt n., Vigil Salt gathered from the eyes of the lidless Eye-lines, the most expensive seasoning on the Table; the Eye-lines eat it on everything. Tear-salted means rich beyond reason. Much tear-salt is lid-salt from beggars, and rich people cannot tell the difference, which pleases the beggars.

Teeth, the n., Fatlands The toothed wheat, first harvested in 204 A.G. and ruled a superior strain. Granny Cracknel keeps the teeth from her milling, eleven hundred sets sorted by village, and says some of them match people she knew. Teeth in the bread: a bad harvest, or a good one.

tenancy n., Brinehollow The legal status of a Tenanted person’s property and marriage, which the Drowned Bench, being Tenanted, has ruled are unchanged. Wreckwives call a bad marriage a tenancy even when nobody has been Called.

Tenanted adj. and n., Brinehollow The Called who come back, weeks later, walking out of the surf heavier than they left, calm, courteous, the same face and the same memories, and someone else looking out. Polite people say returned. The Tenanted now sit on every court in the land, and are fair.

tenterhooks n., Vigil The fine steel hooks a wake-valet uses to hold the skin of a client’s eyelid taut, from Jack Tenterhook. On tenterhooks: awake, in pain, and paying for it. The Compiler notes that the rest of the Table uses the phrase without knowing where it came from, and that this is how the Vigil gets into everything.

Theft, the n., common The oldest doctrine: we murdered them; the Regrowth is justice and we deserve it. In Brinehollow it is called the Debt. Theft-minded: guilty, ascetic, or just Purgation. A Theft sermon begins with We were hungry, say it plainly.

Thimble n., Rim Thimble Cross: a two-storey fieldstone inn of seventeen chimneys where the Rim bends round a lobe of the Fast. A Thimble of: a measure of drink. Thimble-wise: knowing where the Fast begins, to the yard.

Thin, the n., Fatlands Outlawed fasters who believe starving the body starves the god. Gaunt, hunted, and the only people in the south who seem clear-headed. Ranks: Hollow, Lean, Gaunt, Bone, and the Thin Man, Corder Lank, unopposed. Going thin is treason since the Rising of 455.

thinning n., Fatlands Losing weight; the gravest social disgrace in the south, worse than drink. He’s been thinning since his wife was reaped. The Feasting Bailiffs watch the thinning. The Thin welcome them.

Talkative. In Oathen it means a person who will not live long. The canyon schoolmistresses write it on the slate on the first day, and the children are not allowed to say it, only to read it.
the Compiler

Thinwick n., Fast A hamlet of the Fast near the Hem where Decline Marsh and Scant Hollis grew up two doors apart. Thinwick-raised: hard, plain, devout and able to break a table with three blows. The houses of Thinwick have no hearths and no chairs, and one house now has a table, and nobody goes in.

threadbare adj., Sallowreach Of the Kept: so restitched that there is more thread than flesh. Captain Dace Morrow is threadbare and deserting in small pieces. A threadbare argument: one that has been going since 212 A.G. in a room in Lastgate.

Three Knocks, the n., Cradlewrack The knock you give before opening any door in the highlands, to warn whatever is on the other side: three, one, three. Knock twice means be very careful. Something on the other side of the Sill has begun knocking back in the same rhythm.

thumb-ring n., Oathen A ring worn on the thumb by Clausewrights, one per hundred conditions in their longest treaty. Sorrin Vael wears four. Twelve rings is a boast that cannot, in Oathen, be made idly.

tide n., Brinehollow The sea inside the body: twice a day the lungs fill with salt water from nowhere, and it must be coughed out. Also the indoor tide in every cellar, rising twice a day and leaving kelp on the stairs. Your tide’s showing means you are wheezing. Tide-mates: two who bail together.

tide-post n., Brinehollow The carved post at every harbour on which the names of the Called are cut. The Lowmark post bears the old carving: The sea is not going out. It is going in. On the post means gone to the sea.

Tidiers n., Fast The things the Hostwatch say keep the Fast’s empty houses perfect: trimming the hedges, cleaning the windows, lighting the chimneys. Nobody has seen one whole. Tidier-work: housework done by no one. Unfed children who leave their beds unmade are told the Tidiers will come and make it.

toad-mouth n., Oathen, insult A person who says too much and grows ugly by it, from the Breakings of the jaw. Breakdowns children chant it at foreign travelers who chatter at the toll.

Toll Nine n., Rim The Company’s counting-house, long, low, windowless, on the southern Rim, where every ledger of the road is reckoned. Toll-Nine faced: expressionless, calculating, with skin the colour of no daylight.

Tolm n., common The Witness, god of oaths and true speech, eaten in silence in the canyons. What it heard was so. Its name is not said in Oathen, where it is still listening, from the inside. Tolm hears you is the most frightening thing an Oathen mother can say.

tongue-tax n., Oathen The fee paid to a Clausewright to draft a sentence before saying it: one crumb a clause, a lack a promise, a platter a marriage. Pay the tongue-tax means think before you speak.

Tooth, the n., common The d6 added to a roll when a character Partakes: the god’s strength in the blood. A Tooth showing 1 means the god bit back, and Hunger rises. Show your teeth: to Partake openly. Toothy: given to Partaking. She’s all teeth: far gone, hungry, close to the Course.

touch-tax n., Sallowreach The license-levy on Closings, paid to the Court on top of the fee. A Closing costs about four thousand lacks. Touch-tax is also a lover’s joke in the Hand-lines, who are said to pay it on every caress.

trade tables v., Table-speech To betray kin: from the Kitchen Year of the Long Lack, when families who could not bear to eat their own exchanged their dead with neighbors. She traded tables with her own sister. The worst thing one can say of a family, in every land.

Treaty Stair n., Rim The Company depot cut into a canyon wall at the head of the stair down to Tacit, where every contract is copied, sealed in wax and bone, and carried to Jessamy Quill. Down the Stair: sworn, irrevocable. Up the Stair: in the hands of the lawyers.

Trencherman title, Rim A full member of the Second Table, with a course name and a signet ring inscribed It worked once inside the band. A trencherman’s appetite used to mean a hearty eater. In the high houses it no longer does.

tripe-talk n., Fatlands Gossip among the Renderers about what is in the barrels. Don’t give me tripe-talk means do not tell me what you know about the meat. Ivo Stockpot notches the barrels instead.

Tucker n., Vigil A member of the criminal mercy that will, for a price, guard you while you sleep for sixty seconds and then haul you back. Their failures are delivered to the Dormitory steps before the next bell. Tucked: slept, paid for, and returned. Tucked up: not returned.

tunnel-tongue n., Oathen, cant A person who speaks only in questions, like Tavish Crook, called Loophole, who has never asserted or promised anything. Don’t tunnel-tongue me means give me a straight answer, which in the canyons is a dangerous thing to ask.

turned adj., Brinehollow Of a person who has come back from the surf, or of milk, or of the tide in 512 A.G., the first year the sea did not come back. Turned is used of all three in the same breath on the Mile, and the joke is old and still not funny.

Two Columns n., Rim A Cutwright’s ledger layout: one column for a family’s known Cut, one for its suspected Cut. The second is always higher. Two-column family: a noble house with something to hide.

two words phr., Vigil The marriage vow of the Vigil, which is Pinch me. We’ve said our two words means we are married. Elsewhere, two words is the Oathen maximum for a promise between strangers.

U

Ummer n., common The Laden, god of harvest and plenty, eaten fastest of all the gods, its bones cracked for the marrow. Ummer was the god of feeding. Now it feeds. Not said aloud in the south, where people say the field. Ummer-down: the soft fuzz on new rootkin.

Unanswered, the n., Rim The knock heard at the third hour of the night at Rim inns, on the door that faces the middle of the continent. Innkeepers do not answer it. The Unanswered is also what travelers call that door, and the custom is to sleep with your feet toward it, so that if it opens, you will be the first to know.

Unbitting, the n., Oathen The coming of age in Oathen, in Plenty, when twelve-year-olds have the muzzle removed in the Hall of Conditions and speak their first chosen words with a Clausewright present. The words are carved in the family niche. Since my Unbitting means since I became responsible for every sentence I have ever said.

unbread v., Fast, child. To refuse food so politely that the offerer feels foolish. Unfed children practise unbreading on each other with pebbles. She unbreaded the Envoy: she refused the Rim’s food on behalf of her people, and was admired.

Unbricking, the n., Cradlewrack The first of Grace, when every bricked room is broken open at dawn, aired, and its contents Tallied. Contents vary. Unbricking surprises: what was in there with you all winter.

Unclean, the n., Fast Any Unfed who has eaten Godeater food, whether by need, trickery or desire. Scour, the Returned, is Unclean. Unclean is shouted in the streets of Wanting and the shouted-at is left off the next list.

Uncovered, the n., Brinehollow The exposed seabed, a new mile of it every year: weed forests gone to leather, wrecks standing upright, things with too many ribs, salvage, no law. Uncovered is said of anyone caught in a lie and of anyone who has lost their sea. Somewhere far out on it there is a stone table with eight chairs.

Uncut, the n., Cradlewrack People whose birth cords were never severed, who walk through life still attached to their mothers by yards of living cord and consider everyone else amputees. Uncut kin: inseparable. The Uncut call the rest of the Table the Snipped.

underdone adj., Table-speech Cowardly; not cooked through. The commonest insult on the Rim, said with a pinch of the cheek. Underdone and overpriced: a cowardly mercenary. See overdone.

Under-Drafter title, Oathen The second rank of the Clausewrights, who drafts conditions for others to swear. Under-Drafter Lise Amberd is believed to have drafted more marriage vows than anyone living. Under-drafted: a contract that has a hole in it, found too late.

Unending Dinner, the n., Fatlands Dame Suet Marrable’s table, in continuous service for eighty-one years. Guests have been born at it and several have been served at it. An Unending Dinner is any social obligation from which you will not be allowed to rise.

Unfed, the n., Fast The people of the Fast, descended from the survivors of the Refusal, the only people in the world with no god in their blood. They have Want where others have Hunger. Unfed is a title they wear with pride, and on the Rim an insult meaning self-righteous. They are the only innocent people on the Table, and they are insufferable about it.

unfinished adj., Sallowreach Alive, in the fen sense: not finished. The polite fen term for all the Kept, all the living, and all songs. We are all unfinished here. Hushwalkers, on their return, call everyone outside the silence unfinished, with pity.

unhinging n., Cradlewrack The slow loosening of every door in a house in the weeks before a pang, which highland folk read as an omen. She’s unhinging means she is losing her wits, and is said kindly.

Unknotting, the n., Brinehollow The cutting of a sleeper’s name-rope in the night, deliberately, so that the pull will take them. It is a killing, and the coast prosecutes it as murder, when it can prove it, which is never. An Unknotting marriage: one partner is waiting for the other to be Called.

unlaid adj., Rim Of a table: bare. The Rim’s innkeepers keep their tables unlaid between meals, since a laid table with no one at it has come to mean something. Unlaid is also used of a promise never made, and a person never buried.

Unmade Road, the n., Oathen The road behind Captain Renn Hold’s pass, where four hundred soldiers who obeyed his order to retreat broke their oath to hold the pass and came apart. At dusk, strapped-together shapes are said to crawl uphill on it. Unmade means broken by obedience.

Unseamed adj., Sallowreach Of a Kept person whom no Seamer will touch: too poor, too rotten, or under a Court ban. The Unseamed come apart in public and are fined for it. Unseamed is a fen synonym for outcast.

Unvacated, the n., Sallowreach The oldest dead, who hold every title, deed and office in the fens, because owners never die and property never passes. Ansel Grue, the Regent, is the oldest. An Unvacated house: one where the grandparents will own you until about 760 A.G.

unwatched adj., Vigil Without a nudger. The loneliest word in the language. She’s unwatched since the spring. The unwatched go to the Pinchmarket, or to the Lying-Down, or rarely to the Tuckers.

Upper Boards n., Sallowreach The highest, driest storeys of Lastgate, where the Hand-lines and the Closers keep houses that smell of cedar. Upper-Boards perfume: cedar over rot. Boarded up: risen in the world, and dead.

upright adj., Sallowreach Of the Kept: still standing, still in office, still owning things. Jory Welt is seventy and a minor, since his father is three hundred and upright. Upright is the fen word for both alive and respectable and nobody notices the joke.

V

Vashtwater n., Brinehollow Water that has been in a Lung-line prince’s tank, sold after changing as a cure for the pull. It smells of breath. Prince Aurel’s tank-water is a Leaving. To drink Vashtwater is to toady.

veiled adj., Cradlewrack Born in a caul that never comes off: the condition, and the dignity, of the highest Caul-line houses. The Veiled speak through the membrane and are held to be prophetic. Veiled talk: prophecy, blurry and red.

vellum n., Oathen Writing-skin. Since written words began to bind, scribes of the canyons have taken to writing on the skins of the dead, in hopes the dead will take the breaking. It does not work. Vellum-sure: written down, and therefore, now, dangerous.

velvet-hand n., Sallowreach, cant A Closer’s gentle touch, and, by extension, any killing done kindly and for money. Velvet-hand trade: the black market in Closings, carried on by Hand-lines bastards and Pim Sorrel’s imitators.

verge-talk n., Fast Conversation with the Seated from the roadside. It is permitted and it is dangerous, because the Seated describe each course in detail, and people who listen too long pull out a chair. Don’t verge-talk me means do not try to make me want something.

Vey n., common The Opening, god of birth, beginnings, doors and first breaths, the smallest of the Providers and the hardest to kill, because it kept starting again. Nobody calls it Vey aloud in Cradlewrack. They say the Opening, or she, or nothing, and knock first.

Vigil, the n., common The northeastern plateau city, once Ludmere, which ate Iss and has not slept since 341 A.G. Vigil-eyed: red-rimmed, staring, unblinking. To keep vigil elsewhere on the Table means to sit with the dying. In the Vigil itself it means to live.

vigil-candle n., Rim A candle burned at a sickbed. On the Rim, since the Vigil’s trade with Sallowreach, vigil-candles are often Wick Tallow’s, and the sick wake to hear the candle praying for them in a voice they almost know.

vinegar-kiss n., Sallowreach The kiss given to a Kept relative through a cloth soaked in vinegar, to cut the smell. Fen children are taught to give it without flinching. A vinegar-kiss marriage: a match of duty.

visiting n., Fast Walking the verge of a road beside a laid table and talking to the Seated without sitting down. Permitted, because the road is not the table and the verge is not a chair. A visiting family is one with someone at the Long Table. They go on feast days, and come back thinner.

Voice title, Oathen The leader of the Forsworn of the Breakdowns, at present Brakk, whose ribs opened outward like a book. The Voice says means the poor have made up their mind.

Voided, the n., Rim The inner council of the Purgation, who claim to be empty of god, and show their scar, worn bare, as proof. Voided is said of anyone who claims to have no appetite, by people who do not believe them.

voluntary rest n., Vigil The law’s phrase for the Lain-Down. The nudger is prosecuted for negligence and the family is fined. Nobody who has lost someone says it. It appears in the Vigil’s statutes four hundred and eleven times.

vow-eater n., Oathen A fixer who claims to release you from an oath by having you swear a greater one over it, like Grandam Cess. Her clients are free of what they came with, and owe her something worse. Vow-eaten: in debt beyond bone.

W

wage-chit n., Rim A thin bone slip stamped with the Company wheel and a post-number, good for a bed, a meal or a drink at any Company house, worthless off the road. Paid in chits means owned by the Company. Bonded Hands who retire after forty years on the Rim tend to find they cannot afford to leave it.

wake n., Fatlands The funeral of the south, the most sacred rite: the dead are served to the family, by the family, with the best plates. To be buried uneaten is the deepest insult to a life. Wake dishes have names (Hands in a Pie, Heart Seared Thin, Widow’s Dripping, Marrow on Toast). I’ll see you at my wake is a Fatlands lover’s promise.

wakemother n., Fatlands The woman who cooks a wake: a master of the trade, paid in the best cut. Wakemother Pudding Hesk’s glaze is a Leaving. A wakemother’s tenderness: complete, practical and holding a cleaver.

Waker n., Vigil The Vigil’s police, whose job is to hurt people for their own good, and who after three centuries are very skilled. Ranks run Rattle, Needle, Sergeant of the Ward, Inquisitor of the Quick, Captain. Waker-kind: cruel in your interest.

Wake-valet n., Vigil Keeper-awake to the rich, an artist of the precisely tolerable pain, like Jack Tenterhook, who was a torturer before and says the only difference is the tipping. Valeted: kept awake beautifully. Wake-valets’ pincers are silver.

walking west phr., 1. Brinehollow; 2. Fast 1. The pull: sleepwalking toward the sea, or the brine-rouse users of the Vigil drifting to the coast four hundred miles away. 2. Leaving the Fast for the Rim, which is how it loses most of the people it does not starve. She’s walking west is said of a quiet loss in both lands, and nobody likes to be asked which.

walk in singing phr., Sallowreach To go into a Hush with the Finishers, in procession, in song, so that the last thing the world hears of you is a verse, which stops. She walked in singing is the proudest and saddest thing a fen family can say of one of its own, and the families of the Finishers say it more every year.

walk-stone n., common The stone at the edge of every old village from which the Eldest Walk set out, still there in most places. Each is washed in the night, once a year, in late Plenty, by someone who will not say who. Sitting on the walk-stone: getting old. Children are forbidden to play on it, and do.

walk the eldest, to phr., Table-speech To make a sacrifice that is known to be wasted. From the Eldest Walk of the eighth year of the Long Lack, when in every land the old walked out into the cold so that the young might eat, and the young starved anyway, the next year, and the Lack did not lift for them. We walked the eldest for that contract means we gave up what we could not spare and got nothing. In the Fatlands they say it of every Lean Levy, and in the Fast of every winter’s list.

Want n., Fast What the Unfed have where others have Hunger: the slow rising need, not of a god in the blood, but for the god outside the door. To feel the Want is to smell bread on the wind and turn into it, not away. Want-proud: hungry and boasting of it.

Wanting n., Fast The Unfed’s only real town: cold, plain and hearthless, on the eastern edge nearest the Rim, with the Pantry at its heart and the Lean House at its edge. Wanting-cold: the specific chill of a house with no hearth.

Wanting Post n., Rim The only Company station that faces the middle, at the head of the road into Wanting, where Crumb-Runners buy grain at a markup and are spat on for it. Wanting-Post prices: the cost of what you need from people who despise you for needing it.

warm front n., Fast The god passing. The Unfed track Orrum by melted frost and warm ground, and call it company, or a warm front. There’s a warm front by the mill means keep the children in, do not answer the door, and if you smell bread, walk into the wind.

Washing, the n., common The night in late Plenty when each village’s walk-stone is washed by someone who will not say who. It is a custom of every land, and nobody remembers starting it. Washed and not told: forgiven by somebody you do not know.

Watch of Watches n., Vigil The Vigil’s council, which sits in shifts around the clock and has not adjourned in two hundred years, on the Nodding Stair. The Watch’s watch: the attendants who watch the Warden-Prime’s eyes. Who watches the Watch is a proverb in the Vigil and a job title.

watch-self n., Vigil The self that has gone on watching after the mind has failed: a long-waking Vigilant who works, walks and answers questions, and is not there. My husband’s watch-self brought me tea this morning means he is gone, though he is awake.

wax-slate n., Oathen A board of wax and a stylus, for messages that can be smoothed away before they bind. Since writing began to count, wax-slates are scraped clean with frightening speed. Wax-slate love: a love affair conducted with deniability.

weep n., Sallowreach Rain, which in the fens leaves a tea-coloured stain. Weep-weather: wet and warm. Weep-stained: of a person, old, faded, respectable. Lowlanders say that a fen woman who cries is making her own weather.

Weeping Post, the n., Rim The waystation between Cradlewrack and Fogmouth, where weep-rain from the fens meets the warm salt springs of the red hills and the road is always wet; the Purgation’s chief hall, where the Black Draught is given on Retching Day. Weeping-Post wet: soaked through, inside and out.

Weighing, the n., Fatlands The annual public weighing of the Board of Plenty, three days in Grace, at which each Member’s vote is set by weight, with pie-stalls the length of Sated. Weighed and found heavy: approved. Garrick Tripe will fill your pockets with lead for a fee.

welcome n., Fast A forbidden word. Orrum’s Steward is called Welcome Ardent, which the Unfed find unbearable. You are welcome is never said in the Fast; the Unfed say you are tolerated, and mean it as warmly as anyone else means the other. See No, thank you.

well-crowned adj., Cradlewrack Of a well: dilated into a crowning. The well in the square has crowned means something is coming up the rope hand over hand, knocking on the stones as it climbs. Well-crowned in Kest slang also means pregnant, of a man.

west door n., Brinehollow The door of a house that faces the sea, barred every night of the year but Tablenight, when it is left unbarred for whoever might come home. West-door news: a return. West-door niche: the shrine by it where a bowl of seawater stands.

In every land the word for west means something. On the coast it means the sea. In the Fast it means away. In the Vigil it means walking. On the Rim, a Factor once told me, it means nothing, yet.
the Compiler

wet-lung n., Rim, insult A Brinehollower, on the rest of the Rim. They cough in public and spit salt. Wet-lung manners: wiping your mouth on your sleeve after bailing at table, which on the coast is perfectly polite.

wet-nurse n., Cradlewrack One who feeds what no one else will, like Dolour Pym, to whom the Attendance sends the births it permits but cannot look at. She loves all of them. Several have never let go. Wet-nursed means raised on pity and grown up strange.

Wet Tom n., Brinehollow Any very wet beggar; after Old Wet Tom, who has never been dry and on whom it rains indoors. A Wet Tom: a person followed by misfortune. Children who look into his puddles say they are much deeper than the floor.

wheel, the n., Rim The Company’s symbol, and the seven-Spoked council that runs it. On the wheel: employed by the Company. Broke on the wheel: ruined by it, which is to say indebted to a Company inn for life.

whisper-book n., Sallowreach A Loft-Warden’s ledger of what the Set-Aside whisper, kept hall by hall. Senior Wardens may sell what is in them. It’s in the whisper-books means it is known by the dead and will be known by everyone, eventually.

whistle v., Oathen A forbidden act on Tablenight, when the whole country makes no sound for twenty-four hours. A whistler is shunned for a year. To whistle on Tablenight means to commit an outrage in innocence.

white-glove adj., Sallowreach Of a Closer who has never yet closed anyone; and of any newcomer to a killing trade. Still white-gloved: virginal in murder.

wick n., Vigil The lowest Lamplighter, who trims the ten thousand lamps on long poles, burned at the wrist and coughing smoke. Wick-thin: underfed and burning. Wick-talk: the Lamplighters’ cant, of which this Compiler learned only enough to know she was being insulted in it.

wickerman n., Fatlands, child. The scarecrow of any field, especially the one at Low Tilth. Fatlands children chant Wickerman, wickerman, turn round and see, and run before it can. In some villages they have stopped playing it.

Wider Table n., Rim The whole Table, in a sermon; also a Rim euphemism for the dead of all lands together, as in gone to the wider table. In the Fast, nobody says it.

Widow’s Dripping n., Fatlands The first rendering of a wake, on hot bread; the widow skims it herself and weeps into it. Widow’s-dripping tears: tears that are also seasoning. The phrase is used of all grief that has to be got through while cooking.

wife-bucket n., Brinehollow The bail-bucket a sweetheart gives you, exchanged at betrothal. She’s still got his wife-bucket means she has not remarried, though he is ten years in the sea. A Tenanted sweetheart’s bucket is a Leaving, and the water in it does not go stale.

window-warden n., Brinehollow A neighborhood volunteer who walks the street at night looking for people standing at west-facing windows, and knocks to wake them. A window-warden’s knock is a single soft tap. The Called hear it and do not turn.

wishbone n., Fatlands The forked bone of a bird pulled between two eaters at a wake; whoever gets the larger piece gets the dead person’s luck. In the Gut-lines, wishbones are pulled from more than birds. Wishbone siblings: brothers who have fought over an inheritance at the table itself.

Witness, the n., common 1. Tolm. 2. In Rim law, the person before whom a contract is sworn, at present Jessamy Quill. If she dies or breaks, half the trade of the Table comes unbound in an afternoon. Witness-heavy: the burden of being needed to remember.

Wolf-Warden title, Fatlands A Board officer appointed to protect the fields from wolves, of which there are none. Wolf-Wardens walk the dusk lines in white smocks with a lantern, and their lists are the Cullmasters’ lists. Wolf-Warden’s leave: the dusk shift.

wolves n., Fatlands, euphemism The official cause of the Reaping. There are no wolves in the Fatlands. Wolves took him is said with a straight face by Board officials and with a look by everyone else. The Board employs Wolf-Wardens, who hunt nothing and are well paid.

word-bound adj., Oathen Bound by your own words, in the flesh. The commonest Oathen adjective, applied to almost everyone. Not word-bound is said only of Blanks and foreigners, and of Cassian Wry, whom everyone asks to say something false, just to hear it.

worship n., common In Table-speech the same root as eating: orrel and orren. A Fatlands priest says come and worship; a Fatlands child asks what is for supper. (Compiler: I have heard Purgation lecturers argue that if the words share a root, the deeds do. I have heard Second Table lecturers argue the same. I note that they agree on this and on nothing else.)

wrack n., Cradlewrack 1. The red clay highlands themselves, the Wrack. 2. Seaweed, in the speech of the highland coast. 3. Ruin, labor, pain. In the wrack means in labor, which in Cradlewrack may be said of anyone, and of the land.

Wreckwife n., Brinehollow One of the sisterhood of those whose spouses came back Tenanted; they share advice on how to live with a stranger who knows your name. Ranks run Listener, Sister of the Line, Keeper of Names, Elder Wife, Widow-Mother. Wreckwife’s tea: kept warm for two.

wristlet n., Rim The iron wrist-ring of a Bonded Hand of the Company, which never comes off. Wristleted: in the Company’s employ for life. Retired Hands rub the place where it was, years later, without knowing they do it.

Writ of Weight n., Fatlands The Board certificate recording a Member’s weight and vote, renewed yearly. Forged Writs of Weight are the commonest fraud in Sated. A Writ of Weight man: one who is less than he claims.

wyrm-hole n., Brinehollow A hole in the Uncovered where the mud has been pushed up from below, as if something had come out, or gone down. Salvagers mark them with painted stakes. Gone down the wyrm-hole: missing on the seabed.

X

X n., Rim The mark scratched on the door of a household struck from the Pantry list, by the Pantry clerks, so that the Runners know whom to sell to. X-house: a family between lists. Scraplings across the Table sign with an X; in the Fast, nobody does.

xennor n., Table-speech, archaic An old word for the duty of hospitality owed to guests, found in carvings older than the Gorging and in the College’s oldest quires. It is one of the two words for guest-right. Nobody uses the older word. (Compiler: I have found it in one place only, written above a carving of a table, over the eighth seat, which is chiseled out.)

X-stitch n., Sallowreach The crossed stitch a Seamer uses to close a Kept person’s mouth when the jaw has slipped its seam for good. X-stitched means silenced. Grandmothers who are X-stitched are said to hum.

Y

Yardmaster title, Fatlands A Renderers’ Union officer commanding a rendering-house, with a share of export profits. Yardmaster’s word: final, and stamped twice.

yard-warden n., Sallowreach A volunteer who watches the Lofts’ yards at night so that nothing is carried out, or in. The yard-wardens are the first to hear the whispering change. Lately they have asked to be paid more.

Yawn, the n., Vigil The warm wind off the eastern plain. On Yawn days the Wakers double their patrols. Yawn-weather: dangerous comfort. A yawn in the Vigil is never small talk: it spreads through a room like a rumor and can put down a market. See Glass House.

yawner n., Vigil One whose yawns are catching beyond reason, like Lukas Marre, who once put down a whole market square and lives in the Glass House, masked, alone. Don’t be a yawner means do not spread despair.

yawn-tax n., Vigil The fine for yawning in public on a Yawn day. It is a rouse-tab, paid on the spot to the nearest Waker. He’s paying the yawn-tax means he is losing.

Yellowing n., Sallowreach The season in Carving when children gather the rare leaves that fall from the yellow trees of the fens, where leaves stay on the branch for decades, and keep them in boxes. A fallen leaf is the only thing in the north that has ever been allowed to finish. A yellow-leaf child is a fen child who has died properly, abroad, and is envied.

yes interj., Oathen A promise. Oatheners avoid it. Sorrin Vael, Chief Clausewright, has not said an unqualified yes since boyhood, including to his wife. The polite form is as I now intend, or a nod, which is held not to bind, which is being tested.

yesterbed n., Vigil, archaic A bed, in the old Ludmere speech: the thing from yesterday. Used now only in nursery rhymes and by the Bedded, who say it with longing. Yesterbed and yesterdream, never and never wake.

yield v., Fast To give way: to sit at the table, to answer come in, to accept on the first offer. Yield is also a girl’s name, given in hope that she never will. Yield Hartsell has grown a single green sprout in dead soil, and told no one.

yoke-ox n., Fatlands One of the eight oxen that draw Chairman Obb Tullow’s dray. The Chairman’s feet rooted through the cart last spring. Yoke-ox loyal: going on pulling a thing that has stopped moving.

yolk-eyed adj., Fatlands Glazed and yellow from overeating, in the last hour of a Feasting Law supper. A compliment from a host. Yolk-eyed and happy: the ideal guest.

young-dead n., Sallowreach A Kept person who died young and stayed young, like the Smalls. Young-dead envy: a living sibling growing older than their dead brother or sister, and the dead one’s look as they do.

yourself pron., Oathen In Oathen courts, an accused person is addressed only as yourself, never by name, so that their name will not be bound to the sentence by accident before it is passed. Yourself has broken is the shortest verdict in the world.

Z

zealot-salt n., Rim The pinch of salt a Reckoner puts on their tongue before entering a house, so as to taste nothing of what is inside it. Zealot-salted: determined, joyless and armed.

zero n., Rim A Rim factor’s word, from the Company’s counting-house, for the empty circle on the lack. Common folk do not use it. They say a licked plate, or nothing on the board. (Compiler: the College’s counting-masters write the empty circle with a dot in the middle, which they say represents a seat. I asked whose. I was told it was a ledger convention.)

zest n., Fatlands The crackling skin of the wake roast, given to the youngest at the table. Full of zest: lively, young, and soon to be served. Fatlands grandmothers say give the zest to the little one, and the little one is always pleased.

zuzz n., child., Sallowreach The buzzing sound of a Black Noon fly-front, and a nursery word for flies, which in the fens are the weather. Zuzz-zuzz, here comes Justice is a Lastgate skipping rhyme about the Honorable Maggot, and is sung at his door.

Appendix: Numbers, Measures and Time

Count the coins, count the days, count the dead. Do not count the chairs.
— Rim almanac, inside cover

Table-speech counts the way it eats. Its oldest number-words are the words of a shared meal, kept alive by market women, Tally-keepers, children’s rhymes and the College’s counting-masters, who use the old forms in ledgers because they cannot be mistaken for anything else. In daily speech, most people use plain numbers until a sum becomes frightening, and then fall back on the old words, as if they were gentler. They are not.

The Old Count

Every child on the Table learns the old count on the fingers, and every child is corrected at the same place. After table, which is seven, there is no word. The count goes seven, and one more, or a full board, and the finger is folded down without being named. Schoolmistresses in every land give the same reason, which is that it is unlucky. College counting-masters write the eighth figure as an empty circle with a dot in it and call it a ledger convention.

NumberOld wordLiterallyHeard as
0a licked platenothing leftwe came home with a licked plate
1a biteone mouthfula bite of a man: a lone traveler
2a pairtwo at a boarda pair of plates: a married couple
3a messthree at a boarda mess of Reckoners: a raiding party
4a cornerthe four corners of a tablea corner of days: four days
5a handthe fingersa hand of lacks
6a settingthe places at an old tablea setting of chairs
7a tablethe Seven Tablesa table of dead: seven graves
8(not said)a full boardthe finger is folded, unnamed
9a longthe nine years of the Lacka long of pangs: nine pangs
10a lackten crumbsthe market’s ten
12a year of platesthe twelve monthsa dozen
20a plattertwenty lacksa score
100a feastthe old count of a lord’s halla feast of soldiers
1,000a reaping(Fatlands) a district’s yearly losssaid only in the south, and quietly

A counting rhyme, skipped to in Wanting, Lastgate, Kest and on the Mile, with the words changed in each:

A bite for the baby, a pair for the bed,

A mess for the soldiers, a corner for bread,

A hand for the beggar, a setting for kin,

A table for supper, and who’s coming in?

(Fold the finger, fold the finger, nobody’s there.)

A long for the hungry, a lack for the poor,

A platter for Plenty, and bar the back door.

Children who name the eighth finger are not punished. They are simply asked, very gently, where they heard it.
the Compiler

Measures

Every land weighs and measures by its own Rule, and the Company’s factors carry conversion slates. The common ones:

MeasureAmountLandNotes
crumba tenth of a lackcommona bone bead; the price-witness’s fee
lacka day’s breadcommonsalt-cured bone; ten crumbs
plattertwenty lackscommonsealed tablet; sworn redeemable
pound-scripa pound of meatFatlands7 crumbs at home, 3 abroad, falling
sidehalf a beastFatlandsmeat scrip; about 25 lacks
rouse-tabone hour awake (nominal)Vigil3 crumbs; holds twenty minutes now
ration chita day’s Measurethe Fastnot for sale; sold at 3 lacks
Measurea day’s Pantry rationthe Fastone oatcake and a handful of grain
quarter-measurea quarter of thatthe Fastthe daily cut of the Nine Days
stonefourteen poundsFatlandsvotes are counted in stones
hundredweighta Deacon’s voteFatlandsone vote per hundred pounds
fathomsix feet of ropeBrinehollowrope is sold by the fathom on the Rim
Milea section of LowmarkBrinehollowone year’s pier
bowshot and a halfthe edge of Company lawRimmeasured yearly with a knotted rope
Rim-daya day’s wagon travelRimabout twenty miles; a hundred days round
mouthful (of speech)about nine wordsOathenthe most said without a Clausewright
clauseone conditionOathena crumb of tongue-tax each
shelfone Set-AsideSallowreachthe Lofts count bodies in shelves
stitch-countthe Seamer’s billSallowreacha crumb a stitch on Needle Street

Time

The year is 641 A.G., After Gorging. The nine years before Year 0 are the Lack Years, numbered backward. The year turns on Tablenight, the longest night of Lack. It has four seasons, each named for a part of a meal, and each season has three months named for the moon, the Plate. Dates are given as day, Plate and season: the ninth of Middle Plenty. There are no named weekdays; days are numbered within the Plate, and most people know the date by the Plate in the sky.

SeasonMonthsOld senseWeather everywhere but home
GraceFirst, Middle, Last Plate of Gracethe prayer before eatingspring; Oathen’s Kept Rain on the first day
PlentyFirst, Middle, Last Plate of Plentythe meal itselfsummer; the flies breed in the fens
CarvingFirst, Middle, Last Plate of Carvingthe cutting of the jointautumn; the Reaping; Low Water
LackFirst, Middle, Last Plate of Lackthe faminewinter; Tablenight at its deepest point

The phases of the Plate are counted by everyone and trusted by travelers: a full Plate is the time for markets and weddings; being cleared is the waning, when debts are called in; a new moon is licked clean, and on licked-clean nights doors are barred, nobody travels and nobody counts the plates.

Shorter spans of time are measured by the meal and by each land’s Rule:

SpanLengthWhereExample
a graceas long as it takes to say Lack keep away, two breathscommonI’ll be there in a grace
a mouthfula count of twentycommonwait a mouthful
a blinka second or two of sleepVigiltwo breaths is a long time
a bella quarter of an hourVigilthe city’s bells ring every bell; the hours are lengthening
a bailhalf a day, dawn bail to dusk bailBrinehollowtwo bails out: a day’s sailing, once
a sittingan evening at table, about three hourscommona sitting’s work
a coursean hour, in the old Rim countRimthree courses to Thimble
a pangthe interval between quakes, now nine daysCradlewracksee you in a pang
a Platea month, new moon to new mooncommonpay in a Plate
a longnine yearscommon, oldas long as a long: forever

The day itself is rung in Company towns by four bells: First Bell at dawn, Grace Bell at noon (when everyone turns to the nearest stranger and says the grace), Weighing Bell in mid-afternoon in the Fatlands, and Last Bell at dusk, after which nothing lawful is sold. In Oathen, the bells are replaced by flags, since a bell is a kind of voice. In Sallowreach the day has no last bell, only a first, rung every morning to remind the dead that they are still here.

Maud Sexton’s pendulum says each hour in the Vigil is a little longer than the last. The almanac has not been changed. The Company will not print a year that does not end.
the Compiler

Appendix: Forms of Address by Land

What you call someone is a portion of what you owe them. A traveler who gets the forms right is fed. One who gets them wrong is remembered. The table below is the College’s field-guide; it is short, and wrong at the edges, and the Compiler was thrown out of three houses gathering it.

LandTo a superiorTo an equalTo a child or inferiorNever say
SallowreachUpright Sir, Upright Madam; to the Unvacated, Elderthe name, and may you finishsmall one; to the Kept young, by their age at deathLong life
FatlandsYour Weight; to a hill, Eldestheavy friendpudding, little gutYou look thin; I’m full
Brinehollowby ship-rank (Captain, though never afloat); to the Bench, Your Depthneighbor, through the walllittle bucketWhere did you go?; stranded
The VigilUnblinking; to any officer, Watcherlamp-friend; to a spouse, nudgerstarer, pipRest well; you look rested
CradlewrackMother, to any midwife of any sexby mother’s name: Hessa’s Tamby Tally-place, or bit, small, keepWhat are you?; opening a door unknocked
Oathena bow, and if it please; to the King, nothinga nodthe bitted are spoken of, not toan unconditioned I promise; talkative
The FastElder; to the Abstinent, Keeper of the Listthe Refusal-name: Stint, Naylittle Nay, spareWelcome; Come in; Sit down
The RimFactor, Waymaster, Spokeroad-friendlad, lass, Handanything that counts the chairs
Getting the Forms Wrong

A Guest who uses the right form of address in a land for the first time in a scene gains +1 on their next Tongue roll there with that person. A Guest who says the Never say aloud must make a Hard 14 Tongue + Persuade roll to recover; on a failure, the listener’s attitude worsens by one step, and on a Lack, something worse follows: in Oathen the words count; in the Fast someone hears come in and comes; in the Vigil the listener begins to yawn. The Carver should always let the player know the custom exists before the dice are rolled. The Guest may not.

In the fens I said good day, and was asked whose. In Oathen I said good day, and was asked to swear to it.
the Compiler

Appendix: Curses and Blessings

Every land swears by what it fears and blesses by what it lacks. The lists below were gathered over three years on the Rim, from the mouths of carters, nurses, Seamers, Renderers and children, and are given roughly in order of how often the Compiler heard them. The Compiler notes that the curses were easier to collect.

Thirty Curses

  • Long life to you. (Sallowreach; the worst.)
  • May your hands stay warm. (Sallowreach; that is, may you never be able to finish anything.)
  • May you be Set Aside on a high shelf, and nobody read to you. (Sallowreach)
  • Sump take you, and the sack split. (Sallowreach)
  • May you be full. (Fatlands; that is, may you never be. Said with a smile.)
  • Reaped at dusk and served at dawn. (Fatlands)
  • May your wake be cold and your family thin. (Fatlands)
  • May the field know your name. (Fatlands; whispered, and meant.)
  • Go marry the water. (Brinehollow)
  • May your rope be cut by someone who loves you. (Brinehollow)
  • Salt in your bread and sea in your bed. (Brinehollow)
  • May you come back courteous. (Brinehollow; that is, Tenanted.)
  • Rest well. (Vigil)
  • May you sleep on a soft night. (Vigil)
  • Bed one for you, and nobody at the foot. (Vigil)
  • May your nudger blink. (Vigil)
  • May every door you shut stand open. (Cradlewrack)
  • May you bear. (Cradlewrack; said to men, and meant literally.)
  • Unnamed and untallied. (Cradlewrack)
  • May the Question go against you. (Cradlewrack)
  • Be talkative. (Oathen)
  • May your echo find you. (Oathen)
  • May you be the Surety for your own word. (Oathen)
  • Forsworn and well-read. (Oathen; that is, broken in a way everyone can see.)
  • Come in. (the Fast; said to an enemy’s back, and then they run.)
  • May there be a card with your name on it. (the Fast)
  • May you be welcome. (the Fast; the worst.)
  • Lack sit by you. (the Rim; the universal curse of poverty.)
  • May you eat without grace among strangers. (common)
  • May someone count your chair. (common; the most feared, and the Compiler has heard it said only twice.)
The worst curse is a blessing in the next land over. That is the whole Rim, said a carter to me, and spat, and said Lack keep away, though we were not eating.
the Compiler

Thirty Blessings

  • Lack keep away. (common; the grace before every meal with strangers.)
  • May you finish. (Sallowreach)
  • A clean Closing and a quick one. (Sallowreach)
  • Thread in your seams and vinegar in your cloth. (Sallowreach)
  • May your leaves fall. (Sallowreach; a blessing on a child.)
  • You look heavy. (Fatlands; the kindest thing one can say.)
  • Five meals and a sixth. (Fatlands)
  • May you be served with the best plates. (Fatlands; a blessing on the old.)
  • May the field thank you by name. (Fatlands)
  • Cough clean. (Brinehollow; said at dawn.)
  • A good rope and a heavy bed. (Brinehollow)
  • May they call your name and hear you answer. (Brinehollow)
  • May you come home dry. (Brinehollow)
  • Pinch me. (Vigil; love, trust, fear.)
  • A sharp nudger and a loud roof. (Vigil)
  • May the rouse hold. (Vigil)
  • Stand for one, and one, and two. (Vigil; from the Waking Hymn.)
  • Not yet. (Cradlewrack; said over swollen bellies of any kind.)
  • Knock first, and be answered. (Cradlewrack)
  • May what comes stay. (Cradlewrack; said at a birth the Attendance has permitted.)
  • May your doors keep. (Cradlewrack)
  • Say little. (Oathen; a farewell.)
  • If able. (Oathen; the polite reply to anything.)
  • May your word be light. (Oathen; said to a child at the Unbitting.)
  • No, thank you. (the Fast; said three times, as a blessing on the speaker.)
  • May you carry your own bread. (the Fast)
  • Walk into the wind. (the Fast; a farewell to travelers.)
  • Safe road and an unlaid table. (the Rim)
  • May the chair stay to the wall. (the Rim; on Tablenight.)
  • May your portion be small. (common, among Scraplings; a blessing on a newborn, that it carry little god.)
I have finished the word-book. That is the only thing in my life I have been allowed to finish, and I am from the north, and I do not know what to do with my hands.
[ the Compiler, last leaf of the L–Z proofs, Quire, Last Plate of Carving, 641 ]
